en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Beginning of the Book on the Establishment of Words and Forms.
[Ka] To him whose long rays are the thousandfold pure True Dharma,
who has risen from the Yugandhara mountain of the perfectly enlightened Sambodhi;
Having bowed my head in reverence to the Victor,
the sole sun in the field of the Buddha, and to the True Dhamma and the Saṅgha;
[Kha]
Having bowed to the teacher Kaccāyana and relying upon his commentary on the Kaccāyana grammar and other works,
I shall compose this straightforward treatise for the purpose of awakening the ignorant.
The *Byatta-sukaṇḍa*: The Accomplishment of the Form of Words.
1. The Section on Sandhi.

Therein, because proficiency in letters is the root for the attainment of the Conqueror’s Dispensation, this statement regarding the subject matter and purpose is uttered in order to show that such proficiency must be achieved.
1. Meaning is known through syllables.
Whatever meaning of words there may be, whether mundane or supramundane and so forth, all of it is made known by means of syllables alone.

For when there is a corruption of syllables—such as through the softening or hardening of sounds—the meaning becomes difficult to discern; therefore, skill in syllables is of great assistance regarding the words of the Buddha. Herein:
Since words, too, consist of a combination of syllables, they are included within syllables themselves.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should achieve proficiency in syllables by properly attending upon a teacher through the five qualities beginning with exertion.

On the Formation of Technical Terms (Saññāvidhāna): First, in this work on grammatical characteristics (saddalakkhaṇa), the formation of technical terms is undertaken for the purpose of making conventional usage intelligible.
2. There are forty-one syllables and their components.

There are also forty-one primary letters (*akkhara*); specifically, the forty-one phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with the nasal stop (*niggahīta*), which conform to the words of the Victor (*jinavacana*), each individually constitute what is called a "letter.
For example: *ā, ī, ī, u, ū, e, o*; *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*; *ca, cha, ja, jha, ña*; *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa*; *ta, tha, da, dha, na*; *pa, pha, ba, bha*.
The syllables are: *ma, ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ*. They are called "syllables" (*akkhara*) because they do not perish (*na kharanti*).

Those that have *a* and so forth as their beginning are "those beginning with *a*" (*ādayo*). This sequence of the vowels and consonants, however, is based on the order of their places of articulation;

for it is by means of the place, the instrument, and the effort that phonemes are produced. In this regard, there are six places of articulation, consisting of the throat, palate, lips, teeth, nose, and the chest.
Therein: the vowels *a*, the *ka*-group, and the letter *ha* are produced from the throat (*kaṇṭha*).

The vowels *i* and *ī*, the *ca*-group, and the letter *ya* are produced from the palate (*tālū*). The *ṭa*-group, the letter *ra*, and the letter *ḷ* are produced from the head (*muddha*). The *ta*-group, the letter *la*, and the letter *sa* are produced from the teeth (*danta*). The vowel *u*, the *pa*-group, and the letter *va* are produced from the lips (*oṭṭha*). The vowel *e* is produced from both the throat and the palate. The vowel *o* is produced from both the throat and the lips. The letter *va* is produced from both the teeth and the lips.
The *niggahīta* is produced in the place of the nose.
*Ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *mā* are produced in their own respective places and also in the place of the nose.
The letter *ha* is joined only with the fifth [consonants] and with those ending in the dental position (*antaṭṭhā*).
In this context, they say that [the articulation] is produced in the throat for those sounds not joined with others.

The point of articulation (*karaṇa*) is the middle of the tongue for sounds produced at the palate; the tip of the tongue for those produced at the head; the tip of the tongue for those produced at the teeth; and the remaining sounds have their respective locations as the points of articulation.

The effort (*payatana*) is the distinction among the points of articulation such as being closed (*saṃvuta*). The letter *a* has a closed articulation; the remaining vowels, as well as the letters *s* and *h*, have an open (*vivaṭa*) articulation. The consonant groups (*vaggā*) have a complete contact (*phuṭṭha*), while *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v* have slight contact (*īsaṃphuṭṭha*).
Thus, among the phonemes (akkhara) distinguished by their place of articulation, mode of formation, effort, and time of emission, the vowels are the supports and the others are supported.
Therein: first the vowels are stated according to their support; from them, the consonants;
then those belonging to the same class; then those that are numerous; and after that, those that are light in their place of articulation.
And it is said:
“But the sequence of these five bases is stated according to their order,
as well as by way of their classifications such as support and so forth.”
Forty-one, with one additional— by this limit of enumeration—
the Bull among Teachers has declared: "Those containing more than forty-one syllables are not the words of the Buddha."
The inclusion of the word "also" (*api*) is for the purpose of referring back to those [vowels] mentioned previously. 3.
Among those, the vowels ending in *o* are eight.
Among those syllables beginning with *a*, the eight syllables ending in *o* are called vowels (*sara*). They are as follows: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o*—these are the vowels.

Those whose end is *o* are *odanta*; the letter *da* is a euphonic insertion (*sandhi*). They are called *sara* because they flow (*saranti*) or go; they are also called *sara* because they cause [the following] consonants to flow.
“Therein” (*tattha*) is understood from the context. 4.
The three short vowels are due to their lightness (*lahu*).
In that regard, among the eight vowels (*sara*), three vowels of light measure are called "short" (*rassa*). They are as follows: *a*, *i*, and *u*—these are the short [vowels].
Those whose measure (*matta*) or quantity is light are "light-measured. Here, the word "measure" (*matta*) refers to a duration of time consisting of a finger-snap or the closing of an eye.
By that measure, one measure is a short vowel, two measures are long (*dīgha*), and half a measure is a consonant (*byañjana*). And here, the inclusion of the term "light" (*lahu*)...

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), this is for the purpose of including even that which measures one and a half [mātrās]. They are "short" (*rassa*) because of their connection with short duration, or they are "short" because they possess short duration.
Furthermore, the terms "vowel" (*sara*), "shortness" (*rassa*), and "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) are used interchangeably. 5.
Others are long (*dīgha*).
In that regard, among the eight vowels (*sara*), five other vowels—consisting of two measures—are called "long" (*dīgha*). They are as follows: *ā, ī, ū, e, o*—these are the long vowels.

The inclusion of the word "other" (*añña*) is for the purpose of including those [vowels] consisting of one and a half measures (*diyaḍḍhamattika*). They are called "long" because they are connected with a long duration of time, or because they possess that [quality].
In some instances, when preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), the single vowels *o* and *ā* are said to be like short vowels (*rassa*). For example: *ettha*, *seyyo*, *oṭṭho*.
May there be well-being. What is meant by "in some cases" (*kvaci*)? For example: "If you were to bury me in the forest, I am your son, O Great King.

(6) Regarding the term *garu* (heavy): a pair (*du*) is a collection of two; in that *du*, when a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) follows, the preceding short vowel is designated as *garu*. For example: *datvā*, *hitvā*, *bhutvā*.
The term “heavy” (garu) applies. 7. And long:
A long vowel is designated as heavy. For example—nāvā, nadī, vadhū, dve, tayo. Any [vowel] other than a heavy one should be understood as “light” (lahuka).
8. The Consonants (Byañjana).
Excluding the eight vowels, the remaining thirty-three syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *niggahīta*, which have the duration of half a mora (*aḍḍhamatta*), are called consonants.
They are "the rest" (*sesa*) apart from those already mentioned. They are called consonants (*byañjana*) because meaning is manifested (*byañjīyati*) by means of them. For example: *ka*.
kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma;
ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ—these are the consonants (vyañjana). In the case of the letters beginning with *ka*, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
The term "consonants" (vyañjana) continues [to apply].
9. The consonants are grouped in fives.
Of those consonants, the twenty-five beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are called "groups" (*vaggā*) by way of five sets of five.
They are as follows: *ka kha ga gha ṅa*, *ca cha ja jha ña*, *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*.
*ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma*—these are the *vaggas* (consonant groups).

Furthermore, they receive the designations *kavagga*, *cavagga*, and so forth, according to their initial letters. *Vagga* means a collection (*samūho*). In this context, it refers to those that are divided into five each, or those which possess five each; thus, "five-by-five" (*pañcapañcaso*). Those which have *ma* at their end are called *mantā*.
10. *Aṃ* is the *niggahīta* (the nasalized vowel).
The syllable *a* has the sense of pronunciation; the word *iti*, moreover, has the sense of indicating what has been stated immediately preceding.

That which is called *aṃ*—the dot (*bindu*) spoken after the letter *a*—is termed "niggahīta" (suppressed). It is so called because it is grasped by depending on a short vowel, or because it is grasped by suppressing the vocal organ (*karaṇa*).
Having suppressed the *karaṇa* (articulatory organ), that which is uttered with the mouth not opened is called *niggahīta*;
it is said to be the *bindu* following a vowel.
Here, he states a general rule (*paribhāsa*) for the purpose of including even those terms used by others that have not been mentioned here, provided they serve a specific function.
11. Regarding the application of foreign terminology (*parasamaññā*).

Furthermore, whatever terminology, phonology, elision (*lopa*), euphonic combination (*saṃyoga*), gender (*liṅga*), and so forth, belongs to the *Sakkaṭa* (Sanskrit) treatises or to other grammarians (*veyyākaraṇa*), these are applicable here as well when there is an occasion for their use (*payoga*).

"Foreign terminology" (*parasamaññā*) means the terminology belonging to another or the terminology of others; that is to say, the terminology of the grammarians or of those who have studied grammar—this is the meaning. "Application" (*payoga*) means employment or utilization.

Among those, the first and second of the consonant groups (*vaggā*), as well as the letter *s*, are called unvoiced (*aghosa*). The third, fourth, and fifth of the consonant groups, along with *y, r, l, v, h,* and *ḷ*, are called the twenty-one voiced (*ghosa*) sounds.

Furthermore, among these, the second and fourth of the consonant groups are also called "aspirated" (*dhanita*), while the others are called "unaspirated" (*sithila*). "Destruction" (*vināsa*) means elision (*lopa*).
Short vowels are called "homogeneous" (*savaṇṇa*) with their respective long vowels; they are also called "identical in form" (*sarūpa*). [Vowels] separated by other vowels...

Conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) are phonemes. Gender (*liṅga*) is that which possesses meaning, excluding roots, suffixes, and case-endings. A word (*pada*) is that which ends in a case-ending. Such are these and others.
Thus concludes the section on the prescription of technical terms (*saññāvidhāna*). Now follows the section on the rules for vowel sandhi (*sarasandhividhāna*).
Now, the *sarasandhi* (connections by meaning) is explained:
*Loka*, *aggapuggalo*, *paññā*, *indriyaṃ*, *tīṇi*, *imāni*, *no*, *hi*, *etaṃ*, *bhikkhunī*, *ovādo*, *mātu*, *upaṭṭhānaṃ*, *sametu*, *āyasmā*,
*abhibhū*, *āyatanaṃ*, *dhanā*, *me*, *atthi*, *sabbe*, *eva*, *tayo*, *assu*, *dhammā*, *asanto*.

In this context, since [vowels] are not seen here in the designation of "vowel" (*sara*) and so forth, he states a general rule (*paribhāsa*) for the purpose of separating consonants in all instances of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
12. One should separate from a vowel a preceding consonant that stands below it.
The word "from a vowel" (*sarena*) is used in the ablative case, or in connection with the instrumental; it refers to the preceding consonant which is to be combined with a vowel.

Without overstepping [the rule], having made the vowel (*assa*) stand below, one should separate it from the consonant (*sara*); that is, the consonant (*byañjana*) is to be separated from the vowel (*sara*).
And here, by the very power of the mention of the vowel (*assa*), the term "consonant" (*byañjana*) is understood. 13.
*Sarā sare lopaṃ*. (Vowels [are elided] before vowels.)

All vowels (*sara*), when followed by another vowel, undergo elision (*lopa*). Elision means non-appearance or non-utterance. Here, "vowels" (*sara*) is a designation of the grammatical operation (*kāriya*).
The plural number is used here to indicate that elision applies to many [vowels] even when each individual vowel is followed by another.

"Vowel" (*sare*) is a designation of the cause (*nimitta*), and this is a locative case of the cause (*nimittasattamī*); it is understood through the power of taking the cause that there may be an interval of one syllable (*vaṇṇa*) or time.
There is no application of the rule for elision (*sandhikāriya*). The term "elision" (*lopa*) is a designation for a grammatical operation;

however, this sutta should be understood as a prescription for initial elision (*pubbalopa*), because it precedes the prescriptions for subsequent elision (*paralopa*) found later on. Thus, in all instances of the locative case designation (*sattamīniddesa*), it should be understood that the rule applies to what precedes, not to what follows.

The phrase “assaraṃ, adhoṭhitaṃ” recurs [from the previous rule]; it refers to a reproach used in the context of smooth (siliṭṭha) recitation. 14. In the case of *naya* (guiding), when there is a subsequent [consonant] joined (*yutta*).

A consonant (*byañjana*) devoid of a vowel (*sara*) is called *adhoṭhita*; when joined with a subsequent consonant, it should be placed in its position through *naya*, and the guiding of the subsequent [vowel] must be performed.

In this context, the inclusion of the term *yutta* (properly joined) is for the purpose of excluding the *niggahīta* (the nasal stop). By means of that, there is no doubt regarding the application of the subsequent rule in cases such as “*akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ*” and so forth.

[The following are examples: *lokaggapuggalo*, *paññindriyaṃ*, *tīṇimāni*, *nohetaṃ*, *bhikkhunovādo*, *mātupaṭṭhānaṃ*, *sametāyasmā*, *abhibhāyatanaṃ*, *dhanā matthi*, *sabbeva*, *tayassu dhammā*, and *asantettha na dissanti*.

“Of whom now,” “perception,” “like a shadow,” “what indeed is this talk,” “thus also,” “you are not an ascetic,” “the eye-faculty,” “you are ungrateful,” “as in the sky,” “those too,” “I bow to him,” “I am he,” “these four,” “an outcaste,” “Moggallāna was the sower”—
in the morning, when *pubba-lopa* (elision of *pubba*) has occurred, there is the governing rule “when a vowel follows”; however, here, by reason of the sense...
Having applied the rule "change of case-ending" (*vibhattivipariṇāmo*), and while the rules "vowel" (*saro*) and "elision of the vowel after *saramhā*" (*saramhā, lopo*) are in operation— 15.

**Vā paro asarūpā.** A vowel following a vowel that is not of the same form may optionally undergo elision. That which has the same form is "of the same form" (*sarūpo*); [the opposite is] "not of the same form."

It is similar in form, dissimilar in form, and unlike in sound. However, because the particle *vā*—functioning both in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) and in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*)—operates in two ways like a prefix (*upasagga*), it occurs in some instances as an alternative (*vikappa*) and in others as a delimitation of the specific form already established;
here, however, it is the latter, whereby the particle *vā* indicates a rule that is both constant and non-constant, and both existent and non-existent. [In the section on] "Guidance" (*naye*)...
"Furthermore, you must lead [others] beyond.
"Now, for whomsoever... "Perception, perception"—it is like a shadow, like a shadow; "what talk, what talk indeed"—thus even so;
"you are not an ascetic"—you are indeed not an ascetic. "The faculty of the eye," this is constant. "You are ungrateful."

*Akataññū asi*: "You are ungrateful"; *ākāseva ākāse*: "just as in the sky, indeed in the sky"; *tepi te api*: "those very ones, even those"; *vandehaṃ vande ahaṃ*: "I salute, I salute"; *sohaṃ so ahaṃ*:
"that very I, that same I"; *cattārome cattāro ime*: "these four, these very four"; *vasaloti vasalo iti*: "'Outcast'—thus [he is called] an outcast"; *moggallānosi bījako moggallāno āsi bījako*:

"Moggallāna was a seed-sower, Moggallāna was indeed a seed-sower"; *pātova pāto eva*: "at dawn, indeed at dawn. In this [text], it does not occur—as in: *pañcindriyāni*, *saddhindriyaṃ*, *sattuttamo*, *ekūnavīsati*, *yassete*, *sugatovādo*, *diṭṭhāsavo*, *diṭṭhogho*, *cakkhāyatanaṃ*, *taṃ kutettha labbhā*, and so forth.
And there is a fixed rule for the analysis:
after the vowels *a*, *vaṇṇa*, *sarodāni*, *tīveva*, and so forth, the following [consonant] is not elided,
provided it is not one of those beginning with *añña* and is long, excluding [the cases of] *āsevana* and so forth.
In the examples *bandhussa iva*, *upakkhati*, *upito*, *avicca*, *jinīritaṃ*, *na upeti*, and *cando udayo yathā udake*:
here, when the preceding vowels (*pubbāvaṇṇassarā*) have been elided, the rule "the subsequent [vowel], provided they are not of dissimilar form" (*paro, asarūpe*) continues to apply;

likewise, the mention of *ivaṇṇa* from the rule "the *ivaṇṇa* becomes *yaṃ* optionally" (*ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā*) and the mention of *u* from the rule "for those ending in *va*, *ma*, *u*, or *u*" (*vamodudantānaṃ*) must be carried over here by way of the "lion's gait" (*sīhagati*).
16. *Kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte*.

When a following vowel that has become an *ivaṇṇa* or an *ukāra* follows a preceding dissimilar vowel that has been elided, it sometimes attains the status of an *asavaṇṇa*. Those which have no similar vowels (*savaṇṇa*) are called *asavaṇṇa*;
these are the single *e*-vowels and *o*-vowels. In that context, by virtue of proximity to their original positions, the *ivaṇṇas* and *ukāras* become the single *e*-vowels and *o*-vowels.
“He remains equanimous toward his very relatives,” “endowed with,” “having clearly understood,” “proclaimed by the Conqueror,” “does not attain,” “the rising of the moon,” “as in water.

What is the purpose of the word *kvaci* (“in some cases”)? For example: “In this regard, those whose faculties... “One of great psychic power,” “all afflictions,” “he approached him,” “transcending the world. What is the purpose of the elision (*lutta*)? For example:
“These six qualities,” “just as this,” “the undertaking of what is wholesome. What is the purpose of the dissimilar form (*asarūpa*)? For example: “These four,” “attending upon one’s mother.”

And here, although the term *vā* was mentioned previously, it should be understood that this rule stated here applies only when the elision (*lutta*) occurs specifically in cases of censure (*avaṇṇa*), because it is applied in some instances.
Therefore, it does not apply here in the following examples: *diṭṭhupādānaṃ*, *pañcahupāli*, *mudindriyaṃ*, *yo missaro*. In those cases, [the forms are]:
*ayaṃ buddhānussati*, *so atthikā*, *paññavā assa*, *tadā ahaṃ*, *yāni idha bhūtāni*, *gacchāmi iti*, *atito*, *kikīva*, *bahūpakāraṃ*, *madhudakaṃ*, *sūpadhāritaṃ*, *yopi*.
In this case, now I; if this one; one who has heard little; this one by that one; faith is wealth here;

karma is the supporting condition (*upanissaya*); likewise for the simile; night; ceased; *vi* [prefix]; tranquility (*upasama*)—here, when the preceding vowels (*pubba-sarā*) have been elided, the governing rule "kvaci" applies, and the phrase "paro, lutte" (the following [vowel], when there is elision) also continues in effect.
17. Long Vowels (*Dīgha*).
When a preceding short vowel is elided, the following vowel sometimes attains length; thus, by way of proximity to its position, a long vowel of the same class (*savaṇṇadīgha*) replaces short vowels.
Herein, [examples are]: *buddhānussati*, *sātthikā*, *paññavāssa*, *tadāhaṃ*, *yānīdha bhūtāni*, and *gacchāmi*.
The past; like Kikī; of great benefit; honey-water; well-maintained; by means of which; now I; if this;
one of little learning; here and there; faith is wealth in this world; the necessary condition for karma; similar to that; abstaining from food at night;
tranquility. What is "where"? "Truly, this body is not long-lasting"; what indeed is this? These three; in the five aggregates of clinging.
Its meaning is as follows: *pañcaṅgiko*, *munindo*, *satindriyaṃ*, *lahuṭṭhānaṃ*, *gacchāmahaṃ*, *tatridaṃ*, *pañcahupāli*, *natthaññaṃ*.
[In the rule] "when there is elision" (*lutteti*), what [is the purpose]? For example: *yathā ayaṃ*, *nimi iva rājā*, *kikī iva*, *su upadhāritaṃ*.

*lokassa iti*, *deva iti*, *vi ati patanti*, *vi ati nāmenti*, *saṅghāṭi api*, *jīvitahetu api*, *vijju iva*, *kiṃsu idha vittaṃ*, *sādhu iti*. Here, when the elision of the subsequent and preceding sounds has been made—
The phrase “*lutte dīghaṃ*” (long vowel when there is elision) continues [from the previous rule].
18. *Pubbo ca*:

A preceding vowel attains a long vowel when followed by another vowel that has been elided (*lutta*). The inclusion of the particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing back the mention of the long vowel resulting from elision; its purpose is to indicate that what is drawn back does not recur in subsequent rules.
"Of the world," "O deity," they fall away, they pass away; even the outer robe, even for the sake of life, like lightning; what indeed is wealth here? "Excellent. Where? What?
"Of whom now," "of him," "even now," "in those too," the faculty of the eye, "what indeed, alas.

This Dhamma has been attained by me; I am your son; those [defilements] would have been abandoned by him; on the mountain, I; those which would be his—here, when the elision of *pubba* (the former part) occurs.
19. *Yame-dantassādeso* (The substitution of *ya* for a word-final *e*).

In place of the letter *e* that constitutes the end of a word, when followed by a vowel, there is sometimes a substitution (*ādeso*) of the letter *y*. This rule applies only to words such as *ayaṃ*, *ete*, *ime*, etc.

*Yaṃ* is the form [of the pronoun]. *Eva anto* means "that which has *e* as its final [sound]"; it is called a *substitute* (*ādeso*) because it is taught (*ādissati*) in place of the original (*ādi-ṭṭhāne*). [The word] "*byañjane*" [is understood from the previous rule].
By virtue of its function, *dīgha* becomes *dīgho*.
*Adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo*: *putto* [is used] for *tyāhaṃ*; *tyāssa pahīnā*: *pabbatī* [is used] for *yyāssa*.
In what cases [do these substitutions not occur]? *Te nāgatā*, *puttā matthi*. Why is there a mention of the "end" (*anta*)? [As in: *Dhammacakkaṃ pavattento*, *damanto cittaṃ*.
"As much as his body may be, so much may his shadow be; what is the point? Rather, today, whatever this is, let it be that very thing.
From whatever source [the matter arises], it follows every half-month:
'well-come,' 'good form,' 'bad form,' 'within the range of the eye,' 'much affliction,' he has made manifest; but not thus hereafter."
20. *Vamodudantānaṃ*.

In place of the *o*- and *ū*-vowels that occur at the end of a word, there is sometimes a substitution of *va* when followed by a vowel. This refers to the *o*-vowel of words such as *ka*, *kha*, *ya*, and *ta*.
Examples: *yāvatakvassa kāyo*, *tāvatakvassa byāmo*, *kvattho*, *atha khvassa*, *aham khvajja*, *yvāyaṃ*.

*svassa*, *sveva*, *yatvādhikaraṇaṃ*, *anvaddhamāsaṃ*, *anvebhi*, *svāgataṃ*, *svākāro*, *dvākāro*, *cakkhvāpāthaṃ*, *bahvābādho*, *pātvākāsi*, *na tveva*. Why [is it said] "in some cases"? [Examples:
*ko attho*, *atha kho aññatarā*, *yohaṃ*, *sohaṃ*, *cattārome*, *sāgataṃ*, *sādhāvuso*, *hotūti*. What is the purpose of including the word "end" (*anta*)? [Examples: *savanīyaṃ*, *viravanti*.

*Paṭisanthāravutti assa*, *sabbā vitti anubhuyyate*, *vi añjanaṃ*, *vi ākato*, *nadī āsanno*—in these examples, the term "asarūpe" (in the case of dissimilar vowels) is understood from the rule concerning the gait of a frog (*maṇḍūkagati*).
21. *Ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā*.
A preceding *ivaṇṇa* optionally becomes *ya* when followed by a dissimilar vowel. Here, *ivaṇṇo* means "the sound *i*"; the word *nava* is a synonym for the word *kvaci* (sometimes).
In *paṭisanthāravutyassa*, all [the vowels] are experienced as being elided (*vityā*). [The examples are: *byañjanaṃ*, *byākato*, *nadyāsanno*. What is the purpose of the word "optionally" (*navā*)?

[To show that the elision does not occur in the following: *pañcahaṅgehi*, *tāni attani*, *gacchāmahaṃ*, *muttacāgī anuddhato*. What is the purpose of the word "non-homogeneous" (*asarūpe*)? [To exclude cases where the preceding vowel is the same as the following one, such as:

*itihidaṃ*, *aggīva*, *atthīti*. [Examples of the particle *iti* with various preceding sounds: *ati antaṃ*, *ati odātā*, *pati ayo*, *pati āharati*, *pati eti*, *iti assa*, *iti etaṃ*, *itiādi*. 22. *Sabbo ca ti*.
This is the inclusion of the word *ti* from [the rule] *atipatiitīnaṃ*.

This is the rule; otherwise, the inclusion of the word *kvaci* and the sūtra “*atissa cantassā*” would be rendered purposeless.
By the rule “*paradvebhāvo ṭhāne*,” there is doubling of the consonant.
Examples include: *accantaṃ*, *accodātā*, *paccayo*, *paccāharati*, *pacceti*, *iccassa*, *icce taṃ*, *iccādi*.

In the case of the word *ti* which has become part of the prefix *ati*, the form stated as "all [words] ending in *i*" (*sabbo caṃ tī*) does not occur when followed by an *i*-vowel.
*Atissā* is an imitation of the prefix *ati*; for that very reason, there is no elision of the case-ending here.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in this context, because it belongs to the section on phonetic rules and prohibitions, the word *anta* refers specifically to the word *ti* that follows the prefix *ati*, and not to the *i*-vowel itself.
Otherwise, this very sutta would be purposeless.
[The rule] "ivaṇṇo yaṃ navā" (Pāṇini 7.1.2) applies here because of the governing context of "asimilar form" (*asarūpa*);
therefore, the substitution of *y* for an *ivaṇṇa* vowel cannot occur when the following word is similar in form.

The letter *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuttasamuccaya*); by this, there is no [application] of the rule for words ending in *iti* or *pati*. Thus: *atisigaṇo* becomes *atīsigaṇo*;
likewise *atīto*, *atīritaṃ*, *itīti*, *itīdaṃ*, *patīto*. In *abhi akkhānaṃ*, *abhi uggato*, *abhi okāso*—when the letter *ya* is reached here—the word "vowels" (*sare*) is understood to carry over.
24. *Abbhō abhi*.
When the vowel follows this entire word *abhi*, the substitution *abbha* occurs.
The form "abhī" is in the nominative case, but in the commentary it is interpreted as being in the genitive.
It is stated [as such] because of its dependence on a substitute, as in the case of "ammo" and so forth.
There is the elision of the preceding vowel: *abbhakkhānaṃ*, *abbhuggato*, *abbhokāso*.
[In the following cases: *adhi agamā*, *adhi upagato*, *adhi ogāhetvā*—thus here.
25. *ajjho* is a substitute for *adhi*.
When *adhi* is followed by any vowel, there is a substitution of *ajjha*. Examples: *ajjhagamā*, *ajjhupagato*, *ajjhogāhetvā*. [In the following cases, *abhi* becomes *adhi*:
*abhi-icchitaṃ*, *adhi-īritaṃ*. Thus it is here.
The forms *abbho*, *abhi*, *ajjho*, and *adhī* are used [as prefixes].
26. *Te na vā ivaṇṇe*:

These prefixes, namely *abhi* and *adhi*, optionally do not take the forms *abbho* and *ajjho* when followed by a vowel (*ivaṇṇa*). There are elisions of vowels (*saralopa*) and substitutions (*paranayana*). Examples: *abhicchitaṃ*, *adhīritaṃ*. Why say "optionally" (*vā*)? [Counter-examples: *abbhīritaṃ*, *ajjhiṇamutto*, *ajjhiṭṭho*.
*Ekamidha ahantīdha* (27). And *dha*.
Sometimes, when a vowel follows, the letter *da* becomes *dha*.

In this case, the *dha* of *idha* following the word *eka* becomes *dh*, with the elision of the vowel and the lengthening [of the preceding vowel]. Thus: *ekamidāhaṃ*. Why "sometimes"? As in: *idheva*.
By means of the word *kasaddena*, in some instances the sound *dh* of a good person (*sādhussa*) becomes the sound *h*, as in *sāhu dassanaṃ*.
Just as [the particle] *eva* functions here, so too do the words *tathā* and *eva* function here, as well as the word *saramhā*.
28. *Evādissa ri pubbo ca rasso*.

This is the inclusion of the two following words, *yathā* and *tathā*. When the vowel *e*—which follows a long vowel and constitutes the beginning of the word *eva*, etc.—is replaced by *ri*, the preceding vowel optionally becomes short. Examples: *yathariva*, *tathariva*. Why "optionally"?

(Because in cases such as) *yatheva*, *tatheva*. In the following instances—*ti antaṃ*, *ti addhaṃ*, *aggi agāre* (in the sense of the locative case), *pañcamī antaṃ*, *du aṅgikaṃ*, *bhikkhu āsane*, *puthu āsane*, *sayambhū āsane*—since the substitutes for *ya* have been applied here:
The term "saññā" (technical name) is understood [to carry over]. 29. *Ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa* are *jhal*.

These, namely *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa*, are respectively designated by the technical name *jhal*. The inclusion of the term *vaṇṇa* (vowel/sound) is for the purpose of including all homogeneous sounds (*savaṇṇa*).
The designation *jhala* is indeed a technical term (*paññā*), not based on grammatical gender;
for it is seen applied to verbs, to those ending in neuter gender, and to those having two genders. 30. *Jhalānam iyuvā sare vā*:
[The substitutes] *i* and *u* optionally take the place of *jhals* before a vowel.
In these cases, *jha*, *la*, and *icca* are optionally replaced by *iya* and *uva* respectively when followed by a vowel;

there is elision of the vowel (*saralopa*). Examples: *tiyantaṃ*, *tiyaddhaṃ*, *aggiyāgāre* (in the sense of the locative case), *pañcamiyantaṃ*, *duvaṅgikaṃ*, *bhikkhuvāsane*, *puthuvāsane*, *sayambhuvāsane*. Why "optionally" (*vāti*)? [Counter-examples: *agyāgāre* (in the sense of the locative case), *bhikkhuāsane nisīdati*.
Also: *go ajinaṃ*, *go eḷakaṃ*—in these instances [the rule does not apply].
The phrase “go, avo, samāse” is also understood [from the previous rule].
31. *O sare ca*.

In a compound (*samāsa*), when a vowel follows, the substitution of *ava* occurs for the *o*-vowel of the word *go*. Examples: *gavājinaṃ*, *gaveḷakaṃ*. By the inclusion of the word *ca* (“and”), the substitutions *uva* and *ava* also occur for the *u*-vowels. For example: *bhuvi*, *pasavo*.
Putha evātīdha 32.
The augment *ga* sometimes occurs after the particle *putha* when followed by a vowel.
Regarding this particle *putha*, the augment *ga* sometimes occurs at its end when a vowel follows. "Augment" (*āgama*) means that which comes (*āgacchati*).
The arrival of what was non-existent is *āgama*. And here, by virtue of its proximity to the cause (*nimitta*), the word "vowel" (*sare*) is understood to mean the end of the letter *p* (in *putha*).
[Thus,] it is simply separate (*puthageva*), or simply separate (*putha eva*). Here, it is indeed so.
The terms *sara* (vowel), *go* (cow), *āgama* (augment), and *kvaci* (sometimes) recur [in the following rules]. 33.

A vowel at the end of *pā* becomes short. When a vowel follows the final syllable of *pā*, there is sometimes an augment *g* inserted, and the vowel within *pā* becomes short. Thus, for example, *pageva* becomes *pāgeva*.
The word *vā* (or) and *sare* (before a vowel) recur [from the previous rule]. 34. *Yava-ma-da-na-ta-ra-lā cāgamā*:

Before a following vowel (*sare*), the eight augmentations (*āgamā*) beginning with *ya* occur optionally. By the word *ca* (and), the augmentation *ga* is also included; this word *vā* has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*).
In that regard, the insertion of the letter *ya* occurs as in the case of *yathādibho* [from *yathā*] and in the case of the vowels *i*, *e*, and so forth. For example: *yathā* becomes *yathayidaṃ*;
depending on the rule "consonant" (*byañjana*), there is shortening according to the rule "short" (*rassa*). Thus: *yathā idaṃ vā*, *yathā eva*, *yathāyeva*, *yatheva*; likewise:
*māyidaṃ*, *māyevaṃ*, *taṃyidaṃ*, *taṃyeva*, *nayidaṃ*, *nayimassa*, *nayimāni*, *navayime dhammā*, *buddhānaṃyeva*.
There are indeed: *bodhi* itself, *sati* itself, *pathavī* itself, *dhātu* itself, *tesu* itself, *so* itself—each distinct.
Likewise, in the case of vowels (*sare*), there is the reversal [of the vowel]. *Vi-añjanā* is *viyañjanā*, or *byañjanā*;
thus, *viyākāsi* becomes *byākāsi*. *Pari-antaṃ* becomes *pariyantaṃ*; likewise, *pariyādānaṃ*, *pariyuṭṭhānaṃ*, *pariyesati*, and *pariyosānaṃ*.
*niccaṃ*. *Ni-āyoga* is *niyāyoga*. It does not occur here; it is exhausted (*parikkhato*), [as in] he examines (*upaparikkhati*).

The letter *va* occurs after words beginning with *ti* when there is the substitution of *ava*-vowels: *ti-aṅgulaṃ*, *tivaṅgulaṃ*, likewise *tivaṅgikaṃ*; *bhūvādayo*; "the doe looks around" (*migī bhantā vudikkhati*); "it is called" (*pavuccati*); "skillfulness and uprightness" (*pāguññavujutā*).

The letter *ma* occurs after words beginning with *lahu* before vowels for the sake of protecting the meter and so forth: "he will go quickly" (*lahu essati*), "he will go quickly" (*lahumessati*); likewise, "he will go heavily" (*garumessati*).
Regarding this they say: "By what is one purified here? Like a noble steed by the whip, one should honor [the Teacher] in the sky.

[The prefix *u-*, derived from *ud-*, is used] with each individual word to signify "by which," "in this world," "some," "only," "at all," "again," "furthermore," "that very thing," and so forth. It is always attached after a prefix (*upasagga*): *udaggo* (exalted), *udayo* (arising), *udapādi* (appeared), *udāhaṭaṃ* (spoken), *udito* (risen), *udīritaṃ* (uttered), *udeti* (rises).
And by way of particles (*nipāta*): *sakiṃ eva* becomes *sakid-eva*; thus [we have] *sakadāgāmi*, where the vowel *i* becomes *a* according to the *Mahāvuttisutta*.
Likewise: *kenacid-eva*, *kiñcid-eva*, *kismiñcid-eva*, *kocid-eva*, *sammā-attho* becomes *sammadattho*, with the shortening of the vowel.
Thus: *sammadakkhāto*, *sammadaññā-vimuttānaṃ*, *sammadeva*, *yāvad-atthaṃ*, *yāvadeva*, *tāvadeva*, *punadeva*.

By name: for whatever purpose, for that purpose; in whatever interval, in that interval; liberation through its factors—this is the purpose. One should be devoted to one’s own welfare, striving for that very goal.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] for another's purpose, those liberated from mental objects, for much of the night, and indeed much fear.
What does "or" (*vā*) signify? By anyone desiring welfare, having understood rightly: "as long as I," "so long as I," "again and further," for one's own sake.
The letter *na* occurs at the beginning of words such as *āyata*: *ito āyati*, *ito nāyati*, *ciraṃ nāyati*.
The letter *ta* occurs after *yasmā* or *tasmā* at the beginning of words such as *ajja* and *iha*: *yasmā iha*, *tasmā iha*, *ajjatagge*.
The letter *ra* occurs after *ni*, *du*, *pa*, *tu*, *puna*, *dhī*, *pāta*, and *catu*: *ni antaraṃ* becomes *nirantaraṃ*; likewise, *nirālayo*.
Without fuel, effortless, unsurpassed, and devoid of essence. Difficult to transcend, hard to overcome, ill-arrived, and ill-spoken.
He appeared; they appeared. May he come again; a repetition; once more; he returns. Fie! Breakfast. From the group beginning with "four":

fourfold, the fourfold protection, the attainment of the four bases of psychic power, for the purpose of crossing over the four floods. In the sense of a husband, this is a conventional expression; it is simply the earth-element.

Likewise, one should guard one's desire as a charioteer guards his horses; like the moon among the stars, like lightning among the mountain peaks, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, or like an awl on the point of a mustard seed; one should dwell together with the virtuous like a bull among cattle.
What does it blow? It blew twice, it manifested itself, and again.

The letter *la* is used for the number six. There is no distinction between *la* and *ḷ*. "Six higher knowledges" (*cha-abhiññā*), "six-limbed" (*chaḷ-aṅga*), "eighty-six" (*chaḷ-āsīti*), "six parts" (*chaḷ-aṃsa*), "six sense bases" (*saḷ-āyatana*).
What does it blow? The six higher knowledges (abhiññā).
Thus the section on the rules for internal sandhi is completed.
Feminine gender.
Now, the feminine gender endings are stated.
A word ending in the vowel *a* that is feminine in gender is not well-established [in usage].
A word ending in the vowel *ā* that is feminine in gender is the word *kaññā*. When *kaññā* stands [as the base form]—
176. The suffix *āp* occurs after a feminine base ending in *a*.
When expressing a feminine meaning, the suffix *āp* follows a nominal stem ending in the vowel *a*;
these feminine suffixes (*itthippaccaya*) indicate the original meaning of the base, just like the suffixes *si*, etc. (the nominative case endings).
The suffixes beginning with *Ṇ* (Ṇādayo) express both the meaning of the grammatical relation (*paccayattha*) and their own specific meaning (*sakattha*).

When the preceding vowel is elided by rules such as "elision of *sa*" (*saralopo*), and the subsequent guidance (*paranayana*) has been applied, it is stated that "a noun-base (*liṅga*) is that which possesses meaning, excluding roots, suffixes, and case-endings.
Since even a suffix ending [in a consonant] lacks gender, and thus the arising of case-endings is not attained, [the rule applies to] those [forms] ending in *taddhita*, compounds, *kita*, and *ka*.

In the phrase "nāmaṃ vā’tavetunādīsu cā" (or a noun [ending] in -ā, -ī, or -ū, etc.), by the inclusion of the word "vā" (or), even that which ends in a feminine suffix is designated as a "noun" (nāma).
As before, there is the occurrence of the case endings (syādi); by the rule "sesato lopaṃ gasipī," there is the elision of the suffix "si.
That [is] the maiden (sā kaññā). In the plural, the terms "sañño" from the rule "ālapane si gasañño" and "itthikhyā" from the rule "te itthikhyā po" are understood to carry over.

When the long vowel *ā* at the end of a nominal stem (*liṅga*) denotes a female, it is designated as *gha*. Thus, under the designation *gha*, by the optional rule "there is elision of *y* and *on* after a *gha*-stem," there is optionally the elision of *y*. [Examples: *tā kaññā* (those girls), *kaññāyo* (those girls).

In the vocative case, the word "of the *ga*-stem" (*gasse*) follows from the previous rule "optionally for the *ga*-stem" (*sakhato gasse vā*). Thus, "of the *ga*-stem" (*gassā*) continues to apply here.
178. *Ghate ca*.
In the case of *gha*, the vowel *e* of another word becomes [the ending], with the elision of the preceding vowel (*saralopa*), and so forth. Thus: *bhoti kaññe*; *bhotiyo kaññā* and *kaññāyo*.
In the case of the suffix *am*, due to the elision of the preceding vowel and the restoration of the base form (*pakatibhāva*), there are: *kaññaṃ*, *kaññā*, and *kaññāyo*.
In the third [section] and those following, from the rule “*ā* for the fourth singular,” the phrases “*āyo*” and “*ekavacanānam*” also carry over.
179. *Ghato nādīnaṃ*:

after a nominal stem (*liṅga*) marked by the designation *gha*, the case endings (*vibhatti*) beginning with the first singular and ending with the sixth plural (*smiṃ*), excluding those belonging to the feminine (*nādī*), [undergo the following changes].
The substitution of *ā* occurs. There is elision of the final vowel (*saralopa*) and replacement by the following nasal (*paranayana*). [The forms are: *kaññāya*, *kaññāhi*, *kaññābhi*;
*kaññāya*, *kaññānaṃ*, *kaññāya*, *kaññāhi*, *kaññābhi*; *kaññāya*, *kaññānaṃ*. In the case of the suffix *smiṃ*:
180. *Ghapato* means "from the word *gha*.

From the word *gha*, when there is the suffix *yaṃ* belonging to another word, it becomes the substitute *yā*. For example: *kaññāyaṃ*, *kaññāya*, *kaññāsu*. In the same way, others [should be understood] as well.

The difference in form occurs only in the address to mothers (*ammā*). [The forms are: *ammā*, *ammā*, *ammāyo*.
When the *g* [of *ammā*] reaches *e* by rule 180, “*ghate ca*” (and in *gha*), [the following applies]: 181.
Not after *ammā* and so forth.
In forms such as *ammā* and *annā*, when addressing another person in the singular, the vowel does not remain short (*ekāratta*).
According to the rule "or *ākāra*," there is shortening. Thus: *bhodi amma*, *bhodi ammā*; *bhodiyo ammā*, *ammāyo*. Likewise:
*annā*, *annā*, *annāyo*; *bhodi anna*, *bhodi annā*; *bhodiyo annā*, *annāyo*. Similarly: *ambā*, *ambā*, *ambāyo*; *bhodi amba*, *bhodi ambā*; *bhodiyo ambā*, *ambāyo*, and so forth.
Ending in the vowel *ā*.
The feminine noun *ratti* (night) ends in the vowel *i*;
likewise, when the case endings beginning with *si* arise, there is elision of the final consonant, resulting in *ratti*.
In the plural, "saññā" and "ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā" are understood to carry over.
182. *Te itthikhyā po*.
A designation for the feminine is "itthikhyā"; when those vowels *i* and *u* (ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā) are designations for the feminine (*itthikhyā*), then they are designated as *po* (the feminine suffixes).
In the declension [of the word *ratti*], by the rule “*ghapato ca*,” there is the elision of the *y*; by the rule “*yosu kata*,” etc., there is the long vowel.
Thus: *rattī*, *rattiyo*, or *ratyo*; *he ratti*, *he rattī*, *he rattiyo*.
By the rule “*aṃmo*,” etc., there is the nasalization (*niggahīta*): *rattiṃ*, *rattī*, *rattiyo*.
In the third [section] and those following, the phrases “of the singular forms” and “nādīnam” (of those ending in -ā) are understood to carry over. 183. *Pato yā*:

After a word ending in *i* or *u*, there is the substitution of *yā* for the case endings (*vibhatti*) of the singular forms of nouns ending in *-ā*. Thus: *rattiyā*, *rattīhi* / *rattībhi*, *rattihi* / *rattibhi*, *rattiyā*, *rattīnam* / *rattinam*.
**Pañcamiyaṃ (The Fifth Case):** 184. *Amā pato smiṃsmānaṃ vā*.

After the [stems] ending in *pa* and *icca*, the substitutes *smiṃ* and *smā* respectively replace *smiṃ* and *smā*; these replacements may optionally occur. This word *vā* has the sense of a fixed distribution (*vavatthitavibhāsa*); therefore, they do not occur after stems ending in *u-vaṇṇa*, nor after those ending in *i-vaṇṇa*, according to their respective application.
The vowel *ya* occurs [as a substitute] for a vowel, and this applies to both the singular and plural numbers, as well as to the movements of the lion and the frog. 185. And for *pasañña*.
When a vowel follows a *pasañña* (a consonant) that has an *i*-vowel [as its penultimate], the vowel *ya* becomes the substitute for the singular and plural case endings (*vibhatti*). In this case...
And because of the governing rule (adhikāra), only the letter *y* is understood by the mention of the term "vowel" (*saññā*), just as [the vowel] *i* and *u* are [understood].
The mention of *c* is for the purpose of excluding cases such as "ratto" (red). Ratyā, rattiyā; rattīhi, rattībhi, rattihi, rattibhi; rattiyā; rattīnaṃ, rattinaṃ.

In the locative case (*smiṃ-vacana*), there are the substitutions of *am* and *ya*. Thus: *ratyaṃ*. By the rule "after a word ending in *gha*, *p*, or *t*, *yaṃ* optionally [is substituted for *smiṃ*]," there is the substitution of *yaṃ*: *rattiyaṃ*.
Elsewhere, "aṃ," "smiṃ," or "vā" is also applied.
186. From the beginning, "o" also [occurs].

From this very word "ādi," the substitutes "aṃ" and "o" optionally occur for the case-ending *smiṃ*. By the word "ca" (and), from other words as well, "ā," "aṃ," and "o" are the substitutes. [Examples: *ratyā*, *rattiṃ*, *ratto*, *rattiyā*, *rattīsu*, *rattisu*.
Likewise, there are others:

*Rati*, *ruci*, *raśmi*, *aśani*, *vasani*, *auṣadhi*, *aṅguli*, *dhūli*, *dundubhi*, *droṇī*, *aṭavī*, *chavi*, and so forth, are feminine nouns ending in the vowel *i*.
This concludes the section on words ending in *i*. The word *itthī* (woman) is a feminine noun ending in the vowel *ī*.
“Itthā”: here, the phrase “in the feminine, [the suffix] paccaya” is understood.
187. *Ī* after *nada*, etc., or optionally:

after a nominal stem (*liṅga*) denoting the feminine, whether it begins with *nada* or not, the suffix *ī* occurs. The inclusion of the word “or” (*vā*) is for the purpose of including stems other than those beginning with *nada*; therefore, *ī* also occurs after *puthu*, *go*, and so forth.

In the elision of *sa* (saralopa), when a non-homogeneous vowel (*asavaṇṇa*) is reached by the rule "and in some cases, when [sa] is elided, there is no homogeneity," the status of the base form (*pakatibhāva*) receives the designation of a noun, and the case endings (*syādi*) arise.
Thus: *itthī*, *itthī*. By the rule "for a short vowel after a non-nasal consonant" (*agho rassa*), etc., the shortening occurs: *itthiyo*.
In the vocative, by the rule "for a consonant ending in *jha* or *pa*, there is shortening" (*jhalapā rassa*), there is shortening: *bhoti itthi*, *bhotiyo itthī*, *itthiyo*.
In the second singular case, from the rule “*ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā*,” the word “*vā*” (or) is carried over.
188. *Aṃ* optionally becomes *yaṃ* after a suffix ending in *ī*.

*itthiyā*, *itthīhi* / *itthībhi*, *itthiyā*, *itthīnaṃ*, *itthiyā*, *itthīhi* / *itthībhi*, *itthiyā*, *itthīnaṃ*, *itthiyaṃ* / *itthiyā*, *itthīsu*. 190. With the suffixes *ṇava*, *ṇika*, *ṇeyya*, and *ṇantu*:

when the gender is expressed by suffixes ending in *ṇava*, *ṇika*, *ṇeyya*, or *ṇantu*, the suffix *ī* is applied. The phrase “or (*vā*)” from [rule] 190 carries over here as “*guṇavantu ī*.
191. *Ntu* becomes *tam* before the suffix *ī*.

The letter *t* of the entire *ntu*-suffix optionally becomes *m* when followed by the suffix *ī*; elsewhere, there is elision of the vowel (*saralopa*), etc. Thus: *guṇavatī*, *guṇavatī* (nom. sg.), *guṇavatiyo* (nom. pl.); *guṇavantī*, *guṇavantī* (nom. sg.), *guṇavantiyo* (nom. pl.), and so forth, following the same pattern as feminine nouns.
Thus: *kulavatī*, *sīlavatī*, *yasavatī*, *rūpavatī*, *satimatī*, *gottamatī*.

From the word *mahanta* (great), by the rule “*ī* [is added] after words beginning with *nada* etc.,” the suffix *ī* is applied; there is the designation *ntu* (feminine), and optionally the substitution of *t* for the final consonant. Thus: *mahatī* / *mahantī*.
In this context, regarding the rule “*bhavanta ī*,” the term “in the case of *ī*” (*īkāre*) is understood to carry over.
192. *Bhavato* becomes *bhoto*.

The substitution of *bho* for the entire word *bhavanta* occurs when followed by a feminine noun ending in the vowel *ī*. Thus: *sā bhotī*, *bhotī*, *bhotiyo*; *he bhoti*, *he bhotī*, *bhotiyo*, and so forth.
Here, after the word *bhikkhu*, the term *itthiyam* (in the feminine) is understood from the previous rule, as is the particle *vā* (or).

193. The suffix *inī* [is applied] after words ending in *pati*, *bhikkhu*, *rāja*, and others ending in long *ī*. When these words ending in long *ī* occur in the feminine gender, the suffix *inī* is added. According to the rule beginning with "There is elision of *sa* and *ra*;

there is the substitution of *am*," etc., because the inclusion of *tu* in that rule prohibits the elision of the preceding vowel in certain instances, the elision of *sa* and *ra* occurs by the rule "Alternatively, a subsequent [suffix] may be applied when it is not of the same form. Thus: *bhikkhunī*, *bhikkhunī*, *bhikkhuniyo*, and so forth.
From the word *gahapati*, the suffix *inī* is added; the word "ātman" is understood [to apply here]. 194. In *paṭisīnī*:

when the suffix *inī* follows, the final syllable of the prefix *pati* becomes *ātman*. Likewise, when *para-sara* is elided, there is lengthening according to the rule "the preceding [vowel] also. Thus: *gahapatānī*.

In the same way, from the word *rāja*, the suffix *inī* is added; through the elision of the *s* and the restoration of the base form, we have *rājinī*. Among words ending in *ī*, from the word *daṇḍī*, the suffix *inī* is added, with the elision of the *s* and so forth, resulting in *daṇḍinī*. Thus: *daṇḍinī*, *daṇḍiniyo*; likewise *hatthinī*, *medhāvinī*, *tapassinī*, *piyabhāṇinī*, and so on.

Regarding the word *pokkharinī*, by the rule "among those [suffixes], there is a vowel increase" (*tesu vuddhi*), the substitution of *a* for *i* and *n* occurs, resulting in *pokkharaṇī*, *pokkharaṇī*.
By the rule "thereafter, *yu* and *na* are *tū*," through the inclusion of *tū*, the *o* replaces *yu* and *na*, and the *y* replaces the *ī*.

In the sutta beginning with *yavata*, by the inclusion of the causal suffix (*kāra*), the letter *ñ* is substituted for *ṇy*, and doubling occurs: *pokkharañño* or *pokkharaṇiyo*, and so forth. The governing particle *vā* has the sense of an unmentioned conjunction;

therefore, the suffix *inī* is also applied after words such as *vidū* (knower) and *yakkha* (demon): *paracittavidunī* (one who knows the minds of others). There is elision of the preceding vowel and substitution of the short vowel (*rassa*). Thus: *paracittavidunī*, *paracittaviduniyo*; *yakkhinī*, *yakkhiniyo*; *sīhinī*, *sīhiniyo*, and so forth. This concludes the section on words ending in long *ī*.
The word *yāgu* is feminine and ends in the vowel *u*.
Its method of declension is the same as that of the word *ratti* (night). The only distinction is the absence of the *am-ādesa* (the substitution of *am*) and other such changes.
*yāgu*, *yāgū*, *yāguyo*; *he yāgu*, *he yāgū*, *yāguyo*; *yāguṃ*, *yāgū*, *yāguyo*; *yāguyā*, *yāgūhi*, *yāgūbhi*.
Yāguhi, yāgūbhi; yāguyā; yāgūnaṃ, yāgunaṃ; yāguyā; yāgūhi, yāgūbhi, yāguhi, yāgubhi;
yāguyā; yāgūnaṃ, yāgunaṃ; yāguyaṃ, yāguyā; yāgūsu, yāgusu.

*mātarā*, *mātuyā*, *matyā*—here the vowel *u* is elided according to the rule beginning with “*tesu vuddhī*,” and there is also shortening (*rassatta*). [Ablative/Genitive]: *mātarehi*, *mātarebhi*, *mātūhi*.
mātu-bhi, mātu-hi, mātu-bhi; mātu, mātussa, mātuyā; mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ, mātunaṃ;

Neuter Gender:
Now the neuter gender words are being stated.
The word *citta*, ending in the vowel *a*, is neuter.
The arising of *syā* is as if pure; here, in the case of *citta si*, the rule “after neuter [stems], *si* is always [replaced by *e*]” also applies.

*Si*: this consists of two words. After neuter nouns ending in *a*, the suffix *si* is always replaced by *am*. [The rules regarding] elision of vowels (*saralopa*), restoration to the base form (*pakatibhāva*), and so forth, apply; for example, *cittam*.

In the plural, the rule "the replacement of *ya* and *na* occurs after neuter nouns" continues to apply. 196. *Ato niccam*: [after a neuter noun ending in *a*, the suffix *si* is always replaced by *am*].

After neuter stems ending in *a*, the suffix *ni* is always substituted for *ya*. By the rule “*sabbayonīnamāe*,” the vowel *ā* optionally replaces the *i* of *ni*. Elsewhere, by the rule “*yosu kata*,” etc., the long vowel occurs.

Examples: *cittā*, *cittāni*. Although the substitution of *ā* for *e* after *ni* would have been established by the general rule, the specific formulation “*ato niccaṃ*” (always after *a*) indicates that the substitution of *ā* for *e* occurs only in certain instances here.

In address, there is elision. Thus: *he citta*, *he cittā*, *cittāni*—in the second case (*dvitīyā*), the vowel *e* is substituted for *ni* by way of optional variation (*nissakka-vikappa*). *Cittaṃ*, *citte*, *cittāni*.
The remainder is the same as the word *purisa*. In the same way, others also [are declined]: *puñña*, *pāpa*, *phala*, *rūpa*, *sādhanaṃ*.

*kammesu*. Similarly: *thāmunā*, *thāmena*, *thāmasā* or *thāmuno*, *thāmassa*, *thāmunā*, *thāmā*. *Addhunā*, *addhuno*, and so forth, are the same as the preceding [examples].

198. *Aṃ* in the neuter.
For the neuter gender, the suffix *ntu* connected with it becomes *aṃ* when the case ending *si* follows. *Guṇavaṃ cittaṃ* (the virtuous mind).
In the case of *yomhi*, the word *yosu* is the base (*atta*), and the vowel *i* is [the suffix]. For *guṇavanti*, *guṇavantāni*, and so forth, the rest should be understood accordingly.

In *gacchanta si*, the word *nta* is replaced by *a* according to the rule: "In the locative singular (*simhi*), for words beginning with *gacchanta*, the word *nta* becomes *a*. The word *assaddhā* is a neuter gender ending in *-ā*.

When it stands as “*assaddhā*,” with reference to the rule “of a compound” (*samāsassā*), the final vowel of the compound is shortened by the rule “the vowel is short in the neuter” (*saro rasso napuṃsake*). Due to being a compound, it receives the designation of a noun (*nāma*), and the case endings beginning with *si* arise. The rest is the same as for *citta*.
"An unfaithful family," "unfaithful [people]," "unfaithful families," and so forth.

Likewise is the term *mukhanāsika* ("mouth-and-nose"). Because it is a compound of two nouns functioning as a single entity (*dvandeka*), it always takes the singular number. For example: *mukhanāsikaṃ*, *he mukhanāsika*, *mukhanāsikaṃ*, *mukhanāsikena*, and so forth. This concludes the section on words ending in long *ā*.
The word *aṭṭhi* is a neuter noun ending in the vowel *i*.
The suffixes beginning with *si* arise, and there is elision of the final consonant (*silopa*), resulting in *aṭṭhi*. The particle "vā" (or) is understood to carry over.
199. *Yonaṃ ni napuṃsakehi*.
After all [words] ending in the neuter gender, *ni* optionally occurs.

In other cases, there is always elision of *yu*, and the vowel is lengthened: *aṭṭhī*; likewise, *he aṭṭhi*, *he aṭṭhī*, *aṭṭhīni*; *aṭṭhiṃ*, *aṭṭhī*, *aṭṭhīni*; *aṭṭhinā*, and so forth, similar to the word *aggi*.
In this way, there are words such as *satthi*, *dadhi*, *vāri*, *akkhi*, *acchi*, *acci*, and so forth.
These end in the vowel *i*. The word *sukhakārī* is a neuter noun ending in the vowel *ī*.

In the phrase “sukhabhārī si,” because there is no neuter gender here, even in the nominative singular (si), there is shortening according to the rule “agho rassa” and so forth, followed by the elision of the case-ending (silopa).
The word *sukhakāri* [is declined as follows]: Nominative: *sukhakārī*, *sukhakārīni* Vocative: *he sukhakāri*, *he sukhakārī*, *he sukhakārīni* Accusative:
*sukhakārīnaṃ*, *sukhakāriṃ* Nominative (plural): *sukhakārī*, *sukhakārīni*
The remainder is the same as for the word *daṇḍin*. Likewise for *sīghayāyin* and so forth.
[Now] the words ending in *ī*.
The word *āyu*, ending in *u*, is neuter gender. Its method of declension is the same as that of the word *aṭṭhi*.

Āyu, āyū, āyūni; he āyu, he āyū, he āyūni; āyuṃ, āyū, āyūni; āyunā, āyusā—these forms are established because [the stem] belongs to the *manoggaṇa*. [The remaining cases are: āyūhi, āyūbhi; āyuno, āyussa;
āyūnaṃ, and so forth. In the same way are formed: cakkhu, vasu, dhanu, dāru, tipu, madhu, hiṅgu, siggu, vatthu, matthu, jatu, ambu, assu, etc. This concludes the section on stems ending in -u.
The word *gotrabhū* is neuter and ends in the vowel *ū*.

In the nominative singular, it is *gotrabhū*; due to its neuter gender, there is shortening of the vowel, and the elision of the case-suffix (*silopa*). Thus: *gotrabhu cittaṃ*, *gotrabhū*, *gotrabhūni*.
In the vocative: *he gotrabhu*, *he gotrabhū*, *he gotrabhūni*. In the accusative: *gotrabhuṃ*, *gotrabhū*, *gotrabhūni*. In the instrumental: *gotrabhunā*.
Thus, and so forth, in the masculine gender, [words] are equal to the word *abhibhū*.
Likewise, *sayambhū*, *dhammaññū*, and others. [This concludes the section on] words ending in *-ū*.
The word *citta-gosaddo* (the word "mind-cow") ends in *o* and is neuter.

In the sense of “this family has mind-cows,” when a *bahubbīhi* compound is formed, the vowel *o* is shortened because it is situated in the place of [the original] *o* according to the rule “the vowel is short in the neuter.

Thus, the short vowel *u* replaces it; then the case endings (*syādi*) arise, and there is elision of the final consonant (*silopa*). The result is *cittagu kulaṃ* (the mind-cow family); [and in the nominative singular: *cittagu*.
"Cittagūni" and so forth are similar to the word "āyu.
It ends in the vowel "o.
The words *citta*, *kamma*, *assaddha*, *mathaṭṭhi*, and *sukhakāri* [end in "o"].
*Āyu*, *gotrabhū*, *dhammaññū*, and *cittagū* are neuter.
The section on neuter gender is completed. [End of] Pronouns (*sabbanāma*).
Now, all the pronouns (sabbanāmāni) are stated:
sabba, katara, katama, ubhaya, itara, añña, aññatara, aññatama, pubba, para, apara, dakkhiṇa,
uttara, adhara, ya, ta, eta, ima, amu, kiṃ, eka, ubha, dvi, ti, catu, tumha.
*Amha* refers to twenty-seven pronouns (*sabbanāmāni*); because they are pronouns, they possess three genders. Among them, the word *sabba* has the sense of "without remainder" (*niravasesattha*).

When it expresses a meaning qualified by the masculine gender, then the method of declension (*rūpanaya*) is as follows: the addition of the case endings (*syādi*) occurs as before; for *so*, the *si* becomes *o*, and there is the elision of the vowel (*saralopa*) and the substitution of the following sound (*paranayana*).

Thus: *sabba jano*. In the plural, in the expression *sabba yo*, the term "pronoun" (*sabbanāma*) is applied to *sabba* and the others by the rule: "In usage, the technical name of another [term] applies."
The word "yo" (who/which) is understood [to follow]. 200. [The suffix] *paṭhama* occurs after the letter *a* in all masculine names.

"All names"—that is, the names of all feminines, masculines, and neuters—are called "all-name" (*sabbanāma*). After the letter *a* in all those bases designated as "all-name," the first case ending *yo* is substituted. Example: *sabbe purisā* (all men).
What is meant by "the form *akāra*"? It refers to all [forms] ending in *am*.
Thus: *he sabba*, *sabbā*; *he sabbe*, *sabbaṃ*, *sabbe*; *sabbena*, *sabbehi*, *sabbebhi*.
When the substitution of *āy* is due to reach in the singular of the fourth case—
“From this [point], *ā*, *e*, *smā*, *asmim*, *naṃ*, *āya*, and *catutthekavacanassa* are also carried over. 201.
And three [substitutes] do not [occur] after all nouns (*sabbanāma*).
After all nouns ending in *a*, for the following *smā*, *smim*, and the fourth case singular (*catutthekavacana*), these [substitutes]—*ā*, *e*, and *āya*—[are applied].
"Ādesā neva hontīti" means there is an absence of the substitution of *ā*. The inclusion of the particle *ca* is for the purpose of excluding the prohibition in certain instances;
therefore, after words such as *pubba*, the forms *smā* and *smiṃ* become *ā* and *e* respectively. "Of the whole [word]" (*sabbassa*).
"The vowel *a*, *e*" is also carried over (*vattate*).
202. And after all pronouns, when the suffix *naṃ* occurs, the letter *a* of all pronouns undergoes elision (*ettam*).
The phrase “after a pronoun” (*sabbanāmato*) also continues [as a governing rule].
203. *Naṃ* from every [base] ending in *-saṃ*.
