The application (*adhikāra*), moreover, is threefold: by way of the lion’s gait, the frog’s leap, and the gradual sequence. Here, however, it is either by the lion’s gait because of looking back and forward, or simply by the gradual sequence.
Having made the honorific forms non-distinct, he provides a technical rule (*paribhāsa*) for the purpose of establishing the natural state according to the word of the Conqueror.
61. And the gender is inflected.
The gender (*liṅga*) is primary; for in whatever way a gender is connected with the word of the Conqueror (*jinavacana*), in that very way it is applied and established here as the gender.

By the word "and" (*ca*), the sense is "and the roots (*dhātu*)," because, in accordance with the word of the Conqueror, when the gender "masculine" (*purisa*) is established, then for that meaningful sound—excluding the roots, suffixes, and case-endings—the term "other designation" (*parasamaññā*) [is used].
From the word "payoge" (in usage) [in the rule on] gender-designation,
the mention of "gender" (liṅga) recurs in all instances from here onwards in the formulation of case-endings, suffixes, and so forth. And from that [mention],
the case-endings [are introduced].

Following that, there are further case-endings (*vibhattiyo*) associated with the words of the Jina. By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), they include those ending in suffixes such as *tava*, *etu*, and *nādi*, as well as indeclinables (*nipāta*). They are called "case-endings" because they divide the meaning of gender according to functions such as the object (*kamma*) and so forth, and according to numbers such as singularity (*ekatta*) and so forth.
What, then, are those case-endings? The heading is: "The Case-Endings. 63.
*Siyo*, *aṃyo*, *nāhi*, *sanaṃ*, *smāhi*, *sanaṃ*, *smiṃsu*.
The case endings beginning with *syā* are called the dual endings (*dvisatta-vibhattiyo*). Among them: *si*, *yo*—these are the nominative (*paṭhamā*); *aṃ*, *yo*—these are the accusative (*dutiyā*);
*nā*, *hi*—these are the instrumental (*tatiyā*); *sa*, *naṃ*—these are the dative (*catutthī*); *smā*, *hi*—these are the ablative (*pañcamī*);
*sa*, *naṃ*—these are the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*); *smiṃ*, *su*—these are the locative (*sattamī*).
This, however, should be understood as a rule for technical names (*saññā-sutta*) among the rules concerning technical names, prohibitions, and injunctions; for it is said in the *Vutti*:

"What is the purpose of the expression 'vibhatti'? [It is to indicate that] in the case of *amha*, there is *mamaṃ* together with its case-ending, and in the case of *asme*, there is *se*. Otherwise, a single compound would have to be formed with the preceding rule.
And here, the designations such as "nominative" (*paṭhamā*) and so forth, as well as "singular" (*ekavacana*) and so forth, are according to their literal meaning (*anvatthavasena*).
Or, it should be understood that [the term] is established by way of common worldly convention (*parasamaññā*).

A word for one is the singular (*ekavacana*); a word for many is the plural (*bahuvacana*); that which completes two is the dual (*dutiyā*), and so forth. Otherwise, if the technical designation (*saññā*) were made by the particle *ca* in the preceding sutta, there would be the undesirable consequence (*appakatāniratthaka*) of the application of the rule.

Furthermore, the phrase "for gender associated with the Victor’s word is declined" (*jinavacanayuttaṃ hi liṅgañca nipaccate*) is supplied [from the previous context]. However, here he states another paribhāṣā (metarule) in order to make it known that even the formation of words (*padanipphādana*) must not contradict the Victor’s word.
64. *Tadanuparodhena*.
In whatever way there is no contradiction of those words of the Conqueror (*jinavacana*), in that very way the gender (*liṅga*) is produced here;

by the word "and" (*ca*), the verb (*ākhyāta*) is also produced—this is the meaning. For this very reason, both the dual number and the verb are taken here, because they are distinct from the honorific [forms].
And it should be understood that the rules for case endings (*vibhatti*), suffixes (*paccaya*), and so forth, have been established.

In that regard, since there is a general application of all case endings beginning with the nominative (*sabbassādi*), [it is stated]: "The occurrence of words follows the speaker’s intention" (*vatticchānupubbikā saddappavatti*). Thus, by virtue of the speaker’s intention—[rule 65]—the first case ending (*paṭhamā*) occurs in the sense of gender (*liṅgatthe*).
The nominative case occurs when there is the mere expression of the meaning of a gender; thus it is called *paṭhamā* (the first).

Even therein, since both singular and plural would otherwise apply without restriction, the singular nominative occurs when there is a desire to express the singularity of the gender-meaning, according to the paribhāṣā rule: "When singularity is to be expressed, the singular [number] is used.
From the rule "ato nenā," the word "ato" (from this) is carried over, as is the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*).
66. *So si, o iti*: this consists of two words. The vowel *o* replaces the nominative singular suffix *si* that follows a stem ending in the vowel *a*.

For in the Suttas, it should be understood that when the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is indicated by the nominative case, its explanation in terms of the genitive case is required with respect to the substitute (*ādesa*).

And here, the term *sī* (the nominative case ending) is understood because this is a section prescribing grammatical operations (*kāriya-vidhi*) for case endings (*vibhatti*), or because the mention of "case endings" (*vibhattiyo*) from the previous rule [Pāṇini 1.4.104] is carried over;
thus, in all instances where an operation is prescribed for *si* and the other case endings, it should be understood that the case ending itself is intended.

Regarding the rule "or a subsequent [suffix] of a different form," when the elision of the subsequent element would otherwise apply, he states the elision of the preceding element as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
67. *Saralopo’mādesappaccayādimhi*: When there is the elision of a vowel (*sara*) following an *am*-substitute or a suffix beginning with a vowel, the original form (*pakati*) [is restored].

There is an elision of the preceding vowel when there is the expression *am*, and when a vowel belonging to an *am*-substitute or a suffix follows. However, once the elision of the subsequent vowel (*sara*) has been effected, the subsequent vowel assumes its original form (*pakatibhāva*).

And here, the repetition of the term "elision of a vowel" (*saralope*) is for the purpose of indicating that this very rule applies only when the elision of a vowel has already been caused by this [preceding] rule.

When a modification (*vikāra*) of another [element] has occurred, it is for the purpose of restoring its original state (*pakatibhāva*). Because of the inherent capacity of the rule for restoring the original state of both [the preceding and following elements], it is established that even when a vowel follows [the modified element], provided that vowel constitutes the *am*-substitute, the *paccaya* (suffix), and so forth.
Furthermore, the case-endings beginning with *tya* are understood here as being of the nature of suffixes (*paccaya*).

The mention of "ādi" (and so forth) is established by tradition for both nouns (*kitaka*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). Due to the association with suffixes (*paccaya*), a substitute (*ādesa*) follows the original base (*pakati*);
however, there is no elision of the final *sara* vowel of a word when followed by "abbhāha" and so forth.

The inclusion of *tu* is for the purpose of excluding the elision (*lopa*) of *sa* in cases such as *bhikkhunī* and others. According to the rule “*naye paraṃ yutte*” (one should lead the subsequent [word] when joined), the subsequent word must be led forward.
Thus, when one should say *puriso puriso ca*, it becomes *purisa purisa*. 68. *Sarūpānamekasesvasakiṃ*:
Among words that are identical in form (*sarūpa*), there is a single remainder (*ekasesa*), except in the case of the neuter (*asakiṃ*).
Among words that are similar in form—that is, identical in their phonetic shape—only one remains, while the others undergo elision; this is "ekasesa" (single remainder).

Here, although the rule would have been established by the mention of "similar forms" (*sarūpānaṃ*) alone, the explicit inclusion of the term "asakim" (not in the sense of repetition) serves to show that this [ekasesa] applies only when there is a connection with the word *asakim* within the scope of a single case ending, and not in the case of distributive repetition (*vicchā*). Thus, there is no over-extension of the rule to distributive usage.
Regarding the phrase “groups of five by fives, [they are] wise,” here, because the distributive sense is established by the very mention of “five by fives,” it is made known;
or else, this is a single-remainder compound (*ekasesa*) due to the desire for simultaneous expression.
Furthermore, in this case, the single-remainder compound is formed through the analysis of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*).
It remains as the remainder [of the compound], as in the case of "pitūnaṃ" and so forth.

In that very context, when there is a desire to express plurality for the meaning of the gender, the plural of the nominative occurs according to the rule: "The plural is used when plurality is to be expressed. Here, in the words "yo puriso," the terms "ato" and "vā" are understood to carry over.
69. [The suffix] "āe" is substituted for all feminine bases ending in "ā."
After a nominal stem ending in *a*, for all subsequent first-case endings and second-case endings, the substitution of *ā* and *e* respectively occurs optionally;

thus [the forms] *ākāro*, *rūpā*, *rūpāni*, *aggayo*, and *munayo*. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sabba*) is for the purpose of including all substitutions. The elision of vowels (*saralopa*) and so forth are exactly as before; [examples are: *purisā tiṭṭhanti*.
[The forms] *vā*, *icc'eva*, *rūpā*, *rūpāni*, *aggayo*, and *munayo*.
This particle *vā* has the sense of a fixed alternative (*vavatthita-pibhāsa*). Therefore, it is said here:
"Regarding the masculine gender, [the suffix] is always present; in the neuter, it is sometimes absent.
But when the action is completed (*katatte*), the particle *vā* indicates the application [of the suffix]."
In that very context, when there is a desire for an address, the rule "the nominative case [is used] in the sense of gender" continues to apply. 70. And in addressing (*ālapane*).

Addressing (*ālapana*) is speaking while facing someone; it is an invocation. When there is the addition of the sense of addressing, as well as the mere expression of the sense of gender, the first case ending occurs. It takes the singular and other numbers just as before.
Regarding the word *purisa* in this context—71.
In the sense of address (*ālapanatthe*), the [final] *si* is designated as *ga*.
Since that which is prescribed in the sense of address is designated as *ga*, by virtue of this *ga*-designation, the word "ge" is supplied from the rule "bho ge tū. Thus, "ge" is understood here.
72. *Akāra-pitādy-antānam ā*.

The vowel *a* related to a noun stem (*liṅga*), as well as the final [vowel] of words such as *pitā* (father) and *satthū* (teacher), undergoes the substitution of *ā* when followed by the suffix *ge*.
The rule "in *ge*, [the vowel becomes] short" also applies here.
73. Or the *ākāra*.
The *ākāra* related to a grammatical gender (*liṅga*) optionally becomes short when followed by the suffix *ge*, provided this occurs in addressing someone who is not far away. 74.
From the remainder [of the suffixes], there is elision (*lopa*) of both *ga* and *si*.
The term *sesa* (the remainder) refers to those [words] indicated by examples such as “siṃ, so, syā ca, sakhato gasse vā, ghate cā” and so forth;
from that *sesa*, the case endings *gasi* and so on undergo elision (*lopa*). The inclusion of the word *api* is for the purpose of including the second sense [of *sesa*].
And here, even though the word *si* is included, the statement *vaiti* itself is the indicator (*ñāpaka*) that when *si* is included in another sense, the term *ālapanā* (vocative) is also included.
Some employ the word *bhavanta* or the word *he* for the sake of clarity in address. For example: "O man, stand" (*bho purisa tiṭṭha*), or "O men" (*he purisā*).
There is no difference in the plural; [one may say] "O sirs, stand" (*bhavanto purisā tiṭṭhatha*).
In that very context, when there is a desire for a word expressing the object (*kamma*), the particle *va* follows.
75. That which one does is *kamma* (an object).
Whatever one does, whatever one transforms, or whatever one attains—that which is the agent, the cause of the action—receives the designation *kamma*. 76.
The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The second case ending occurs in the sense of the object (*kamma*). As before, the singular form is *am*; when the vowel is elided by the rule "elision of vowels" (*saralopa*), and the rule "long vowel" (*dīgha*) applies, the original base form (*pakatibhāva*) is restored: *purisaṃ passa* (see the man).
In the plural, by the rule "for all [stems] ending in *i*, *u*, or *n*, [substitute] *ā* and *e*," the *i* of the suffix is replaced: *purise passa* (see the men).
In that same context, when there is a desire for the agentive expression (*kattuvacana*):
77. He who performs [an action] is the agent (*kattā*).
One who performs an action with self-exertion receives the designation "agent.
The term "the third case" (*tatiyā*) is understood to carry over.
78. And in the case of the agent (*kattar*).

When the agent (*kattar*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), the third case ending occurs; thus, the singular form of the third case is *nā*. 79. After [a stem ending in] *a*, [the suffix] *na* [is substituted for the third case singular].

*Enā* is a designation for that which lacks a case ending (*avibhattika*). After a gendered noun (*liṅga*) ending in *a*, the substitution of *enā* occurs for the following word *nā*; there is elision of the vowel (*saralopa*), etc.: *purisena kataṃ*.
In the plural: 80. *Suhisvakāro e*. (The letter *e* is substituted for *su*, *hi*, and *sva*.)
In these subsequent case-endings—*su*, *hi*, and *icceta*—the vowel *a* related to the gender undergoes the change to *e*. 81. *Smā-hi-smiṃ-naṃ mhā-bhi-mhi vā*:
After every gender, for *smā*, *hi*, and *smiṃ*, the substitutes *mhā*, *bhi*, and *mhi* respectively occur optionally; as in *purisehi* and *purisebhi kataṃ*.
In that very context, when there is a desire to express the instrument: 82. That by which one performs is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Whatever performs, whatever sees, or whatever hears—that agent is designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

83. The third case ending occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the instrumental case, the third case ending is used; the rest is the same as for the agent (*kartr*). For example: "by the man who has entered" (*āviṭṭhena purisena*), he performs merit (*puññaṃ karoti*); [also] *purisehi*, *purisebhi*.
In that very same context, when there is a desire to express the recipient (*sampadāna*):
84. That person to whom one wishes to give, or who approves [of the gift], or who receives it, is the recipient (*sampadāna*).
Whether it be the one to whom one wishes to give, or the one who approves, or the one who receives, that *kāraka* (participant in an action) is designated as the recipient.
85. The fourth case ending (*catutthī*) is used for the recipient.
The fourth case ending occurs in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna-kāraka). Thus, the singular of the fourth case is *sa*.
[Rule 86: *Sāgamo se*:
the letter *s* is inserted after the final consonant of every nominal stem (*liṅga*) when the case ending *se* follows. [Example: *purisassa dhanam dadāti* (He gives wealth to the man).
In the case of the plural number, the word "long" (dīgha) is understood to carry over. 87.

And in the presence of *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*: when these follow, all short vowels at the end of a stem undergo lengthening. The inclusion of the letter *ca* is for the purpose of excluding the vowels *i* and *u* in certain instances. Example: *purisānaṃ*.
In that very context, regarding the desire for the term *apādāna*: 88.
That from which one departs (*apeti*), or from which one takes fear (*bhayaṃ ādatte*), is the *apādāna*.

Or, that which serves as the limit (*avadhi*) from which one departs, or from which fear arises, or from which one takes [something], that grammatical factor (*kāraka*) receives the designation *apādāna*.
89. The fifth case ending is used for the ablative (*apādāna*).
Since the fifth case ending occurs in the sense of the ablative factor (*apādānakāraka*), the singular form of the fifth case is *smā*.
Furthermore, the rules “*ato*” (from *a*) and “*sabbesaṃ, ā e*” (for all [vowels], *ā* becomes *e*) continue to apply.

90. *Smā* or *Smiṃ*. From a noun ending in *a*, the forms *smā* and *smin* undergo, respectively, the substitutions of *ā* and *ī*; otherwise, the substitution of *mhā* occurs. Thus: *purisā* (from), *purisamhā*, *purisasmā*.
In the plural, it is the same as the third case in all instances, for its substitute is *bhi*. Thus: *purisehi*, *purisebhi* (from).
In that very context, regarding the desire for the possessive case: 91.
Or, that which is the possession of someone is his "owner" (sāmi).
Or, that which is the possession of someone is designated as "possessive" (sāmisaññā).

92. The sixth case ending occurs when there is a sense of "belonging to" (sāmismiṃ). With the exception of the substitution of *ā* [for *e*], the forms for the fourth and sixth cases are identical in all instances. For example: "this wealth belongs to the man" (*purisassa*), or "to the men" (*purisānaṃ*).
In that very same context, when there is a desire to express location:
93. The locus (*adhāra*) of darkness.
That factor which is the locus for the performance of actions to be done is designated as the "locus" (*okāsa*) kāraka. 94. The seventh case ending is used for the locus.

The locative case ending occurs when there is a locus (okāsa). The singular form of the locative is *smiṃ*; by the rule "for *smā*, *smiṃ*, and *naṃ*, [the vowel] *e* [is substituted]," the vowel *e* is replaced, and *mhi* is the substitute: *purise paṭṭhitaṃ*, *purisamhi*, *purisasmiṃ*.
In the plural, by the rule "for *su*, *hi*, and *sva*, the vowel *e* [is substituted]," the vowel *e* is applied:
*purisesu*. [The nominative forms are: *puriso*, *purisā*, or *bho purisa*, *bho purisā*; [the vocative: *bhavanto purisā*; [the accusative: *purisaṃ*, *purise*; [the instrumental: *purisena*.
*Purisa*: purisehi, purisebhi; purisassa; purisānaṃ; purisā, purisasmā, purisamhā;
purisehi, purisebhi; purisassa, purisānaṃ; purise, purisasmiṃ, purisamhi;
purisesu. Likewise: *sugata*, *sugatā*; *bho sugata*, *bho sugatā* or *bhavanto sugatā*; *sugataṃ*; *sugate*.
Sugatena, sugatehi, sugatebhi; sugatassa, sugatānaṃ; sugatā, sugatasmā, sugatamhā;
sugatehi, sugatebhi; sugatassa, sugatānaṃ; sugate, sugatasmiṃ, sugatamhi; sugatesu.
Thus [are declined] sura, asura, nara, uraga, nāga, and yakkha.
Gandhabbas, kinnaras, humans, pisācas, and petas;
mātaṅgas, moving creatures, horses, boars, and lions;
tigers, bears, tortoises, hyenas, deer, antelopes, and jackals.
The Sangha— whose light is the world’s abode, who possess the yoga of generosity and the wind of effort, who delight in the Dhamma of the villages, towns, and scriptures,
and who have destroyed the flood of misfortune, resentment, the taints, anger, and greed.
Aggression, stubbornness, intoxication, pride, negligence, and hypocrisy;
the punnāga, pūga, panasa, āsana, campaka, and ambā trees;
the hintāla, tāla, bakula, arjuna, and kiṃsuka trees.
The mandāra, kunda, pucimanda, and karañja trees;
and the peacock, the bird born from an egg, the krauñca, the swan—
these and others as well.
But for the masculine *manogaṇa* class, there is no distinction between the singular and plural forms.
In other respects, it is the same as the masculine [class]. [The forms are: *mano*, *manā*; *he mana*, *he manā* (or); *bhavanto manā*; *manaṃ*, *mane*.
The word "vā" (or) continues [to apply].
95. *Manogaṇādito smiṃnānamiā*.

From the group beginning with *mano* (the *manogaṇa*), before the suffixes *smiṃ*, *na*, *ā*, *mi*, and *ā*, the vowels *i* and *ā* are optionally substituted respectively for the final letters of these [words]. By the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), this also applies to words such as *bila* and others.
The phrase "*manogaṇādito*" continues [to the following rule].
96. *Sa-sare vā āgamo*.
After these same groups beginning with *man*, when a vowel follows, the augment *ā* optionally occurs. Examples: *manasā*, *manena*.

This word "optionally" (*vā*) has the sense of a fixed distribution (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*); therefore, it does not occur in cases such as "mano, manā, manaṃ, mane, mana-āyatanaṃ," etc. However, in cases such as "mānasikaṃ, cetasikaṃ," it occurs invariably. Examples: *mane-hi*, *mane-bhi*.
The phrase “or from a consonant-group beginning with *man*” also recurs [from the previous rule]. 97. *Sassa co*.
After a consonant-group beginning with *man*, the vowel *o* optionally replaces the case-ending *sā* (nominative singular). There is the augment *sā*.

Of *mano*: *manassa*, *manānaṃ*; from *mano*: *manā*, *manasmā*, *manamhā*; by *mano*: *manehi*, *manebhi*; for *mano*: *manaso*, *manassa*, *manānaṃ*; in *mano*: *manasi*, *mane*, *manasmiṃ*, *manamhi*; in *manos*: *manesu*.
Thus also for *vaco*, *vayo*, *tejo*, *tapo*, *ceto*, *tamo*, and *yaso*.
Ayo, payo, siro, chando, saro, uro,
raho, aho— these and others are the *manogaṇa* (consonant groups).
The analysis of the word *guṇavantu*. Here, in the case of *guṇavantu si*, there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of both “*savibhattissa, ntussa*” and [the present rule].
98. *Ā simhi*. (In the presence of the suffix *si*, [the final *u* of *guṇavantu*] becomes *ā*.)
The *ntu* suffix, along with its case-ending (*savibhatti*), undergoes substitution by *ā* when the nominative (*si*) case-ending follows. [Thus: *guṇavā*.
In the rule “*yo* in the first [case]” (Pāṇini 7.1.13), the word “*vā*” from the *Sīhagati* [section] is understood to carry over.
99. The *ntu* suffix becomes *nto*.
For every *ntu*-suffix ending in a case-ending, the substitute *nto* optionally occurs when the first person plural suffix *yu* follows; thus, [the forms] *guṇavanto* and *tiṭṭhanti* arise.

The phrase "and *atta* in the case of *su* and *naṃ*" is also understood to apply here. 100. *Ntussa anto yosu ca*. (In the case of the *ntu*-suffix, *anta* is substituted before the first person plural suffixes *yu* and *su*).

In the case of the *ntu* suffix, the vowel *u* becomes *a* before the endings *sunam*, *hi*, and *yo*; by the inclusion of "or" (*ca*), it also occurs before other endings such as *aṃ*, *nā*, *smā*, and *smiṃ*.

Although the substitution of *anta* for the genitive was already established [by a previous rule], because the term *anta* is mentioned again here, the vowel *i* is substituted for *yu* in some instances. Examples: *guṇavantā*.
The word "A" is understood [to apply]. 101. *Avaṇṇā ca ge*:
When *ge* follows, the substitutes *aṃ*, *avaṇṇa*, and so forth, occur in place of the entire suffix *ntu* along with its case ending.
"Bho guṇavaṃ, bho guṇava, bho guṇavā; bhavanto guṇavanto, guṇavantā; guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. The word "vā" (or) is understood [to apply here].
102. In the case of *sasmin* and *āsu*, [the suffixes] *to* and *ti* [are applied].

In the case of all *ntu*-suffixes accompanied by case endings, the substitutions *tā* and *to* optionally occur respectively before the suffixes *sasmiṃ* and *nā*. For example: *guṇavatā*, *guṇavantena*; *guṇavantehi*, *guṇavantebhi*.
103. *Ntassa se vā*:
In the case of all *ntu*-suffixes accompanied by case endings, the substitution *nta* optionally occurs for the suffix *ntu* before the case ending *se*. For example: *guṇavantassa*, *guṇavato*.

104. *Naṃmhi taṃ vā*. In the case of the suffix *naṃ*, the substitution of *taṃ* optionally occurs for the entire *ntu* suffix when it is accompanied by a case ending. [Thus: *guṇavataṃ* (of those possessing virtue), *guṇavantānaṃ* (of those possessing virtue).
By the rule beginning with "amha tumha ntu," the designation *nā* is applied to the *smā* case ending.

From *guṇavā*: *guṇavantā*, *guṇavantasmā*, *guṇavantamhā*; from *guṇavantehi*, *guṇavantebhi*; of *guṇavato*, *guṇavassa*; of *guṇavantānaṃ*, *guṇavataṃ*; in *guṇavati*, *guṇavante*, *guṇavantasmiṃ*, *guṇavantamhī*; in *guṇavantesu*.
In the same way, [the forms of] *gaṇavā*, *kulavā*, *balavā*, *yasavā*, *dhanavā*, *sutavā*, *bhagavā*, *himavā*, *phalavā*, *sīlavā*, *paññavā*, and so forth [are formed].
When the nominative singular suffix (*si*) is applied to the word *himavant*:
While the rule “*attaṃ*, *ntussa’nto*” is being stated:
105. *Simhī vā*.
In the locative case ending *simhi*, the suffix *ntu* optionally becomes *attaṃ*. For example: *himavanto* or *himavā*; the rest is the same.
The inclusion of the word *vā* again is for the purpose of precluding [the application of the suffix] to anything other than the word *himavanta*;
this *vā* has the sense of a restrictive alternative (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*). By means of that, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) to words such as *guṇavanta*. Thus:

*satimā*, *dhitimā*, *gatimā*, *matimā*, *mutimā*, *muttimā*, *jutimā*, *sirimā*, *hirimā*, *thutimā*, *ratimā*, *yatimā*, *sucimā*, *kalimā*, *balimā*, *kasimā*, *rucimā*, *buddhimā*, *cakkhumā*, *bandhumā*, *hetumā*, *setumā*.
[The suffixes] -ketumā, -rāhumā, -bhāṇumā, -khāṇumā, -vijjumā, and so forth.

In that context, there is a difference in form for the words *satimantu* and *bandhumantu* before the [suffixes] *-aṃsa*. The terms *attaṃ* and *ntussa* also recur. Or, [the suffix] *-aṃsa* may be applied to all [of these].

The suffix *ntu* occurs after every [stem] before the endings *atta*, *vā*, and *aṃsa*. Here too, because the particle *vā* has a restricted optionality (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), there is no over-extension.
Thus: *satimaṃ*, *satimantaṃ*; *bandhumaṃ*, *bandhumantaṃ*; *satimassa*, *satimato*, *satimantassa*;
*bandhumassa*, *bandhumato*, *bandhumantassa*; the rest is the same.
There is an analysis of the word *gacchantasadda*: *gacchantasi*. The particle *vā* is understood [from the previous rule]. 107.
In the nominative singular (*simhi*), the suffix *-nta-* of words such as *gacchant-* becomes *-am*.

In words such as *gacchant* ending in the suffix *-nta*, the word-element *-nta* optionally assumes the form *aṃ* when the nominative case-suffix (*si*) follows. By the rules of elision of *sara* and *silopa*, it becomes *so gacchaṃ*, or [alternatively] *gacchanto gaṇhāti*.
And while the rule "the word-element *-nta* of *gacchant* and others" is being stated—108.
In the remaining cases, only *ntu* [is substituted].

In the case of *gacchant-ādi*, the suffix *-nt-* should be regarded as the primary suffix *-ntu* (*ntupaccaya*) among the remaining case-suffixes; this is an extension of grammatical operation (*kāriyātidesa*) to the form *asmim*. The rest is the same as for *guṇavant*. They: *gacchanto*, *gacchantā*; O you:
*bho gacchaṃ*, *bho gaccha*, *bho gacchā*; Your honors: *bhavanto gacchanto*, *gacchantā*;
[Accusative: *gacchaṃ*, *gacchantaṃ*; [Ablative: *gacchante*; [Instrumental: *gacchatā*, *gacchantena*; [Ablative/Genitive: *gacchantehi*, *gacchantebhi*.
Of one going, of the one who is going; of those going, of the ones who are going; from one going, from the one who is going, from those going, from the ones who are going;
by one going, by the one who is going; by those going, by the ones who are going; in one going, in the one who is going, in those going, in the ones who are going; in those who are going.
Thus: *mahaṃ* (I), *caraṃ* (walking), *tiṭṭhaṃ* (standing), *dadaṃ* (giving), *bhuñjaṃ* (eating),

*suṇaṃ* (hearing), *pacaṃ* (cooking), *jayaṃ* (conquering), *jīraṃ* (aging), *cavaṃ* (falling away), *mīyaṃ* (dying), *saraṃ* (remembering), *kubbaṃ* (doing), *japaṃ* (muttering), *vajaṃ* (avoiding)— and so forth.
There is no difference in the various case endings of the word *bhavant*. It is *so bhavaṃ* (“that venerable one”).
The form *bhavato* is understood [to follow]. 109.
In some instances, the substitution of *o* occurs for the letter *va* in the nominative and accusative cases.

In the case of this word *bhavanta*, the substitution of *o* for the letter *va* occurs optionally before these [suffixes]: *yo*, *te*, *bhonto*, *bhavanto*, and *bhavantā*. The term "of *bhavato*" (genitive of *bhavant*) is understood [as governing the following rules].
110. But in the case of the vocative singular (*ge*), it is *bho*.

For the entire word *bhavanta*, *bho* is substituted when followed by a *ge*-case suffix. With the word *tusa*, there is elision (*galopa*) of *bhante*, *bhontādi*, and so forth: *bho bhante*, *bhonta*, *bhontā*; *bhonto*, *bhavanto*, *bhavantā*; *bhavantaṃ*; *bhonte*, *bhavante*.
In the neuter forms, by the rule "obhāvo kvaci" through the division of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*), there is the substitution of *obhāva*:
*bhotā*, *bhavatā*, *bhavantena*; *bhoto*, *bhavato*, *bhavantassa*, and so on.
111. *Bhaddanta* [becomes] *bhaddanta* and *bhante*.

These substitutions—*bhaddanta* and *bhante*—occasionally apply to the entire word *bhadanta* when followed by *ge*, *kvaci*, or the dual endings (*yosu*). Thus: *bho bhaddanta bhante*, *bhadanta*, or *bhadantā*, etc., following the same pattern as the word *purisa*.
112. For the word *santa*, [the final *a* becomes] *so*, *bhe*, or *bo* before the ending *ante*.
The substitution of *sa* for the entire word *santa* occurs when the letter *bha* follows, and the letter *ba* is inserted at the end.
By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), in some compounds where *bha* does not follow, there is also the substitution of *sa*. Examples: *sabbhi*. What is the purpose of [mentioning] *bha*?
[To show it does not apply in cases like] *santehi*; the rest is the same as for the word *gacchanta*.

There is a distinction between *rāja*, *brahma*, *atta*, *sakha*, *sadda*, and so forth; likewise, there is the arising of *syā*. When "rāja si" is established—the governing rule being "from *brahma*, *atta*, *sakha*, *rāja*, etc."—there is also [the substitution of] *syā*.

The form *rājā* arises from *brahma*, *atta*, *sakha*, *rāja*, and so forth, at the beginning [of a compound]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is also derived from words such as *ātumā*. [There is] elision of the vowel and other changes. *Rājā tiṭṭhati* (the king stands). 114. *Yonaṃ āno*: After *brahma*, *atta*, *sakha*, *rāja*, and so forth, the substitution of *āno* occurs for the nominative plural ending (*na*).
*Rājāno tiṭṭhanti* (the kings stand), *bho rāja* (O King), *bho rājā* (O King), *bhavanto rājāno* (your majesties, the kings).
The word “vā” (or) is understood [from the previous rule]. 115. *Amāna* after *brahma*, *atta*, *sakha*, *rāja*, etc.
After words such as *brahma* and so forth, the suffix *āna* optionally replaces the vocative ending *-aṃ*. For example: *rājānaṃ passa* or *rājaṃ*, and *rājāno*.
The phrase “of the word *rāja* with its case ending” is understood [from the previous rule].
116. *Nāmhi raññā vā*.
In the locative case (*nāmhi*), the substitute *raññā* optionally occurs for the entire word *rāja* when it has a case ending. [Examples: *raññā kataṃ* or *rājena kataṃ* (“done by the king”).
117. *Rāja* becomes *rāju* before *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*.

The substitution of *rāju* occurs for the entire word *rāja* when these suffixes—*su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*—follow. The word *ca* has the sense of an alternative; thus, because of the phrase “or before *su* and *naṃ*,” there is a long vowel: *rājūhi* or *rājūbhi*, or *rājehi* or *rāje bhi*.
“Accompanied by case endings” (*savibhattissa*) is the governing heading.
118. *Rājassa* (of the word *rāja*), *rañño*, *rājino*:
for the entire word *rāja*, when accompanied by a case ending, these substitutes *rañño* and *rājino* occur before the case ending *se*. [Examples: *rañño*, *rājino deti*.
The term "*rājassa*" continues [as a governing rule].
119. *Raññaṃ* or *naṃ*.
In the case of the genitive case ending, the substitution of *raññaṃ* optionally occurs for the entire word *rāja*, including its case ending. Thus: *raññaṃ*, *rājūnaṃ*, or *rājānaṃ*.
In the fifth [case ending]—
120. *Amha*, *tumha*, *tunra*, *rājā*, *brahmā*, *atta*, *sakha*, *satthu*, *pitā*, etc., [are treated] as *nā* [in the vocative].

The extension (*atidesa*) of the absence of the *nā*-suffix applies to words such as *amha*, *tumha*, *tunra*, *rājā*, *brahmā*, *atta*, *sakha*, *satthu*, *pitā*, and so forth; for it is to be understood that the word *smā* [the vocative suffix] does not occur after these. Furthermore, this extension is sixfold.
And it has been said:
“Specification, the characteristic mark, that form, that nature, the sutta itself, and likewise extension by analogy—thus it is sixfold.
In this context, among [terms] such as *brahmattasakha*, there is an extension of the grammatical form (*rūpātidesa*) based on the power of the reading. The remainder is equal to the third [chapter].
From the king: *raññā*, *rājūhi*, *rājūbhi*, *raññehi*, *raññebhi*; [belonging] to the king: *rañño*, *rājino* (possessive); [of] the kings:
*raññaṃ*, *rājūnaṃ*, *rājānaṃ*. The term “of the king” (*raññassa*) recurs. 121. In the locative case (*smim*): *raññe*, *rājini*.

In place of the entire word *rāja*, together with its case ending, the substitutes *rañño* and *rājino* occur when the case ending *smiṃ* follows. Thus: *raññe*, *rājini* (established); *rājūsu*, *rājesu*.
There is a specific rule for the word *brahma* regarding the endings *nā*, *sa*, and *smiṃ*: *brahmā*, *brahmāno*.
And in the vocative, the substitute *e* is applied.
122. *Brahmato gassa ca*.

After the word *brahma*, the letter *g* becomes *e*; the inclusion of *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing in the inclusion of *e* from the previous rule. Examples: *bho brahme*, *bhavanto brahmāno*, *brahmānaṃ brahmaṃ*, *brahmāno*.
By way of transposition, the phrase "*brahmassa, anto*" is also understood to follow.
123. *Uttaṃ sanāsu*.

The word *brahma* undergoes the substitution *uttama* before these case-endings (*nādiccesu*). The designation *uttama* is made in some instances for the purpose of showing the absence [of other operations]. Thus: *brahmunā*, *brahmehi*, *brahmebhi*.
When *utta* has been substituted, by the rule "vowels *i* and *u* are *jhal*" (*ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā jhalā*), it receives the technical name *la*.
124. *Jhalato sassa no vā*.

After vowels (*ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa*) that are designated as *jhala*, the substitution of *no* optionally occurs for the nominative singular ending *sa*. Thus, *brahmuno* or *brahmassa*; *brahmānaṃ* or *brahmūnaṃ*. By means of a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), it is stated elsewhere as well that [the form] ends in *-utta*.
In the fifth case (instrumental), there is no extension of the *nā* substitution. Thus: *brahunā*, *brahmehi*, *brahmebhi*; *brahmuno*, *brahmassa*; *brahmānaṃ*, *brahmūnaṃ*.
125. *Brahmato tu smiṃ ni*.

After the word *brahma*, the suffix *ni* occurs for the case ending *smiṃ*. By means of the particle *tu*, it also occurs after *kamma*, *camma*, *muddha*, and so forth, in some instances. Examples: *brahmani*, *brahmesu*.
There is a specific rule regarding the word *atta* only in the third case (*tatiyā*) and those that follow.
*Attā*, *attāno*, *bho atta bho attā*, *bhavanto attāno*, *attānaṃ attaṃ*, *attāno*.
In the phrase "and of one who is inactive" (*akammantassa ca*), by the word *ca* (and), [it includes] *attantassa* or *attaṃ*. [It also includes] *attanā* or *attena*.
126. For *attanto* here is a non-case form (*anattaṃ*).
The word *atta* (self) undergoes the substitution of *anatta* when followed by the suffixes *him*, *sme*, or *pare*. [In the plural,] it becomes *attanehi* and *attanebhi*.
Furthermore, the forms *tato* and *attato* are used. 127. [When the suffix] *sā* follows, it becomes *no*.
From that word *atta*, the case-ending *sassa* becomes *no*. [Thus: *attano*, *attānaṃ*.
128. *Smā nā*:
From that word *atta*, the case-ending *smā* becomes *nā*. [Thus: *attanā*, *apeti*.

Although [the desired form] would have been established by the extension of the previous rule (*atidesa*), the fact that a separate rule (*bhinnayoga*) is made instead of a single continuous rule (*ekayogamakka*) in the subsequent sutta is for the purpose of indicating a different meaning.

By this, the letter *ra* replaces the letter *ta* of *attanta* before the letter *ja* in certain cases: *atraja* or *attaja*. [The forms] *attanehi*, *attanebhi*, *attano*, and *attānaṃ* [are also formed].
The word "from oneself" (*attato*) is understood to carry over.
129. *Tato smiṃ ni*.
After the word *atta*, the suffix *ni* occurs in place of the case ending *smiṃ*. [Examples: *attani*, *attesu*.
The declension of the word *sakha* is as follows: *sakhā*, *sakhāno*.
The term “yonaṃ” is understood [to apply here].
130. *Sakha* and *ayonaṃ*:
after the word *sakha*, the substitution of *yonaṃ* and *āya* occurs for the nominative plural ending (*no*). Thus: *sakhāyo*.

132. *Sakhato gassa vā*. After a word ending in *sakha*, the substitutions for the letter *ga* are *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *e*. By the word *vā* ("or"), the substitution *e* occurs after other words as well in certain instances; for example: *bhaddante ise*. Furthermore, *e* is a contraction of *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *e*;
there is the successive elision (*lopa*) of the preceding and following vowels.
Bho sakha, bho sakhā, bho sakhi, bho sakhī, bho sakhe; bhavanto sakhāno, sakhāyo, sakhino.
The forms "sakhantassa" and "āro ca" also occur. 133.
Or they were heard as such.

The letter *ā* is optionally substituted for the final vowel of a word ending in *sakha*, when followed by *vā*, *sunaṃ*, *aṃ*, or *iccete*. [Examples: *sakhāraṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*, *sakhaṃ*, *sakhāno*, *sakhāyo*, *sakhino*, *sakhinā*.
The phrase “of a word ending in *sakha*” continues to apply. 134. The letter *ā* is optionally substituted before the suffix *him*.
For the word *sakha*, there is optionally the substitution of *ā* when the case-ending *him* follows. [The forms are: *sakhārehi*, *sakhārebhi*; *sakhehi*, *sakhebhi*.
When the substitution of *i* occurs, the rule “after a consonant (*jhal*), the genitive suffix *sassa* optionally becomes *no*” applies, resulting in *sakhino* and *sakhissa*.

[The plural forms are: *sakhārānaṃ*, *sakhīnaṃ*. There is no substitution of *nā* for the suffix *smā*. [The instrumental forms are: *sakhinā*; *sakhārehi*, *sakhārebhi*; *sakhehi*, *sakhebhi*; [the genitive forms are: *sakhino*, *sakhissa*; *sakhārānaṃ*, *sakhīnaṃ*.
The term *sakhato* continues [from the previous rule].
135. *Smime*.
The vowel *e* occurs in place of the locative case ending *smiṃ* after *sakha*. This rule is commenced for the sake of permanence [of the form]. [Examples: *sakhe*, *sakhāresu*, *sakhesu*.

The method for the forms of the word *ātuma* in the first and second [cases] is the same as that for the word *atta*. Thus: *ātumā*, *ātumāno*; *bho ātuma*, *bho ātumā*; *bhavanto ātumāno*; *ātumānaṃ*, *ātumaṃ*; *ātumāno*; *ātumena*, and so forth, which are the same as those for *purisa*.
Now follows the analysis of the word *puma*. *Puma si*: the governing rule "savibhattissā" (with all case-endings) applies.
136. *Pumantassā simhi*.

In the locative case ending *sim*, the substitution of the vowel *ā* occurs for the word *pum* together with its case ending. By the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*), this also applies to the end of words such as *maghavan* and *yuvan*. Thus: *pumā*.
The phrase "*pumantassā*" is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).
137. *Yosvāno*.

For a masculine stem, the substitution of *āno* occurs in place of [the final vowel] when the case endings *yus* and *su* follow. Example: *pumāno*. 138. *Amālapanekavacane*. [The same substitution occurs] before the singular case ending *am*. Example: *pumanam*.

The substitution *aṃ* occurs for the [stem] *pumān* when it is accompanied by a case ending (*savibhatti*) and followed by the singular vocative case. Thus: *he pumaṃ*, *he pumāno*; *pumaṃ*, *pumāno*. The phrase “*ā*, optionally” (*ā, vā*) also continues to apply.
139. And before the locative case suffix *nāmhi*, [the final vowel of *pumān* becomes *u*].

In the case of the word *pumān*, the substitution of *ā* occurs optionally before the nominative singular ending (*nāmhi*). By virtue of the word *ca* (“and”), the substitution of *cu* for the final syllable of *pumakamma-thāman* occurs optionally before the endings *sasmā*. Thus: *pumānā*, *pumunā*, or *pumena*.
The term *āne* is understood [from the previous rule]. 140. And [the substitution occurs] before the dative singular ending (*hivibhattimhi*).

In the case of a masculine stem ending in *m*, the substitution of *ān* occurs before a case ending (*vibhatti*). The mention of "case ending" is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] when a case ending is not present.
Thus: *pumānehi*, *pumānebhi*. By the word "and" (*ca*), the substitution of *ān* optionally occurs for the final syllable of stems such as *yuvan* and *maghavan* in all case endings.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "optionally before the ending *smi*" (*u nāmhi cā*), the vowel *u* is optionally substituted for the final syllable of a masculine stem before the endings *sā*, *smā*, and *ssu*. By the rule "after a consonant (*jhala*), the ending *sā* optionally becomes *no*," it becomes *no*.
From *pum* [comes] *puṃso*, *puṃsaḥ*, *puṃsām*.
The term "smā, nā" continues [from the previous rule]. 141.
And after a *jhal* [consonant].

The substitution *nā* occurs for the nominative singular ending after [stems ending in] *jha*, *la*, *i*, and *cc*. The inclusion of *ca* (and) is for the purpose of occasional exclusion. Nominative: *pumā*, *pumunā*, *pumā*, *pumasmā*, *pumamhā*; *pumānehi*, *pumānebhi*, *pumehi*, *pumebhi*.

Genitive: *pumuno*, *pumassa*; *pumānaṃ*. 142. *Āne smiṃmhi vā*: For a stem ending in *pu*, the substitute *āne* optionally occurs in place of the locative case ending *smiṃ*. Locative: *pumāne*, *pume*, *pumasmiṃ*, *pumamhi*.
143. *Susmimā vā*.
For a word ending in *pum*, there is optionally the substitution of *su* when followed by a vowel (*ā*). Thus: *pumasu* or *pumesu*.
In the case of *yuvan* and others, as in the example "yuva si": [the *si* is elided].

In the rule *“pumantassā simhī”* (the final vowel of *pum* becomes *si* before *m* and *h*), the letter *ā* is included by the mention of the term *anta* (“end”). And in the rule *“hivibhattimhi cā”* (and before the case-ending *hi*), the letter *ā* is substituted for *an* by the word *ca* (“and”).
Thus: *yuvā*, *yuvāno*, *yuvānā*; *yuvā*, *yuvā*, *he yuva*, *he yuvā*, *he yuvāna*, *he yuvānā*; *bhavanto*, *yuvānā*; *yuvānaṃ*, *yuvaṃ*; *yuvāne*, *yuve*.

In the rule *“akammantassa cā”* (and for that which does not end in *kamma*), the letter *ā* is optionally substituted for the final vowel of words such as *yuvan* and *maghavan* before the endings *nā* and *su* by the word *ca* (“and”). Thus: *yuvā*.
yuvānā, yuvānena, yuvānena; yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi;
yuvānassa, yuvassa; yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ; yuvānā, yuvānasmā, yuvānamhā; yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi;
yuvānassa, yuvassa; yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ; yuvāne, yuvānasmiṃ, yuvānamhi, yuve, yuvamhi, yuvasmiṃ.
*Yuvānesu*, *yuvāsu*, *yuvesu*.
Thus, *maghavā*, *maghavāno*, *maghavānā*, and so forth, are the same as the word *yuvan*. [This concludes the section on] words ending in the vowel *a*.
The word *sā*, ending in the vowel *ā* and being masculine, [is declined as follows]:
*sā* (nominative singular), with the elision of *si*: *sā sunakho*. In the plural: —
144. *Agho rassamekavacanayosvapi ca*.

With the exception of the vowel *ā* belonging to the term *ghasa*, a final vowel of a noun (*liṅga*) becomes short when followed by the singular cases and the two [nominative and accusative] plural cases; this is the shortening.

The inclusion of the particle *api* is for the purpose of excluding the locative singular (*simhi*). The rest is to be understood accordingly. Sā tiṭṭhanti: he sā, he sā, saṃ, se, sena, sāhi, sābhi, sassa, sāya, sānaṃ, sā, sasmā, samhā, sāhi, sābhi, sassa, sānaṃ, se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sāsu.
Thus are those whose dhammas are directly perceived, such as Gāṇḍīvadhanvan and others.
This concludes the section ending in the vowel *ā*. Now, the masculine word *aggi* (fire), which ends in the vowel *i*: the derivation of the case endings begins with *aggi si*.
The rule “*anto simhi vā*” (the final vowel becomes *a* optionally before the locative suffix *sim*) applies here. 145. *Aggissini*.
Before the locative case ending *sim*, the suffix *ini* is optionally added after the word *aggi*. By the rule “*sesato lopaṃ gasipī*,” the *s* is elided. Thus: *aggini*, *aggi*.
In the plural, by the technical designation *jhal* according to the rule “*ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā jhalā*,” the phrase “*jhalato vā*” also applies. 146.
There is elision (*lopa*) of *y* and *n* after *gha*.

The elision of the *yu* suffixes following words denoting feminine gender that possess the *ghapa*-designation (i.e., ending in *ā*, *ī*, or *ū*) or the *jhal*-designation (i.e., ending in consonants) is optional. This is a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*). 147.
When the *ni* and *kāra* suffixes have been elided, the vowel becomes long.

All short vowels (*rasassarā*) occurring at the end of a grammatical base (*liṅga*) undergo lengthening when the *ni* and *kāra* suffixes have been elided. Those from which the *ni* and *kāra* suffixes have been elided are called "those whose *ni* and *kāra* have been elided. Example: *aggī*.
The phrase “the self of the five and so forth” follows from this as “self.
148. *Yosvakatarasso jho*: among those others, that which does not perform [an action] becomes *jha*, and it assumes the status of the self (*atta*). [This applies to] the *agga* (superior) ones.
What is the vocative singular? It is *rattiyo*.
The same applies to the vocative as well: *he aggi*, *he aggī*, *he aggayo*.
When the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubba-saralopa*) is reached in the second case singular—
149. *Aṃ* is the substitute for the *niggahīta* [anusvāra] when followed by *jha*, *la*, or *pa*.
When these—namely *jha*, *la*, or *pa*—follow, the *niggahīta* becomes the substitute for the word-final *aṃ* and for the letter *m*.

[Examples: *aggiṃ*; *aggī*, *aggayo*; *agginā*; *aggīhi*, *aggībhi*. Regarding the rule *“sunamhisu ca”* (and in *su*, *naṃ*, *hi*, *su*), because of the inclusion of the word *ca* (and), in some instances there is an absence of the long vowel. [Examples: *aggihi*, *aggibhi*.
“Not after *jhala*,” it is not [the case]. [The forms] *aggino*, *aggissa*, and *aggīnaṃ*.

When the rule “*smā nā*” is in force, by the alternative rule “*jhala-to cā*,” there is *nā*. [The forms] *agginā*, *aggismā*, *aggimhā*; *aggīhi*, *aggībhi*, *aggihi*, *aggibhi*; *aggino*, *aggissa*, *aggīnaṃ*, *agginaṃ*; *aggimhi*, *aggismiṃ*; *aggīsu*, *aggisu*. In the same way, others as well—
Light, hand, fist, handful; belly, bladder, rice, grain;
disease, limit, enlightenment, joint; heap, hair, satisfaction, leopard;
seer, sage, jewel, wealthy, ascetic, mountain, sun, poet.
You are the monkey, the ink, the treasure, the creator, the serpent, and the lord of worms;
you are Hari’s enemy, the darkness, the Kali age, the demon Bali, the ocean, and the householder;
you are the one of vast radiance, the one of excellent intellect, the one free from substrate, and the sovereign lord.
Añjali, sārathi, atithi, samādhi, udadhi, and so forth.
[These end in] the letter *i*. The masculine noun ending in the vowel *ī* is the word *daṇḍī*.
Regarding the rule “*daṇḍī si*”:

here, when shortness (*rassatta*) is reached by the rule “*agho rassamekavacanayosvapi ca*,” although the absence of that [long vowel] would already be established in *si* by the inclusion of the word “also” (*api*), he states it for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).
While the term “short” (*rassa*) is being applied—
150. *Na sismiṃ napuṃsakāni*.

In the nominative case (*sismiṃ*), genders other than the neuter do not undergo shortening; thus, there is an absence of shortening, and the elision of the suffix (*silopa*) occurs. Example: *daṇḍī tiṭṭhati* (the man with a staff stands).
Why say "other than the neuter"? [Example]: *sukhakāri dānaṃ* (a gift that produces happiness).

And here: "That which is free from both the designations of 'clear' and 'unclear,' and which serves as the cause for the cognition of [gender] such as masculine and so forth, is called *liṅga* (grammatical gender)."
In the first case, it is *yolope daṇḍī tiṭṭhanti*.
In the other case, after shortening (*rassatta*) has been applied by [the rule] “*agho rasso*” and so forth—
“*jhato, katarassā*” is also stated as the governing context.
151. *Yonaṃ no*:
For all [words] ending in *y*, when followed by a word beginning with *s* or *l*, the substitution of *no* occurs for the others (*para*). Example: *daṇḍino tiṭṭhanti*.
What is meant by "for which one" (*katarassa*)? [It refers to] *aggyo*.
Without a governing rule (*adhikāra*),
[the answer is determined] by the analysis of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*) as "yes" or "no"; in some cases, even for one who has not performed [an action], [the result follows].
Not as in the case of *sāramati*.
In address, the sound "ge" occurs. 152.
Before *jhal* and *p*, [the preceding vowel] becomes short.
The *jhala* [consonants] become short when followed by a *ge* [vowel]. *Bho daṇḍi*.

Although the shortening is already established by the rule beginning with “*agho rasso*,” this repetition is for the sake of restriction; therefore, it does not occur in cases such as “*bho go*. *Daṇḍī*, *daṇḍino*.

When the shortening has been made in the second case, the term “*a*” is understood from the previous context. From the rule “*ghapato smiṃ yaṃ vā*,” the term “*vā*” is understood here by means of the “frog-leap” (*maṇḍūkagati*) method.
153. *Naṃ* occurs after *jhata*.
After *jhata*, *naṃ* optionally occurs for another case-ending (*aṃ*). [Examples: *daṇḍinaṃ*, *daṇḍiṃ*; *daṇḍī*, *daṇḍino*; *daṇḍinā*, *daṇḍīhi*, *daṇḍībhi*; *daṇḍino*, *daṇḍissa*; *daṇḍīnaṃ*.
By the rule "also after *jhalata*," *nā* occurs. [Examples: *daṇḍinā*, *daṇḍismā*, *daṇḍimhā*; *daṇḍīhi*, *daṇḍībhi*; *daṇḍino*, *daṇḍissa*; *daṇḍīnaṃ*.
“Of what [is it]? (*jhato katarassā*) continues [to apply], and as before, “or” (*vā*) also applies.
154. *Smiṃ* is substituted for *ni*.
For the word *jhata*, when followed by the suffix *smin*, the substitution of *ni* occurs optionally. Thus: *daṇḍini*, *daṇḍismiṃ*, *daṇḍimhi*; [and] *daṇḍīsu*.
Likewise, there are others as well:
the righteous one, the communal one, the wise one, the elephant, the wheel-turner, the bird, the tusked one, the ruler of the realm;
the one with the parasol, the garlanded one, the armored one, the yogi, the sharer, the enjoyer, the desirous one, and the master.
Dhaji, Ganī, Sasī, Kuṭṭhī, Jaṭī, Yānī, Sukhī, Sikhī;
Dantī, Mantī, Karī, Cāgī, Kusālī, Musalī, Balī;
Pāpakārī, Sattughātī, Mālyakārī, and Dīghajīvī.
“Dhammacārī sīghayāyī, sīhanādī bhūmisāyī”—
these and others are names ending in the vowel *ī*. However,
there is a variation in the locative case of the word *gāmaṇī*.
Gāmaṇī, gāmaṇī, gāmaṇino; bho gāmaṇi, bhonto gāmaṇī, bhonto gāmaṇino; gāmaṇinaṃ, gāmaṇiṃ; gāmaṇinā, gāmaṇinā; gāmaṇismiṃ, gāmaṇismiṃ; gāmaṇino, gāmaṇino. The remainder is the same as *daṇḍī*;
the only difference is the absence of the *niādesa* (substitution). Thus it is for *senānī*, *sudhī*, and so forth. This concludes the section on words ending in the vowel *ī*.
The word *bhikkhu* is masculine and ends in the vowel *u*.
Likewise, after the word *bhikkhu*, the suffix *si* [is applied], and there is elision of the *s*. Thus: *so bhikkhu* (that monk).

In the plural, by the rule “there is elision of *ya* and *na* after a word ending in *gha*,” there is elision of *ya*; then, by the rule “in the case of *yosu*, lengthening occurs,” etc., the vowel is lengthened. Thus: *te bhikkhū* (those monks).
In the absence of elision (*lopābhāve*), the phrase “or *yo* and *na*” also applies.

155. *La* becomes *vo*. For those words following a term marked with the *la*-designation, the substitution of *vo* for *yo* occurs optionally. By the inclusion of the word “cause” (*kāra*), the substitution of *no* for *yo* also takes place.
The inclusion of the word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of exclusion in certain instances. Alternatively, the inclusion of *ca* is for the purpose of following the non-inclusion of *na*;
by this, the substitution of *no* does not occur after words such as *jantu*, *sabbaññū*, and so forth. The word *vā* has the sense of a fixed alternative (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*).
By this [rule]: After *bhikkhu* and so forth, [the substitution of] *vo* is constant; after *hetu* and so forth, [the substitution of] *yo* and *no* [is constant].
In the *Vibhāsā*, there is neither *vo* nor *no*; it would be from the point of origin (*amuppabhutito*).
And the phrase “self, not of two-fold nature” (*attaṃ, akatarasso*) continues [to apply].
156. In the case of *vevu*s, there is *lo*.
"Among these others, one who is not distressed in mind attains self-mastery. O monks, "bho bhikkhu," "bhavanto bhikkhū.
In the absence of elision (lopābhāve): 157. *Akatarassā* [is derived from] *akata-rasa*, where *ve* is the substitute for the vocative (*yvālapanassa vevo*).

In the case of *akatarassa* (the non-agential form), when another person is addressed, the following substitutions (*vo-ādesā*) occur for *yo*: *ve* and *vo*. *Attaṃ* (the reflexive pronoun): *bhavanto bhikkhave bhikkhavo*. By the rule *“aṃ mo niggahītaṃ jhalapehi”* (the nasal *aṃ* becomes a *niggahīta* before *jh*, *l*, or *ap*), the *niggahīta* is applied.
Thus: *bhikkhuṃ*, *bhikkhū*, *bhikkhavo*; *bhikkhunā*, *bhikkhūhi*, *bhikkhūbhi*, *bhikkhuhi*, *bhikkhubhi*;
*bhikkhuno*, *bhikkhussa*; *bhikkhūnaṃ*, *bhikkhunaṃ*; *bhikkhunā*, *bhikkhusmā*, *bhikkhumhā*; *bhikkhūhi*.
Bhikkhūhi, bhikkhuhi, bhikkhubhi; bhikkhuno, bhikkhussa; bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhunaṃ; bhikkhumhi, bhikkhusmiṃ;
bhikkhūsu, bhikkhusu. In the same way:
setu, ketu, rāhu, bhānu, paṅgu, ucchu, veḷu, maccu, sindhu, bandhu, neru, meru, sattu, kāru, hetu, jantu, ruru, paṭu, and so forth.
There is a distinction between the words *hetu* and *jantu* in their nominative singular and dual forms.
*Hetu*: *hetu*, *hetū*, *hetavo*, *hetuyo*; *bho hetu*, *bhonto hetū*, *hetave*, *hetavo*; *hetuṃ*, *hetū*, *hetavo*, *hetuyo*. The remainder is the same as for *bhikkhu*.

*Jantu*: *jantu*, *jantū*, *jantavo*. By the inclusion of the suffix *-ka*, the *ya*-suffixes become *na*. [Thus: *jantuno*, *jantuyo*; *bho jantu*, *jantū*, *jantave*, *jantavo*; *jantuṃ*, *jantū*, *jantavo*, *jantuno*, *jantuyo*, and so forth.
The analysis of the word *satthu*: regarding the phrase "of the Teacher" (*satthu si*) here, the term "internal" (*anto*) is supplied from the previous context. 158.
In the case of *satthupitā* and so forth, when the suffix *si* follows, there is elision of the final vowel.

The suffix *āttam* is applied after words such as *satthu*, *pitu*, *mātu*, *bhātu*, *dhītu*, and *kattu*, with the addition of *icc-eva-m-ādīnam*; furthermore, there is elision (*silopa*) of the final vowel. Thus: *satthā*.
The governing rule "after *satthu*, *pitā*, and so forth" continues to apply. 159. The suffix *ārattaṃ* is applied after other [words].

After the word *sivacanato* (from the neuter case), [the suffix] *ār* occurs in place of other case-endings (*vacana*). By the designation *ārattaniddesa*, it shows that in some instances there is no fixed rule.
The mention of *āra* continues [into the following]. 160. *Tato yo namo tu*.
From that point on, for all [words ending in] *yona*, there is the substitution of *okāra*.

By the inclusion of *tu*, the *okāra* of *yona* is also applied after other [words] such as *catu*, *ubha*, *nadī*, and *gava*, with the elision of the vowel (*saralopa*) and so forth. Thus: *satthāro*.

In the vocative, by the rule “*ā* replaces *akāra*, *pitā*, and those ending in *ā*,” there is the substitution of *ā*. Then, depending on the rule “*rassa* in *ge*,” there is optionally (*vā*) the shortening (*rassatta*), and the elision of *va* (*valopa*). Thus: *bho sattha*, *bho satthā*, *bhavanto satthāro*, *satthāraṃ*, *satthāre*, *satthāro*.
The word “tato” (from that) is understood to carry over. 161. *Nā*:

After the substitution of *ār* [for *ā*], there is the substitution of *ā* for the word ending in *nā*. This is established by the rule stating "after *satthārā*, *satthunā*, and *āratta*. [Examples: *satthārehi*, *satthārebhi*.
“*Vā naṃmhī*” (or not in the locative case): the word “*vā*” (or) is understood from here [and applies to what follows]. 162. *U sasmiṃ salopa ca*:

In the locative case (*sasmiṃ*), the final vowel of words such as *satthu*, *pitu*, and so forth, optionally becomes *ut*, and there is also the elision of the *s*. This is an exception to the rule regarding the substitution of *ā*. In other instances, when expressing the state of being (*bhāva*), the form is *ārā*. Thus: *satthussa* and *satthuno*.
The term "āratta" is understood [to follow]. 163.
*Vā* is used before the suffix *naṃ*.
Before the case-ending *naṃ*, the word following "satthu," "pitu," and so forth, optionally becomes "āratta. For example: *satthārānaṃ*.
In the absence of *ārā*, the phrase "or not" (*vā naṃmhī*) applies.
164. *Satthu-attañ-ca*.

For the final syllable of the word *satthu* and for the final syllable of words such as *pitā*, the substitution *atta* optionally occurs before the case-ending *naṃ*. The repetition of the term *satthu* is for the purpose of making the rule compulsory for *satthuno*. [Examples: *satthānaṃ*.

In the phrase “*amhatumhanturājabrahmattasakhasatthupitādīhi smā nāvā*,” the substitution of *nā* for the suffix *smā* occurs. [The forms are: *satthārā*, *satthārehi*, *satthārebhi*; *satthu*, *satthuno*, *satthussa*; *satthārānaṃ*, *satthānaṃ*.
The word “*āratō*” (from) follows. 165. From that [stem], the suffix *smiṃ* [is applied].
From that point on, there is the substitution of *i* for the suffix *smin*. By the subsequent mention of "from that" (*tato*), the *i*-sound of the suffix *smin* occurs even after other [vowels].
For example: *bhuvi*, *divi*. 166. *Āro rassamikāre*:
The substitute *ā* becomes short when followed by the vowel *i*; as in *satthari*, *satthāresu*.
Thus: *kattā*, *kattāro*; *bho katta*, *bho kattā*; *bhavanto kattāro*; *kattāraṃ*, *kattāre*, *kattāro*; *kattārā*, *kattārehi*, *kattārebhi*.
It is stated [in the rules] that "there is elision of *s* when *u* follows," and there is also elision of *s*.
[The forms are: *kattu*, *kattuno*, *kattussa*; *kattārānaṃ*, *kattānaṃ*, *kattūnaṃ*, *kattunaṃ*; *kattārā*, *kattārehi*, *kattārebhi*; *kattu*.

Of *kattuno*, *kattussa*, *kattārānaṃ*, *kattānaṃ*, *kattūnaṃ*, *kattunaṃ*; in the locative singular, *kattari*; in the locative plural, *kattāresu*; and in the absence of the suffix *āra*, *kattūsu* or *kattusu*.
Likewise:
*bhattu*, *vattu*, *netu*, *sotu*, *ñātu*, *jetu*, *chettu*, *bhettu*, *dātu*, *dhātu*, *nattu*, *boddhu*, *viññāpetu*, and so forth.
“*U* and *sa* [are substituted], and there is elision of *s* in *sasmin*”:
this continues [to apply]. 167. *Sakam*, *mandhātu*, and so forth:

for *sakam*, *mandhātu*, and the like, the final vowel becomes *u* before *sasmin*, and there is elision of *s*; this is because of the constant re-statement [of the rule]. The power of King Mandhātu was like that of *sakam*; the rest is the same. Thus [it applies] to Mahāmandhātu and others as well.
The analysis of the word *pitu*: in the locative case (*simhi*), there is *ātta* [substitution], and the elision of the suffix (*silopa*), resulting in *pitā*.
In the instrumental case (*yomhi*), the rules "āro" and "rassa" also apply. 168. For *pitu* and other such words, [the substitution occurs] in the locative case (*asimhi*).
The substitution of *ār* for *pit* and other [terms] occurs when followed by a short vowel ending in the locative case (*asmiṃ*).

Although there is no substitution of *ār* when the locative suffix *si* follows, the specific mention of "in the locative" (*asmiṃ*) is for the purpose of indicating a different meaning; by that, the vowel *i* is also substituted for *pit* and others when followed by *to* and so on.
For example: *pitito*, *mātito*, *bhātito*, *dhītito*, *pitipakkho*, *mātipakkho*.
*Pitaro*: the rest is the same as for the agent (*kattusama*). Bho pita, bho pitā; bhavanto pitaro; pitaraṃ, pitare, pitaro;
pitarā, pitunā; pitarehi, pitarebhi. By the description of the base ending in *-u*, when there is no substitution of *ār*, [the forms are] pitūhi, pitūbhi, pituhi, pitubhi;
pitu, pituno, pitussa; pitarānaṃ, pitānaṃ, pitūnaṃ; or, in the absence of the long vowel, pitunaṃ; [and] pitarā.
pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbhi, pituhi, pitubhi; pitu, pituno, pitussa;
pitarānaṃ, pitānaṃ, pitūnaṃ, pitunaṃ; pitari; pitaresu, pitūsu, pitusu.
In the same way: bhātā, bhātaro, and so forth.
Ending in *u*. The word *abhibhū*, ending in *ū*, is masculine. The formation of the case endings (*syādi*) occurs in the same manner, followed by the elision of the suffix (*silopa*).
Thus: *so abhibhū* (he is the conqueror); when the *y* is elided, it becomes *te abhibhū* (those are the conquerors).

By the rule beginning with “*agho rassan*,” there is shortening (*rassatta*), which is a vowel modification (*vokāra*). From which short vowel is the self-form (*attābhāva*) derived? It is from the long vowel of *abhibhū*. Thus: *abhibhū*, *bho abhibhū*, *bhavanto abhibhū*, *abhibhūvo*.

From which short vowel does the substitution (*veādesa*) not occur? The remainder is the same as for the word *bhikkhu*; the only difference is the shortening. For example: *abhibhum*, *abhibhū*, *abhibhūvo*; *abhibhunā*, *abhibhūhi*, *abhibhūbhi*; *abhibhuno*, *abhibhussa*, *abhibhūnam*, and so forth.

Likewise, *sayambhū*, *vessabhū*, *parābhibhū*, *sahabhū*, and so forth. The distinction in the word *sahabhū* lies solely in the substitution of *no* for the *yo* [ending]. Thus: *sahabhū*, *sahabhū*, *sahabhuvo*, *sahabhuno*, and so on. Similarly, there is a distinction only in the *yo* ending of the word *sabbaññū*.
When that *yo* is present: *so sabbaññū*, *te sabbaññū*; when there is an absence of *yo-lopa*, there is shortening (*rassatta*).

Regarding the rule "after *la*, the *vo*-kāra [is substituted]," the mention of the letter *ka* therein indicates that *no* is the substitute for *yo*. This is because the governing term *vā* (or) is understood as a restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*).
And there is no *vokāra* [substitution]. For example: *sabbaññuno*, *bho sabbaññu*, *bhonto sabbaññū*, *sabbaññuno*, *sabbaññuṃ*, *sabbaññū sabbaññuno*, and so forth.
Likewise: *maggaññū*, *dhammaññū*, *atthaññū*, *kālaññū*, *rattaññū*, *mattaññū*, *kataññū*, *tathaññū*, *viññū*, *vidū*, *vedagū*, *pāragū*, and so on. This concludes the section ending in *ū*.
The word ending in *e* is rarely used.
The word *go*, ending in *o*, is masculine. From it, the addition of the case endings (*syādi*) occurs;
with the elision of the final vowel (*silopa*), we have *go gacchati*.
“*Gāva se*” means that from here the governing rule is “*go*,” and the term “*āv*” also continues [from the previous rule].
169. *Yosu ca*:

In the case of the locative dual (*yosu*), the vowel *o* of this word “*go*” is replaced by *āv*. By the word “*ca*,” [the substitution also occurs] in the cases of the ablative singular (*smā*) and the locative singular (*smim*). In the rule “*tato yonamo tū*,” the inclusion of the letter *t* indicates that in the case of *yo*, the *o* is replaced by *āv*, with the elision of the preceding vowel (*saralopa*), and so forth. *Gāvo tiṭṭhanti* (The cows stand).
170. *Avaṃhi ca*.

In place of the vowel *o* of the word *go*, the substitutes *āva* and *ava* occur when the case ending *aṃ* follows. Furthermore, the substitute *ava* occurs for that [vowel *o*] which is preceded by *se* (the nominative plural marker) before the endings *nā*, *smā*, and *smiṃ*. Examples: *gavo gacchanti* (the cows go); *he go*, *he gāvo*, *he gavo* (O cow! O cows!).
In the second [section], the term "*aṃhi*" is understood as being in force.
171. *Āvassu vā*.

For the word *gāva* and others ending in *ā*, there is optionally the substitution of *ū* for the final vowel when the case-ending *am* follows. Of *āva*—that is, of that word ending in *āva*—there is the substitution of *ū*. The nasalization (*niggahīta*) occurs by the rule beginning with "ammo. Thus: *gāvuṃ*, *gāvaṃ*, *gavaṃ*; *gāvo*, *gavo*.
The phrase "*goṇa, vā*" (or "cow") continues [as a governing rule].
172. *Suhināsu ca*.

After the words *su*, *hi*, and *nā*, there is optionally the substitution of *goṇa* for the entire word *go*. By the word *ca* ("and"), this also applies to the remaining [cases]. *Goṇo*, *goṇā*; *he goṇa*, *he goṇā*; *goṇaṃ*, *goṇe*; *goṇena*, *goṇehi*, *goṇebhi*; *goṇassa*. 173. *Goṇa naṃmhi vā*.
Optionally, the substitution of *goṇa* occurs before the suffix *naṃ*.

The substitution of *goṇa* optionally occurs for every instance of the word *go* before the case-ending *nam*. [Thus: *goṇānaṃ*, *goṇā*, *goṇasmā*, *goṇamhā*, *goṇehi*, *goṇebhi*, *goṇassa*, *goṇānaṃ*, *goṇe*, *goṇasmiṃ*, *goṇamhi*, *goṇesu*.
In the absence of the substitution of *goṇa*: *gāvena*, *gavena*, *gohi*, *gobhi*.
174. *Gāva se*.

“Go āva se”: this consists of three words. In the case of the word *go*, when the suffix *se* follows, the vowel *o* of the word *go* undergoes substitution by *ā*. Thus, *gāvassa* (genitive singular) from *gavassa*.
In the case of the suffix *naṃ*, the sequence “*go, āva*” also applies. 175.
Thereafter, in the case of the suffix *nām*, when there is elision (*lutta*) in a compound (*samāsa*), [the same rule applies].

Then, when the word *go* is followed by another word beginning with *naṃ*, there is the substitution of *aṃ* for the suffix *naṃ* and the substitution of *ava* for the vowel *o* of the word *go*, provided that *pati* follows or the compound is not elided (*alutta*). By the word *ca* (and), these substitutions of *aṃ* and *ava* also occur even when it is not a compound. Thus: *gavaṃpatissa therassa* (of the Elder Gavampati), *gavaṃ*.

In the rule *“Suhināsu cā”* (and in *su*, *hinā*, and *su*), by the word *ca* (and), there is the substitution of *gu* for *go* when *naṃ* follows. In the sutta *“No ca dvādito naṃhī”* (and not after *du* or *ādi*, there is the augment *n* in *naṃ*), by the word *ca* (and), there is also the augment *n*. Thus: *gunnaṃ* or *gonaṃ*.

From the cow: *gāvā*, *gāvamhā*, *gāvasmā*; by the cow: *gavā*, *gavamhā*, *gavasmā*; with the cows: *go-hi*, *go-bhi*; of the cow: *gāvassa*, *gavassa*; of the cows: *gavaṃ* (of cattle), *gunaṃ*, *gonaṃ*; in the cow: *gāve*, *gāvamhi*, *gāvasmiṃ*, *gave*, *gavamhi*, *gavasmiṃ*; in the cows: *gāvesu*, *gavesu*, *gosu*. This concludes the section ending in the vowel *o*.
The virtuous man, the king, the one with fire, the staff-bearer, and the monk.
*Satthā*, *abhibhū*, and *sabbaññū*—the word *goti* is included in the masculine gender. The masculine gender is completed. [The declension of the pronoun *ta-* (that):

Nominative: *asmā*, *nasmā*, *tasmā*; *namhā*, *tamhā*. Instrumental: *nehi*, *nebhi*; *tehi*, *tebhi*. Dative: *assa*, *nassa*, *tassa*. Genitive: *nesaṃ*, *tesaṃ*; *nesānaṃ*, *tesānaṃ*. Locative: *asmiṃ*, *nasmiṃ*, *tasmiṃ*; *namhi*, *tamhi*. Plural Locative: *nesu*, *tesu*.

In the case of *itthi* (feminine), the forms *tā* and *si* arise here through the substitution (*sādesa*) and the elision of the suffix (*silopa*). *Sā* is the nominative singular (*kaññā*, "the girl"). The forms *nā*, *tā*, *nāyo*, *tāyo*; *naṃ*, *taṃ*; *nā*, *tā*, *nāyo*, *tāyo*; *nāya*, *tāya*; *nāhi*, *tāhi*, *nābhi*, *tābhi* [are derived].

Regarding the rule *“etimāsamī”* (Pāṇini 7.3.103), the mention of *eti* from that source and the mention of *ta* from the rule *“tassā vā”* (Pāṇini 7.3.106) apply by way of the fifth case ending (*pañcamyantavasena*), and the word *“vā”* (or) is also included.
215. From that [base], *sassa* becomes *ssāya*.
Then, for these [feminine stems], there is optionally the substitution of *ssā* for the genitive case-ending *sā* of another word.
The phrase “and in the singular of the locative and nominative, *i*” also continues to apply. 216. *Tassā vā*. (There is optionally the substitution of *tassā* for *sā*.)

Furthermore, for this [pronoun] *ta* when used in the feminine, the vowel *i* optionally replaces the final syllable in the singular case-substitute endings *sa*, *m*, and *ā*. Thus: *tissāya* (her), *tassāya* (her), *assāya* (her), *nassāya* (her); *assā* (her), *nassā* (her), *tissā* (her), *tassā* (her), *nāya* (her), *tāya* (her); *nāsaṃ* (them), *tāsaṃ* (them).

"Those who say 'He is ours' and 'He is not ours,' those who say 'He is our brother' and 'He is not our brother,'" and so forth.
And through renunciation, those [afflictions] do not exist.
As it is said: "I do not grieve, nor do I weep, O young man, having heard from you."
"And for you too, O Great King, and for me, O Increaser of the Realm—thus have we both wandered and transmigrated through this long stretch of time.
What is meant by "from a footing"? "Your relative, my relative."
“*Te* and *me*” are subject to this rule.
248. Not before *am*.

The substitutes *te* and *me* do not occur for all forms of the words *tumha* and *amha*, including their case-endings, when they follow a word [ending in a consonant] and the case-ending *am* follows. One might see you for a hundred years in good health. He spoke to me.
The phrase “in the case of the word *teme* (you)” is understood [from the previous rule]. 249. *Vā tatiye ca*:
After a word ending in any case-ending, the substitutes *te* and *me* optionally occur in their respective order for all forms of the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*.

When followed by a third-person singular ending. *Kataṃ te pāpaṃ* (evil was done by you), *kataṃ tayā pāpaṃ* (evil was done by you [feminine]), *kataṃ me puññaṃ* (merit was done by me), *kataṃ mayā puññaṃ* (merit was done by me).
The phrase “vā, tatiye” (or, in the third person) also continues to apply. 250. In plural endings, [the forms] *vo* and *no* [are used].

After a word ending in the plural case, the substitutes *vo* and *no* optionally occur in place of all forms of the pronouns *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*, respectively, when followed by the third-person plural suffix. For example: *kataṃ vo kammaṃ* (the work was done by you), *kataṃ no kammaṃ* (the work was done by us).

By the rule for the plural designation, in certain instances where the first-person singular suffix *yaṃ* occurs, *vo* and *no* are also used: *gāmaṃ vo gaccheyyātha* (you might go to the village), *gāmaṃ no gaccheyyāma* (we might go to the village).

Likewise, for the group of eighteen words beginning with *pañca* (five), and for the word *kati* (how many), the form remains the same across all three genders because they are devoid of gender (*aliṅga*). Precisely because they lack gender, feminine suffixes do not occur after *pañca* and the others.
Regarding the phrase “pañca yo” here:

from the rule “yosu dvinnaṃ dve cā,” the term “yosu” continues [into this context], as does the phrase “itthipumanapuṃsakasaṅkhyam. (251) In the case of the words beginning with *pañca*, the letter *a* [is substituted].

In the case of the sixth [case-ending], when the numbers five and so forth up to eighteen—which denote feminine, masculine, or neuter—are followed by the dual suffixes *yu* and *su*, the final vowel of the stem, together with its case-suffix, becomes *a*. This is an exception to the substitution of *ā* and *e*. Examples:
*pañcakkhandhā*, *pañca gatiyo*, *pañca indriyāni*. The same applies in the second case.
The phrase “su naṃ hisu” is understood [to apply here]. 252.

The final syllable of numbers beginning with five becomes *at* when followed by *su*, *naṃ*, *hi*, or *iccete*. This means that the final syllable of the eighteen numbers beginning with five takes the form *at* when these suffixes follow.
This is the declension for *dīgha*. [The forms are: *pañcahi pañcabhi*, *pañcannaṃ*, *pañcahi pañcabhi*, *pañcannaṃ*, *pañcasu*.
The same applies to the words *cha*, *satta*, *aṭṭha*, *nava*, and *dasa*.
When the sense is "one and ten," a *dvanda* compound is formed as *ekañca dasa ca*; or, when the sense is "ten plus one," a *tappurisa* compound is formed.
The term "in enumeration" (*saṅkhyāne*) is understood [from the previous rule]. 253. *Dve-eka-aṭṭha*:

the vowel *ā* optionally occurs at the end of these words—*dve*, *eka*, and *aṭṭha*—when followed by a subsequent word in an enumeration. This is an optional rule with fixed application (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*). Examples: *ekādasa* (eleven), *dvādasa* (twelve), *aṭṭhārasa* (eighteen).
For what purpose is the term *saṅkhyāne* (in counting) used? [Examples: *ekadanto*, *dvidanto*, *aṭṭhathambho*. The word *vā* (or) is understood [from the previous rule].
254. In counting, *ra* replaces *da* after *eka* and so forth.
In enumeration, the letter *ra* optionally replaces the initial *da* of the word *dasā* (ten) following a numeral ending in *eka*. The rest is the same.
Thus: *ekārasa*, *ekādasa*. Regarding *dvidasa*—meaning both two and ten, or ten plus two—the term "optionally" (*vā*) applies here as well.

255. *Vīsati-dasesu bā dvissa tu*: Before the words *vīsati* and *dasa*, the word *dvi* optionally becomes *bā*. By the inclusion of the word *tu*, this also applies before *tiṃsa*. There is also the substitution of *ra* and the elision (*ātta*) of the vowel. Thus: *bārasa* (twelve), *dvādasa* (twelve).

*Tayo ca dasa ca* (three and ten) or "ten increased by three" is *terasa* (thirteen). Here, by the rule beginning with *tesu vuddhī*, the substitute *te* replaces *ti* in the word *ti* before numbers up to ninety.
Regarding the term *cuddasa* (fourteen): it means "four and ten" or "ten with four added.

Here, the rule "in counting, [the elision] of *dasa*" applies. 256. When the prefix *catu-* is present, its elision occurs before the beginning of the subsequent word, and the initial consonant (*ca*) of that subsequent word may optionally become *cu*.

In the context of numerals, when the word *catu* stands at the beginning of a compound followed by the suffixes *-icca* or *-ittha*, the syllable *tu* is elided. Optionally, when the word *catu* stands as a prefix to a subsequent word, the letter *c* may undergo the substitutions *cu* or *co*. Thus: *cuddasa*, *coddasa*, *catuddasa*.

By the inclusion of the particle *api*, even when there is no suffix, the letter *c* at the beginning of a numeral may be elided; optionally, it becomes *cu* or *co*. For example: *tālīsaṃ*, *cuttālīsaṃ*, *cottālīsaṃ*, *cattālīsaṃ*.

*Pañca ca dasa ca*, or *pañcahi vā adhikā dasa*, in these senses, there is the term *pañcadasa*. By the rule beginning with “*tesu vuddhī*,” the word *pañca* undergoes the substitution of *panna* or *paṇṇa* in certain instances before the words *dasa* and *vīsati*.
Thus: *pannarasa*, *paṇṇarasa*. Regarding *cha ca dasa ca*, or *chahi vā adhikā dasa*, in these senses there is the term *chadasa*;
here the word “*chassā*” is understood to carry over.
257. *Dasa* becomes *so* permanently when followed by *niccaṃ*. When the numeral word *cha* is followed by *niccaṃ*, it becomes *so* when *dasa* follows.
The phrase "of numerals, optionally" also continues to apply.
258. *La-daranaṃ*. In the numerals containing the letters *da* and *ra*, there is optionally a substitution of *la* for them. There is no distinction between *la* and *ḷa*.

This word "optionally" (*vā*) has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*); therefore, in the case of "sixteen" (*soḷasa*), it is constant, while in "thirteen" (*teḷasa*, *terasa*), "forty" (*cattālīsaṃ*, *cattārīsaṃ*), and so on, it is optional; however, it does not occur in words such as "ten" (*dasa*) or "fifteen" (*pannarasa*).
Seven and ten, or ten with seven added, mean seventeen (*sattarasa*, *sattadasa*).
Eight and ten, or ten with eight added, mean eighteen (*aṭṭhadasa*);
here, when *aṭṭha* is substituted [for *aṭṭha*], the rule "or, for *da*, *ra*, in enumeration" also applies.
259. And from *aṭṭha*.
In the enumeration of numbers, the letter *d* of the word *dasan* optionally becomes *r* after *aṭṭha*. Examples: *aṭṭhārasa*, *aṭṭhādasa*. Why "after *aṭṭha*" (*aṭṭhādito*)?
[To exclude cases such as] *catuddasa*.
The word *kati* ends only in the plural.

In this context, as in "kati yo," there is always the elision of *yo* and so forth, along with the shortening of the vowel: *kati tiṭṭhanti*, *kati passasi*, *katibi*, *katibhi*, *katinaṃ*, *katihi*, *katibhi*, *katinaṃ*, *katisu*.
The section on nouns without gender is completed.
The Rules for the Formation of Case Endings (Vibhattippaccayavidhāna).
Now, those [suffixes] ending in case endings (vibhatti) are discussed.
Since they possess no gender and are indeclinables (nipāta), their form is identical across the three genders and the two numbers.
Regarding the meanings "from a man" (*purisasmā*) or "by means of men" (*purisehi*):
260. In certain instances, *to* occurs in the sense of the ablative case.
In some cases, the suffix *to* occurs in the sense of the ablative after a pure noun stem (*sabbasmā*) as well as after a nominal stem that includes gender markers (*sabbanāmato*).
261. *Tvādayo* (the suffixes beginning with *tvā*) are designated as case-endings (*vibhatti*).

Those suffixes beginning with *to* and ending with *dāni*, which are [added after nouns], are called *tvādi*-suffixes; these suffixes are designated as case-endings. By this, it is established that words ending in those suffixes also possess the status of being "words ending in a case-ending" (*vibhatyanta-pada*). For example:
*purisato* (from a man), and likewise *rājato* (from a king), *corato* (from a thief), *aggito* (from fire), *gahapatito* (from a householder), *hatthito* (from an elephant), *hetuto* (from a cause).

From the perspective of *sabbaññu*, *kaññā*, *yutta*, *itthi*, and *bhikkhunī*: here, by the rule “*kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ dīgharassāpaccayesu cā*” (in certain instances, for words beginning with *ka*, *ma*, or *ja*, and for those ending in long vowels, there is shortening before the suffix *to*), there is shortening of the vowel.

Thus: *yāguto*, *jambuto*, *cittato*, *āyuto*, and so forth. From the pronoun *sabba*: *sabbasmā* or, in the sense of “by all,” *sabbato*. Likewise: *yato*, *tato*, *katarato*, *katamato*, *itarato*, *aññato*, *ekato*, *ubhayato*, *pubbato*, *parato*, *aparato*, *dakkhiṇato*, *uttarato*, *amuto*.
The form *kissa* and *ku* are used [in place of *kassa*].
262. Also before *trato*, *thesu*, and *ca*.
When followed by *ico*, *iccetassa*, *ku*, *hoti*, *trato*, *tha*, *iccete*, *su*, and *ca*, the word *kim* becomes *ku*. For example: *kasmā* or *kehi*; or *kuto*.
