The term “tothesu” is being discussed. 263.
The vowel *a* optionally replaces the entire word *eta*.
In the presence of these [suffixes] beginning with *to* and *tha*, the vowel *a* optionally takes the place of the entire word *eta*. Thus, from *etasmā* or *etehi*, we have *ato*.
The phrase “of the whole of this” (*sabbassetassa*) recurs [from the previous rule].
264. And in the case of *etto* and *thesu*:
the vowel *e* optionally replaces the final syllable of the word *eta* before these two words, *etto* and *thesu*. There is doubling of the consonant: *etto*.
“Of all” (sabbassa) is understood [to apply here].
265. In the case of *imassa*, *thaṃ*, *dāni*, *hata*, and *idha*:
the vowel *i* replaces the entire word *ima-* when followed by *thaṃ*, *dāni*, *hata*, or *idha*. Thus, *imasmiṃ* becomes *ito*.
“In some cases, *to*”: by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), *to* following *ādi* and other words occurs in the sense of the locative case;
and in the sense of the instrumental case following *anicca* and others. For example: in the sense of “in the beginning,” *āditobhi*;
likewise, *majjhatō*, *ekatō*, *puratō*, *pacchatō*, *passatō*, *piṭṭhitō*, *pādatō*, *sīsatō*, *aggatō*, *mūlatō*, *paratō*, and so forth.

In the third sense, *aniccenā* means "as impermanent"; one comprehends [it] as impermanent (*aniccato*). Likewise for "as suffering" (*dukkhato*), "as a disease" (*rogato*), "as a boil" (*gaṇḍato*), and so forth.
The phrase "in the sense, in some cases" (*atthe, kvaci*) also continues [to apply].
266. In this context, [the suffix *-tā*] occurs after all nouns in the seventh case (*sattamiyā*).
The suffixes *tra* and *tha* come after all nominal stems (*sabbanāma*) optionally in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*).
Thus: *sabbasmiṃ* and *sabbesu* become *sabbatra* and *sabbattha*. Likewise:

*yatra* and *yattha*, *tatra* and *tattha*, *itaratra* and *itarattha*, *aññatra* and *aññattha*, *ubhayatra* and *ubhayattha*, *paratra* and *parattha*, *kutra* and *kuttha*; [and] according to the rule "also after [stems ending in] *-tra* and *-tha*."
The *kutta* [is as follows]: In the sutta “Kissa ka ve ca,” the substitution of *kā* occurs by means of the word *ca*. [Examples: *kattha*, *amutra*, *amuttha*.
The phrase “the vowel *a* of *sabba* and *etassa*” continues [to apply]. 267.
[The suffix] *tre* is always [substituted].

The vowel *a* always replaces the entire word *eta*, when followed by *tre*. For example: *atra*. [In this case], because of the rule *“sabbassetassākāro vā”* (the vowel *a* optionally replaces the whole of *eta*), we have *atta*; and because of the rule *“e tothesu ca”* (the vowel *e* replaces *eta* before *to* and *thesu*), we have *attha* and *ettha*.
Furthermore, there is the governing rule *“kvaci, atthe, sattamiyā”* (sometimes, in the sense of ‘in’, in the locative case); thus, in the sense of “from all,” we have: 268. *sabbato dhi*.
The suffix *icca* occurs after *sabba* in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*) in certain instances.
*Sabbadhi*. 269. *Kismā vo*:
the suffix *vo* occurs after *kiṃ* in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*) in certain instances.
270. *Kissa ka ve ca*.

When the suffix *va* follows, the substitute *ka* occurs for the word *kim*. By the inclusion of *ca*, it also occurs when the suffixes *tha*, *ha*, and so forth follow, even though they are not *va*-suffixes. Furthermore, according to the rule beginning with "In those [cases], there is *vuddhi*," there is the elision of the vowel *a* before the letter *k*, and the substitution of *va* [for *kim*]. Examples: *kva gato si tvam* ("Where have you gone?").
The word *kismā* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
271. *Hiṃ*, *haṃ*, *hiñcanaṃ*.

From what [root] do these suffixes—*hiṃ*, *haṃ*, and *hiñcanaṃ*—occur? They occur in certain instances in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*). The word "of what" (*kissa*) is understood [from the previous rule].
272. *Ku hiṃhaṃsu ca*. Why [is this said]?

Because of the words *ku*, *hiṃ*, and *haṃ*. By the inclusion of *ca* (and), it also applies to *hiṃcanaṃ*, *haṃdanaṃ*, and so forth. In the sense of "where" (*kismiṃ*), there are the forms *kuhiṃ*, *kuhaṃ*, *kuhiñcanaṃ*, and *kahaṃ*, where *ka* is the substitute.
The terms *hiṃ* and *haṃ* are understood to follow.
273. And from *tamhā*. From this [base] *ta*, the suffixes *hiṃ* and *haṃ* occur here in the sense of the locative (*sattamī*), optionally. Thus: *tasmim* → *tahiṃ*; *tasmim* → *tahaṃ*. 274.
And from *imasmā*, the suffixes *ha* and *dhā* [occur].

From the word *ima*, the suffixes *ha* and *dha* occur optionally in the sense of the locative (*sattamī*). By the rule “*imasmiṃ tha*” and so forth, the vowel *i* is elided. Thus, *imasmiṃ* becomes *iha*, meaning “here.
275. *Yato hiṃ*:
From the pronoun *ya*, the suffix *hiṃ* occurs optionally in the sense of the locative. Thus, *yasmiṃ* becomes *yahiṃ*.
“Kāle” (at the right time) is the governing heading here. Regarding the meaning “at what time,” [the following applies]:
*kiṃ-sabbaññ-eka-yaku-hi-dā-dā-canaṃ*.

Does the suffix *dā* occur after all nouns ending in *kiṃ*, *sabba*, *añña*, and *eka*? After a word ending in *ku*, the suffixes *dā* and *cana* occur optionally in the sense of time (*kāle*), and sometimes in the sense of the locative (*sattamyatthe*).
In the rule *“kissa ka ve cā,”* the substitution of *ka* for *ki* occurs by virtue of the word *ca*; thus, *kadā*. 277.
The substitution of *sa* for *sabba* occurs optionally before the suffix *dā*.

The word *sabba* optionally undergoes the substitution *sa* when followed by the suffix *dā*. Thus: *sabbasmiṃ kāle* becomes *sadā* (always) and *sabbadā* (always). Similarly, from *aññasmiṃ kāle* comes *aññadā*;

from *ekasmiṃ kāle*, *ekadā*; and from *yasmiṃ kāle*, *yadā*. From *kasmiṃ kāle* comes *kudācanaṃ*; the form *kuttaṃ* is derived either by the rule *“ku hiṃhaṃsu ca”* where the word *ca* [indicates the addition of the suffix], or by the grammatical convention (*nipātana*) of the word *“ku”*.
The term *“dā”* continues [as a governing heading].
278. From *tamha* and *ta*, the suffixes *-dāni* and *-dā* occur optionally in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*) at certain times. At that time: *tadāni*, *tadā*. 279.
From *ima*, the suffixes *-ra*, *-hi*, *-du*, *-na*, and *-dāni* occur.
From the word *ima*, the suffixes *ra* and *hi* now become conditional suffixes (*paccaya*) in certain instances when expressing time in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*).
The phrases “of all” (*sabbassa*) and “of this” (*imassa*) are also understood to recur [in the following rules]. 280. *Eta* [is substituted] before *ra* and *hi*.
The substitution of *eta* occurs for the entire word *ima* when the suffix *rahi* follows. "At this time" is *etarahi*. 281. And in *adhunā*:
the vowel *a* is substituted for the entire word *ima* when the suffix *dhunā* follows. *Adhunā*. The vowel *i* is substituted for the word *ima*. "At this time" is *idāni*.
The exposition of the case endings is completed.
Now, the prefixes and particles,
which are distinguished by their lack of gender and number and by their case endings, will be discussed.
*Pa*, *parā*, *ni*, *nu*, *du*, *saṃ*, *vi*, *ava*, *anu*, *pari*, *adhi*, *abhi*, *pati*, *su*, *ā*, *ati*, *api*, *apa*, *upa*, and *iti* are the prefixes (*upasaggā*).

Among them, the prefix *pa-* occurs in the following senses: excellence (*pakāra*), beginning (*ādi*), action (*kamma*), predominance (*padhāni*), sovereignty (*issariya*), inclusion (*antobhāva*), separation (*viyoga*), devotion (*tappara*), intensity (*bhusattha*), occurrence (*sambhava*), satisfaction (*titti*), lack of turbidity (*anāvila*), aspiration (*patthana*), and so forth.
This prefix *pa-* functions in these senses, such as those beginning with "excellence. For example:

— *pakāre* (in the sense of manner): *paññā* (wisdom); *ādikamme* (in the sense of an initial action): *vippakataṃ* (half-done); *padhāne* (in the sense of exertion): *paṇītaṃ* (excellent); *padhānaṃ* is the state of being an exertion; *issariye* (in the sense of sovereignty):

*pabhū* (lord) [of this country]; *antobhāve* (in the sense of inclusion): *pakkhittaṃ* (placed within); *viyoge* (in the sense of separation): *pavāsī* (a traveler abroad); *tappare* (in the sense of devotion): *pācariyo* (a teacher); *bhusatthe* (in the sense of intensity): *pavuddhakāyo* (one whose body has grown large); *sambhave* (in the sense of origin):

from Himavat, the Gaṅgā originates (*pabhavati*); *tittiyaṃ* (in the sense of satiety): abundant food (*pahūtamannaṃ*); *anāvile* (in the sense of being untroubled): clear water (*pasannamudakaṃ*); *patthane* (in the sense of a foundation): firmly established (*paṇihitaṃ*).

*Parā-* occurs in the senses of decline (*parihāni*), defeat (*parājaya*), movement (*gati*), stepping forward (*vikkamā*), touching (*āmasana*), and so forth. For example: in decline, *parābhava*; in defeat, *parājito*; in movement, *parāyana*; in stepping forward, *parakkamati*; in touching, *aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ*.

*Ni-* occurs in the senses of remainderlessness (*nissesa*), emergence (*niggata*), taking out (*nīharaṇa*), entering within (*antopavesana*), non-existence (*abhāva*), negation (*nisedha*), having gone out (*nikkhanta*), manifestation (*pātubhāva*), determination (*avadhāraṇa*), analysis (*vibhajana*), comparison (*upamā*), support (*upadhāraṇā*), conclusion (*avasāna*), skill (*cheka*), and so forth.
In the sense of remainderlessness, it is *nirutti*; [one] gives without remainder (*niravasesaṃ deti*); in the sense of having emerged, *niggate*.
*Nikkilesa* means free from defilement; *niyyāti* means it leads out; *niddhāraṇa* means selection from among many; *nikhāta* means firmly fixed when referring to being driven inside;

*nimmakkhikaṃ* means "free from flies" when referring to absence; *nivāreti* means he prevents as a prohibition; *nibbāna* means blown out when referring to having departed; *nibbānaṃ* means extinction; *nimmitaṃ* means created when referring to manifestation;

*nicchayo* means certainty when referring to determination; *niddeso* means description when referring to analysis; *nidassanaṃ* means illustration when referring to a simile; *nisāmanaṃ* means attending to when referring to investigation; *niṭṭhitaṃ* means finished when referring to the conclusion; *nipuṇo* means clever.
*Nī* occurs in the senses of leading out, concealing, and so forth. In the sense of leading out, it is *nīharati*; in the sense of concealing, it is *nīvaraṇaṃ*.
*U* occurs in the senses of rising, upward action, exertion, separation, origin, acquisition of wealth, power, description of essential nature, and so forth.

In the sense of rising, it is *uggacchati*; in the sense of upward action, it is one who has risen from his seat (*āsana*), or "lifting up" (*ukkhepo*); in the sense of exertion, it is "supreme" (*uttamo*), or "supramundane" (*lokuttaro*).
In separation, it is *ubbāsita*; in arising, *ubbhūta*; in the attainment of a goal, knowledge has *uppanna*; in capability, one is able to go; in the statement of form, one *uddisati* the sutta.

*Duti* is used in the senses of non-beauty, absence, loathsomeness, lack of prosperity, difficulty, deformity, and so forth. In the sense of non-beauty, there is a foul odor (*duggandha*); in the sense of absence—

In *dubbhikkha* (famine), it means contemptible; in *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), it means lack of success; in *dussassa* (bad harvest), it means difficulty; in *dukkara* (hardship), it means misfortune; in *dubbaṇṇa* (ugliness), it means having a bad face. The prefix *sam-* signifies:

conjunction (*samodhāna*), equality (*sammā-sama*), being on all sides (*samanta-bhāva*), being joined together (*saṅgata*), the sense of brevity (*saṅkhepa*), excellence (*bhūsattha*), together with (*sahattha*), reaching (*appattha*), origin (*pabhava*), facing toward (*abhimukha-bhāva*), inclusion (*saṅgaha*), covering (*pidhāna*), repetition (*punappuna-karaṇa*), and success (*samiddhi*), etc. In the sense of conjunction (*samodhāna*), it is a euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
In the sense of right measure, *samādhi*; in the sense of association, *sampayutta*; in the sense of being all-around, *saṃkiṇṇa* (mixed);

in the sense of speaking together, *samullapanā*; in the sense of coming together, *saṅgama*; in the sense of brevity, *samāsa*; in the sense of intensity, *sāratta*; in the sense of dwelling together, *saṃvāsa*;

in the sense of worthlessness, *samaggha*. In the sense of origin, *sambhava*; in the sense of facing toward, *sammukhaṃ*; in the sense of gathering, *saṅgaṇhāti*; in the sense of covering, *saṃvutaṃ*; in the sense of doing repeatedly, [saṃsaya].
*Sandhāvati* means "runs" (*samiddhiyaṃ sampanno*).

*Vi* is used in the senses of distinction (*visesa*), variety (*vividha*), opposition (*viruddha*), disappearance (*vigata*), separation (*viyoga*), and deformity (*virūpatā*), etc. In the sense of distinction, it is *vimutti* (liberation) or *visiṭṭho* (distinguished); in the sense of variety, *vimati* (doubt) or *vicitraṃ* (variegated); in the sense of opposition, *vivādo* (dispute); in the sense of disappearance, *vimalaṃ* (stainless); in the sense of separation, *vippayutto* (dissociated); and in the sense of deformity, *virūpo* (deformed).

*Ava* is used in the senses of downward direction (*adhobhāga*), separation (*viyoga*), contempt (*paribhava*), knowing (*jānana*), purity (*suddhi*), certainty (*nicchaya*), place (*desa*), theft (*theyya*), etc. In the sense of downward direction... [text ends].

*Avakkhittacakkhu*: with downcast eyes. In the sense of separation: *omukkaupāhano* (one who has taken off his sandals). In the sense of contempt: *avakokilaṃ vanaṃ* (a forest devoid of cuckoos); *avajānanaṃ* (disrespect); *avamaññati* (despises). In the sense of knowing:
*avagacchati* (understands). In the sense of purification: *vodānaṃ* (cleansing). In the sense of determination: *avadhāraṇaṃ* (ascertainment). In the sense of place: *avakāso* (space).

In the sense of theft: *avahāro* (stealing). Regarding *anu*: it means followed (*anugata*), uninterrupted (*anupacchinna*), behind (*pacchattha*), intense (*bhusattha*), similar (*sādissa*), inferior (*hīnatatiyattha*), and the sense of a characteristic or a statement of how something actually is (*lakkhaṇi’tthambhūtakkhāna*).

In the sense of a portion or a division: *anugate* (followed), *anveti* (he follows); in the sense of being uninterrupted: *anusayo* (latent tendency); in the sense of "behind": *anuratham* (behind the chariot);

in the sense of intensity: *anuratto* (intensely attached); in the sense of similarity: *anurūpam* (conformable). In the sense of inferiority: *anusāriputtam paññavanto* (those possessing wisdom follow Sāriputta); in the sense of the third case: *nadimanvavasitā senā* (the army has encamped along the river);

in the sense of a characteristic mark: *rukkham anu vijjotate vijju* (the lightning flashes along the tree); in the sense of describing one who is thus: *sādhu devadatto mātaram* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother).

*Anu*: in the sense of "portion" (*bhāga*), as in "whatever portion of this is mine, let that be given"; in the sense of "along" (*anu*), as in "the moon shines along every tree in the thicket. *Pari*:

in the sense of "all-around state" (*samantatobhāva*), "delimitation" (*pariccheda*), "avoidance" (*vajjana*), "embracing" (*āliṅgana*), "clothing" (*nivāsana*), "honoring" (*pūjā*), "eating" (*bhojana*), "disregarding" (*avajānana*), "declaring a fault" (*dosakkhāna*), and "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*), etc.
[Examples: in the sense of all-around state, *parivuto* (surrounded); in the sense of delimitation, *pariññeyyaṃ* (to be fully understood); in the sense of avoidance, *pariharati* (he avoids).

In the sense of embracing, it means to embrace (*parissajati*); in the sense of clothing, it means to put on a garment (*vatthaṃ paridhassati*); in the sense of honoring, it means service (*pāricariyā*);

in the sense of feeding, it means to serve food to a monk (*bhikkhuṃ parivisati*). In the sense of despising, it means to treat with contempt (*paribhavati*); in the sense of speaking ill, it means to revile (*paribhāsati*);
and in the context of characteristics and so forth, it means that lightning flashes around a tree (*rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijjū*), and so on.
*Adhi* is used in the senses of superiority, supremacy, presiding over, study, determination, and attainment.

In the sense of superiority: *adhisīlaṃ* (higher morality). In the sense of supremacy: *adhipati* (lord). In the sense of presiding over: *adhi brahmadatte pañcālā* (the Pañcālas [live] under Brahmadatta).

In the sense of being above: *adhirohati*. In the sense of lying upon: *pathaviṃ adhisessati* (he will lie upon the earth). In the sense of overcoming: *adhibhavati*. In the sense of study: *byākaraṇam adhīte* (he studies grammar). In the sense of determination: *adhiṭṭhāne*.
He resolves upon the earthquake and so forth; *adhimokkha* is resolution in certainty; in attainment, he acquires a mass of wealth.

*Abhi-* signifies facing toward (*abhimukhabhāva*), excellence (*visiṭṭha*), superiority (*adhika*), action directed toward something (*uddhakamma*), suitability for a family (*kulassa sāruppa*), salutation (*vandana*), characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), being established (*itthambhūta-akkhāna*), and distribution (*vicchādi*).
Regarding facing toward: he faces toward, he approaches (*abhikkamati*). Regarding excellence: the *Abhidhamma*. Regarding superiority: it rains excessively (*abhivassati*).

In ascending to a high position, being born into a noble family, being handsome in a fitting manner, and bowing in salutation—these are equal to what precedes them in the section on characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).

The prefix *pati-* occurs in the senses of: reaching, returning, inverse, counterpart, deposit, giving back, prohibition, turning away, similarity, making amends, taking, awakening, dependence, characteristic, pillar-like statement, portion, distribution, and so forth. In the sense of "reached," it means direct perception (*paccakkha*).
In the sense of reverse direction, it is *paṭisotaṃ* (against the current); in the sense of a substitute, a pupil is *pati* to the teacher;

in the sense of giving in exchange, one gives ghee *pati* to one who desires oil; in the sense of prohibition, it is *paṭisedhanaṃ*; in the sense of turning back, one *paṭikkamati*; in the sense of similarity, it is *patirūpakaṃ*;

in the sense of making amends, it is *patikāro*; in the sense of taking up, one *patiggaṇhāti*; in the sense of awakening, it is *paṭivedho*; in the sense of dependence, it is *paccayo*. In the case of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, it is the same as the preceding [section].

*Su-* is used in the senses of beauty (*sobhana*), well (*suṭṭhu*), rightly (*sammā*), prosperity (*samiddhi*), and happiness (*sukha*). In the sense of beauty: *sugandho* (fragrant). In the senses of "well" and "rightly": one who has gone well is a *Sugata*; likewise, one who has gone rightly is also a *Sugata*. In the sense of prosperity: *subhikkhaṃ* (abundance of food). In the sense of happiness: *sukaro* (easy to do).

*Ā-* is used in the senses of facing toward (*abhimukhabhāva*), upward action (*uddhakamma*), boundary (*mariyādā*), pervasion (*abhividhi*), attainment (*patti*), longing (*icchā*), embracing (*parissajana*), undertaking an action (*ādikammaggahaṇa*), dwelling (*nivāsa*), proximity (*samīpa*), and summoning (*avhāna*).
In the sense of facing toward: *āgacchati* (he comes). In the sense of upward action: *ārohati* (he ascends). In the sense of a boundary... [text ends]...
*Āpabbatā* means "as far as the mountains" regarding a field; *ākumāraṃ* means "up to children" in the sense of inclusion;

*pattiyaṃ* means "having fallen into an offense"; *icchāyaṃ* means "desire"; *parissajane* means "embracing"; *ādikamme* means "the beginning of an action"; *gahaṇe* means "it is taken up" or "grasped";
*nivāse* means "dwelling"; *samīpe* means "nearby"; *avhāne* means "in addressing."

*Ati* is used in the senses of surpassing, exceeding, pre-eminence, intensity, and so forth. In the sense of surpassing: *atirocati amhehi* (he outshines us); in the sense of having passed: *atīto*; in the sense of having transcended: *accantaṃ*; in the sense of pre-eminence: *atisayo*; in the sense of intensity: *atikodho*, *ativuddhi*.

*Api* is used in the senses of possibility, expectation, conjunction, censure, inquiry, and so forth. In the sense of possibility: *api dibbesu kāmesu* (even regarding celestial pleasures); in the sense of expectation: *merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya* (he might even go piercing right through Mount Meru);
in the sense of expectation: *ayampi dhammo aniyato* (this phenomenon also is indeterminate); in the sense of conjunction: *itipi*.
The Arhat, having taken even the interior and the inner lining [of the garment], said: "O wise one, we are indeed censured; O Venerable One, you have received alms even for our sake.

*Apaiti* occurs in the senses of departing, being gone away, censure, avoidance, worship, offense, and so forth. *Apeta*: free from negligence (*apamāna*). *Apagabbha*: free from reproach (*garahe*). *Apasālāya*: merchants come to the marketplace (*vajjane*). *Apūjāyaṃ*: one who honors the elders (*vuddhāpacāyī*). *Aparajjhati*: he offends (*padussane*).
*Upaiti* occurs in the senses of approaching, going near, rebirth, similarity, superiority, cultivation, dwelling, accusation of fault, perception, and prior karma.

*Upa-* is used in the sense of taking hold (*gayha*) in cases such as *bhusattha*. It is used in the sense of approaching (*upagamana*): one should sit down near (*upanisīdeyya*) someone who is already seated; or in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*): *upanagaraṃ* (near the city);
or in the sense of rebirth (*upapatti*): he is reborn in the heavenly world (*saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati*). Alternatively, *upa* signifies connection (*yutti*), as in:

equanimity (*upekkhā*) is so called because it views [things] from a position of rebirth (*upapattito ikkhati*); or likeness (*sādisse*): a comparison (*upamānaṃ*) is a comparison (*upamā*); or excess (*adhike*): a *doṇa* measure is *upa* more than a *khāri*; or superiority (*uparibhāve*): one who is fully ordained (*upasampanno*).
In the sense of fasting, it is *upavāsa*; in the sense of proclaiming a fault, it is *upapadati*; in the sense of perception, it is *upadhā* or *upasagga*;
in the sense of prior action, it is *upakkama* or *upakāra*; in the sense of veneration, it is *buddhupaṭṭhāka*, *mātupaṭṭhāna*, or *soceyyapaccupaṭṭhāna*;
in the sense of intense application, it is *upādāna*, *upāyāsa*, or *upanissaya*. Thus, prefixes (*upasaggā*) indeed have many meanings.
And it is said:
"Prefixes, particles, and suffixes—these three have various and single meanings respectively; so say the grammarians."

In this context, because prefixes (upasagga) qualify both nouns and verbs, they are not restricted by gender designation; thus, when the nominative case ending (syādi) is reached, since they lack distinctions such as number or object, the singular nominative alone occurs after them.
While the rule "elision" (lopa) is being observed: 282. [The elision of the case ending occurs] after all [prefixes], including *ā*, *vu*, prefixes (*upasagga*), particles (*nipāta*), and so forth.

After the word *āvuso*, as well as after prefixes (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*), there is the elision of all case endings (*vibhatti*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood that in some instances the elision occurs after words such as *sutta* and *pada*.
Furthermore, the separate mention of the word *āvuso* here should be seen as intended to indicate that it possesses a number.
Prefixes (*upasagga*) are so called because they attach themselves to the meaning of a root (*pāda*).
Particles (nipāta) fall [as grammatical units] at the beginning, middle, and end of words such as *ca* and so forth.

"Striking" is *pahāra*; likewise, there are *parābhava*, *nivāsa*, *nīhāra*, *uhāra*, *duhāra*, *saṃhāra*, *vihāra*, *avahāra*, *anuhāra*, *parihāra*, *adhihāra*, *abhihāra*, *patihāra*, *suhāra*, *āhāra*, and *atihāra*.

*Apihāra*, *apahāra*, and *upahāra*. One should apply [the following] accordingly: *paharati*, *parābhavati*, *nivasati*, *nīharati*, *uddharati*, and so forth. Sometimes a prefix obstructs the meaning of the verbal root;
sometimes it conforms to it; and another [prefix] qualifies that very same [root].
Thus, the function of prefixes is threefold.
The section on prepositions (*opasaggika-pada*) is completed.

The section on indeclinables (*nepātika-pada*): An indeclinable word (*nepātika-pada*) is that which expresses non-substantiality (*asattva-vācaka*) and serves purposes such as conjunction, option, negation, and completion.

In this context, *ca* is used in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), subsequent addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*), collection (*samāhāra*), restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and so forth. *Vā* is used in the senses of option (*vikappa*), comparison (*ūpamāna*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), and fixed alternative (*vavatthitavibhāsā*).
*Na*, *no*, *mā*, *a*, *alaṃ*, and *halaṃ*—these are used in the sense of negation (*paṭisedha*).
Enough with ornaments such as *pariyatti*.
For the purpose of completion, there are two kinds: completion of meaning (*atthapūraṇa*) and completion of words (*padapūraṇa*).

Among these, examples of word-completions include: *atha*, *khalu*, *vata*, *vata*, *atha*, *kho*, *assu*, *yagghe*, *hi*, *carahi*, *naṃ*, *taṃ*, *vā*, *ca*, *tuva*, *vo*, *pana*, *have*, *kīva*, *ha*, *tato*, *yathā*, *sudaṃ*, *kho*, *ve*, *haṃ*, *enaṃ*, *seyyathidaṃ*, and so forth.
In this context: *atha* is used in the senses of "then," "question," "immediacy," "sequence," and so forth;
*khalu* is used in the senses of "negation," "restriction," and "establishment";
and *vata* is used in the senses of "certainty," "sorrow," and "compassionate intention."
*Atho* is used in the sense of a subsequent reference (*anvādesa*) and so forth;
*hi* is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and so forth;
*tu* is used in the sense of distinction (*visesa*), cause (*hetu*), exclusion (*nivattana*), and so forth.
*Panaiti* is used in the sense of "even though there is a distinction. *Have* and *ve* are used in the sense of "certainly" (*ekamsattha*).
*Haṃ* is used in the senses of "dejection" and "alarm."
"Seyyathīdaṃ" means "that which is what," and it also has the sense of "namely.
The fulfillment of meaning is twofold: that connected with a case ending and that not connected with a case ending.
"Atthi," "sakkā," and "labbhā" belong to the nominative case.
*Āvuso*, *ambo*, *haṃbho*, *re*, *are*, *hare*, and *je* are used for addressing.
*Divā*, *bhiyyo*, and *namo* occur with the first case ending (*nominative*), as do those ending in the suffixes *-sota*, *-dhā*, and *-pa*.
Examples include: *suttaso*, *padaso*, *aniccato*, *dukkhato*, *ekadhā*, *dvidhā*, and so forth. These occur in the sense of the third case (*instrumental*).
The suffix *tuṃ* with the *paccayantā* (gerundive) ending occurs in the sense of the fourth case (*catutthī*): *kātave*, *dātave*, *kātuṃ*, *kāretuṃ*, *dātuṃ*, *dāpetuṃ*, and so forth.
The suffix *so* with the *topaccayantā* ending occurs in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*): *dīghaso*, *oraso*, *rājato*, *corato*, and so forth.

The suffix *to* also occurs in the sense of the seventh case (*sattamī*), as do those with the *trathādi-paccayantā* endings: *ekato*, *purato*, *pacchato*, *passato*, *piṭṭhito*, *pādato*, *sīsato*, *aggato*, *mūlato*, *yatra*, *yattha*, *yahiṃ*, *tatra*, *tattha*, *tahiṃ*, *tahaṃ*, and so forth.
*Samantā*, *sāmanta*, *parito*, *abhito*, *samantato*, *ekajjhaṃ*, *ekamantaṃ*, *heṭṭhā*, *upari*, *uddhaṃ*, *adho*, *tiriyaṃ*, *sammukhā*,
*parammukhā*, *āvi*, *raho*, *tiro*, *uccaṃ*, *nīcaṃ*, *anto*, *antarā*, *ajjhattaṃ*, *bahiddhā*, *bāhirā*, *bāhiraṃ*,
*bahi*, *oraṃ*, *pāraṃ*, *ārā*, *ārakā*, *pacchā*, *pure*, *huraṃ*, *pecca*— these [words] belong to the seventh case.

*Sampati*, *āyati*, *ajja* (today), *aparajju* (tomorrow), *parajju* (the day after tomorrow), *suve* (the day after tomorrow), *sve* (the day after tomorrow), *parasuve* (the day after the day after tomorrow), *hiyyo* (yesterday), *pare* (yesterday), *sajju* (immediately), *sāyaṃ* (evening), *pāto* (morning), *kālaṃ* (time), *kallaṃ* (fitting time),
*divā* (by day), *nattaṃ* (by night), *niccaṃ* (constantly), *satataṃ* (continuously), *abhiṇhaṃ* (frequently), *abhikkhaṇaṃ* (repeatedly), *muhuṃ* (momentarily), *muhuttaṃ* (for a moment),

*bhūtapubbaṃ* (formerly), *purā* (formerly), *yadā* (when), *tadā* (then), *kadā* (when)— these and others are [particles] used with the locative case of time (*kālasattamī*). Thus end those connected with case endings.
In the case of those joined with indeclinables (*avibhattiya*), *appeva*, *appevanāma*, and *nu* have the sense of doubt (*saṃsaya*).
*Addhā*, *aññadatthu*, *taggha*, *jātu*, *kāmaṃ*, and *sasakkaṃ* have the sense of certainty (*ekaṃsa*).
*Eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
*Kaccin*, *nu*, *kim nu*, *kim*—these are used in the sense of questioning.
*Evam*, *iti*, *ittham*—these are used as demonstratives.
*Iti* is also used to indicate cause or the completion of a statement.
*Yāva*, *tāva*, *yāvatā*, *tāvatā*, *kittāvatā*, *ettāvatā*, and *kīva*—these have the sense of delimitation (*paricchedanatthe*).
*Evaṃ*, *sāhu*, *lahu*, *opāyikaṃ*, *patirūpaṃ*, and *āma*—in the sense of acceptance (*sampaṭicchanatthe*), as in "it is good," "it is well," "quickly," "suitable," "appropriate," and "yes.
*Yathā*, *tathā*, *yatheva*, *tatheva*, *evaṃ*, *evameva*, *evamevaṃ*, *evampi*, *yathāpi*, *seyyathāpi*, and *seyyathāpināma*.
*Viya*, *iva*, *yathā*, *iva*, *tathā*, *iva*, *yathānāma*, *tathānāma*, *yathāhi*, *tathāhi*, *yathācatathāca*, and *iccaite* are used in the sense of resemblance (*paṭibhāga*).
*Yathā* is used in the senses of fitness (*yoggatā*), desire (*vicchā*), and the indication of not overstepping the meaning of a word (*padatthānativattanidassana*).
*Evaṃ* is used in the senses of instruction (*upadesa*), questioning (*pañha*), and so forth.
*Kiñcāpi* is used in the sense of favoring (*anuggaha*).
*Aho* is used in censure, praise, and aspiration.
*Nāma* is used in censure, praise, designation, and questioning.
*Sādhu* is used in the senses of praising and requesting;
*iṅgha* and *handa* are used in the sense of exhortation;
and *sādhu*, *suṭṭhu*, and *evam etam* are used in the sense of expressing approval.
*Kirāti* is used in the sense of hearsay or things not to be believed.
*Nūna* is used in the sense of inference, recollection, or deliberation.
*Kasmā* is used in the sense of asking for a reason.
Because of that, therefore, "tathā" and "tena" are used in the sense of cutting off the reason.
"Saha," "saddhiṃ," and "amā" are used in the sense of simultaneous action.
"Vinā" and "rite" are used in the sense of dissociation.
*Nānā* means various, diverse, and of many kinds.
*Puthu* means separate, distinct, and uncombined.
*Duṭṭhu* means badly, in the sense of loathing.
Furthermore, [the suffix -ma] occurs in the sense of "not first" (*appaṭhama*). It also occurs in the sense of difficulty (*kathañci kiccha*).
[The suffixes] *-dhā*, *-kkhattum*, and *-sakim* occur in the sense of numerical division (*saṅkhyāvibhāga*).
*Īsakaṃ* means slightly;
*saṇikaṃ* means slowly;
*khippaṃ*, *araṃ*, *lahuṃ*, *āsuṃ*, *tuṇṇaṃ*, *aciraṃ*, and *sīghaṃ* mean quickly.
*Ciraṃ* means for a long time; *cirassaṃ* means after a long period.
*Ce* means if. *Saṅkāvaṭṭhāne* means in a place of doubt.
*Dhuvaṃ* is used in the senses of constant, firm, or certain.
Hā expresses sorrow.
Tuṇhī denotes silence or non-speaking.
Sacchi signifies presence or being before the eyes.
*Musā* is used in the sense of falsehood and untruth;
*suvatthi* is used in the sense of wishing well, and so forth.
The suffixes *-tuna*, *-tvāna*, and *-tvā* occur in the sense of longing or exertion (*ussukkana*).
For example: *passituṃ*, *passiya*, *passitvāna*, *passitvā*, *disvā*, *disvāna*, *adassetvā*;
*dātuṃ*, *datvā*, *datvāna*, *upādāya*, *dāpetvā*, *viññāpetvā*, *viceyya*, *vineyya*, *nihacca*, *samecca*, *apecca*, *upecca*, *ārabbha*, *āgamma*—and so forth.
Thus, whatever possesses the characteristic of an indeclinable (*abyaya*), being free from nouns, verbs, and prefixes, all that should be understood as a particle-word (*nipātapada*).
And it is said:
"Because it is released from the three cases, it therefore falls in between;
that which possesses the characteristic of an indeclinable is called *nepakika*."
The section on Nepātika words is concluded.
Nouns are established as being fivefold: masculine, feminine, neuter, those possessing all three genders, and those that are genderless.
Thus ends the second section, the Section on Nouns, within the *Padarūpasiddhi*.
3. The Section on Case-Endings (*Kārakakaṇḍa*).
Now, the distinctions in the meanings of the case-endings are stated.

In this context, the case endings (*vibhatti*)—namely, *si* and the others—are so called because they divide even a single meaning according to functions such as action (*kamma*) and so forth, and according to categories such as singularity (*ekatta*) and so forth. These, moreover, are sevenfold through the divisions of the nominative (*paṭhamā*) and the rest.
Among these, in what sense is the nominative used?
283. The nominative is used in the sense of grammatical gender (*liṅga*).
The nominative case ending occurs when there is the mere expression of the meaning of a gender (liṅga).
"Liṅgattha" means the meaning of a gender. In this context, "liṅga" refers to that which is hidden (līna) as a limb (aṅga); it is an unmanifested part.
For nominal words—which are counterparts to sounds produced by the conceptualization of the divisions of bases, suffixes, and so forth, such as "purisa" (man)—[the gender is thus defined].
First, the basic form (*pakatirūpa*) should be established; because it is not manifest and because it is a constituent part, it is called a "gender" (*liṅga*).

Alternatively, it is called a "gender" by way of its etymological name (*anvatthanāma*), because it causes one to go toward (*gamanato*) or to mark (*liṅganato*) meanings that possess the threefold gender—designated by the conventional expression of forms devoid of both clarity and lack of clarity—as well as meanings such as prefixes which are distinct from those [roots], and because it marks what is latent (*līnassa*).
Thus, excluding roots, suffixes, and case-endings, it is that which possesses meaning.

Regarding the word "liṅga": either according to common usage (*parasamaññā*) it is called a "gender" (*liṅga*); here, however, it should be understood as referring specifically to the form of a nominal base (*pakati-rūpa*) ending in case-terminations (*syādi-vibhatti*), which is another name for the "first day of the lunar fortnight" (*pāṭipadika*).

The meaning of gender (*liṅga-attha*) is that which is designated by depending upon forms such as "visible form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, as they occur in the specific mode of a particular grammatical construction (*pabandha-visesākāra*).

Furthermore, there is that which cannot be defined as being either identical to or different from those [constituents], consisting of the categories of "aggregate" (samūha), "continuum" (santāna), and so forth, termed "derived designation" (upādāpaññatti);
and there is the aspect of commonality such as hardness or contact, termed "specific designation" (tajjāpaññatti), which— though distinct from the individual phenomena of the earth-element,

contact, and so on that are differentiated by time, place, and other factors— is established through superimposition according to convention, being shared by those of the same class and serving as the referent for conventional expressions such as "jar" or "cloth."
That [base meaning], moreover, is twofold: that which is connected with a verbal root (kamma) and so forth, and that which is pure.

Among these, because the second and subsequent cases are prescribed for those connected with a verbal root and so forth, the base meaning of a word here termed "gender-meaning" (liṅgattha) is that which is free from connection with a verbal root and so forth, endowed with gender, number, and measure, and which constitutes the referent of words such as prefixes when they are excluded from those [verbal roots].

Furthermore, the meaning associated with the object (kamma) and so forth, which is expressed by verbs, primary derivatives (kitaka), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds—that too is the domain of the nominative case alone.

This is because it is not the domain of the accusative and other cases, as there is no further specific meaning to be expressed by them in their own right; moreover, since the mere sense of gender is possible [in that context], it falls under the nominative.
And herein there is:
[the use of] particles (*nipāta*) in the sense of prefixes (*upasagga*), in the sense of some [other] meanings, and when gender and so forth are expressed purely,
as well as when the objects of action (*kamma*) and other such meanings are expressed.
First, with respect to gender (liṅga): "this man," "these men," "this girl," "these girls," "this consciousness," "these consciousnesses.
With respect to number (saṅkhyā): "one," "two.
With respect to measure (parimāṇa): "a doṇa," "a khārī," "an āḷhaka."
In the mere existence [of a thing], even when devoid of gender and so forth—as in *sattāmatte*—there are forms such as *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *ahaṃ*, *atthi*, *sakka*, *labbhā*, and so on.

With reference to the rule “The first case ending (*paṭhamā*) is used in the sense of gender,” the phrase “and in addressing” (*ālapane ca*) indicates that the first case is also used in the sense of addressing. Addressing (*ālapana*) means speaking to someone by making them face oneself;

the meaning is calling out or summoning. Here, “calling out” (*āmantana*) refers specifically to making someone who has already received their name turn toward one by means of sound. Once they have been made to face oneself...

However, it is joined with an action by way of the sequence beginning with "Go" (*gaccha*); therefore, because there is no connection with an action at the time of addressing, this does not receive the designation of a *kāraka*.
And it has been said:
“Bringing [something] before one’s mind by means of sadness regarding an existing object;
addressing [someone] regarding what is to be done: there is no such thing as ‘May I become a king.
O man, come! Or, O men, come, sirs! Come, you men!
In what sense is the second case used? 284. The second case is used in the sense of the object.
The second case ending occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the object.
This [rule] applies only when [the case] is not already expressed; here, the statement "the second case is used for the object" (*kammani dutiyā*) serves as the indicator.
What is the object (*kamma*)?
From the rule "that by which one performs [an action] is the instrument" (*yena vā kayirate taṃ karaṇaṃ*), the word "or" (*vā*) is carried over from that [preceding rule].
285. That which one does is *kamma*.
Or, whatever one does, or whatever one transforms, or whatever one attains—that agent is designated as *kamma*. Here, gender, tense, number, and case-endings are not restricted.
It is called *kamma* because it is "acted upon" (*karīyati*). In that context, the agent (*kāraka*) is that which accomplishes the production of the action.

The cause is stated; furthermore, that causal agent (*kāraka*) is sixfold: the object (*kamma*), the agent (*kattā*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), and the location (*okāsa*).

In this regard, because an action exists only when there is an object and so forth—whether by way of its own nature or through conceptual designation—the designation "causal agent" is established for all six, beginning with the object.
Furthermore, that karma is threefold: productive (*nibbattanīya*), transformative (*vikaraṇīya*), and purificatory (*pāpaṇīya*). For example:
"A mother gives birth to a son," "Food produces happiness";
"Devadatta makes a pot," "He makes wood into charcoal," "He makes gold into an armlet or a bracelet," or "He reaps rice"; "Devadatta enters his house."
One sees the sun, hears the Dhamma, and attends upon the wise.
And it is said:
"It is considered to be threefold, by way of the distinctions of arising, transformation, and attainment."
"Having approached that deed, it is like entering a house of glowing embers. And here,
because it is stated as "whatever one does is action" (*kamma*) by way of including everything without regard for distinctions such as desired or undesired,
spoken or unspoken, and because this is the context for defining alternative meanings, the designation "action" (*kamma*) applies everywhere by means of this very definition.
In this context, an unintended object (*anicchitakamma*) is, for example: one tramples upon a thorn, swallows poison, or, while going to a village, approaches the foot of a tree.
An unstated object (*akathitakamma*) is, for example: "The Brahmin asks Yaññadatta for a blanket.

Here, "blanket" (*kambala*) is the stated object because it is what is most desired to be attained by the act of asking, which possesses two objects; whereas "Yaññadatta" is [the unstated object] because of its subordinate status.

The "unexpressed object" (*akathitakamma*). For example: *samiddhaṃ dhanaṃ bhikkhate* (he begs for abundant wealth), *ajaṃ gāmaṃ nayati* (he leads the goat to the village), *parābhavantaṃ purisaṃ* (the man who is perishing), *mayaṃ pucchāma gotamaṃ* (we ask Gotama), and *bhagavā bhikkhū etadavoca* (the Blessed One said this to the monks).

However, it does not occur when the object is expressed [as the agent], as in: *kaṭo karīyate devadattena* (a mat is being made by Devadatta), *sugatena desito dhammo* (the Dhamma was taught by the Sugata), and *yaññadatto kambalaṃ yācīyate brāhmaṇena* (Yaññadatta is being asked for a blanket by the brahmin).
“*Dutiya* (the second [section])” indicates the governing heading.
286. For the roots *gam*, *budh*, *bhuj*, *path*, *har*, *kar*, *say*, etc., the suffix *kārita* (causative) is optionally applied.
*Gam* (in the sense of going), *sapp* (to move); *budh* (in the sense of awakening), or *budh* (in the sense of understanding); *bhuj* (in the senses of protecting and dealing/trading).

In the usage of verbal roots such as *paṭha* (to recite), *vāca* (speech), *hara* (to take), *kara* (to do), and *si* (to lie down), when they are used in the causative (*kārita*), the second case ending optionally occurs for the object that has become the instigating agent (*payojaka-kartṛ*).
Since [the second case] is already established by a permanent rule (*niccasampatti*), this [present rule] has the sense of an option;
therefore, in its alternative case, the third case ending occurs.
When any man goes to a village, another employs him; one man causes another man to go to the village, or causes him to go to the village by means of another man.
Likewise, the teacher causes the pupil to understand the Dhamma; the mother causes the son to eat food;
the teacher causes the pupil to recite the Dhamma; and likewise, one man causes another man to carry a burden.
He causes a man to do work, or he has work done by a man, or one man makes another man lie down.
Thus, in all such cases where there is a causative action (*kārita*), the second case is used for the agent of that action. Why "causative" (*kārita*)?
[Because] "the man goes to the village" [does not take the second case].

When [the object] is already expressed, [the suffix] does not occur; for example: *purisena puriso gāmaṃ gamīyate* ("a man is made to go to the village by a man"), *sisso dhammaṃ bodhīyate* ("a student is made to understand the Dhamma," etc.).
287. *Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge*:

"Accantasaṃyoga" (absolute connection) means a connection that is continuous and uninterrupted. When there is absolute connection between time (*kāla*) or distance (*addhāna*) and a substance (*dabba*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*kiriya*), the second case ending (*dutiyāvibhatti*) occurs after those words expressing time or distance.

First, regarding time (*kāla*): "For seven days he drinks cow's milk; for a month, meat and rice; in autumn, the delightful river; at all times, the delightful Nandana grove. Regarding study: "He studies for a month; he teaches the Abhidhamma for three months. Regarding distance (*addhāna*):
"A row of forest trees for a league (*yojana*); a long mountain for a league; he studies for a *kosa*. What is the purpose of the term "absolute connection" (*accantasaṃyoga*)?
[Examples: "He eats every month"; "He established a monastery every league."
288. When joined with *kammappavacanīya* particles.
When there is a construction joined with particles (*nipāta*) or prefixes (*upasagga*) that are *kammappavacanīya*, the second case ending occurs after the noun stem.
Those for whom an object is to be expressed are *kammappavacanīya*; or, according to another convention, particles such as *anu* and so forth are *kammappavacanīya*.

In this context, it is stated that the prefix *anu* has the designation of a "karmapravacanīya" (prepositional particle) when it signifies a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), accompaniment (*sahattha*), or inferiority (*hīna*). For example:

*pabbajitamanu pabbajiṃsu* ("they went forth after those who had gone forth"), *nadimanvavasitā Bārāṇasī* ("Bārāṇasī is situated along the river"); the meaning is "bound together with the river. Also:
*anu Sāriputtaṃ paññavā* ("one who is wise is second only to Sāriputta").

Regarding the *Lakkhaṇa* (Characteristic) and other rules, it is stated in the rule "pati, pari, anu [are used] in the senses of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), state of being thus (*itthambhūta*), narration (*akkhāna*), portion (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vicchā*)": that *pati*, *pari*, and *anu* are designated as *kammappavacanīya* (governing accusative).

In the sense of a characteristic: "Divine foods might appear in relation to the rising of the sun" (*sūriyuggamanaṃ pati*); "the moon shines in relation to the tree" (*rukkhaṃ pati*, *rukkhaṃ pari*, *rukkhaṃ anu*).
In the sense of a state of being thus: "Devadatta is good in relation to his mother" (*mātaraṃ pati*, *mātaraṃ pari*, *mātaraṃ anu*).
Whatever portion of this there may be for me, let that be given to me—*pati*, *pari*, *anu*.

The word *pati* is employed in the sense of distribution (*vicchā-yoga*): "The moon shines toward every tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati*), [meaning] toward each tree, around each tree, or along each tree.

Regarding the rule "abhi in the sense of non-distribution," the designation of object-indicative (*kammappavacanīya*) is stated for *abhi* when used in the senses of indication (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, excluding the sense of distribution: "This excellent report of the venerable Gotama has spread abroad; it is well that Devadatta is against his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ abhi*).
In the *Nipāta* [section], there is the example: "O Brahmin, [I am] the slayer of my enemies," and so forth.
(289) In some instances, the accusative case (*dutiyā*) occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*).
In certain cases, the accusative case-ending (*dutiyāvibhatti*) is used in the sense of the genitive. This occurs in connection with the words *antarā*, *abhito*, *parito*, *pati*, and *paṭibhāti*.
This [means]: having set out on the highway between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda;
the meaning is "in the middle of Rājagaha and Nāḷanda. He dwells near a village, he dwells around a village;
"towards the river Nerañjarā" means in the vicinity of the river Nerañjarā. "May the factors of awakening occur to you, Cunda; let a simile come to me."
"It occurs to me," means "a simile presents itself to me.
And the phrase "in some cases, the second case [is used] when there is a meaning" continues [to apply].
Also [the same applies] to the third and seventh cases.
In the sense of the third and seventh cases, and in some instances, the second case ending occurs after a noun. In the sense of the third case:
"If he will not address me, and you do not speak to me," "Where is there happiness without the True Dhamma? and "Without a means, there is no accomplishment of the goal.

In the sense of the seventh case—the second case is used after a verb meaning "to dwell near" (upān-vajjhāvasa), after verbs meaning "to preside over" (adhisitthāvasāna), and in the context of "drinking that" (tappānacāra).
First, regarding time: "At one time, having dressed in the morning," refers to a certain occasion when the Blessed One [was so]. Regarding this night, it refers to the four Great Kings.

Regarding the application of the verbal root *vas* preceded by *upa* and others: he dwells near the village (*upavasati*), he dwells along the village (*anuvasati*), he dwells in the monastery (*adhivasati*), he dwells in the village (*āvasati*), he dwells in the household (*ajjhāvasati*).
Likewise: he will lie upon the earth (*pathaviṃ adhisessati*), he stands upon the village (*gāmaṃ adhitiṭṭhati*), he dwells in the village (*gāmaṃ ajjhāvasati*).
In the case of tappanacāra (actions involving satisfying): "He drinks from the river," "He wanders through the village," and so forth.
In what sense is the third case used? 291. The third case is used in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa).
The third case ending occurs in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa-kāraka).
What is the instrument?
292. That by which something is performed is the instrument.

That instrument by which the agent performs an action without intervention—whether it be that by which he acts, that by which he transforms, or that by which he reaches [the object]—is termed the *karaṇa* (instrument). It is called *karaṇa* because "it is done (*karīyate*) by means of this.

And although all factors of action (*kāraka*) are equally effective in accomplishing an action, the specific statement "by which it is performed" is made here in order to include only that factor among the agents—which serves as the agent's instrument—that is the most effective (*sādhakatama*). And it has been said:
“That whose state as the cause for the successful accomplishment of an action is possible through every distinction—
that is called the *karaṇa* (instrument) among the factors of action (*kāraka*).
Furthermore, it is twofold, by way of being internal or external.”
For example: "He performs work with his hand," "he sees a form with his eye," "having cognized a mental object with the mind"; "he reaps rice with a sickle," "he burns a hut with fire.
The term "third" (tatiyā) is the governing heading. 293. And [the third case ending is used] for the agent (kattar).

The third case ending occurs after a noun in the sense of an agent (*kattari*) and an instrument (*kārake*). By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ca*), the third case is also used: (1) to denote a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*); (2) in connection with the group of verbs beginning with *kriyā*;

(3) in connection with words having the sense of "similar to," "assemblage," "decrease," "quarrel," "skilled," "mixed," "together with," and so on; (4) in the sense of time and distance; and (5) in the sense of the nominative (*paccatta*), the accusative (*kammattha*), and the ablative (*pañcamiyattha*), etc.
And who is the agent?
294. He who acts is the agent.
He who performs an action by making himself the primary focus is designated as the "agent" (kattā).
Thus, there are three kinds of agents: the pure agent (*suddhakattā*), the causal agent (*hetukattā*), and the object-agent (*kammakattā*).
Among these, one who performs the action oneself is the pure agent. One who directs another who is capable of acting but is not yet acting is the causal agent;
for example, Devadatta is capable of going, and another person instigates him, [expressed as] "he causes Devadatta to go" (*gamayati devadattan*).
Furthermore, when Devadatta goes here and there, another person instigates him, which is indicated as "he causes Devadatta to go" (*gamayati devadatta*);
this too should be understood as stated by way of demonstrating the capacity [of the agent].
Otherwise, if he were to go by himself, what would be the use of the instigating activity? How could one force someone who is not acting to act? [It is like] a stone.
Furthermore, [expressions] such as "he causes to arise" would not be established.
Here, however,
the term "agent" (kattā) is understood to carry over.
293. That which causes [something] to be done is the *hetu* (cause).
That which causes the agent to act receives the designation *hetu*, and the agent [of that cause] receives the designation *hetukattā* (causal agent).

However, when something, although it has become an object (*kamma*) in dependence on another’s action, is as if accomplished by itself because it is easy to do, it is called a *kammakattā* (object-agent), as in: “The mat is being made by itself,” or “The rice is cooking by itself.”
And it is said:
“The agent who, making himself the primary focus, produces an action—
whether unassociated or associated with that action— is called the ‘doer.’”
That which is called "hetukatta" (causative agency) is the instigator of the agent;
that which is called "kammakatta" (object-agency) is easily accomplished.
"...is said to be the agent of the action.
But surely, in cases such as "a conjunction arises," how can there be the status of an agent for the act of arising when [the agent] did not previously exist?
It is replied: the application of words is established by worldly convention; for even that which does not [yet] exist is, in the world, made the denotation of a word.

One expresses [the object] as if it were being grasped while actually present; for it is precisely the aspect grasped by a conceptualizing consciousness (*vikappa-buddhi*) that is denoted by the word, and not the intrinsic nature (*vatthu-sabhāva*) of the thing itself.

Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that even knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*suta-maya-ñāṇa*) would realize the intrinsic nature of the thing as if it were directly perceived (*paccakkha*), and there would also follow the non-existence of false speech, wrong views, and so forth. Therefore, [this is possible] even by way of a designation (*paññatti*) constructed by the intellect.
"The occurrence of the word" means that even for a non-existent thing, such as a conjunction, there is indeed the status of being the agent (*kattū*) of the action of producing.
As it has been said:
"The word is the domain of conventional usage; it does not exclusively pertain to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*)."
"The purpose intended by the intellect is called its 'purpose.
Because it is grasped by the intellect, a conjunction arises;
and that conjunction, while existing, becomes the agent of birth."

In that context, the third [type of compound] is the *dharmapada* taught by the Conqueror: "The Buddha, having conquered Māra, awakened the world; a man bitten by a snake was awakened by the Buddha; a monastery was built by the faithful.
It does not occur when [the action] is already expressed. For example: "Devadatta makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti devadatto*) or "he causes it to be made.
Regarding the characteristic of one who has become thus: "With her head broken and blood flowing, [she went] to the neighbors..."
He complained; he had another new bowl made with a bowl that had fewer than five mends; he saw a wandering ascetic with a triple staff.

Regarding *apavagga* (completion): he set out for Bārāṇasī in a single day; he completed the monastery in nine months; he mastered the grammar in a league’s distance—this refers to the swift completion of an action, as in "the completion of the action.
Regarding *pubba*-type compounds (*pubbādiyoga*): "pus" [is cured] in a month; "equal to his father"; "the same as his mother"; "less by a kahāpaṇa coin"; "destitute of wealth."
A quarrel with salt; skilled in conduct; skilled in speech; mixed with sugar;
mixed with sesame; friendly in speech; purpose served by a gem; purpose served by wealth; equal to one's father.
Regarding time and distance: he eats for a month; he travels a league.
In the sense of identity (paccatte): he appoints himself by himself.
In the sense of the object (kamm-atthe): he sows in the field with sesame seeds.
In the sense of the ablative (pañcamiyatthe): we are well released from that Great Ascetic.

296. And [the third case ending occurs] in connection with *saha* and so forth. When used in conjunction with *saha*, *saddhiṃ*, *samaṃ*, *nānā*, *vinā*, *alaṃ*, *kimañca*, and similar words, the third case ending occurs after a noun; by the word *ca*, this also applies when used with *sahattha*.
In that context, the connection with the word *saha* occurs in relation to action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*dabba*), or inherence (*samavāya*). For example: *vitakkena saha*.
It is permissible; the teacher and preceptor may receive gains together with their resident pupil and co-resident students, even if they are physically large.
The Blessed One sat down together with the community of monks. Measured by a thousand [units], there is separation and parting from all those who are dear and pleasing to me.
The Saṅgha may perform the Uposatha even without Gagga. Enough for you to dwell here.
"What is the use of my alone having crossed over, by a man who perceives his own strength? What use have you for matted hair, O dull-witted one?
What use have you for your deerskin garment?"—with these words, Devadatta entered Rājagaha with Kokālika as his attendant monk; living together with fools is painful.
(297) And [the suffix -tā] is used in the sense of "because of" (*hetvatthe*).

The term *yogaggahaṇa* (the mention of connection) follows here; when used in the sense of a cause (*hetvattha*), the third case ending occurs after a noun (*liṅga*) employed in that sense of a cause.

A cause is a reason whose efficacy has been observed in relation to some result; that itself is the "meaning" (*attha*). In that sense of a cause: he dwells because of food, he dwells because of the Dhamma, he dwells because of knowledge.
One does not become an outcast by birth.
One is not a brahmin by birth;
by one's deeds one becomes an outcaste,
and by one's deeds one becomes a brahmin.
Through giving one possesses wealth; through conduct, one is well-born.
By what does one hand become a giver of desires? By what does one hand have the fragrance of honey?
Through what holy life does merit succeed in the hand?
In the usage of *hetu* (cause) and *attha* (purpose): for what sign (*nimitta*), for what purpose (*payojana*), for what meaning (*attha*), for what cause (*hetu*) does he dwell?
298. And in the sense of the locative:
the third case ending occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the locative as well.

And this [usage] occurs in relation to time, duration, direction, place, and so forth: "at that time," "at that moment," "listening to the Dhamma from time to time," "after my passing, he will be your teacher," "he eats for a month," "he runs for a league. Also:
"Dhataraṭṭha in the east, Virūḷhaka in the south, Virūpakkha in the west, Kasivanta in the north, and Janogha beyond."
"He approached where the Blessed One was," and so forth. 299.

*Yena-aṅgavikāro* (The case of bodily deformity caused by a limb). When a deformity of the whole body (*aṅgin*) is indicated by a diseased limb (*aṅga*), the third case ending occurs there. In this context, "limb" (*aṅga*) refers to the body, in the sense that "it has limbs. Examples: blind in the eye; club-footed in the hand; lame in the foot; hunchbacked in the back.

300. And [the third case ending occurs] after a qualifier (*visesana*). That by which something is qualified, or that which is to be qualified, is a qualifier (*visesana*), such as lineage (*gotta*) and so forth. The third case ending occurs in the sense of a qualifier—consisting of lineage, name, birth, craft, age, or quality—and by the word "and" (*ca*), it also occurs after *pakati* and other such terms. For example: "The Lord is Gotama by lineage;
he is known as Sāriputta by name, and he is possessed of wisdom."
The Buddha, by birth a kshatriya, is the peerless person in the world.
Even though he went forth on the very day he was seven years old by birth, may he too instruct me; I accept it upon my head.
He was a reed-worker by clan, twenty-nine years of age, excellent in learning, excellent in wisdom, supreme in asceticism, and handsome in appearance.

Regarding [the use of] *pakati* and so forth: “handsome by nature,” “mostly clay,” “he runs on level ground,” “he runs on uneven ground,” “he buys grain for two *doṇas*,” “he buys horses for a thousand.
In what sense is the fourth case used?
301. The dative case is used for the recipient (sampadāna).
In the grammatical factor of the recipient, the fourth case ending occurs after a nominal stem.
And what is the recipient?
302. That person for whom one desires to give, or who approves [of the gift], or who receives it, is the *sampadāna* (recipient).

Or rather, that *kāraka* (participant) for whom one desires to give, or who approves, or who receives, is designated as the *sampadāna*. It is called *sampadāna* because "it is properly given to him" (*sammā padīyate assa*); thus, it refers to the recipient.
Furthermore, that [recipient] is threefold, by way of not preventing what is being given, requesting it, or consenting to it. For example: "A flower for the Buddha."
He sacrifices; he offers water to the Bodhi tree. In the case of entreaty—he gives wealth to beggars.
In the case of consent—he gives a gift to the bhikkhus.
As it has been said:
“Indeed, the recipient (sampadāna) is said to be threefold, according to non-repudiation, propitiation, and permission: [as in] ‘the tree,’ ‘the beggar,’ and ‘the bhikkhus.
What is meant by “desiring to give”? He gives a punishment to the king.

But in the case of *rocana* (to please) and so forth: "The truth pleases the ascetic; may it also please the venerable ones that there should be a schism in the Saṅgha; for whichever venerable one approves, let Yaññadatta hold the golden parasol for Devadatta. The term "recipient" (*sampadāna*) also recurs [from the previous rule].
303. [The following roots take the recipient as their object:

*silāgh* (to praise), *han* (to strike), *ṭhā* (to stand), *sap* (to swear), *dhāra* (to bear), *piha* (to love), *kudha* (to be angry), *duhi* (to milk), *ssāsūya* (to envy), *rādhikkha* (to succeed), *paccāsuṇa* (to promise), and those whose sense is to follow, to enter, to precede, to do, or to express approval.

[The suffix -tu occurs] after roots meaning "to think" (maññati), "to respect" (ādara), "sentient beings" (pāṇin), roots with the sense of "going" (gati), roots with the sense of "action" (kamman), roots with the sense of "wishing" (āsisa), conventional terms (sammuti), and in the sense of the locative case (bhiyyasattami). This consists of four words. [It occurs] in the employment of these verbal roots:

*silāgha* in praise, *hanu* in taking away, *ṭhā* in stopping from going, *sapa* in reviling, *dhara* in supporting, and *piha* in longing; as well as *kudha* in anger and *duha* in the desire to injure.

In the employment of the roots *issa* (to envy) and *issāyaṃ*, as well as those roots expressing the sense of *usūya* (malice) and *dosāvikaraṇa* (exposing faults); in the employment of *rādha* in the senses of harming (*hiṃsā*) and propitiating (*saṃrādhesu*);
in the employment of *ikkha* in the senses of seeing (*dassana*) and counting (*aṅka*); in the employment of *su* preceded by *pati* in the sense of hearing (*savaṇa*);
and in the employment of the root *ga* preceded by *anu-pati* in the sense of announcing (*ārocanattha*), when used with a prior agent (*pubbakattā*) and in that same sense (*tadatthe*).

In the sense of "enough" (*tumatthe*), in the application of "sufficient for" (*alamatthappayoge*), in the application of "to think" (*maññatippayoge*), in disregard (*anādare*), with respect to non-living beings (*appāṇini*), as the object (*kammani*) of verbs meaning "to go" (*gatyatthānaṃ*), in the application of the sense of "wishing" (*āsisatthappayoge*), in the applications of "consent" (*sammuti*) and "moreover" (*bhiyyappayogesū*), and in the sense of the locative case (*sattamyatthe*)—that karmic factor (*kammādikāraka*) is designated as the recipient (*sampadānasañña*). By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), [the following are also included]:
the application of *pahiṇati*, *kappati*, *pahoti*, comparison (*upamā*), making the añjali gesture (*añjalikaraṇa*), and well-being (*phāsu*).
In the case of the *atthaseyya* (bed for the sake of another) and similar constructions, the dative case is used as before.
First, regarding the usage with *silāghati* (to praise) and so forth: *buddhassa silāghate*. *Upajjhāyassa silāghate*; the meaning is "he praises" or "he extols.
*Hanute mayhameva*, *hanute tuyhameva*; the meaning is "he denies" or "he disclaims."

"A carpenter should attend upon the sons of the Sakyans. Here, "attending" (*upatiṭṭhāna*) means approaching. One should attend upon a monk while he is eating, either with drinking water or with a fan.
"He owes you," "he owes me"—here, "owing" (*sapana*) means making a formal agreement.
In the usage of "to owe" (*dhārayati*), the creditor alone is the recipient (*sampadāna*): "He owes you gold"; the meaning is that he owes a debt. "We owe a nāga to that king."

In the application of the word *pihā* (longing), it is precisely what is desired; even the gods long for such a person (*tādino*). "Even the gods long for them" means they yearn for those who are perfectly enlightened (*sambuddha*) and mindful.
In the application of the words *kodha* (anger) and so forth: "O Great Hero, be angry with that toward whom your anger is directed, if I were to be angry with him.
The cloud parches the quarters of the sky, but he who does not deceive his friends does not parch them.
The sectarians envy the ascetics.
The wicked envy those possessed of virtue; what envy can there be for those who possess true knowledge?

In the application of the term *rādhikkha*, there is an inquiry for the purpose of proclaiming the action (*kamma*); and because of the governing rule (*vādhikāra*), the second case ending is also used. *Ārādho*.

"I have offended against the king, I am offending against the king, or I have offended against the king; what offense have I committed against you, noble ladies, or what offense have I committed against you, noble ladies?
Upatissa desires the full ordination from the Venerable Elder Upāli, or [he desires it] from the Venerable [Elder]."

When the verbal root *suṇati* (to hear) is used in conjunction with *paccā*, and the root *giṇāti* (to take) is used in conjunction with *anupati*, the agent of the preceding action is designated as the recipient (*sampadāna*).

For example: "The Blessed One said this to the monks. Here, "the monks" (*bhikkhū*) is the unexpressed object (*akathitakamma*), while "this" (*etaṃ*) is the expressed object (*kathitakamma*). [This applies] to the preceding act of speaking.
The Blessed One is the author. The monks listened to the Blessed One; the monks heeded the Buddha.
In the same way, the monk proclaims the Dhamma to people; people follow that monk;
people respond to that monk—the meaning is that they encourage him by giving shouts of "Well done! and so forth.
"He who speaks is the agent"; that which is spoken is called the "object" (kamma).
One should understand that he who is the recipient of that [speech] is the "indirect object" (sampadāna).
In the usage of the sense of announcing, that to whom one announces is the indirect object. "I announce to you, O monks; I make it known to you."

"O monks, I address you; O Great King, I address you; 'I address you,' or 'I shall go, having addressed you'—in these cases, because the word *ārocanā* (addressing) has the sense of a mode of speaking, the fourth case is used even when the meaning is that of teaching and so forth.

For example: *dhammaṃ vo desessāmi* (I will teach the Dhamma to you), *desetu bhante bhagavā dhammaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ* (May the Blessed One, venerable sir, teach the Dhamma to the monks), *yathā no bhagavā byākareyya* (so that the Blessed One might explain it to us), *niruttiṃ te pavakkhāmi* (I will declare the etymology to you), and so on."
The designation "dative" (sampadāna) applies to that meaning, and the fourth case (catutthī) is used as well.
The phrase "or from this" (ato vā) also recurs.
304. [The suffix] āya replaces the singular dative ending.
After a noun ending in the letter *a*, the fourth case singular suffix optionally undergoes the substitution *āy*;
there is the elision of the vowel and so forth. "For the sake of the Buddha, for the sake of the Dhamma, for the sake of the Saṅgha, I renounce life;

I partake of almsfood neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification, but for the fulfillment of what is deficient, and it conduces to welfare, benefit, and happiness."

*Tumatthe*: "Out of compassion for the world"; the meaning is that he has compassion for the world. Likewise, it is for the sake of living in comfort (*phāsuvihārāya*). The meanings of the word *alaṃ* include "worthiness" (*araha*) and "refusal" (*paṭikkhepa*).

In the sense of worthiness: *Alaṃ me rajjaṃ* (Sovereignty is enough for me); *Alaṃ bhikkhu pattassa* (Enough, O monk, with the bowl); *Akkhadhutto purisapuggalo nālaṃ dārabharaṇāya* (A man who is a gambler is not fit to support a wife); *Alaṃ mallo mallassa* (One wrestler is a match for another wrestler); *Mallo mallassa arahati* (A wrestler is worthy of [being matched by] a wrestler).

In the sense of refusal: *Alaṃ te idha vāsena* (Enough of your dwelling here); *Alaṃ me hiraññasuvaṇṇena* (I have had enough of gold and bullion); *Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena* (What is the use of my being one who has crossed over?); *Kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha* (Of what use are your matted locks, O dull-witted one?); *Kiṃ tettha catumaṭṭhassa* (What is the use of those four matters to you?).

In construction with the verb *maññati* (to think), when expressing disregard (*anādara*) toward a non-living thing (*appāṇini*), the second case is used only for the object—*kaṭṭhassa tuvaṃ maññe*, "I think you are a mere log"; *kaḷiṅgarassa tuvaṃ maññe*, "I think you are a mere clod"; *jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññamāno*, "not regarding even life as a blade of grass. Why "when expressing disregard"? Witness:

*suvaṇṇaṃ taṃ maññe*, "I think that is gold" (which expresses esteem). Why "non-living thing"? Witness: *gadrabhaṃ tuvaṃ maññe*, "I think you are a donkey" (which expresses disregard toward a living being).

By virtue of the governing rule concerning verbs meaning "to go," the second case is also used for the object: *appo saggāya gacchati*, "few go to heaven"; *appo saggaṃ gacchati*, "few go to heaven"; *nibbānāya vajantiyā*, "for those going toward Nibbāna"; *mūlāya paṭikasseyya*, "he should drive back to the root"; *mūlaṃ paṭikasseyya*, "he should drive back to the root."

In the sense of a blessing (*āsīsana*), it refers specifically to the application of longevity, welfare, skillfulness, and so forth. [Examples include: "May the Venerable One have long life" (*āyasmato dīghāyu hotu*);

here, the substitution of *to* for the word *tassa* when accompanied by a case ending occurs according to the rule "in *sasmin*, *to* becomes *ntu*. "May there be welfare for you" (*bhaddaṃ bhavato hotu*); "may there be well-being for you" (*kusalaṃ bhavato hotu*);

"may there be health for you" (*anāmayaṃ bhavato hotu*); "may there be happiness for you" (*sukhaṃ bhavato hotu*); "may there be prosperity for you" (*atthaṃ bhavato hotu*); "may there be benefit for you" (*hitaṃ bhavato hotu*); "welcome! (*svāgataṃ*).
May it be well with you; may there be welfare for all beings.
Regarding the application of *sammuti*: "It is good that I have the opportunity to see that Blessed One.
Regarding the application of *bhiyyo*: "To a greater degree."

In the sense of the seventh case (locative), [the particle *ca*] occurs in connection with revealing (*āvikaraṇa*), manifesting (*pātubhavana*), and so forth—as in: "I reveal it to you" (*tuyhañcassa āvikaromi*) and "Sakka appeared to me" (*tassa me Sakko pāturahosi*).
By the inclusion of the word *ca*, it also occurs in connection with actions such as sending (*pahiṇādi*), and in connection with nouns such as "comfort" (*phāsū*):

"one should send him" (*tassa pahiṇeyya*), "he sent a messenger to the monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ dūtaṃ pāhesi*), "exertion is appropriate for ascetics" (*kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo*), "what was given to one suffices for two or three," and "a simile."
“I shall do for them; I raise my joined palms to you. “In such a way he finds ease; it is for the welfare of the world;
I have need of the jewel; my welfare is better”—and so forth.
The term “the dative” (catutthī) recurs.

305. Also [the fourth case ending occurs] in connection with *namas* and so forth. When in connection with the word *namas*, as well as in connection with *sotthi*, *svāgata*, and so on, the fourth case ending (*catutthīvibhatti*) occurs after the noun stem.

Examples: *namo te buddha vīratthu* (Homage to you, O Heroic Buddha); *namo karohi nāgassa* (Pay homage to the Naga); *namatthu buddhānaṃ* (May there be homage to the Buddhas); *namatthu bodhiyā* (May there be homage to the Bodhi tree); *sotthi*...
“Knowing [this], welcome to you, O Great King; indeed, your arrival is not ill-timed.
And it is said: ‘It will happen at the right time.
(306) When expressing a state of being (*bhāva*), the fourth case is used.

The fourth case ending occurs in the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) when referring to the future tense. Becoming is *bhāva*. "He will cook" (*paccissate*), or "cooking" is *pāka*; "he goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vajati*) means "he goes in order to cook. Likewise, "he goes for the sake of enjoyment" (*bhogāya vajati*), and so forth.
In what sense does the fifth case ending occur? 307. The fifth case ending occurs in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
What is the ablative (apādāna)? 308. That from which fear departs or from which one takes [something] is the ablative.

Or, that from which there is departure—limited by a boundary—or that from which fear arises due to a cause of fear, or that from whom one receives knowledge through a teacher; such an agent is designated as the ablative. It is called the ablative (apādāna) because, having moved away (apanetvā) from it, one takes [something] from it (ito ādadāti).

That [ablative] is further specified as threefold according to the distinction of its objects: the indicated object (*niddiṭṭhavisaya*), the retained object (*upāttavisaya*), and the inferable object (*anumeyyavisaya*).

It is called the "indicated object" because it indicates a specific action whose designation is "ablative" (*apādāna*). For example: *gāmā apenti munayo* (the sages depart from the village), *nagarā niggato rājā* (the king has gone out from the city).

And here, in cases such as *pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye* (one should restrain the mind from evil) and *pāpā nivārenti* (they restrain [it] from evil), although there is no departure preceded by physical contact, nevertheless, because a departure preceded by mental contact is possible, the designation "ablative" applies by this rule.

However, when [an action] occurs by taking as its object a domain that is implied or brought in (*ajjhāhaṭa*) through the act of departing (*apagamanakriya*), that is one whose object is implied (*upāttavisaya*).
For example: "Lightning flashes from the clouds" (*valāhakā vijjotate vijju*) and "He cooks from the granary" (*kusūlato pacati*).
And here, the prior action—"having emerged from the clouds" (*valāhakā nikkhamma*) and "having removed from the granary" (*kusūlato apanetvā*)"—is supplied (*ajjhāharīyati*).

An example of a case where the object is to be inferred (*anumeyya-visaya*) is: "The people of Mathurā are more handsome than those of Pāṭaliputta. For here, they are being excelled by some quality; thus, the specific action (*kriyā-visesa*) is indeed that which is to be inferred. However, in this context, in the sutta beginning with *dūranta-*, the designation of the ablative (*apādāna-saññā*) occurs through the inclusion of the case-ending (*vibhatti*). And it has been said:
"In some cases the object is explicitly stated (*niddiṭṭha*), and likewise in others the object is included (*upātta*)."
"And the object of inference; thus the ablative is considered to be threefold. That very [ablative] is also twofold, by way of being mobile or immobile.
As for the mobile, for example: "The goad-bearer fell from the running elephant."
As an immovable example: "The forest-dwellers descend from the mountains.

Regarding the cause of fear: "Fear arises from thieves; fear arises from craving; one trembles before evil. Regarding the declarer: "One receives the training from the preceptor (upajjhāya); one studies from the teacher (ācariya); one hears from the teacher.
The governing term is "apādāna" (ablative case).

309. Also [the term] *apādāna* applies to that which is connected with verbal roots (*dhātu*), nouns (*nāman*), prefixes (*upasagga*), and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), with particles (*nipāta*). Verbal roots and nouns are "verbal-roots-and-nouns" (*dhātunāmāni*). When such verbal roots and nouns—whose specific grammatical characteristics have not been otherwise prescribed—are employed, and when there is connection with a prefix, and by the word "and so forth," also connection with a particle, the case-factor (*kāraka*) associated with them receives the designation *apādāna*.

First, regarding connection with a verbal root: in connection with *parā-ji* (to defeat), that which is "unbearable" (*asayha*); in connection with *pabhu* (powerful/master), the "source" (*pabhava*); in connection with *jani* (to be born), that which is being born.
And by way of nature (*pakati*). For example: non-Buddhist sectarians are defeated by the Buddha;
the five great rivers originate from the Himalayas, they originate from the great lake Anavatatta, and the small streams originate from the Aciravatī;
sorrow is born from desire, for from that [desire] fire is born; a son is born from the breast, and the faculty is born from karma.

In connection with nouns (*nāmappayoge*), when joined with words such as *aññatra*, *itarā*, etc.: "Nothing arises other than suffering; nothing ceases other than suffering"; "by karma other than that"; "the other than that"; "a son well-born from both [parents]"; and so forth. In connection with prefixes (*upasaggayuttesu*):

when joined with *apa* and *pari* in the sense of exclusion (*vajjanatthe*); when joined with *ā* in the sense of limit (*mariyādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*); and when joined with *pati* in the sense of substitution (*patinidhi*) or replacement (*patidāna*).
For example: "Merchants come from outside the hall" (*apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā*), meaning "excluding the hall."
