Meaning: likewise, "paripabbatā devo vassati" means "the rain-god rains, avoiding the mountain. In the sense of a boundary: "āpabbatā khettaṃ" [means] "a field up to the mountains. In the sense of pervasion:
"ābrahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchati" means "the sound rises up reaching as far as the Brahma-world. In the sense of a representative:
"buddhasmā pati sāriputto dhammadesanāya ālapati temāsaṃ" [means] "for three months, Sāriputta speaks on the teaching of the Dhamma as the Buddha’s representative. In the sense of giving back...
He gives him a vessel from the oil; he gives him gold from the treasure.
In the case of compounds with indeclinables (*nipāta*), when joined with *rite*, *nānā*, or *vinā*: "Apart from the True Dharma (*saddhamma*), where could one obtain happiness?
Those monks have gone forth from various clans. Apart from the True Dharma, no other protector is found in the world. This [person] is indeed distinct from the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
The sound of the people rises up as far as the Brahma-world.
By the inclusion of the word "api" (also), the ablative case is used even among the factors of action such as the instrument and the object;

for example, *pakkhasmā vijjhati migaṃ luddako* means "the hunter pierces the deer from one side," which is to say he pierces the deer from this flank. Likewise, *māsasmā bhuñjati bhojanaṃ* [means "he eats food once a month"].
The sheath pierces the elephant.

By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, [it indicates] the sense of "starting from" (*pabhuti*) and so forth, as well as its application in that sense—as in: "Sister, from the time I was born with noble birth;
from when I remember myself; from the time I attained discernment; on account of which; starting from when."
"From which point," "starting from which point," and so forth.
310. That which is intended as the object of protection [is the apādāna].
In the usage of verbal roots whose meaning is protection, that factor which is intended becomes designated as the *apādāna* (ablative) case; this is due to the governing rule of the letter *ca*.
And [the term] *anicchitaṃ* (the undesired). Here, protection (*rakkhaṇaṃ*) consists of warding off (*nivāraṇaṃ*) and safeguarding (*tāyaṇaṃ*). For example: "The rice wards off the crows;

the barley keeps the cows away. As for the undesired: "One should ward off the mind from evil"; or "May they provide protection against evil," or from kings, thieves, fire, water, various dangers, various diseases, or various calamities.
The word "desired" (*icchitaṃ*) carries over [from the previous rule].
311. Or, that by which there is non-seeing (*adassana*).

That agent by which non-seeing is intended, while [the object] disappears, receives the designation of the ablative (*apādāna*); this refers to the act of disappearing itself. For example: "The pupil disappears from the preceptor" (*upajjhāyā antaradhāyati sisso*), meaning he hides himself.
"The son disappears from his parents. Why say "or"? [Consider: "He disappeared in the Jeta Grove. Why say "by which" (*yena*)? [Consider: "The yakkha disappeared right there."

312. [The suffix *tā* is used] in the sense of distance (*dūra*), proximity (*antika*), measurement of space (*addhanimmāna*), measurement of time (*kālanimmāna*), elision of the suffix *-tvā* (*tvālopa*), connection with a direction (*disāyoga*), division (*vibhatta*), application of the word *ārata*, application of the sense of purity (*suddhattha*), application of the sense of release (*pamocanattha*), the sense of cause (*hetvattha*), application of the sense of separation (*vivittattha*), the sense of measure (*pamāṇattha*), words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*), questions (*pañha*), narration (*kathana*), and in cases where the agent is not explicitly mentioned (*athokākattūsu*).

[In detail: in the sense of distance; in the sense of proximity; in the measurement of space; in the measurement of time; in the elision of the suffix *-tvā*; in connection with a direction; in the case of division;

in the application of the word *ārata*; in the application of the sense of purity; in the application of the sense of release; in the sense of cause; in the application of the sense of separation; in the sense of measure.

In the case of *pubbayoga* (prior connection), *bandhanatthappayoga* (connection with the sense of binding), *guṇavacana* (words expressing qualities), *pañha* (question), *kathana* (telling), *thokattha* (the sense of "a little"),
and that which has become a limit (*avadhibhūta*) as well as that which has become a cause (*hetu*) or an object (*kamma*), that *kāraka* receives the designation *apādāna*;
by the word *ca* ("and"), the second, third, and sixth cases are applied as appropriate.

And here, in the phrase "distant and near, and the meaning of distant and near," it should be understood that *dūrantika* is stated using the *sarūpeka-śeṣa* (single-remainder) compound; therefore, when used in the sense of distance or nearness, as well as in that specific sense, it receives the designation of *apādāna*.
First, regarding usage in the sense of distance: "How far from here is Naḷakāra village? "Indeed, they say it is even further than that. "Not very far from the village.
"Those foolish men are far removed from this Dhamma and Vinaya. "The Blessed One is far removed from them. In the sense of distance...
“They pay homage from afar”—he saw him coming from afar.
In the usage of words meaning “near”: *antikaṃ gāmā*, *āsannaṃ gāmā*, *samīpaṃ gāmā*—the meaning is “from near the village” or “in the vicinity of the village.
For the second and third cases: *dūraṃ gāmaṃ āgato*, *dūrena gāmena āgato*, *dūrato gāmā āgato*—the meaning is “he has come from a distant village.”
“By means of a distant village” (*dūraṃ gāmena vā*). “He has come from a near village,” or “by means of a near village” (*antikaṃ gāmena vā*), meaning a proximate village;

and so forth. Regarding the formation of distance and time (*addhakālanimmāne*): “formation” (*nimmāna*) here means measurement; when that is being expressed—as for example, Sāṅkassa is four *yojanas* from Mathurā, or Sāvatthī is at a distance of forty-five *yojanas* from Rājagaha.

Regarding the formation of time—as for example, the Blessed One Vipassī appeared in the world ninety-one aeons ago, or a Buddha will appear in the world after the passing of one thousand years from now.
The elision (*lopa*) of the *tvā*-suffix means its non-existence even when its meaning is present. When that *tvā*-elision occurs, in the case of the accusative and locative cases:
*pāsādā saṅkameyya* means "having ascended the palace, he would cross over. Likewise: *hatthikkhandhā saṅkameyya*;
*abhidhammā pucchanti* means "having heard the Abhidhamma" or "having asked about the Abhidhamma"; *abhidhammā kathayanti* means "having [studied] the Abhidhamma. The Abhidhamma...
Having recited [it], he should rise from his seat, or sit upon the seat.
In connection with words expressing direction, and regarding the meaning of direction: "From here is that eastern direction;

from here is that southern direction; from here is that western direction; from here is that northern direction; from Avīci up to the peak of existence; upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards..."

"From the tips of the hair," and so forth. In the sense of direction: "from the east," "from the south," and so forth. Here, however, the suffix *-to* will also occur in the sense of the locative case.
What is called "divided" (*vibhatta*) is the act of dividing by means of a quality that which is already divided from something else; in that which is thus divided—
Since there is nothing more excellent or more distinguished than this, self-restraint is therefore better.
Although virtue is indeed better than giving, yet that which I have heard is much more than what I have not heard; thus, virtue is superior to mere learning.
And among the ninety-six sects, the discipline of the Sugata is the most preeminent.

The application of terms in the sense of abstaining is called *ārati-p-payoga*. In this regard: "Abstention from unrighteous things," "refraining from evil," "abstinence from taking life," "he refrains from taking what is not given," "he does not refrain from false speech.
In the application of terms in the sense of purity: "Pure and unadulterated by things that provoke greed," "pure on the mother's and father's side, irreproachable and beyond censure.

In the application of terms in the sense of liberation: "I declare him completely released from suffering," "freed from the bonds of Māra," "they are not released from death," "I am freed from all snares."
In the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*), because the form of the *ekasesa* (inclusion) is taken—since it is used in the sense of a cause from a pronoun—the following examples occur:
"Why indeed do your young ones not die? Why will death occur right here? Why? Because of the cause;
and because they perform karmas. And: "Because, monks, therefore, monks, you should train thus"; "Therefore, I am the Buddha."
*Brāhmaṇa*, *yasmā kāraṇā*, *tasmā kāraṇā*, *kiṃ kāraṇā*: here the second and sixth cases [are used].

*Kiṃ kāraṇaṃ*, *taṃ kissa hetu*, *kissa tumhe kilamatha*, *kena hetunā*, *kena kāraṇena*, *yena midhekacce sattā*, *tena nimittena*, *tena vuttaṃ*—in such instances as these, the third case is used according to the rule "and in the sense of cause" (*hetvatthe ca*).

"Secluded" (vivitta) means separation; in its application to that purpose—as in "secluded from evil states," "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and "secluded from unwholesome states"—it refers to this.

In the sense of measurement, the third case is used: one *yojana* in length and breadth is the measure for Candabhāgā; one *yojana* in depth and width is the measure for the middle country (*majjhimapadesa*), which is nine hundred *yojanas* in circumference.
In terms of length, it should be made according to the measure of nine spans of the Sugata’s span.
And here, following the rules beginning with "smāhismiṃnaṃ," while the words "smā" and "so vā" are in effect:
313. *Dīghorehi*.
After the long vowels *ī* and *ū*, the substitution of *so* for the word ending in *smā* occurs optionally.

"Longwise" (*dīghaso*), "from the long" (*dīghamhā*); or "nearwise" (*oraso*), "from the near" (*oramhā*). The third [case ending] is used: one *yojana* in length, one *yojana* in breadth, and one *yojana* in height—a heap of mustard seeds.

The term *pubbayoga* (prior connection) is a compound with the word *pubba* ("prior") functioning as the first member expressing the meaning. Here, the inclusion of the word *pubba* should be understood as an illustration for the inclusion of *pubba* and other such terms that function as the first members of a compound;
therefore, it applies even in connections with *para* and so forth. For example: *pubbeva me*.
"Monks, prior to this awakening there was [no such thing]; after that, the border regions, conditions beyond the marks of the elements;
then at a later time, and even further than that," and so forth.

In the application of the sense of "bondage," when there is a cause of bondage, namely a debt, the fifth case (pañcamī) occurs, as well as the third case (tatiyā): "The man is bound because of a hundred by the king," or "the man is bound for a hundred."

A "quality-word" (guṇavacana) is a word expressing a quality that serves as the cause for the accomplishment of a result; in such a quality-word, both the fifth (ablative) and third (instrumental) cases are used, as in:
"The king protects the people by his sovereignty" (*issariyā*), or "by his sovereignty" (*issariyena*); "They praise him for his virtue" (*sīlato*), or "by his virtue" (*sīlena*);
"One whose mind is liberated through wisdom," and so forth.
In the *Pañhakathā* (Explanations of Questions): "From where are you? From where is your lordship? [The answer is: "From Pāṭaliputta. Here, "speaking" (*kathana*) means answering.

The third case ending (*tatiyā*) is used in the sense of "a little" (*thoka*), provided it does not denote a sentient being (*asatvavacana*) and functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Examples: "He is released by a little" (*thokā muccati*), or "he is released with a little" (*thokena muccati*); "he is released by a small amount" (*appamattakā muccati*), or "with a small amount" (*appamattakena*); "he is released with difficulty" (*kicchā muccati*), or "with difficulty" (*kicchena*).

When there is no agent (*akattarī akārake*)—that is, when the cause is one that makes known (*ñāpaka-hetu*)—[the third case is used] because of the performance, accumulation, increase, or abundance of an action (*kamma*).

When eye-consciousness has arisen, this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is certainly not without cause, because otherwise it would result in a state of being identical for everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
It is not permanent because it exists after having been non-existent, and it is subject to oppression by arising and passing away.
“Suffering because of lack of mastery; ‘non-self’—these are the three characteristics.
The term “the fifth” carries over. 314.
And [it applies] in the sense of cause.

That which produces its own fruit is the "productive cause" (*kāraka-hetu*); and in the sense of this causal factor, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī-vibhatti*) occurs, as it is prescribed optionally along with the third case ending in the sense of a cause.
Through non-comprehension, through lack of penetration, and through not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, one has thus run on and wandered through this long course of existence.

“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, [feeling ceases],” and so forth.
In what sense is the genitive case used here?
315. The sixth case [ending] is used for the owner (*sāmī*).
And who is the owner?
316. Or, that which is someone's possession, he is the owner.

"It is grasped" (*pariggayhati*) thus it is "possession" (*pariggaho*). Whatever is someone's possession—that which is dependent upon or connected to it—that object is designated as "possessive" (*sāmisa*). By the inclusion of the word "or," this applies even when there is a connection with pain (*rujā*) and so forth that ought to be possessed.

And here, because there is no connection with an action (*kriyā*), the status of a "factor of action" (*kāraka*) is not possible. For the state of being a possessor (*sāmibhāva*) is understood as a result of the relationship between an action and its factors;
for instance, when it is said, "the king’s man," since the king gives [to him] and the man [receives].

Because he accepts [the commands], he is therefore known as "the king’s man. Thus, whoever is dependent upon another—whether by way of being a servant and so forth, or by way of being a commodity, or through proximity, collection, part, modification, effect, state, genus, quality, action, and so on—for all such cases, that [dependent] person is the basis for the relationship;
it serves as a qualifier and is threefold according to its mode of arrival (āgamī).
The meaning should be understood as "the master.
And it has been said: "Born from the action and the agent..."
The genitive case ending (assedaṃ) is based on the cause of the state;
that meaning is called "relation" (sambandha),
and therein the sixth [case] is prescribed.
For dependence is indeed a relation;
therefore, the genitive case would apply there.
It is understood by means of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
"Not because of a qualification, etc. First, regarding "because of a qualification":
in the phrase *rañño puriso* ("the king's man"), here the king qualifies and distinguishes the man from other masters;

thus, he is a "qualification" (*visesana*). The man is that which is to be qualified by him; thus, he is "to be qualified" (*visesitabba*). In this way, in all instances involving that which is to be qualified, the genitive case is used precisely because of the qualification.
In the sense of connection by ownership (*sambandhe*): "I have abundant wealth, Sakka; this is the share for him—the bowl and robes of the bhikkhu.
In the sense of connection by proximity (*samīpasambandhe*): "Not far from the mango grove," or "in the very presence of Nibbāna.
In the sense of connection by collection (*samūhasambandhe*): "A heap of gold," or "a multitude of bhikkhus."
In the case of a relationship of parts (*avayava-sambandha*): "The head belongs to the person; the branch belongs to the tree.
In the case of a relationship of modification (*vikāra-sambandha*): "A transformation of gold"; "flour from cooked grain.
In the case of a relationship of effect (*kāriya-sambandha*): "A sprout of barley"; "the sound of a cloud"; "his sons are many"; "the fruit is the ripening of actions."
In relation to states (*avasthā*): the manifestation of the aggregates, the aging of the aggregates, the dissolution of the aggregates.
In relation to birth (*jāti*): the state of being human, the birth of humans.
In relation to qualities (*guṇa*): the color of gold, the color of the Tathāgata does not fade, the sound of the Buddha’s qualities.
The fragrance of flowers, the taste of fruits, the contact of the mind, the hundred [types of] craftsmen, a handful of sesame seeds,
their combination, the release from bondage, concerning the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom,
or his former conduct, "What is your pleasure? What is your pain?"— thus a reflection arose in the mind, the proficiency of wisdom regarding form.
Lightness, malleability of matter, and integration of matter.
In relation to action: the lifting of the foot, or the lowering of the foot; the bending of the hand; the stretching out of the feet;
the going of the elements, as well as the standing, sitting, or lying down of the elements themselves. Likewise...
[Examples include: his name and clan, etc.; the reason for that; his mother and father; it appeared before him; behind him;
to the south of the city; in the third month of the rains; there is no simile for him; the offering to Kuvera, and so forth.
Regarding the grammatical position (*ṭhānito*): *ya* is the substitute for *edanta*, and *o* is the substitute for *ava*.
In the sense of "arrival": *puthassāgamo* ("the arrival of many"), and so forth. In connection with the genitive (*sāmiyoge*):
*devānamindo* ("lord of the gods"), *migānaṃ rājā* ("king of the deer").

In connection with the suffixes *-tabba*, *-ruja*, etc.: *mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ* ("it is to be lamented, wailed, and cried out by the great generals"), *devadattassa rujati* ("Devadatta suffers pain"), *tassa rogo uppajjati* ("a disease arises for him"), *rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti* ("he gives cloth to the washerman"), *musāvādassa ottappaṃ* ("shame regarding false speech"), and so forth.
The phrase “in some cases, [the case endings] of the third and seventh [cases]” is understood [to carry over]. 317.
And the sixth [case].
In some instances, the sixth case ending occurs in the sense of the third and seventh cases.
In the sense of "offering": one offers a flower to the Buddha, or with a flower; one makes an oblation of ghee into the fire. In connection with the sense of "fullness":
having filled the bowl with rice—meaning "with rice. One contemplates this very body as full of various kinds of impurity; it is full of gold and silver; the fool is filled with evil.

In the case of construction with *tulya*, *attha*, *kima*, *alaṃ*, and so forth: "equal to the father," or "equal by means of the father"; "similar to the mother," or "similar by means of the mother. The meaning is: "What to him who is satisfied? or "What [use] to him who is satisfied? "Enough for him who is satisfied.

In the case of construction with the *ki* suffix (*kitappaccaya*) when denoting the agent: "The *kati* (verse) of Kaccāyana is beautiful," or "by Kaccāyana"; "approved by the king," or "by the king. Likewise:
"honored by the king," "respected by the king," "venerated by the king," "esteemed by the king. "The Deathless for them..."
“Monks, it is unused... for those by whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been used,” and so forth.
In the sense of the seventh case (locative), when joined with *kusala* and other terms: “Women skilled in the training of dance and song”;
“You are skilled in the parts and members of the chariot”; “skilled in the path”; “skilled in the non-path”; for there are, O Blessed One, sublime [beings]...
The *yakkhas* were devoted to the Blessed One; three times a day, or three times during the day, or twice a month, and so forth.
The term "in some cases, the sixth [case]" also recurs. 318. And [the sixth case is used] for the second and fifth cases as well.
The sixth case ending occurs in the sense of the second and fifth cases, and in some instances, it also occurs in the sense of the sixth case.
Regarding the sense of the second case (the object) in connection with the agent of an action (*kamma-kāraka*):

they are the speakers of that [truth], the performers of deeds with haste, the givers of the Deathless, the reconcilers of those who are divided, the promoters of those who are united, the awakener of the world, [and] of the deed.
There is no agent, nor is there an experiencer of the result; one does not deceive the world. Not committing evil deeds is happiness.
Sensitivity arises dependent upon the four great elements. It is marvelous how cloth is dyed by one who is not a dyer;
it is marvelous how cows are milked by one who is not a cowherd.

Likewise, regarding the function of rivers and so forth: *mātu sarati*, *mātaraṃ sarati* (he remembers his mother), or *na tesaṃ koci sarati* (no one remembers them); [these occur] due to the condition of the karma of sentient beings. Regarding *puttassa icchati* (he desires a son) and *puttamicchati* (he desires a son):

[this refers to] the basis for its performance (*karotissa patiṭṭhāne*). The basis is volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*). *Udakassa patikurute* (he remedies the water), *udakaṃ patikurute* (he remedies the water), *kaṇḍassa patikurute* (he remedies the wound), *kaṇḍaṃ patikurute* (he remedies the wound).

In the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamiyatthe*), when joined with the meaning of fear of decline (*parihānibhayattha*): *assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti* (through not hearing the Dhamma, they decline); *kiṃ nu kho*...?
"I fear that pleasure; all tremble at punishment, all fear death" (Dhp 129), and "fearing four venomous snakes," and so forth. What is the meaning of "in some cases"?

One who delivers a profound discourse, one who speaks a timely discourse on the Dhamma, one who rejoices in the merits of others, one who has awakened to the Truths, a doer of what is beneficial, and a slayer of cattle.

Likewise, it does not occur in the case of *niṭṭhā* (completion) and so forth—as in: *sukhakāmī vihāraṃ kato*, *rathaṃ katavanto*, *rathaṃ katāvī*, *kaṭaṃ katvā*, *kaṭaṃ karonto*, *kaṭaṃ karāno*, *kaṭaṃ kurumāno*, and so on.
In what sense is the locative case used? 319. The locative case is used in the sense of location (*okāsa*).
The seventh case ending occurs when expressing the location (*okāsa*).
And what is the location?
It is that which serves as the basis for the recitation. 320. That which is the basis for the recitation is the location.

That in which something is supported is the *ādhāra* (locus), that is, the *adhikaraṇa* (substratum). That factor which serves as the support for actions such as sitting or cooking—actions inherent in the agent or the object—in the sense of being their foundation, is the grammatical factor known as the *okāsa* (locative).

For example: "Devadatta sits on a mat" (*kaṭe nisīdati devadatto*) and "He cooks rice in a pot" (*thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati*). Here, because it supports the agent Devadatta and the object rice, it is said to support the actions termed "sitting" and "cooking" which are inherent in them.
This locus is fourfold: pervasive (*byāpika*), contiguous (*opasilesika*), proximate (*sāmīpika*), and absolute (*vesayika*).

In this context, "pervasive" (*byāpika*) refers to that wherein the entire substratum (*ādhāra*) is spread over by the superstratum (*ādheya*), or that which remains after having pervaded some superstratum;
for example: "there is oil in sesame seeds," "water in dewdrops," and "ghee in curds.
"Adhesive" (*opasilesika*) refers to that wherein there is an approach through adhesion (*upasileśa*) among entities established individually, and wherein—

The *ādheyya* (the supported) remains by clinging to it, as for example: "the Saṅgha is seated on the seat," "he cooks rice in the pot," "there is water in the jars," "standing far away," or "standing nearby.

The *sāmīpika* (proximate) [locative] is that where, by applying the designation of proximity to what is near, the state of being a support is indicated for the purpose of showing dependence upon that.
It is designated [metaphorically], as for example: "A sound dwells in the Ganges" means that a sound dwells near the Ganges;
"The Blessed One dwells at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove" means he dwells near Sāvatthī.
What is called a "locative relation" (vesayika) is that state of being a locus by virtue of the absence [of the object] elsewhere, or by virtue of delimiting it from other regions.

A hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*), such as: "birds fly in the sky," "people walk on the ground," "fish [swim] in water," "fallen at the feet," "the mind delights in evil," "confident in the Buddha’s teaching," "skilled in wisdom," "proficient in the discipline (*vinaya*)," "good toward one's mother," "skillful toward one's father," and so forth.
Furthermore, this entire basis should be understood as being called "the occasion" (okāsa) because it serves as the foundation for action, either by way of exertion or by way of conceptualization.
And this has been said:
"Action [is the cause] of the agent and the object..."
Wherever it is established,
that is called an "occasion" (okāsa);
it is fourfold, beginning with that which pervades.
The pervasive [metaphor] is exemplified by sesame milk and the like; the metaphorical (kaṭa) is exemplified by the plastering;
the proximate (sāmīpika), however, is exemplified by the Ganges and the like.
“Space is considered the object.

The sixth and seventh [cases] are the governing rule. 321. [The sixth case is used] with the words *sāmi* (owner), *issara* (lord), *adhipati* (ruler), *dāyāda* (heir), *sakkhin* (witness), *patibhū* (surety), *upa* (near), *sūta* (born), and *kusala* (skilled).

The sixth case ending occurs with the words *sāmī* (owner), *issara* (lord), *adhipati* (master), *dāyāda* (heir), *sakkhi* (witness), *patibhū* (surety), *pasūta* (born of), and *kusala* (skilled) when used in conjunction [with these senses]. The seventh case ending also occurs. The statement applies to both cases.
Examples: *gavāṃ sāmī*, *gosu sāmī*; *gavāṃ issaro*, *gosu issaro*; *gavāṃ adhipati*, *gosu adhipati*;
*gavāṃ dāyādo*, *gosu dāyādo*; *gavāṃ sakkhi*, *gosu sakkhi*; *gavāṃ patibhū*, *gosu patibhū*.
*gavaṃ pasūto* (born among cows), *gosu pasūto* (born among cows); *gavaṃ kusalo* (skilled among cows), *gosu kusalo* (skilled among cows). 322.
*Niddhāraṇe ca* (and in the sense of selection).
Selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is the act of setting apart after having extracted; it is the separation of a single part from a whole by means of genus, quality, action, or name.
When the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is implied, the sixth case ending (*chaṭṭhīvibhatti*) and the seventh case ending (*sattamī*) occur after a word expressing a collective group.
For example: *manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo* (among men, the warrior is the most courageous), *manussesu khattiyo sūratamo*;

*kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā* (among black cows, the one with the most abundant milk), *kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā*; *addhikānaṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo* (among travelers, the runner is the swiftest), *addhikesu dhāvanto*.
The Venerable Ānanda was one of the most swift [in attaining] among the Arahants, or among the Arahants, and so forth.
323. And in the sense of disregard (*anādara*).

When disregard is implied, the sixth case ending occurs after a word expressing a state, and the seventh case ending as well. He went forth while his unwilling mother and father were weeping; he went forth while his mother and father were weeping.
Striking him, Death leads him away while King Sivi looks on;
taking him, Death departs.
While the great multitude was looking on.

324. The seventh case ending occurs after a word [ending in] a nominal stem when expressing the meanings of "object," "instrument," and "cause. That is to say, the seventh case ending occurs after a nominal stem when these meanings—object, instrument, and cause—are intended.
In the sense of the object (*kamma-attha*): "When they salute the monks, having kissed their heads, they take hold of the man by his arms.

In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa-attha*): "They wander for alms with their hands; they wander for alms with their bowls; they walk on paths; may he also instruct me; I accept it upon my head. In the sense of the cause or motive (*nimitta-attha*):

"The leopard is killed for its skins; the elephant is killed for its tusks; seeing fear even in the slightest faults, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for intentional lying. The meaning is: "on account of lying, by reason of lying."
“Seventh” is the governing heading. 325.
And in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna).

The seventh case ending occurs after a noun when it signifies the recipient. “What is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit; give, Gotamī, to the Saṅgha. When you have given to the Saṅgha, I myself will be honored.”
The woman who, having offered a garland made of straw at a shrine, obtained a garland made of gold and [attained] the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). 326.
And in the sense of the fifth case.
The seventh case ending occurs after a noun in the sense of the fifth case (ablative). For example: *kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti* ("They protect the elephants among the plantains").
327. It also occurs in the sense of time (*kāla*) and state (*bhāva*).

"Time" refers to such units as a blink of an eye (*nimesa*), a moment (*khaṇa*), a beat (*laya*), an instant (*muhutta*), morning (*pubbaṇha*), and so forth; "state" refers to action (*kriyā*), and in this context, it is specifically characterized by another action.
The seventh case ending occurs after a noun when it signifies time (*kāla*), as well as when it signifies a characteristic of a state (*bhāva-lakkhaṇa*) or a state itself (*bhāva*).

**Regarding time:** *Pubbaṇhasamaye gato* (He went at the time of forenoon); *sāyanhasamaye āgato* (He returned at the time of evening); *akāle vassati tassa* (It rains for him out of season); *kāle tassa na vassati* (It does not rain for him in season); *phussamāsamhā tīsu māsesu vesākhamāso* (From the month of Phussa, Vesākha is three months [later]); *ito satasahassamhi kappe uppajji cakkhumā* (A hundred thousand aeons from now, the Visionary One arose).

**Regarding a characteristic of a state:** *bhikkhusaṅghesu bhojīyamānesu gato* (He went while the community of monks was being fed); *bhuttesu āgato* (He returned after they had eaten); *gosu duyhamānāsu* (While the cows were being milked).
When he had gone and returned from his search, Sāriputta, at the very moment the Bodhisatta was being born, this ten-thousandfold world system trembled,
shook, and quaked. Stones and pebbles,
gravel, stumps, and thorns— [all were leveled].
All paths avoid [the Buddha] as he goes, the Leader of the World.
"When this exists, that comes to be," and so forth.
328. In the statement regarding the essential meaning of the *Upajjhā* (Preceptor).

This is a two-line [rule]. When used in conjunction with the words *upa*, *adhi*, and *īsa*—which express the senses of "excess" (*adhika*) and "lordship" (*issara*)—the seventh case ending occurs after a noun when the sense of "excess" or "lordship" is implied.

Regarding the sense of excess: *upa khāriyaṃ doṇo* (a *doṇa* measure is in excess of a *khārī*); the meaning is that a *doṇa* is more than a *khārī*. Likewise: *upa nikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ* (one *kahāpaṇa* is in excess).

Regarding lordship: *adhi devesu buddho* (the Buddha is above the gods). Here, the term "gods" (*deva*) refers to the threefold classification of gods: conventional, rebirth-born, and purified. The Omniscient One [is above] all these types of gods.
The meaning is: “the Buddha alone is superior.
In the sense of sovereignty (*issaravacana*): *adhi brahmadatte pañcālā*, meaning “the Pañcālas have Brahmadatta as their sovereign. 329.
In the sense of ornamenting (*maṇḍita*) and desiring (*ussukka*), the third case is also used.
When these meanings—*maṇḍita*, *ussukka*, and so forth—are understood, the third case ending occurs after the word [ending in] a nominal stem, as does the seventh case ending.
Here, the word *maṇḍita* expresses the sense of "clear" (*pasanna*), while the word *ussukka* means "exerting effort" (*sa-īhā*).
A good person is one who is clear through knowledge, clear in respect to knowledge; one who exerts effort through knowledge, or exerts effort in respect to knowledge.
The *kāraka* is sixfold, yet becomes twenty-sixfold by way of its designations;
action (*kamma*) is sevenfold by its divisions, and the agent (*kattā*) may be fivefold.
The instrument (*karaṇa*) is twofold, and the recipient (*sampadāna*) is considered to be threefold.
The ablative (*apādāna*) is fivefold, while the locative (*ādhāra*) is fourfold.

Furthermore, the case endings (*vibhatti*) are eightfold, according to the nominative (*paccatta*), accusative (*upayoga*), instrumental (*karaṇa*), dative (*sampadāniya*), and so forth. As it has been said:
"The nominative, the accusative, the instrumental, the dative..."
"The ablative, the genitive, the locative, and the vocative are the eighth.
Thus ends the third section, the Section on Kārakas, in the *Padarūpasiddhi*.

4. The Section on Compounds (Samāsakaṇḍa) Now, because it depends upon nouns—since a compound (*samāsa*) is defined as the mutual connection of nouns—and because it is itself nominal in nature, the compound is discussed immediately after the nouns.
Furthermore, by way of technical designation (*saññā*), it is sixfold: *abyayībhāva*, *kammadhāraya*, *digu*, *tappurisa*, *bahubbīhi*, and *dvanda*.
The *Abyayībhāva* Compound:
First, the *abyayībhāva* compound is explained;
it is an obligatory compound (*niccasamāsa*) with the analytical phrase (*assapadaviggaha*) "with that" (*tatra*).

Regarding the term "upanagaraṃ": here, from the prefix *upa*, there is the nominative singular; because it follows a prefix, its [final] vowel is elided by the rule "of all [vowels], O friend, after prefixes, particles, and so forth.

From the word *nagara*, there is the genitive singular *sa*. In the analysis (*viggha*) as "in the vicinity of the city" (*nagarassa samīpaṃ*), which is a compound of different words (*aññapada*), the rule for forming compounds—"A compound of nouns [expressing] a connected meaning"—applies in all instances.
330. *Abyayībhāva* is that which is preceded by a prefix (*upasagga*) or a particle (*nipāta*).
A nominal base (*nāmika*) whose meaning is connected [to another] is always compounded with those very prefixes or particles that precede it;
and that compound is designated as *abyayībhāva*. Here, we shall deal only with the sūtras that prescribe the technical designations (*saññā*) such as *abyayībhāva*.
Or rather, they should be understood as rules prescribing compounds by way of designating technical terms (*saññā*).
In this context, "indeclinable" (*abyaya*) is the designation for prefixes and particles because they are devoid of change (*byaya*), even though they differ in gender and number.

It is called *abyayībhāva* because it clarifies the meaning of indeclinables; it is so named because the meaning of the indeclinable comes first, or because that which was not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable.
Or it is an *abyayībhāva* compound. For an *abyayībhāva* has the meaning of the preceding member as its primary focus;
and since it is stated here that [the compound] "is preceded by prepositions (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*)," only prepositions and particles are placed first. 331.
A compound of nouns (*nāma*) is one whose meaning is connected [with the members].

The connected meaning (*yuttattha*) of those nouns when their referents are being employed is designated as a compound (*samāsa*); anything other than that is conventionally known as a sentence (*vākya*). Nouns are those ending in case-suffixes such as *si*, etc.;
"compound" (*samāsa*) means that which is condensed (*samassati*), that is, it is abbreviated (*saṅkhipiyati*).
For it has been said:
“A compound (samāsa) is a contraction of words;
that which is joined with suffixes to a word is called a secondary derivative (taddhita). Thus they should be understood as distinct from one another.
Furthermore, its compounding is twofold: the compounding of sounds and the compounding of meanings; both of these occur in elided compounds (luttasamāsa).

Only the complete form is obtained. However, in the case of an *alutta*-compound (where the elided case-ending is not restored), only the form with identical meaning is found due to the absence of the case-ending elision;
yet even there, both types are indeed possible because it attains the status of a single word (*ekapada*). For there are two purposes for a compound:
being a single word and having a single case-ending.
“Yuttattha” means that whose meaning is joined (*yutta*) or connected (*saṅgata*), or whose meaning is related;

by this expression “yuttattha,” which signifies being joined, it is stated that the unification of meanings (*ekatthībhāva*) of words with different meanings is the defining characteristic of a compound (*samāsa*).
And here, by the mention of the word “nāmānam” (of nouns), there is no compounding with a verb in cases such as “Devadatto pacati” (Devadatta cooks).
This shows that there is no [compound]. Furthermore, by taking the sense of connection as the appropriate meaning,

it illustrates that there is no compound due to the lack of appropriateness (*ayuttattha*) in cases such as "The king’s servant is Devadatta’s son," where the terms do not depend on one another, and in cases such as "Devadatta’s teeth are black," where they depend on something else.
“By reason of purpose, there is a change of case-ending”—by this change of form, the term “connected meaning” (*yuttattha*) is understood [to carry over]. 332.
Of those, there are case-endings and elisions.
Here, “connected meanings” refers to those that have become unified in sense either by means of another word, or by *taddhita* suffixes, or by suffixes such as *-āya* and so forth.

The meaning is that, by this [rule], "the case endings of those compounds whose meanings are joined together, as well as those ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *aya*, *i*, etc., are to be elided.

However, when the governing heading of "compounds" (*samāsa*) is present, the elision of the case endings occurs either through the inclusion of "those" (*tesaṃ*) or through the inclusion of "ending in secondary suffixes such as *aya*, *i*, etc.
The mention of "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of preventing the elision in cases such as "pabhaṅkaro" and so forth.
By way of modification, the phrase "when case-endings (*vibhatti*) have been elided" continues [from the previous rule], as does the inclusion of the sense of connection (*yuttattha*). 333.
And its original form (*pakati*) belongs to that which ends in a vowel.
When case-endings have been elided, the original form of that which ends in a vowel—namely, the threefold gender (*liṅga*) which constitutes the sense of connection—is maintained.

[The particle] *ca* [is used here] because even in cases such as "origination from what" (*kiṃsamudaya*) or "this-conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*), there is a suppression (*niggahīta*) [of the final vowel]. This extended application (*atidesa*) is employed because the absence of the effect is not intended here when the cause is absent.

Furthermore, since the compound here lacks its own specific meaning and possesses neither gender nor number, the case endings do not arise; thus, he states this extended application of the designation "noun" (*nāma*).

334. Words ending in *taddhita* suffixes, words ending in *ki* suffixes, and compounds (*samāsa*) are to be regarded as nouns (*nāman*), with the exception of those ending in the suffixes *tava*, *tuna*, *tvā*, *tvāna*, *tvādo*, and so forth.

The inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of extending the designation of "noun" to those ending in kṛt suffixes, verbal suffixes (*kicca*), feminine suffixes such as *ā*, *ī*, and *īnī*, and others.
Others say that here the mention of "compound" (samāsa) serves as a restriction, meaning that the designation "name" (nāma) applies only to compounds consisting of meaningful aggregates.
The term "abyayībhāva" is understood [from the previous rule]. 335. It is neuter in gender.

Thus, the *avyayībhāva* compound should be regarded as being exclusively neuter; this is its neuter gender. For here, even though there is an extension (*atidesa*) of gender, one must observe that in cases such as *adhipañña*, there is no undesirable consequence of the form becoming *adhiñāṇa* and so forth, because it is a different word (*saddantara*), just as in the case of *tipañña*.
Furthermore, this is not an extension [of gender], because in the Sutta, the word *iva*—which is the marker for an extension—is absent.
Because it is not seen [as such]. There may be the arising of *syā* as before.

The word "kvaci" (sometimes) is understood [to apply here]. 336. The case endings (*vibhatti*) following an indeclinable (*abyayībhāva*) compound ending in a vowel other than *a* take the suffix *am*.
Therefore, after neuter *avyayībhāva* compounds ending in *-am*, the suffix *am* optionally occurs before the following case endings;
the rest should be understood accordingly. *Tam upanagaram*: it stands near the city—this is the meaning. *Tāni upanagaram*: likewise in the vocative; "see that *upanagaram*," *tāni upanagaram*.
This change to *am* does not occur after the fifth (ablative) case, because of the governing rule "optionally" (*kvaci*).
The third, seventh, and sixth cases occur optionally.
By that [suffix], one says: *upanagaraṃ kataṃ* (a suburb was made), or *upanagarena* (by a suburb); *tehi upanagaraṃ* (a suburb by them), or *upanagarehi* (by suburbs);
*tassa upanagaraṃ dehi* (give a suburb to him), or *tesaṃ upanagaraṃ* (a suburb of theirs); *upanagarā ānaya* (bring from a suburb), or *upanagaramhā*, *upanagarasmā*, *upanagarehi*.

*Upanagaraṃ* means belonging to the vicinity of the city (*santakaṃ*), or of the vicinity of the city (*upanagarassa*); [it may refer to] those [things] of the vicinity of the city (*tesaṃ upanagaraṃ*), or of the vicinities of the city (*upanagarānaṃ*).
One should place [it] in the vicinity of the city (*upanagaraṃ nidhehi*); [the locative forms are] *upanagaramhi* or *upanagarasmiṃ*; [and the accusative forms are] *upanagaraṃ* or *upanagaresu*.
In the same way, *upakumbhaṃ*. Regarding absence (*abhāve*): the absence of distresses (*darathānaṃ*) is *niddarathaṃ*, as is *nimmasakaṃ*.
In the sense of "behind": *pacchā-rathaṃ* means behind the chariot (*anurathaṃ*), or downwind (*anuvātaṃ*).
In the sense of "suitability": *yathā-sarūpaṃ*, *anurūpaṃ*; the meaning is "suitable to form" (*rūpa-yoggaṃ*). In the sense of "distribution":
*paccattaṃ* means for each individual self (*attānaṃ attānaṃ pati*); *anvaddhamāsaṃ* means every half-month (*addhamāsaṃ addhamāsaṃ anu*).
*Anupubbiyaṃ*: In the sense of sequence—*anupubbo* means "one who follows in order" (*anujeṭṭhaṃ*).

In the sense of reverse order—*sotassa paṭilomaṃ* means "against the stream," *paṭisotaṃ*, *paṭipathaṃ*, or *pativātaṃ*. That which occurs with reference to oneself is *ajjhattaṃ*. In the senses of inclusion and limit:

*āpāṇakoṭiyā* [means] "as far as the limit of living beings" (*āpāṇakoṭikaṃ*). By the rule "in some cases, when the final member of a compound ends in a vowel, the suffix *-ka* is added," the suffix *-ka* is applied; thus, *ākumārehi yaso kaccāyanassa* becomes *ākumāraṃ* ("from childhood").

In the case of *samiddhiyaṃ*—where the meaning is "success in alms-food" (*bhikkhāya samiddhi*) and the compound has been formed with the neuter gender—the rule "at the end of a compound" (*samāsassa anto*) continues to apply. 337.
A vowel is shortened in the neuter.
The vowel at the end of a compound that occurs in the neuter gender becomes short.

In this context, the mention of *abyayībhāva* need not be repeated; therefore, the shortening of the final vowel of a compound occurring in the neuter is established even for *dig-*, *dvanda*, and *bahubbīhi* compounds.
By the rule "the substitution of *am* for the case endings," etc., there is the replacement with *am*. Thus: *subhikkham*. Near the Ganges (*gaṅgāya samīpe*).
The term *vattati* (is supplied) means "following after" (*upagaṅgaṃ*). *Upamaṇikaṃ* means "near the jewel-house" (*maṇikāya samīpaṃ*).

When compounds such as neuter gender and so forth have been formed in the sense of "among women" (*itthīsu amikicca*), the rule "from indeclinable compounds, [the elision] of case-endings" (*abyayībhāvā, vibhattīnaṃ*) is also supplied.
338. *Aññasmā lopa ca*.
There is also elision (*lopa*) of the case endings following an *abyayībhāva* compound other than one ending in the vowel *a*. For example:
*adhitti*, meaning "the discourse proceeds by depending upon women" (*itthīsu adhikicca kathā pavattati*). [Examples include: *adhitthi passa*, *adhitthi kataṃ*, and so forth; likewise, *adhikumāri*.
In *upavadhū* (near the bride), *upagu* (near the cattle), the long vowel *o* becomes short *u*. Thus [the prefix] is preceded by an upasagga. As for that preceded by a nipāta:
in *vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi* (the sequence of the elders) and *ye ye vuḍḍhā vā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ* (whichever elders, according to their seniority), there is no transgression of the word-meaning.

In *yathākkamaṃ*, *yathāsatti*, and *yathābalaṃ karoti* (he acts according to order, according to ability, according to strength), the meaning is that he acts without overstepping his strength (*balamanatikkamitvā*).
Whatever the extent of a living being’s limit is—namely, for as long as life lasts, for as long as the lifespan endures, or for the duration of an aeon—that is *yāvajīvam*.
Whatever the measure of what is needed is *yāvadattham*. The far side of a mountain is *tiropabbatam*; beyond a rampart, *tiropākāram*; beyond a wall, *tirokuṭṭam*.
Inside a palace is *antopāsādam*; inside a city, *antonagaram*; inside the rainy season, *antovassam*. Outside a city is *bahinagaram*; above a palace is *uparipāsādam*.

*Uparimañcaṃ*: the upper bed; *heṭṭhāmañcaṃ*: the bed below [another] bed; *heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ*: the lower story of a palace. *Purebhattaṃ*: before the meal; likewise, *pacchābhattaṃ* (after the meal). In the sense of "together with" (*sākalla*):

*samakkhikaṃ bhuñjati*—he eats together with flies; the meaning is that he avoids nothing. In the phrase "among these, there is the substitution of *sa*" and so forth, there is the substitution of *sa* for the word *saha*. Examples include *oragaṅgaṃ* (this side of the Ganges), and so on.
The indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva-samāsa*) is concluded.
The Kammadhāraya Compound:
Now the kammadhāraya compound is explained.

It is of nine kinds: that which has a qualifier as the first member, that which has a qualifier as the final member, that which has qualifiers as both members, that which has a simile as the final member, that which has a superlative as the first member, that which has an emphasis as the first member, that which has the negative particle *na* as the first member, that which has the particle *ku-* as the first member, and that which has the particle *pa-* as the first member.

In that regard, first concerning the compound where the qualifying term precedes: in the expression “*mahanta-purisa*,” there is the nominative singular in both cases here. The use of the particle *ca* and the word *ta* is for the purpose of establishing the state of having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa-bhāva*).

In the analysis (*viggahe*)—“and he is great, and he is a person”—from this point forward, the term “optionally” (*vibhāsā*) applies everywhere in the rules for forming compounds, starting from “*vibhāsā rukkhatiṇa*” and so forth.
339. When two words have a common substratum, it is a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive) compound.

Two nominal words that have the same grammatical referent (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) are optionally compounded with one another; when those two words have the same grammatical referent, that compound is designated as a *kammadhāraya*.
"Two words" means a pair of words. That which has a "same" (*tulya*) or identical referent (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning an object (*attha*), is "having the same grammatical referent" (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).

[This occurs] in that pair of words having the same grammatical referent, [namely] two words whose grounds for application (*pavatti-nimitta*) are distinct, existing in the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*visesana-visesitabba-bhāva*).
The occurrence of two words in a single meaning is "tulyādhikaraṇatā" (co-referentiality).

It is called *kammadhāraya* because it "holds" (*dhārayati*) a pair [of meanings] like an object (*kamma*). For just as an object holds a pair—namely, the action (*kriyā*) and the purpose (*payojana*)—since both action and purpose are possible only when there is an object;
so too this compound holds two names for a single meaning within that compound.
Because two names expressing a single meaning can occur together.

As before, there is the designation of a compound (*samāsa*), the elision of case-endings (*vibhattilopa*), and the retention of the base form (*pakatibhāva*); and since the state of having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇabhāva*) is already expressed by the compound itself, there is no employment of the words *ca* and *ta*, according to the rule: "There is no employment of [words] whose meaning has already been stated.
340. *Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade*: "The word *mahā* is substituted for *mahant* when it occurs in a word that has a common substratum."
The word *mahanta* becomes *maha* when followed by a subsequent member of the compound that has the same grammatical base (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).

By the inclusion of the plural form *mahantāni*, it is understood that in some instances there is also the substitution of *maha*. Furthermore, the fact that the qualifier is placed first [in the compound] is understood precisely from the rule prescribing the substitution of *maha* for the preceding member which serves as the qualifier.
The terms *kammadhāraya* and *digū* are understood [from the preceding rules].
341. Both are *tappurisa*.
Both the *kammadhāraya* and *digū* compounds receive the designation *tappurisa*.
*Tappurisa* means "his man" (*tassa puriso*). Because it resembles *tappurisa*, this compound is also called *tappurisa* by way of a designation that conforms to its meaning.
For just as the word *tappurisa* transcends its specific quality, so too does this compound. Indeed, a *tappurisa* has the meaning of the final member as its predominant factor;

thus, it receives the designation of a noun and the production of case endings (*syādi*). However, this *tappurisa* expresses its own referent (*abhidheyyavacana*) and takes the gender of the subsequent word (*paraliṅga*).

*Mahāpuriso*, *mahāpurisā*, and so forth, are examples where the word *purisa* (person) is preceded by *mahā*. Similarly, *mahāvīro* (Great Hero), *mahāmuni* (Great Sage). And because it is both "great" (*mahanta*) and "strength" (*bala*), it is *mahābalaṃ* (Great Strength);
likewise, *mahabbhayaṃ* (Great Fear), where the substitution of *maha-* occurs. Because he is both "virtuous" (*santo*) and "a person" (*puriso*), he is a *sappuriso* (True Person).

In the rule "In the case of the word *santa*, [the final vowel] becomes *so*, *be*, or *bo* before a consonant," the word *ca* (and) indicates that this change occurs even when the word *santa* is part of a compound, provided it is not followed by the letter *bh*.

There is substitution [of the suffix -a]: likewise, *pubbapuriso* (former man), *parapuriso* (other man), *paṭhamapuriso* (first man), *majjhimapuriso* (middle man), *uttamapuriso* (supreme man), *dantapuriso* (tamed man), *paramapuriso* (excellent man), *vīrapuriso* (heroic man), *setahatthī* (white elephant), *kaṇhasappo* (black snake), *nīluppalaṃ* (blue lotus), *lohitacandanaṃ* (red sandalwood).
In some cases, it does not occur due to the governing rule of optionality (*vibhāsā*), as in: *puṇṇo mantāniputto*, *citto gahapati*, *sakko devarājā*.
When the compound "pumā ca so kokilo ca" (he who is both a man and a cuckoo) has been formed, the term "elision" (lopa) applies.
342. [This occurs] in compounds where the masculine gender and other such factors are involved.

In compound words where the subsequent members are *liṅga* (gender) and so forth, the final vowel *a* of this [word] undergoes elision. According to the rule “*aṃmo niggahītaṃ jhalapehi*,” the *m* becomes a *niggahīta*. Thus: *puṅkokilo* (the male cuckoo). Likewise: *punnāgo* (the male *nāga* tree).
When the analysis (*viggaha*) “she is both a *khattiya* and a maiden” is formed into a compound, the following applies:
“When the case-referents (*adhikaraṇa*) are identical, in the feminine gender, if the word spoken as masculine is feminine, it remains masculine. This [rule] also continues in effect.

343. And in a compound designated as *kammadhāraya*. In a compound designated as *kammadhāraya*, when a feminine form is present and the following word (*uttarapada*) has a common referent (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), if the preceding word denoting a female was previously used in the masculine, that [preceding word] is to be regarded as if it were masculine;
thus, there is the elision of the feminine suffix in the preceding word.

“Khattiyakaññā,” “khattiyakaññāyo,” and so forth. Likewise, *rattalatā* (red creeper), *dutiyabhikkhā* (second alms-offering). And *brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā ca* becomes *brāhmaṇadārikā* (Brahmin girl); [the same applies to] *nāgamāṇavikā* (Naga maiden).

This transfer of the masculine form (*pumbhāva*) applies only to the preceding member; therefore, in cases such as *khattiyakumārī* (Brahmin princess), *kumārasamaṇī* (young female ascetic), and *taruṇabrāhmaṇī* (young Brahmin woman), the feminine suffix in the subsequent member is not elided. Why say “in the sense of a female”?
[Because otherwise it would apply to] *kumārīratanaṃ* (the jewel of a maiden) and *samaṇīpadumaṃ* (the lotus of a female ascetic).

What is that which has been stated as masculine? The river Gaṅgā, the river of craving (taṇhānadī), and the earth element (pathavīdhātu). However, in cases such as "the Nandā lotus pond" or "Queen Nandā," it does not apply because they are conventional terms (saññāsadda).
Likewise, "the eastern part of the body" is *puratthimakāya*; here, the word *kāya* refers to a portion of the body. Similarly:

"the western part of the body" (*pacchimakāya*), "the lower part of the body" (*heṭṭhimakāya*), "the upper part of the body" (*uparimakāya*), "the whole body" (*sabbakāya*), "the old monastery" (*purāṇavihāra*), "the new dwelling" (*navāvāsa*), and "which group? (*kataranikāya*).
"Which category? refers to the condition of cause (*hetu-paccaya*). "Made much of" means practiced extensively.
"The life-effort group of nine" refers to the *jīvita-navaka*, and so forth.
Furthermore, when a qualifying term follows a supreme term, such as "Thera," "Ācariya," or "Paṇḍita," it serves as a qualification in accordance with the words of the Victor (*jinavacana*).
For example: *sāriputto ca so thero ca* means "the Elder Sāriputta. Likewise: the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the teacher Buddhaghosa, the teacher Dhammapāla, or the teacher Guttila;
or *mahosadho ca so paṇḍito ca* means "the wise man Mahosadha. Similarly: the wise man Vidhura.
These are specific instances of the subject matter.
An example of a compound with both members as qualifiers (*visesanobhayapada*) is as follows: that which is cold and hot is "cold-and-hot" (*sītuṇha*);
that which is smooth and hot is "smooth-and-hot" (*siniddhuṇha*), [referring to] the month. That which is lame and hunchbacked is "lame-and-hunchbacked" (*khañjakhujja*). Likewise:

blind-and-deaf (*andhabadhira*), done-and-undone (*katākata*), perforated-and-unperforated (*chiddāvachidda*), high-and-low (*uccāvaca*), cut-and-split (*chinnabhinna*), sprinkled-and-swept (*sittasammaṭṭha*), gone-and-returning (*gatapaccāgata*).

In the case of a compound with an incomparable object of comparison (*upamānuttarapada*), the qualifying term that serves as the object of comparison (*upamāna*) comes last, in accordance with the rules of expression. For example:
*sīho viya sīho* (like a lion, a lion), or *muni ca so sīho ca* (he is both a sage and a lion), thus *munisīho*. Likewise: *munivasabho*, *munipuṅgavo*, *buddhanāgo*, *buddhādicco*. Also:
*raṃsi viya raṃsi* (like a ray, a ray), or *saddhammo ca so raṃsi ca* (it is both the True Dhamma and a ray), thus *saddhammaraṃsi*. Similarly: *vinayasāgaro*.

Like a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), he is a *puṇḍarīka*; and because he is both an ascetic (*samaṇa*) and a *puṇḍarīka*, he is an "ascetic-white-lotus" (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*), or an "ascetic-lotus" (*samaṇapaduma*).

Like the moon (*canda*), it is the moon; and because that face is the moon, it is a "moon-face" (*mukhacanda*). In the same way, there are terms such as "lotus-face" (*mukhapaduma*). An example of a compound with a preceding word of esteem (*sambhāvanāpubbapada*) is:

the understanding (*buddhi*) that is the Dhamma is "Dhamma-understanding" (*dhammabuddhi*). Likewise, there are terms such as "Dhamma-perception" (*dhammasaññā*) and "designated as Dhamma" (*dhammasaṅkhāta*).

Perception of phenomena (dhammasaññā), perception of living beings (pāṇasaññā), perception of the foul (asubhasaññā), perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), perception of non-self (anattasaññā), perception of elements (dhātusaññā), perception of the body (kāyasaññā), perception of self (attasaññā), perception of existence (atthisaññā), view of self (attadiṭṭhi), and so forth.
An example of a compound with a restrictive preceding member (*avadhāraṇapubbapada*) is:
"virtue alone is wealth" is *guṇadhana*. Likewise, *saddhādhana* (the wealth of faith) and *sīladhana* (the wealth of virtue).

The wealth of wisdom; the eye itself as a faculty is the "eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriya*). Likewise: the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*), the eye-door (*cakkhudvāra*), the visible-form object (*rūpārammaṇa*), and so forth.

As for a compound with the negative particle *na* as the prior member—such as in the sense of "not a brahmin" (*na-brāhmaṇo*) when formed as a *kammadhāraya* compound, after the elision of the case-ending and so on—this is [an example].
“*Ubhe tappurisā*”: this is the technical designation *tappurisa*.
344. *Attaṃ nassa tappurise*:

in a *tappurisa* compound, when the following member (*uttarapada*) is a particle (*nipāta*), the word *na* becomes *atta* throughout. Because it is a part of the *tappurisa*, it is called *tappurisa*; for example, *abrāhmaṇo* (“one who is not a brahmin”).
A negation of that which exists is not tenable without a restriction of place and so forth; nor is it fruitful [to negate] that which does not exist. Therefore...
If it is asked, "How is one a non-Brahmin?"—
it is by way of restating a negation. In some cases,
a prohibitive injunction serves to make known another person's state of false knowledge.
And this negation (assattha) is twofold, by way of absolute negation (pasajjappaṭisedha) and relative negation (pariyudāsa).

Therein, that which indicates the total non-existence of the meaning of the subsequent term—as in "the king's wives are not to be seen by the sun" (asūriyapassā rājadārā)—is called the expression of absolute negation.
However, that which [indicates the subsequent term] as in "non-Brahmins, non-ghosts" (abrāhmaṇa amanussa)—where the subsequent term...
Having excluded [the object] from its locus, it establishes the action upon a similar locus; this is called the "exclusionary negation" (*pariyudāsavācī*). And it is said:
"The characteristic of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) is the non-existence of the locus."
“Functioning apart from the substance [itself] is the characteristic of a relative negation (pariyudāsa).
But even if this is so, how can there be predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member in cases such as “non-Brahmin” (abrāhmaṇo)?
It is said: because words such as “Brahmin” denote not only the referent that is a Brahmin and so forth, but also referents similar to them and the like.
For words such as *brāhmaṇa* are well-known only in the sense of a "Brahmin" and so forth; the word *bhū*, however, [is well-known] in the sense of "existence.

But when they are joined with the particle *na*, which expresses similarity to something else and so on, they then function to denote similarity to that, otherness than that, opposition to that, and the absence of that—just as the word *bhū* functions in connection with *anu* and *abhi* to denote experiencing, overcoming, and so forth. Therefore, in this context, it is only that which expresses the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound].

The word *na* is a particle; thus, there is no fault [in its usage]. By this, "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) means one who resembles a Brahmin. Likewise for "non-human" (*amanusso*) and "non-recluse" (*assamaṇo*).
In the sense of "other than": "unexplained" (*abyākatā*) means not explained; "undefiled" (*asaṃkiliṭṭhā*) and "not included [within the mundane]" (*apariyāpannā*).
In the sense of "opposite": "unwholesome" (*akusalā*) means not wholesome; the meaning is "antithetical to the wholesome. Likewise for "non-greed" (*alobho*) and "non-friend" (*amitto*).
In the prohibition of the *pasajja* (subordinate) [compound]: not having done, not having made; not having performed merit, one who does not perform it.
The phrase “*nassa tappurise*” (let there be elision in a *tappurisa*) continues [from the previous rule]. 345. *Sare ana*. (Before a vowel, *ana* [is substituted for the suffix]).
In a *tappurisa* compound, the word *na* becomes *an-* when followed by a vowel-initial following member (*uttarapada*).
Examples: *na asso* = *anasso*; *na ariyo* = *anariyo*. Likewise: *anissaro*, *aniṭṭho*, *anupavādo*, *na ādāya* = *anādāya*, *anoloketvā*, and so forth.

An example with *ku-* as the first member: "despicable food" (*kucchitaṃ annaṃ*)—because it is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), the analysis is made with a different word; once the *kammadhāraya* compound is formed: [the form *kukamma* follows].
The phrase “in a tappurisa compound, before a vowel” (tappurise, sare) also continues [from the previous rule]. 346. *Kad* replaces *ku*.

When this particle *ku* occurs in a tappurisa compound with a following word that begins with a vowel, it is replaced by *kad*. For example: *kadannaṃ* (bad food). Likewise, *kadasanaṃ* (bad conduct).
What does it cause to arise? A bad wife, a bad son, a bad slave, and wrong view. The term "of what" (kussa) is understood [to apply here]. 347.
And also in the sense of "suitable for."
What [substitute] occurs for *ku* when it is used in the sense of "unfit" (*appattha*) while standing before a *tappurisa* compound with a following final member?

Because of its explicit mention in the plural, it also occasionally occurs in the sense of "contemptible" (*kucchita*) within a *tappurisa*. For example: "little salt" is *kālavaṇaṃ*; likewise, *kāpupphaṃ* ("bad flower");
and "a contemptible man" is *kāpuriso* or *kupuriso*.
A compound where the first word is primary is always a *niccasamāsa*. "Pāvacana" means a preeminent teaching (*padhānaṃ vacanaṃ*). "Pavaddha" means greatly increased (*bhusaṃ vaddhaṃ*).
"Samādhāna" means the body, or a balanced or correct placement (*samaṃ, sammā vā ādhānaṃ*). "Vimati" means various opinions (*vividhā mati*).

"Vikappa" means various possibilities (*vividho kappo*), or a distinct possibility (*visiṭṭho vā kappo*). "Atideva" means a superior god (*adhiko devo*). Likewise, there are *adhideva*, *adhisīla*, and *sundara*.
"Sugandho" means a pleasant smell; "duggandho" means a foul smell; "sukataṃ" means well-done, beautiful work; "dukkataṃ" means ill-done, ugly work, and so forth.
Regarding those nouns, particles, and prefixes whose characteristics are not specifically prescribed here, a compound should be understood by means of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*), namely:

"there is a compound of nouns. For example: *apuna-geyyā gāthā* (verses not to be sung again), *acanda-mullokikāni mukhāni* (faces that do not look up at the moon), *assaddha-bhojī* (one who eats without faith).
In cases such as *alavaṇabhojī* ("one who eats without salt"), there is no compound with another word because the meaning is inappropriate.
Likewise, *diṭṭhapubbo* ("seen before") is [an example of] a *tathāgata*; similarly, *sutapubbo* ("heard before") refers to the Dhamma, and *gatapubbo* ("gone before") refers to the Path.
In the passive sense (*kamma*), *diṭṭhā pubbā* ("seen before") means "the gods were seen by him"; similarly, *sutapubbā* refers to the teachings, and *gatapubbā* refers to the directions.
*Pahāra*, *parābhava*, *vihāra*, *āhāra*, *upahāra*, and so forth.
These are examples of *kammadhāraya* compounds. [Next is] the *digu* compound.
Now, the *digusamāsa* (numeral compound) is explained.

When the meaning is "the three worlds brought together, combined by the mind," or "the collection of the three worlds"—while the rule "A compound of nouns [expressing] a connected meaning" (*nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho*) is applicable—the *kammadhāraya* compound is formed by the rule "in two words," etc. Then, when the technical designation of a compound (*samāsasaññā*) has been applied, the case endings elided, and the original form restored—
The term "kammadhāraya" is understood [from the previous rule].
348. A compound preceded by a numeral is a *digu*.
A *kammadhāraya* compound that is preceded by a numeral receives the designation *digu*.
The *digu* compound is so called because it resembles a *digu*; that is, like the [compound] "two cows" (*dve gāvo*), this compound is also termed a *digu*.

Alternatively, it is called a *digu* because it has gone to or understood two characteristics—namely, having a numeral as its first member, being neuter, and being singular—or because it goes to (i.e., functions according to) those two characteristics.

Furthermore, because it is stated here that "it has a numeral as its first member," the numeral word itself is placed first; and because it is stated that "both are *tappurisa* compounds," it receives the designation of *tappurisa*.
“Neuter gender” is understood [from the previous rule].
349. *Digu* compounds are singular.
A *digu* compound takes the singular number and the neuter gender.
This is the inclusion of *samāhāra-dvigu* compounds; therein, the singular number always occurs, whereas elsewhere the plural may also occur.

The origin of the designation "noun" (*nāma*) begins with the substitution of *am* (*amādesa*), and so forth. *Tilokaṃ*, *he tiloka*, *tilokaṃ*, *tilokena*, *tilokassa*, *tilokā* (ablative), *tilokasmā*, *tilokamhā*, *tilokassa*, *tiloke*, *tilokamhi*, *tilokasmiṃ*.
In the same way: *tayo daṇḍā* (three sticks) is *tidaṇḍaṃ*; or, three impurities (*malāni*) brought together, or the collection of the three impurities, is *timalaṃ*.

The three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), the four truths (*catussacca*), the four directions (*catuddisa*), [the form *catuddisa*] having its short vowel by the rule "the vowel is short in the neuter" (*saro rasso napuṃsake*);

the five training rules (*pañcasikkhāpada*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), seven days (*sattāha*), the eightfold morality (*aṭṭhasīla*), the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttara*), the tenfold morality (*dasasīla*), and one hundred yojanas (*satayojana*).

Likewise: two nights (*dve rattiyo*) is *dviratta*, three nights (*tisso rattiyo*) is *tiratta*, two fingers (*dve aṅguliyo*) is *dvaṅgula*, seven Godāvarīs, or the collection of them (*tāsaṃ samāhāro*) is *sattagodāvara*.
And here, regarding "ratti aṅguli godāvarīnam antassa": 350. In some cases, there is an *a*-ending for those words situated at the end of a compound.
This is the inclusion of the group beginning with *rāja*; therefore, in some cases, there is an *a*-vowel at the end of names such as *rāja* and others that occur at the end of a compound.
The meaning is "it becomes. By the inclusion of the letter *ka*, the suffix *k* occurs in certain instances within compound endings such as the *bahubbīhi*;
furthermore, the nasalization (*antassikāra*) occurs after *su*, *ru*, *du*, and *pūti*.

Alternatively, *akā* consists of *a* and *ko*; the letter *ra* serves to join words (*padasaṃdhikaro*). Therefore, in some cases, it functions as the final element of those [words] situated at the end of a compound.

The meaning is: "these [suffixes] such as *a* and *ka* are conditions. Consequently, when the sense is "five cows have been brought together," having formed a compound (*samāsa*) and applied the suffix *ap* at the end of the compound, and having substituted *o* for the vowel according to the rule "o sara-cā," forms such as "pañcagavam" are established.
However, in cases such as "dvirattam," once the suffix *ap* has been applied, there is elision of the preceding vowel according to the rule "saralopa" and so forth.

An example of a non-compound *digu* (numeral compound) is: *eko ca so puggalo ca* = *ekapuggalo* (one person). Likewise: *ekadhammo*, *ekaputto*, *tayo bhavā* = *tibhavā* (the three states of existence), *catasso disā* = *catuddisā* (the four quarters), *dasasahassacakkavāḷāni*, and so forth.
This is the *digusamāsa*.
[Next is] the *tappurisasamāsa*.
Now the *tappurisa* compound is explained.

It is sixfold according to its occurrence with the six case endings, beginning with the accusative. Among these, a *tappurisa* in the accusative case arises through [the use of] words such as *gata*, *nissita*, *atīta*, *atikkanta*, *patta*, and *āpanna*.
For example, in the analysis (*viggahe*) of "one who has gone for refuge" (*saraṇaṃ gato*):
The term *tappurisa* is understood [to carry over]. 351. *Amādayo parapadebhi*:

Words ending in the case-terminations beginning with *am* (accusative), which possess a connected meaning, are optionally compounded with subsequent words (*parapada*) that are nouns; such a compound is designated as a *tappurisa*. Furthermore, this *tappurisa* takes the gender of the word expressing its referent (*abhidheyya*).

Words such as *gata* and others, being formed with the suffix *-ita*, possess all three genders; the elision of case endings and so forth are all identical to those of the preceding [chapter]. Examples include: *so saraṇagato* (he has gone for refuge), *te saraṇagatā* (they have gone for refuge);

*sā saraṇagatā* (she has gone for refuge), *tā saraṇagatāyo* (those women have gone for refuge); *taṃ kulaṃ saraṇagataṃ* (that family has gone for refuge), *tāni kulāni saraṇagatāni* (those families have gone for refuge), and so forth.
Thus, having gone to the forest, having gone to the ground, he is supported by the Dhamma, supported by the Dhamma; he has transcended existence, transcended existence;
he has transcended time, transcended measure; he has transcended the world; he has attained happiness, attained happiness;
he has attained suffering, entered the stream, attained cessation, and mounted the chariot.
*Rathāruḷho* (mounted on a chariot); *sabbarattiṃ sobhano* (shining all night), hence *sabbarattisobhano* (all-night-shining); [these denote] momentary pleasure.

In the case of a compound with a subordinate term (*upapada-samāsa*), however, the grammatical operation (*vutti*) itself is permanent because of its obligatory nature. For example: one who performs work is a *kammakāro* (laborer); a potter is a *kumbhakāro*; one who desires wealth is an *atthakāmo*;
one who desires the Dhamma is a *dhammakāmo*; one who upholds the Dhamma is a *dhammadharo*; one who upholds the Vinaya is a *vinayadharo*.
"One whose nature is to speak truth" is a *saccavādī* (truth-speaker), and so forth.

By means of suffixes such as *-tavant*, *-māna*, *-anta*, and *-ika*, the sentence itself [functions as the agent], because of the governing rule regarding optional application (*vibhāsā*) for those whose case endings are fixed. For example:

*odanaṃ bhuttavā* (having eaten rice), *dhammaṃ suṇamāno* (while listening to the Dhamma), *dhammaṃ suṇanto* (listening to the Dhamma), *kaṭaṃ karāno* (making a mat). Or, due to non-expression (*anabhidhānato*), it is characterized by expression (*abhidhānalakkhaṇā*).
Indeed, [the following] are derivative (taddhita) compounds, possessive (samāsa) compounds, and those ending in -ka or -ika: the second type is the tappurisa compound;
the third type consists of those where the first member is similar to, or has the sense of, "collection," "quarrel," "skillful," "mixed," "friendly," and so forth, followed by words such as *kitaka*.
The Dhamma spoken by the Buddha is "spoken by the Buddha. Likewise, it is "taught by the Victor," "praised by the Teacher," and "praised by the Teacher.
It is "condemned by the wise" [in its opposite], while it is "extolled by the wise.
It is "created by Īśvara," "self-created," "brought by crows," "crow-made," "struck by a king," "king-struck," "afflicted by disease," "burnt by fire," "bitten by a snake," or "pierced by an arrow."
Pierced by an arrow; overcome by desire, one who is overcome by desire; endowed with virtue, one who is endowed with virtue. Thus: accompanied by pleasure;
associated with knowledge; association with friends; separation from the beloved; stiff with birth; deficient in qualities; increased in qualities; that which is to be performed by a group of four;
that which is to be done by a group of four and so forth; drinkable by crows, a river.

In some cases there is only a compound (vutti): *uraga* (“going with the belly”) and *pādapa* (“drinking with the foot”). In other cases there is only a sentence (vākya): “cut by an axe,” “to be eaten by crows,” “to be abandoned by seeing.
In connection with the prefix *pubba-* and others: *māsena pubbo* (“swollen for a month”) becomes *māsapubbo*. Likewise:

*mātusadiso* (“like a mother”), *pitusamo* (“equal to a father”), *ekūnavīsati* (“nineteen”), *sīlavikalo* (“deficient in virtue”), *asikalaho* (“a sword-fight”), *vācānipuṇo* (“skilled in speech”), *yāvakālikasaṃmissaṃ* (“mixed with what is to be taken at the proper time”), *vācāsakhilo* (“harsh in speech”), *satthārā sadiso satthukappo* (“resembling the Teacher, like the Teacher”).
One who seeks merit is a *puññatthika*; one who possesses superior qualities is a *guṇādhika*; rice mixed with molasses is *guḷodana*; rice with milk is *khīrodana*;
a chariot yoked with a horse is an *assaratha*; the path-consciousness is *maggacitta*; the island known and marked by the Jambu tree is *Jambudīpa*;
ten plus one is eleven (*ekādasa*); one blind from birth is a *jaccandha*; naturally wise is a *pakatimedhāvī*, and so forth.
The third type of tappurisa compound:

[a word] in the fourth case is compounded with words meaning "for that purpose" (*tadattha*), "good for" (*attha*), "beneficial to" (*hita*), "to be given" (*deyya*), and so forth. Regarding "for that purpose": *kathinassa dussaṃ* (cloth for the kathina) is *kathinadussaṃ*; the meaning is "for the sake of the kathina robe. Likewise, *cīvaradussaṃ*.
The price of a robe; rice for the sake of conjey is "conjey-rice" or "rice for a meal";
a meal for the sake of the Saṅgha is "Saṅgha-meal"; a meal for the sake of newcomers is "newcomer-meal. Likewise, a meal for those going away is "going-away-meal";
grass for the sake of a palace is "palace-grass."
A monastery for the sake of the community of bhikkhus is a “monastery for the sake of the community of bhikkhus”;

rice gruel for the sake of the community of bhikkhus; a robe for the sake of the community of bhikkhus. Whatever is for the sake of someone is “for whose sake” (*yassatthāya*), “of which purpose” (*yadattho*), “of which purpose” (*yadatthā*), or “for which purpose” (*yadatthaṃ*).

Likewise, “of that purpose” (*tadattho*), “of that purpose” (*tadatthā*), or “for that purpose” (*tadatthaṃ*). This effort is for this purpose; this talk is for this purpose; this application of the ear is for this purpose.

For what purpose? For one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the sake of restraint, for the sake of happiness and concentration, for the sake of disenchantment and dispassion, and for the sake of dispassion and liberation.
Likewise, that which is beneficial to the world is "beneficial to the world" (*lokahita*); that which is to be given to a Buddha is "Buddha-gift" (*buddhadeyya*), namely flowers;
that which is to be given to the Sangha is "Sangha-gift" (*saṅghadeyya*), namely robes. Herein, it does not exist [as a gift to the Buddha]; it is to be given to the Sangha.
"Intended to be given to the Saṅgha," and so forth.
This is a fourth-case tappurisa compound.
The fifth case [is used] with meanings such as departure, fear, abstention, and release.

One who has departed from sexual intercourse is "one who has departed from sexual intercourse" (*methunāpeto*). Likewise, one who has gone away from chaff, one who has gone out from the city, one who has turned back from alms-food.

One who has gone out from the village is "one who has gone out from the village" (*gāmanikkhantaṃ*); one who has fallen from the top of a tree is "one who has fallen from the top of a tree" (*rukkhaggapatito*); one who has fallen away from the Teaching; one who has emerged from an offense; one who has risen up from the surface of the earth;
one who has escaped from all states of existence is "one who has escaped from all states of existence" (*sabbabhavanissaṭo*).

In the case of the *bhayātthādi-yoga* (compounds where the first member denotes fear), for example: fear of a king is *rājabhaya*, fear of thieves is *corabhaya*, fear of non-human beings is *amanussabhaya*, and fear of fire is *aggibhaya*.
One who is afraid of evil is *pāpabhīto*, one who fears evil is *pāpabhīruko*.

Abstinence from what should not be done is *akattabbavirati*. Likewise, there is abstinence from bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita-virati*) and abstinence from verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita-virati*).

"Released from bondage" (*bandhanā mutto*) means released from bondage; "released from the forest" (*vanamutto*); "release from bondage" (*bandhanamokkho*). "Arising from karma" (*kammato samuṭṭhitaṃ*) means arisen from karma. "Extremely high" (*ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭhaṃ*); "extremely low" (*omakomakaṃ*).
