In some cases there is simply an elision [of the suffix], as in "born of karma" (*kammajaṃ*). Likewise for "born of mind" (*cittajaṃ*), "born of temperature" (*utujaṃ*), and "born of nutriment" (*āhārajaṃ*). Here it is not used [in this way]: "the palace has fallen."
The Genitive Tatpurisa (Chaṭṭhītappurisa):

"The king’s son" is *rājaputta*. Likewise: *rājapuriso* (king’s man), *ācariyapūjako* (teacher’s worshipper), *buddhasāvako* (Buddha’s disciple), *buddharūpaṃ* (Buddha’s image), *jinavacanaṃ* (Conqueror’s word), *samuddaghoso* (ocean’s roar), *dhaññarāsi* (a heap of grain), *pupphagandho* (flower’s fragrance), *phalaraso* (fruit’s juice), *kāyassa* (of the body).

Lightness (lahutā), lightness of body (kāyalahutā), mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), the foot of a tree (rukkhamūla), an iron bowl (ayassa patto = ayopatto), likewise a golden basin (suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ), a water vessel (pānīyathālakaṃ), and a jar of ghee (sappikumbho).

When the compound "king of the gods" (devānaṃ rājā) is formed, the final vowel is replaced by the letter *a* according to the rule: "In some cases, for those [words] ending in a compound, the suffix *a* is applied."
Therefore, the form "syā ca" does not occur. *Devarājo*, *devarājā*, *devarājaṃ*, *devarāje*, and so forth, are the same as the word *purisa*.
In the sense of the self (*attā*), *so devarājā* (that king of gods), *te devarājāno* (those kings of gods), and so forth, are the same as the word *rāja*.
Likewise, *devānaṃ sakhā* (a friend of the gods) becomes *devasakho*; *devasakhā*, *so devasakhā*, *te devasakhāno*, and so forth.

The characteristic of a male is the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*). Likewise, there is the state of being male (*pumbhāva*), as well as the elision of the final *pum* sound and so forth. Examples include:

*hatthipadaṃ* (the footprint of an elephant), *itthirūpaṃ* (the form of a woman), *bhikkhunisaṅgho* (the community of nuns), and *jambusākhā* (a branch of the rose-apple tree). In these cases, by the rule beginning with "kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ," the long vowels *ī* and *ū* in the middle are shortened.

Due to the governing heading of "optionally" (*vibhāsā*), in some instances the sentence remains unchanged: *sahasā kammassa kattāro* (those who perform an action impulsively), *bhinnānaṃ sandhātā* (the reconciler of those who are divided), *kappassa tatiyo bhāgo* (the third part of an aeon), *yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī* (and that which is the eighth day of the fortnight), and *manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo* (among men, the most courageous is the noble warrior).

Is it only when the meaning is appropriate? In the case of “*bhaṭo rañño puriso devadattassā*” (“the king’s servant, Devadatta’s man”), because there is no mutual dependence—since the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) is used here in the sense of a connection with the servant (*bhaṭa-sambandhe*)—there is no compound due to the state of having an inappropriate meaning.
However, in cases such as “*kosalassa rañño putto*” (“the son of the King of Kosala”), [no compound occurs] because of the inability [of the words] to be dependent [on each other].
Yet, even though related words are always dependent, [a compound may still occur].

A compound is used for the sake of clarity, as in: "Devadatta’s teacher's family" (*devadattassa gurukulaṃ*) or "the Blessed One’s community of disciples" (*bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho*), and so forth. This is a genitive tappurisa compound.
A locative tappurisa is, for example:
"perception regarding form" (*rūpe saññā* = *rūpasaññā*), likewise "volition regarding form" (*rūpasañcetanā*), "the suffering of saṃsāra," or "that which is dependent upon the eye."

Consciousness is eye-consciousness; delighting in the Dhamma is *dhammarata*, delight in the Dhamma (*dhammābhirati*), fondness for the Dhamma (*dhammaruci*), reverence for the Dhamma (*dhammagārava*);

linguistic expression regarding the Dhammas is *dhammanirutti*; inclination toward giving is *dānādhimutti*; performed in another existence is *bhavantarakata*; gratification in seeing is *dassanassāda*; dwelling in the forest is *araññavāsa*;
eating at the wrong time is *vikālabhojana*; rain during the proper season is *kālavassa*; in the woods...
"Flower" means a wild forest flower. Likewise: a wild buffalo; a village pig; a sea fish; a pond tortoise;

a pond frog; a well frog; a ferry-boat; a rogue among women is a "woman-rogue"; one dried in the shade is "shade-dried"; roasted on coals is "aṅgārapakka"; one bound in prison is "cārakabaddha. Here, however, it is simply a matter of derivation (*vutti*), as for example:
one who wanders in the forest is a "forest-wanderer" (*vanacara*); one who lies in the belly is a "belly-lie" (*kucchisaya*); one [who stands] on dry land...
"It stands" means "standing on dry land. Likewise: *jalaṭṭho* (standing in water), *pabbataṭṭho* (standing on a mountain), *maggaṭṭho* (standing on a path); *paṅkajaṃ* (born in mud);
*siroruhaṃ* (growing on the head). Here it does not occur:
*bhojane mattaññutā* (moderation in eating), *indriyesu guttadvāratā* (guarding the doors of the sense faculties), *āsane nisinno* (seated on a seat), *āsane nisīditabbaṃ* (one should sit on a seat).

This is a *sattamī-tappurisa* (genitive determinative compound). Because it is stated [in the rule] as “without obstructing that,” in certain instances of a *tappurisa* such as *accanta* and so forth, a following word ending in the *am*-case (accusative) and other cases may occur as the first member according to its specific designation.

For example: *antaṃ atikkantaṃ* (that which has gone beyond the end) becomes *accantaṃ*; *accantāni*. *Velaṃ atikkanto* (one who has transgressed the limit) becomes *ativelo*, with the shortening of the vowel.
Thus, *mālam atīto* means "having transcended pride" (*atimālo*). *Pattajīviko* means "one who has attained livelihood. *Āpannajīviko* means "one who has entered into livelihood.
*Akkhaṃ patigataṃ nissitaṃ* refers to direct perception (*paccakkhaṃ*), which is seeing; it is direct perception as one's own person (*attabhāvo*), direct perception as wisdom (*buddhi*).

*Anvatthaṃ* means that which has followed the meaning (*atthaṃ anugataṃ*). *Avakokilaṃ vanaṃ* means a forest "pecked by cuckoos" (*kokilāya avakuṭṭhaṃ*); the sense is "abandoned" (*pariccattaṃ*). *Avamayūraṃ* [is used] for the purpose of study (*ajjhayanāya*).
One who has swallowed up [the teachings] and mastered them is *pariyajjhāyana*; one who is capable and competent in action is *alaṃkamma*; one who is sufficient for speech is *alaṃvacana*.

*Nibbāna* is that which has emerged from craving (*vāna*); *nikkilesa* is that which has emerged from defilements; *niraṅgaṇa* is free from passion; *nikkosambī* is that which has emerged from Kosambī;
*nibbana* is that which has departed from the forest (*vana*); *pācariya* is one beyond the teacher (*ācariya*). In this same way, *payyaka*, *parahiyyo*, and so forth.
"Upstream of the Ganges" is *uparigaṅgaṃ*. Likewise: "downstream river" (*heṭṭhānadī*); "within meditative attainment" (*antosamāpatti*); "king of swans" is *rājahaṃso*, or *haṃsarājā*;
"half of a month" is *addhamāsaṃ*, or *māsaddhaṃ*; "half of an āmalaka fruit" is *addhāmalakaṃ*, or *āmalakaddhaṃ*;
"half of a kahāpaṇa coin" is *aḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ*, or *aḍḍhamāsakaṃ*; "half of a night" (*rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ*).

*Addharattaṃ*, *rattiyā pubbaṃ pubbarattaṃ*, and *rattiyā pacchā pacchārattaṃ*. Herein, by the rule “in some cases, when at the end of a compound, the final vowel becomes *a*,” the final syllable of the word *ratti* becomes *atta*;
and for *aha* (day), there is *pubbaṃ pubbanhaṃ*. Likewise, *sāyanhaṃ*; and by the rule “in those [cases], there is a substitution of *anha* for *aha*,” there is the replacement of *anha* for *aha*.
This is an *amādi-tappurisa* compound.
In certain instances within a *tappurisa*, there is no elision of the case ending (*vibhatti-lopa*), as in the case of "pabhaṅkara" and others.

For example, in the sense of "one who makes light," the compound "pabhaṅkara" is formed by the rule "amādayo parapadehi" (amā and so forth [combine] with subsequent words), according to the rule "nāmānaṃ samāso yuttattho" (a compound of nouns [expresses] a connected meaning).

There is the designation *samāsa*. Then, when the elision of case-endings (*vibhattilopa*) is reached by the rule “*tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca*,” the mention of *ca* (and) in that very rule prevents the elision of the case-ending in the first member of the compound.
The rest is the same. [Examples: *pabhaṅkaro* (light-maker); *amatandado* (giver of the deathless), from *amataṃ dadāti*;
*raṇañjaho* (quitter of strife), from *raṇaṃ jahāti*; *jutindharo* (bearer of splendor), from *jutiṃ dhāreti*; likewise *sahasākataṃ* (done hastily). These are in the third person (*parassapada*).
*Attanopadaṃ*, *bhayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ* (the appearance as terror), *paratoghoso*, *gavaṃpati-thero*, *manasikāro*, *pubbenivāso*,
*pubbenivāsānussati*, *majjhekalyāṇaṃ*, *antevāsī*, *antevāsiko*, *janesuto*, *urasilomo*,
*kaṇṭhekāḷo*, *sarasijaṃ*, and so forth.
Alopa tappurisa.
The tappurisa compound is finished.
The bahubbīhi compound.
Now, the *bahubbīhi* compound is explained.

It is of nine kinds: the two-word *bahubbīhi* with identical referents (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), the two-word *bahubbīhi* with different referents (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), the three-word *bahubbīhi* preceded by a negative particle (*na*) or an indeclinable (*nipāta*), [the three-word *bahubbīhi*] preceded by the word *saha*, [the three-word *bahubbīhi*] preceded by a term of comparison (*upamāna*), the two-word *bahubbīhi* having a numeral as its first member, the two-word *bahubbīhi* expressing the meaning of "between the directions" (*disantarāla*), and that characterized by reciprocal exchange (*byatihāra*).
Among these, the two-word *bahubbīhi* with identical referents occurs in the six case-meanings beginning with the object (*kamma*).
Regarding that, first, in the case of the second sense—in the analysis (*viggahe*) of the phrase “The ascetics have come to this monastery” (*imaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ āgatā samaṇā*)—it is stated: **352.

Bahubbīhi in the sense of other words.** Names (*nāmāni*) whose meanings are connected with the meanings of words other than those being compounded—which end in the first, second, and so forth, case endings—are optionally (*vibhāsā*) compounded; that compound is designated as *bahubbīhi*.

That which has many grains is a *bahubbīhi*. Because it resembles a *bahubbīhi*, this compound is also called a *bahubbīhi* by way of a designation based on its meaning; for a *bahubbīhi* has another word as its primary referent.

This *bahubbīhi* is of two kinds, according to whether the quality of that [referent] is understood (*tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*) or the quality of that is not understood (*atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*). Among these, where the meaning existing as a qualifier is grasped by the inclusion of another word’s referent, that is one where the quality of that is understood, such as:
"Bring the long-eared one. But where it is not grasped, that is one where the quality of that is not understood, such as: "Bring the one with much wealth."
Here, as in the case of the word *bahubbīhi*, the qualifier is placed first; the rest is the same as the previous [type].

"The monastery of the monks who have arrived" (*āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo*). In this instance, the words *āgata* and *samaṇa*, instead of remaining in their own primary sense, function with reference to another referent—the compound meaning "monastery"—which constitutes the object of the second case ending. This is solely for the purpose of indicating that meaning.

Immediately after that, the word "saṅghārāmo" (the monastery) is employed; because the object (kamma) has already been expressed by the compound itself, the accusative case ending does not occur again.
Furthermore, there is no employment of the pronoun *idaṃ* (this), and so it is in all instances. This is a bahubbīhi compound, which takes the gender and number of the thing designated.
Thus: "Sāvatthī where the monks have arrived," "Jetavana where the monks have arrived," and "the road on which the travelers have set out."
This is the path for those who have set out; that ship which the merchants have boarded is "the ship boarded by the merchants.
Thus is the *bahubbīhi* compound used in the sense of the object (*kamma*).

An example of the *bahubbīhi* in the sense of the agent (*tatiyattha*) is as follows: that ascetic by whom the faculties have been conquered is "the ascetic who has conquered his faculties" (*jitindriyo samaṇo*).

Thus, he has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, and accomplished what was to be done; because Māra has been conquered by him, the Blessed One is "one who has conquered Māra" (jitamāra), having penetrated all phenomena.

This is a *bahubbīhi* compound used in the sense of the fourth case (the recipient). For example: "The king to whom tax has been given" is a "king to whom tax is given" (*dinnasuṅko rājā*); "The ascetic to whom food has been brought" is an "ascetic to whom food is brought" (*upanītabhojano samaṇo*); "The yakṣa to whom tribute has been brought" is a "yakṣa to whom tribute is brought" (*upahaṭabali yakkho*). This is a *bahubbīhi* compound used in the sense of the fifth case (the source). For example:
"The village from which people have gone out" is a "village from which people have gone out" (*niggatajano gāmo*); "gone out... [and so forth].

Because iron (*ayo*) is present in it, it is "hell" (*niraya*); because defilements (*kilesa*) have departed from it, it is "free from defilement" (*nikkilesa*); because consciousness (*viññāṇa*) has departed from it, it is a "corpse devoid of consciousness" (*apetaviññāṇo matakāyo*);
because fear and terror (*bhayabherava*) have departed from him, he is an "arahant free from fear and terror" (*apagatabhayabheravo*).
This is a *bahubbīhi* compound in the sense of the sixth case (genitive), as for example: "that man whose hands are cut off is 'one with cut-off hands' (*chinnahattho*)."
A person. Thus, one whose intention is fulfilled and whose taints are exhausted is "one free from lust" (*vītarāgo*). One who has two feet is "two-footed," like a cloth with two hands;

one who possesses three knowledges is "three-knowledge"; one who possesses four feet is "four-footed"; one who possesses five eyes is the Blessed One, "five-eyed"; one who possesses six direct knowledges is "six-fold direct knowledge. [The word] *rassattaṃ* [is used for brevity]. The Teacher’s dispensation has nine factors; one who possesses ten powers is "ten-powered"; one who possesses infinite knowledge is "infinite-wisdom. Three...
The word *tīdasā* means "the gods" whose measure (*parimāṇa*) is ten; *samāsa* is its own [etymological] self.
Here, because of the proximity of the word for "measure," the word *dasa* functions in the sense of number. "Those which have this as their condition" are *idappaccayā*.
"What is its origin? is *kiṃpabhavo*; "this body. "That from which impurity has departed" is *vimalo*; "that which possesses a beautiful fragrance" is *sugandhaṃ*.
"Candana" means sandalwood. Likewise, one who possesses good virtue, a pleasant countenance, and foul-smelling excrement is "duggandha" (foul-smelling) or "kuṇapa" (corpse-like);

one who possesses a corrupted mind is "dummana" (dejected). Similarly, one who possesses bad virtue and a dejected countenance; one whose wealth consists solely of austerity is "tapodhana" (wealthy in austerity);
one who possesses the strength characterized by patience is "khantibala" (strong in patience); and one whose name is "Inda" is "indanāma" (named Inda).
In compounds such as *chandajāta* and others, because both the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*visesitabba*) may be placed first according to one's preference, both positions are possible.
For example: *chando jāto assā* (desire has arisen for him) is *chandajāto*; likewise, *jāto chando assā* (desire has arisen for him) is *jātachando*. In the same way:

*sañjātapītisomanasso* (one who has produced joy and happiness) and *pītisomanassasañjāto*; *māsajāto* (born a month ago) and *jātamāso*; *chinnahattho* (one whose hand is cut off) and *hatthacchinno*.

When the analysis “*dīghā jaṅghā assā*” has been performed and the beginning of the compound is formed—given that the rule “*tulyādhikaraṇe pade*” (when the words have a common substratum) is still in force:
if [the first member] is feminine and its corresponding masculine form exists, it remains masculine.
353. In the feminine, if the word is one whose masculine counterpart exists, it remains masculine.
When a feminine word denoting a male being occurs before another word in grammatical apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), that word is to be regarded as if it were masculine;
consequently, there is no feminine suffix in the preceding word. This applies specifically to the domain of *bahubbīhi* compounds, because it will be stated later:
"and also when there is the designation *kammadhāraya*."
354. In some cases, among the suffixes *dīgha* (long) and *rassa* (short), there are [changes] for vowels occurring at the beginning, middle, or end.

In certain instances—namely, in the case of *taddhita* (secondary derivative) suffixes, compounds (*samāsa*), nouns (*nāma*), prefixes (*upasagga*), and so forth—the vowels situated at the beginning, middle, or end become long or short according to the rules of the Jina’s word (*jinavacana*). This applies both when followed by suffixes and when not followed by suffixes, as well as when they occur in subsequent positions.
Regarding that:
Lengthening occurs in words such as *madhu-vādi* (one who speaks sweetly), provided there is no injury to the natural form (*anūpaghātādo*).
Shortening occurs in words such as *ajjava* (straightforwardness) and *itthirūpa* (the form of a woman), provided they are of that kind.

When a *bahubbīhi* compound exists, the final vowel of the last member becomes short when the compound is in the masculine gender. For example: *dīghajaṅgho puriso* (a man with long shanks). Likewise...
He who possesses an abundant tongue is "one with an abundant tongue" (*pahūtajivho*); the Blessed One is such. He who possesses great wisdom is "one of great wisdom" (*mahāpañño*).
Regarding the form *mahā*, there is the rule: "The substitute *mahā* occurs when [the word] *mahant* stands in grammatical apposition with another word.
Why is it specified "in the feminine"? [Consider: *khamādhano*. Why is it specified "when the original stem is masculine"? [Consider: *saddhādhuro*, *saddhāpakatiko*, *paññāpakatiko*.

[The suffix -ika] is for the purpose of expressing purification by wisdom (*paññāvisuddhi*). And here, the suffix *ka* (kappaccaya) is applied according to the rule: "In some cases, [the suffix -ika is added] to words ending in a compound with the letter *a*.

Is it only when there is a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*)? [Yes. Examples: *samaṇibhattiko* (one who eats the food of a female ascetic), *kumāribhattiko* (one who eats the food of a maiden), *kumāribhatti* (the meal of a maiden).

This transfer of the masculine state (*pumbhāva-atideso*) applies only to the preceding member (*pubbapada*); therefore, it does not occur here: *bahudāsiko puriso* (a man who has many female slaves), *bahukumārikaṃ kulaṃ* (a family with many daughters).
In the analysis [of the compound] “*gāṇṭhiva-dhanu-assa*,” when the compound has been formed, [the rule] states:
355. *Dhanumhā ca*. This consists of three words.

The suffix *āp* occurs after the word *dhanu* when it appears at the end of a compound; by the word *ca* (“and”), it also occurs after *dhamma* and so forth. By the rule “*vamodudantānam*,” the letter *v* is substituted [for the final *u*], resulting in *gāṇṭhivadhanvā*. Thus, [we have] *paccakkhadhammā*.
What is meant by "in some places"? [He was] one whose strength is like that of a thousand, one who has realized the Dhamma, one who has understood the Dhamma.

Regarding the phrase "the ridges scented by flowers fallen from various trees": various kinds of trees are "various trees" (*nānādumā*); those fallen from various trees are "fallen from various trees" (*nānādumapatitāni*);
and those which are both fallen from various trees and flowers are "flowers fallen from various trees" (*nānādumapatitapupphāni*).

"Scented by them" means scented by the flowers fallen from various trees; that mountain whose ridges (*sānu*) are scented by the flowers fallen from various trees is "the mountain with ridges scented by flowers fallen from various trees.
This, moreover, is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a common substratum, containing within it a *kammadhāraya* and a *tappurisa*.
Likewise, *byālamba-ambudhara* means "a cloud hanging down"; *byālambambudhara-bindu* means "drops from that hanging cloud";
*byālambambudharabinducumbita* means "kissed by those drops"; and one whose peak (*kūṭa*) is such is called *byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭa*, and so forth.
An example of a bahubbīhi compound used in the sense of the locative case is: *sampannasassa*, meaning "that country in which the crops have flourished."
A "country" (*janapada*) is so called because alms-food is easily obtained there; thus, a region where alms-food is easily obtained is a "place of easy alms.
A royal capital where people are crowded together is a "royal capital crowded with people"; a hermitage where many ascetics reside is a "hermitage with many ascetics";
a body where flesh and blood have accumulated is a "body with accumulated flesh and blood"; and a city where many masters reside is a "city with many masters."
When the meaning “bahū nadiyo asmiṃ” has been formed with the initial member of a compound—[it is stated]:
“The inclusion of the end of a compound applies, and the suffix *ka* also applies. (356) And [the suffix *ka* applies] after the word *nadi*.
The *kappa* suffix occurs after a word ending in *nadi*; by the word "and" (*ca*), it also occurs after words ending in *tu*. This statement has the sense of necessity (*nicca*).
Here, the term *nadi* is a conventional designation for feminine nouns ending in *ī* and *ū*.

Therefore, by the rule beginning with "kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ," there is shortening of the vowel in the *kappa* suffix when it bears the technical name *nadi*, as in *bahunadiko janapado* (a country with many rivers). Likewise, *bahujambukaṃ vanaṃ* (a forest with many jackals).
The form *bahunāriko* is established by means of a genitive *bahubbīhi* compound. A place where there are many agents (*kattāro*) is called *bahukattuko*;
likewise, one where there are many meals (*bhattuko*).
An example of a *bhinnādhikaraṇa* (compound with different substrata) is: that which has a dwelling for a single night is *ekarattivāso*, [as well as] together with people of the same [caste].

One who has the same dwelling is a "co-resident" (samānavāsa) person. One who possesses both sexual organs is a "hermaphrodite" (ubhatobyañjanaka). One who has an umbrella in his hand is an "umbrella-handed" (chattapāṇi) person.

Likewise, there are those who are "staff-handed" (daṇḍapāṇi), "sword-handed" (satthapāṇi), and "thunderbolt-handed" (vajirapāṇi); one who has a sword in his hand is "sword-handed" (khaggahattha), and one who has a knife in his hand is "knife-handed" (satthahattha).
One whose inclination is toward giving is "one whose inclination is to give" (dānajjhāsaya), one who is devoted to giving (dānādhimuttika), and one who is devoted to the Buddha (buddhabhattika).
"Veneration for the true Dhamma," and so forth.

An example of three words [forming a compound] is as follows: those by whom prosperity has been attained through exertion are "great beings who have attained prosperity through exertion" (*parakkamādhigatasampadā mahāpurisā*).

Likewise, those who have acquired wealth through the Dhamma are "those who have acquired wealth through the Dhamma" (*dhammādhigatabhoga*); one by whom the hand has been lowered from the bowl is "one who has lowered his hand from the bowl" (*oṇītapattapāṇi*).
“Sīhapubbaddhakāyo” means one whose body is like the forepart of a lion; “mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ” means a forest containing many (*matta*) elephants (*bahumātaṅga*), and so forth.
Regarding compounds preceded by the particle *na*:

for example, “asamo bhagavā,” meaning the Blessed One for whom there is no equal (*natthi etassa samo*). Here, [the rule] applies: “*attaṃ nassa tappurise*” (in a *tappurisa* compound, *na* becomes *a*).
In the Sutta, by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), [the compound] *nassa-attaṃ* is analyzed as "his self has perished.

Likewise, in *appaṭipuggalo*, *aputtako*, and *ahetuko*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule beginning with "kvaci samāsanta" (Pāṇini 5.4.73). Those for whom there is no communal living are *asaṃvāsā*.
A country where no rain exists is *avuṭṭhiko*. A monastery where no monks reside is *abhikkhuko*. That which has nothing superior to it is *anuttaro*.

In the phrase “*sare ana*,” *ana* is the suffix; the mention of the masculine gender (*tappurisa*) is illustrative (*upalakkhaṇa*). Alternatively, according to the rule “*tesu vuddhī*” and so forth, there is *ana* for *na*.
Thus, that which has no end (*anta*) is *ananta*; those in whom taints (*āsava*) do not exist are *anāsava*, and so on.
When used in the sense of the first case (*paṭhamāyatthe*), the word is preceded by *saha*: that which exists together with a cause (*hetu*) is *sahetuka*, or it is simply *sahetu*.
In the phrase “*tesu vuddhī*,” etc., there is the substitution of *sā* for *sa*, and by the rule “*kvaci samāsanta*,” etc., the suffix *ka* is added;
thus, “those which exist together with joy (*pīti*)” are *sappītikā*. Likewise, “those which exist together with conditions (*paccaya*)” are *sappaccayā*;
[the terms] *sakileso* (with defilement), *saupādāno* (with clinging), and *saparivāro* (with retinue); and “a tree uprooted together with its root” is *samūluddhato*.

First, regarding compounds where the first member is a simile (upamānapubbapada) in the sense of the nominative case: the employment of the word *iva* is for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the object of comparison and that which is compared.
Because his bodily proportions are equal to those of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*), the prince who is thus well-proportioned is called "the prince Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala.
Regarding the phrase "non-employment when the meaning has been stated": there is no employment of the word *iva*, as in: "They go white like a conch shell (*saṅkha*)."
"Saṅkhapaṇḍaro": like a crow, he goes toward the sun; thus, "kākasūro" (crow-sun). "Cakkhubhūto": he has become like an eye for the seeing of the ultimate truth;
thus, the Blessed One is "cakkhubhūto. In this way, he is "atthabhūto" (become the goal). He is "dhammabhūto" (become the Dhamma) and "brahmabhūto" (become the Brahma).

"Andhabhūto": like a blind man, they go toward [darkness]; thus, the fool is "andhabhūto. "Muñjapabbajabhūtā": like the reeds of the muñja grass, they go toward [destruction]; thus, wrong view is "muñjapabbajabhūtā."
Those who have become like a tangled skein are called *tantākulakajāta*.
In the sense of the genitive case (*chaṭṭhiyatthe*): he whose complexion is like the color of gold is the "gold-colored" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇa*) Blessed One.

This is an elision of the middle term (*uttarapadalopa*); his gait is like that of an elephant, thus it is "elephant-gait" (*nāgagati*). Likewise, "lion-gait" (*sīhagati*), "elephant-stride" (*nāgavikkama*), "lion-stride" (*sīhavikkama*), and "lion-jaw" (*sīhahanu*).
He has shanks like those of an antelope, thus he is "antelope-shanked" (*eṇijaṅgho*); his body has the fore-part like that of a lion, thus he is "lion-fore-bodied" (*sīhapubbaddhakāyo*);
his voice is endowed with the eight qualities like that of Brahmā, thus he is "Brahmā-voiced" (*brahmassaro*).

The word *vā* is used in the sense of "and"; when both members of a compound are numerals, it forms a numeral compound (*saṅkhyobhayapado*), such as "two or three bowls" (*dvattipattā*). [As in: "The letter *ā* occurs in two or one place."

In the word *vā*, the vowel *ā* of the word ending in *dvi* is shortened; thus, two days or three days is *dvīhatīhaṃ*; six or five utterances is *chappañcavācā*. Likewise for seven or eight months, and one or two *yojanas*.
The sense of being in between two directions is as follows: that which is the intermediate space between the eastern and southern directions is the southeastern direction (*pubbadakkhiṇā*).
*vidisā*. Here, because there is an absence of the status of being words in apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), there is no extension of the masculine gender (*pumbhāvātideso*).
By the rule beginning with "kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ," the first member of the compound is shortened when it signifies an intermediate direction. Thus: *pubbuttarā*, *aparadakkhiṇā*, *pacchimuttarā*.
However, when there is a *kammadhāraya* compound such as "that which is both south and east" (*dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā ca*), then there is an extension of the masculine gender.

Because the meaning of the latter member of the compound is predominant, the application of the pronominal suffixes also occurs invariably, as in *dakkhiṇapubbassā* (of the south-east) and *dakkhiṇapubbassaṃ* (to the south-east). The example characterized by reciprocal exchange (*byatihāra*) is:
"Having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeds," thus *kesākesi*.
*Daṇḍādaṇḍi* means "this battle proceeds by striking with sticks against sticks. According to the rule beginning with *kvacādimajjhuttarānaṃ*, the middle vowel is lengthened;
according to the rule beginning with *tesu vuddhī*, the final syllable is replaced by *-ika*.
This is a bahubbīhi compound expressing the sense of the first case ending.
The Bahubbīhi compound is finished.
Now the Dvandva compound is stated.
And that [compound] is of two kinds, distinguished by the meanings of mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*) and collective aggregation (*samāhāra*).

Regarding these, first, in the case of mutual conjunction—as in “Sāriputta-Moggallāna”—the nominative singular is used for both members, and the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of indicating a conjunction.
In the analytical statement (*viggahe*): “Sāriputto ca Moggallāno ca.”
357. A *dvanda* is a collection of names (*nāmānaṃ samuccayo*).
Whatever collection there is of various names that possess a single case-ending and have a connected meaning, that optionally becomes a compound and is designated as a *dvanda*.

Herein, "collection" means a grouping together; furthermore, by way of meaning, it is fourfold: simple collection (*kevalasamuccaya*), addition (*anvācaya*), mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*), and aggregate (*samāhāra*).

In that regard, a compound does not occur in the case of a simple conjunction (*kevalasamuccaya*) or a subsequent addition (*anvācaya*), because the nouns, being dependent on the action, do not have a mutually connected meaning, as in:

"He gave robes, alms-food, requisites, and lodgings," or "Give a gift and guard your virtue. However, a compound does occur in the case of mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*) and collective aggregation (*samāhāra*); therein—

Because their meanings are mutually connected, two by two words are *dvanda*s; or rather, they are *dvanda*s because they possess the state of being a *dvanda*, and since this compound is similar to a *dvanda*, it is also called "dvanda" by virtue of its derivative meaning (*anvattha-saññā*), for a *dvanda* has both word-meanings as its primary referents.
But surely, if both word-meanings are the primary referents in a *dvanda*, how can there be a unification of meaning (*ekatthībhāva*)? It is said in reply:

—Even when there is a similarity of meaning, because the occurrence of the word is possible [in both senses], there is no contradiction, since two words can indicate two meanings simultaneously in a single moment;
and this applies specifically to the domain of *dvanda* (copulative compounds), because they indicate those two meanings.

For just as the word *bhū*, when accompanied by prefixes such as *anu* or *abhi*, indicates meanings such as "experience" or "overpowering," but not when it is alone, so too in cases such as *gavassa-kaṃ*, the words *go* and so forth [indicate their respective meanings].

It should be understood that the illustration of the two meanings applies only to those [words] accompanied by *assādi*, *sadda*, and *antara*, and not to them alone; furthermore, this applies specifically to the domain of *dvanda* compounds and not in all instances.
Alternatively, since both [types of words] indicate the aforementioned conjunction (*samuccaya*), there is no contradiction in the fact that *dvanda* compounds possess a single referent (*ekattha*).

Consequently, the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saññā*), the elision of case endings (*vibhatti-lopa*), and so forth, follow the previously stated method; indeed, the meaning is conveyed by the compound itself.
Because it has been stated [in the rule], there is no application of the word *ca* (and) according to the principle:

“there is no application [of *ca*] where the meaning has already been expressed. Here, in a *dvanda* compound, that which is more important (*accitatara*) is placed first, and the gender of the subsequent member alone is maintained. Because in a reciprocal conjunction (*itarītarayoga*) the individual members are predominant, the plural number is used in all instances.
For example: *sāriputtamoggallānā*, *sāriputtamoggallāne*, *sāriputtamoggallānehi*, and so forth; as well as *samaṇo ca*.

A brahmin and ascetics and brahmins; likewise, brahmin householders, kshatriyas and brahmins, gods and humans, the moon and the sun, and mother and father—“parents”—in these dvanda compounds, the vowel *ā* replaces the initial syllable of the preceding word such as "mother" and so forth.
Likewise, "father and son."
In the phrase “jāyā ca pati ca = jāyāpati,” the word “kvaci” (sometimes) is understood here.
[The suffix] *tu* is added after *jāyā* to form *jāni* when referring to the husband.
The words *jāyā* and *jāni* undergo these substitutions when followed by the word *pati*, in certain instances: *tudaṃpati*, *jānipati*, *jayampatikā*.
Here, there is the insertion of a nasal (*niggahīta*), and shortening [of the vowel] according to the rule beginning with "kvacā. In some cases, the shorter member is placed first;

for example: *cando ca sūriyo ca* becomes *candasūriyā*; *nigamā ca janapadā ca* becomes *nigamajanapadā*; and *surā ca asurā ca garuḷā ca manujā ca bhujagā ca gandhabbā* [becomes *surāsuragarulamanujabhujagagandhabbā*].
And [the same applies to] *sura*, *asura*, *garuḷa*, *manuja*, *bhujaga*, and *gandhabba*.

In some cases, there is the prior placement of those ending in the vowels *i* and *u*, as in: *aggi ca dhūmo ca* = *aggidhūmā* (fire and smoke). Likewise: *gati*, *buddhi*, *bhujapaṭha*, *harakara*, *rasa*, *yā*, *dhātavo*, and *liṅgāni* = *dhātuliṅgāni* (elements and genders).

In some cases, there is the prior placement of those beginning with a vowel and ending in the vowel *a*, as in: *attho ca dhammo ca* = *atthadhammā* (meaning and doctrine). Likewise: *atthasaddā* or *saddatthā* (words and meanings).

In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), however—having formed a *dvanda* compound according to the rule "the conjunction of nouns is a *dvanda*," as in the sense of "the eye and the ear" (*cakkhu ca sotañca*), and having performed the elision of case endings and so forth—the following applies:
"The neuter gender and the singular number. 359.

Likewise, in a *dvanda*, this applies to the categories of living beings (*pāṇa*), musical instruments (*tūriya*), equipment (*yogga*), parts of an army (*senāṅga*), small creatures (*khuddajantuka*), various things, opposites (*viruddha*), heterogeneous things (*visabhāga*), and so on.

Just as in the case of a *digu* compound, so too in a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvanda* compound there is singularity and neuter gender for such terms as "limbs of living beings, musical instruments, vehicles, and armies," as well as "small creatures, various [things], enemies, and incompatible things. Thus:
*pāṇino ca tūriyāni ca yoggāni ca senā ca* = *pāṇitūriyayoggasenā*; their limbs are *pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅgāni*.
Because it follows a *dvanda*, the word *aṅga* is connected with each individual member. Furthermore, *khuddā ca te jantukā ca* = *khuddajantukā*.
“Vividhaviruddhā” means those that are opposed in various ways; they are constant adversaries. “Sabhāgā” refers to those whose parts are similar;

by the rule beginning with “tesu vuddhi,” there is the substitution of *sa* for *sama*. They are called “visabhāgā” because they are diverse in their characteristics (*lakkhaṇato*) yet similar in their function (*kiccato*).
Furthermore, the limbs suitable for living beings and musical instruments, as well as small creatures, are both diverse and opposed, and thus are “visabhāgā.”

The term *cāti* is a *dvanda* compound; here, because there is a plurality [of items], the priority of the first member is not fixed. Those whose objects are these—namely, living beings (*pāṇi*), musical instruments (*tūriya*), equipment for vehicles (*yoggasenaṅga*), small creatures (*khuddajantuka*), various hostile things (*vividhaviruddha*), and dissimilar things (*visabhāgattha*)—are "those beginning with those" (*tadādayo*).
By the inclusion of the word "etc.
(*ādi*), other categories are also included: those distinguished by mutual gender, number, measure, meaning, cooking, outcastes (*caṇḍāla*), meaning, direction (*disattha*), and so forth.

In a *dvanda* compound, there is singularity and neuter gender; thus, because they are parts of the body (pānyaṅga), singularity and neuter gender are applied to the words *cakkhu* (eye) and *sota* (ear).
Having formed the compound, when the designation of a noun (*nāmavyapadesa*) is made, the case endings (*syādi*) arise, along with the substitution of *am* and so forth.
Thus: *cakkhusotaṃ*, *he cakkhusota*, *cakkhusotaṃ*, *cakkhusotena*. In this way, it remains in the singular throughout.
“Mukhañca nāsikā ca” becomes “mukhanāsikaṃ”; the shortening of the final vowel occurs according to the rule “a vowel is shortened in the neuter.

“Hanu ca gīvā ca” becomes “hanugīvaṃ. In the same way: “kaṇṇanāsaṃ,” “pāṇipādaṃ,” and “chavimaṃsalohitaṃ. However, in cases such as “hatthapādā maṃsalohitāni,” the formation is established through mutual conjunction (itarītarayoga). Thus it is in the sense of a limb of the hand.

"Singing and instrumental music" (*gītavāditaṃ*) refers to singing and instrumental music; "clapping and rhythmic percussion" (*sammattāḷaṃ*)—*sammas* refers to bronze cymbals; *tāḷas* refers to hand-clapping.
"Conch shells, drums, and kettledrums" (*saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ*) means conch shells, drums, and kettledrums;
alternatively, it may be analyzed as "conch shells, drums, and kettledrums. Both "drums" (*paṇava*) and so forth are specific types of large drums (*bheri*).
In the sense of equipment (*yoggaṅga*): a plow and a sickle are "plow-and-sickle" (*phālapācana*); a yoke and a plow are "yoke-and-plow" (*yuganaṅgala*). In the sense of military units (*senāṅga*):
elephants and horses are "elephants-and-horses" (*hatthiassa*); chariots and infantry are "chariots-and-infantry" (*rathapattika*);

sword and shield are "sword-and-shield" (*asicamma*)—where "shield" (*camma*) refers to a wooden board for warding off arrows; bow and quiver are "bow-and-quiver" (*dhanukalāpa*)—where "quiver" (*kalāpa*) refers to a case for arrows.

In the sense of small creatures: *ḍaṃsa* (gadflies) and *makasa* (mosquitoes) make *ḍaṃsamakasaṃ*. Likewise, *kuntha* (ants), *kipillika* (ants), *kīṭa* (insects), *paṭaṅga* (grasshoppers), and *kīṭasarīsapa* (insects and reptiles). Herein, *kunthā* are tiny ants; *kīṭā* are insects that crawl on the backs of skulls. In the sense of various opposites:

*ahi* (snake) and *nakula* (mongoose) make *ahinakulaṃ*, or alternatively, *ahī* (snakes) and *nakulā* (mongooses). Likewise, *biḷāra* (cat) and *mūsika* (mouse); *anta* (end) with its shortening [of the vowel]; *kāka* (crow) and *ulūka* (owl); *sappa* (snake) and *maṇḍūka* (frog); *garuḷa* (eagle) and *sappa* (snake). In the sense of things that are dissimilar:
*sīla* (virtue) and *paññāṇa* (wisdom) make *sīlapaññāṇaṃ*; *samatha* (tranquility) and *vipassanā* (insight) make *samathavipassanaṃ*.

Thus, there are *nāmarūpa*, moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*), mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), greed and delusion (*lobhamoha*), hatred and delusion (*dosamoha*), lack of shame and lack of dread (*ahirikānottappa*), sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*), and so forth.

Regarding the rule “*aṃmo niggahītaṃ jhalapehi*,” it should be understood that because the term "*aṃmo*" is shown as a demonstrative reference (*niddesa*), it does not possess the neuter gender in certain instances; by this, [the compound] *ādhipaccaparivāro* [is formed].
The [terms] *chandapārisuddhi*, *paṭisandhi*, *pavatti*, and so forth, are established.

In a *dvanda* compound where the members are distinguished by different genders, as in *dāsī ca dāso ca* (a female slave and a male slave), the form becomes *dāsidāsaṃ*; here, shortening occurs in the middle according to the rule beginning with "kvacādī. Similarly, one finds *itthipumaṃ*, *pattacīvaraṃ*, *sākhāpalāsaṃ*, and so on.
In a *dvanda* compound where the meaning is numerical measure, as in *ekakañca dukañca*, the form is *ekakadukaṃ*; in a numerical *dvanda*, the smaller number [comes first].
The former word falls first. Thus: *dukatikam*, *tikacatukkan*, *catukkapañcakam*; *dīgho ca majjhimo ca* = *dīghamajjhimam*.
In a *dvanda* compound, the place of the "cooking outcaste" (*pacana-caṇḍāla*) is as follows: *orabbhikā ca sūkarikā ca* = *orabbhikasūkarikam*. Likewise:
*sākuṇikamāgavikam*, *sapāko ca caṇḍālo ca* = *sapākacaṇḍālam*, *pukkusachavaḍāhakam*, *venarathakāram*. Therein:
The *venā* (weavers), *tacchakā* (carpenters), *rathakārā* (chariot-makers), and *cammakārā* (leather-workers).
Regarding the meaning "the eastern and western directions," a *dvanda* compound is formed;

after the elision of the case endings (*vibhatti*), by the inclusion of the word "here" (*idha*) in the rule for singularity and the neuter gender, the shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule: "The vowel is short in the neuter."
*Pubbāparaṃ*, *he pubbāpara*, *pubbāparaṃ*, *pubbāparena*, *pubbāparassa*, and so forth. Likewise for *puratthimapacchimaṃ*, *dakkhiṇuttaraṃ*, and *adharuttaraṃ*.
The phrase "neuter gender, singular number, in a dvanda" also continues [to apply].
360. *Vibhāsā* (optionally) applies to trees, grass, cattle, wealth, grain, countries, and so forth.

In a *dvanda* compound, the singularity and the neuter gender of trees, grass, cattle, wealth, grain, countries, and so forth, are optional. In the absence of singularity, the plural is used, as well as the gender of the subsequent member.
In that regard, for a *dvanda* compound of trees, such as in the sense "the *assattha* and the *kapittha*," when it is a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvanda* compound, [the rules apply].

When combined by this alternative [rule], there is unity and the neuter gender. For example: *assatthakapitthaṃ* (the *assattha* and *kapittha* trees), or *assatthakapitthā* (the *assattha* and *kapittha* trees).

Likewise: *ambapanasaṃ* (the mango and breadfruit trees), or *ambapanasā*; *khadirapalāsaṃ* (the acacia and *palāsa* trees), or *khadirapalāsā*; *dhavassakaṇṇakaṃ* (the *dhava* and *assakaṇṇaka* trees), or *dhavassakaṇṇakā*. In a copulative compound (*dvanda*) of grasses:

*usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca* (the *usīra* and *bīraṇa* grasses) becomes *usīrabīraṇaṃ*, or *usīrabīraṇāni*; likewise: *muñjapabbajaṃ* (the *muñja* and *pabbaja* grasses), or *muñjapabbajā*; *kāsakusaṃ* (the *kāsa* and *kusa* grasses), or *kāsakusā*.
In the case of animals in a dvanda compound: *ajā* (goat) and *eḷakā* (sheep) form *ajeḷakaṃ* or *ajeḷakā*;
*hatthī* (elephant), *gāvo* (cows), *assā* (horses), and *vaḷavā* (mares) form *hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ* or *hatthigavassavaḷavā*.

By the rule beginning with "kvacā," there is shortening of the vowels, and by the rule "osare ca," there is the substitution of *ava*. Thus: *gomahiṃsaṃ* or *gomahiṃsā*; *eṇeyyavarāhaṃ* or *eṇeyyavarāhā*; *sīhabyagghataracchaṃ*.

Or lions, tigers, and leopards. In a copulative compound of wealth-terms: *hiraññañca suvaṇṇañca* becomes *hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ*, or *hiraññasuvaṇṇāni*. Likewise, *jātarūparajataṃ*, or *jātarūparajatāni*; *maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyaṃ*, or *maṇimuttasaṅkhaveḷuriyā*.
In a copulative compound of grain-terms: *sālī ca yavā ca* becomes *sāliyavaṃ*, or *sāliyavā*. Likewise, *tilamuggamāsaṃ*, or *tilamuggamāsā*.

In the case of a dvanda compound of names of countries, there is optionally a singular form and neuter gender: *kāsī ca kosalā ca* becomes *kāsikosalaṃ* or *kāsikosalā*; *vajjī ca mallā ca* becomes *vajjimallaṃ* or *vajjimallā*; *aṅgā ca magadhā ca* becomes *aṅgamagadhaṃ* or *aṅgamagadhā*. By the inclusion of the word "etc.
(*ādi*), there is optionally a singular form and neuter gender for dvanda compounds of mutually opposing phenomena and of birds:
*kusalañca akusalañca* becomes *kusalākusalaṃ* or *kusalākusalā*.
Thus, the blameworthy and the blameless, or the blameworthy and the blameless; the inferior and the sublime, or the inferior and the sublime;
the dark and the bright, or the dark and the bright; pleasure and pain, or pleasures and pains;
aversion and attachment, or aversions and attachments; shade and sunlight, or shades and sunlight; light and darkness, or lights and darkness; night and day, and the night-and-day.

*Rattindivā* means night and day; *ahorattaṃ* means day and night (*ahar* and *rattaṃ*). From *ahorattā*, the long vowel *ā* is substituted for the short vowels *a* and *i* according to the rule beginning with "kvaci samāsanta.

In a copulative compound (*dvanda*) of birds: *haṃsā ca bakā ca* becomes *haṃsabakaṃ* or *haṃsabakā*. Likewise, *kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ* or *kāraṇḍavacakkavākā*; *mayūrakoñcaṃ* or *mayūrakoñcā*; *sukasālikaṃ* or *sukasālikā*. These are examples of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvanda*).
And here, for the most part:
first, there is the expansion of vowels; in some cases, there is the substitution of *i* and *u* vowels;
in a dvanda compound, that which begins with a vowel and ends in the letter *a* [comes first]; and there is no fixed rule regarding the number of syllables.
The section on *dvanda* compounds is concluded.
This compound is fourfold because it is predominant in the first member, the second member, both, or another meaning; furthermore, this compound is sixfold when including *digu* and *kammadhāraya*.
The *abyayībhāva* compound is of two kinds, the *kammadhāraya* is ninefold;
the *digu* is twofold, the *tappurisa* would be eightfold or ninefold;
the *bahubbīhi* is twofold, and the *dvanda*—thus the compound is of four and eight types.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Section on Compounds, within the *Padarūpasiddhi*. 5.
The Section on Secondary Derivatives (*Taddhita*).

**Non-Derivatives (Apaccataddhita):** Now, since secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) arise after nominal stems (*nāma*) ending in case endings to express specific meanings such as "descendant" (*apacca*) and so forth, the rules for the formation of secondary suffixes are commenced following the nominal stems.

In this context, they are called *taddhita* because they are beneficial (*hita*) or associated (*sahita*) with the three types of gender (*liṅga*) that follow them; this is a designation for suffixes such as *ṇa* and others.
A *taddhita* [suffix] is so called by way of a derivative technical term (*anvatthabhūtaparasamaññā*) based on the sense that it is "beneficial" (*hita*) or "helpful" (*upakāra*) to those names,
thus being a "derivative of that" (*tassa hita*).
In the analysis of the compound "the offspring of Vasiṭṭha":
In the phrase “liṅgañca nipaccate,” the mention of *liṅga* (gender) from the preceding rule is carried over here. 361. *Vā ṇa’pacce*:
After a word ending in the genitive case that denotes gender, the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs in the sense of “his offspring.”
And so—362. "The suffixes follow from the roots and the genders.
According to the Paribhāṣā rule, "the suffixes follow after the roots and the genders," [it is understood] that the gender is not connected with the meaning of the suffix.

The suffix *anta* ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) alone constitutes the "other" [member]. It is called a *paccaya* (condition) because meaning (*attha*) comes from it; or alternatively, it is a *paccaya* because meaning is understood (*pati-iyanti*) by means of it.

There is no application of the word *appa* in the rule "there is no application of the word *appa* when the meaning has already been stated," and there is also the elision of the case-ending according to the rule "the case-endings of those [suffixes] are elided."
363. *Tesaṃ ṇo lopaṃ*.

The letter *ṇ*, which is an *anubandha* of those *taddhita* suffixes, undergoes elision (*lopa*). 364. *Vuddhādisarassa vāsaṃyogantassa saṇe ca*. [The elision of the *ṇ* occurs] optionally after a vowel that begins with a *vuddhi* vowel, provided it is not at the end of a conjunct consonant, even when followed by the suffix *saṇ*.
Vṛddhi occurs for the first vowel (ādisara) or the initial consonant (ādibyañjana) that does not end in a conjunct (asaṃyoganta), when followed by the suffix *saṇ*.

That which has a conjunct at its end is "ending in a conjunct" (*saṃyoganta*); other than that is "not ending in a conjunct" (*asaṃyoganta*). Alternatively, the word "or" (*vā*) here has the sense of a restrictive distribution (*vavatthitavibhāsa*);
in that case, when the gender is in its original form (*pakatibhūta*), vṛddhi occurs for the first vowel of the vowels that do not end in a conjunct, when followed by *saṇ*.
The meaning is "in a taddhita suffix. By this—
[it is shown that] in cases such as *Vāsiṭṭha* and so on, [the suffix] is permanent (*nicca*), whereas in cases such as *olumpika* and so on, it is not permanent (*anica*).
There is no growth [of the vowel] in the case of "blue," "yellow," and so forth, because they are fixed in their specific expressions.
The inclusion of the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of restriction.
Since there is a possibility of that growth being unrestricted, he states a grammatical maxim (*paribhāsa*) for the sake of restriction.
365. *Ayuvannañca āyo vuddhi*.
For those [sounds], namely the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u*, the corresponding *vuddhi* (increment) sounds are *ā*, *e*, and *o* respectively.

The inclusion of the word *ca* (*and*) is for the purpose of including the non-*vuddhi* sounds, or for the purpose of restriction. *I* and *u* are *yu*; *yu* itself are the *yuvanna* (consonant-vowel) sounds; *a* and the *yuvanna* sounds are *ayuvanna*.

Ā, e, and o are called *āyo*. The repetition of the term "vṛddhi" (increase) is for the purpose of indicating that there is an increase in the subsequent member of the compound in cases such as *negamajānapadā* ("townspeople and countryfolk").

And here, the statement of the restriction of position, namely "*of the vowels a and i*," is for the purpose of precluding the possibility of an increase (*vṛddhi*) occurring in place of the *āyo* sounds.
For just as there is no further increase for those [sounds] in which an increase has already been effected, so it is here.
Likewise, for those [vowels] whose nature is growth (*vuddhi*), there is no further growth.

Therefore, the change of *a* to *ā* is "growth" (*vuddhi*). According to the rule, "When *sara*, elision (*lopa*), augment (*āgama*), substitute (*ādesa*), affix (*paccaya*), etc., occurs, in the case of elision of *sara*, the original form (*pakati*) remains," there is the state of being the original form due to the elision of *sara*.

Then, by applying the subsequent guidance according to the rule, "In a derivative (*yutta*), lead [the preceding] to the following," because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it receives the designation of a noun (*nāma*) by the rule beginning with "A secondary derivative and a compound... and so forth.
The arising of a clan-name (*gotra*) may be like that of a *kate* (a derivative suffix).

For example, "Vāsiṭṭha," "the son of Vasiṣṭha," or "the Vāsiṭṭhas" and so forth are identical to the word for the person (*puruṣa*). His grandsons, great-grandsons, and so on, are also called "Vāsiṭṭhas" by metaphorical designation (*tadupacāra*).
Thus, in all cases involving a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) of a clan-name, the suffix is applied from the very first base form (*pakati*).
Because the word *vāsiṭṭha* ends in the feminine suffix *ṇī*, the suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule “*ṇava ṇika ṇeyya ṇa ntūhī*.

After performing the elision of the vowel (*saralopa*) and other operations, since it now ends in a feminine suffix, the designation “noun” (*nāma*) is applied by the inclusion of the word “optionally” (*ca*) in the sutta beginning with “*taddhita-samāsa*,” which triggers the addition of the case endings (*syādi*).
Thus, *vāsiṭṭhī kaññā*, *vāsiṭṭhī*, *vāsiṭṭhiyo*, and so forth, are identical to feminine words.

In the neuter gender, *vāsiṭṭhaṃ apaccaṃ* (the descendant of Vasiṣṭha) and *vāsiṭṭhāni apaccāni* (the descendants of Vasiṣṭha), and so forth, are similar to the word *citta*. In this way, the three-gendered nature of words ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) should be understood in subsequent cases as well.
The son of Bhāradvāja is *bhāradvāja*; the son of Vesāmitta is *vesāmitta*; the son of Gotama is *gotama*.
And here, because of the absence of the vowels *i* and *u*, there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) of the long vowels such as *ā*. The descendant of Vasudeva is *vāsudeva*.
Baladeva states: In cases such as *cittaka*, there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) because of the final conjunct consonant.

In the analysis (*viggahe*) "the descendant (*apacca*) of Vaccha," when the suffix *ṇa* is reached, the rule "optionally (*vā*) before *ṇa-apacca*" from this [section] applies throughout the section on the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita-vidhāna*).
Therefore, in all instances, there are syntactic applications (*vākya-vuttiyo*). The word "descendant" (*apacce*) continues to apply as far as the mention of "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*).

366. From *Ṇāyana*, *Ṇāna*, *Vacchādita*, *Vaccha*, *Kacca*, and so forth—from the sixth case ending, from a clan or group (*gottagaṇa*)—the suffixes *Ṇāyana* and *Ṇāna* optionally occur in the sense of "his descendant" (*tassāpaccam*).
In all instances, the letter *Ṇ* as an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) serves to indicate vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*); the remainder is the same as the preceding [rules].
The distinction lies in the presence or absence of the suffix *-anta*. [For example:
from *Vaccha*, [we have] *Vacchāyana*, *Vacchāna*, or *Vacchassa-putta* (the son of Vaccha). Likewise, from *Kacca*, [we have] *Kaccāyana*, *Kaccāna*;
from *Moggalla*, [we have] *Moggallāyana*, *Moggallāna*. Similarly, from *Aggivessa*, [we have] *Aggivessāyana*, *Aggivessāna*; from *Kaṇha*, [we have] *Kaṇhāyana*, *Kaṇhāna*.
*Sākaṭāyana* from *sākaṭa*, *muñcāyana* from *muñca*, *kuñjāyana* from *kuñja*, and so forth. This is a class of words (*ākati-gaṇa*).
In the analysis "the descendant of Kattikā," [the suffix] 367.
*Ṇeyya* is applied after *kattikā* and others.

This word *ādi* (and so forth) functions in the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). After nominal stems occurring in the feminine gender, such as *kattikā*, *vinatā*, and *rohiṇī*, the suffix *ṇeyya* optionally occurs in the sense of "her offspring" (*tassā apaccaṃ*).
Upon the elision of the case ending, the original stem form (*pakati*) is maintained by the rule "and for a stem ending in a vowel.

Thus: *kattikeyyo*, meaning the offspring of *kattikā*. Similarly, the offspring of *vinatā* is *venateyyo*; here, the long *ī* is replaced by the short *i* as the vowel-increment (*vuddhi*). The son of *rohiṇī* is *rohiṇeyyo*.
The offspring of Gaṅgā is *Gaṅgeyyo*; the son of a sister is *bhāgineyyo*; the son of a river is *nādeyyo*. Likewise, *anteyyo*, *āheyyo*, and *kāmeyyo*.
The offspring of Sucī is *Soceyyo*—here, the vowel *u* becomes *o* through *vuddhi* (vowel strengthening); the offspring of Bālā is *Bāleyyo*, and so forth.
When the suffix *ṇa* is reached in the analysis “the offspring of Dakkha,” [the following applies]:
368. *Ato ṇi vā*.
The suffix *ṇi* optionally occurs after a feminine stem ending in *a* in the sense of "her offspring" (*tassāpacca*).
For example: *dakkhi*, *dakkhī*, *dakkhayo*; the offspring of a *doṇa* is *doṇi*. Likewise: *vāsavi*, *sakyaputti*, *nāṭaputti*, *dāsaputti*, *dāsarathi*.
Vāruṇi, Kaṇḍi, Bāladevi, Pāvaki, Jinadattassa apaccaṃ (the offspring of Jinadatta) is Jenadatti; likewise Suddhodani, Anuruddhi, and so forth.
Again, by the inclusion of the word "vā" (or), the suffix *ṇika* is applied in the sense of offspring, and the suffix *ṇya* is applied after words such as Aditi.
For example: the son of Sakya-putta is *Sakyaputtiko*; according to the rule beginning with "tesu vuddhī," the letter *k* becomes *y*, resulting in *Sakyaputtiyo*. In the same way: Nāṭaputtiko.
*Jenadattika* means "son of Jenadatta"; *vemātiko* means "son of a stepmother.
When the meaning is "son of Aditi," the suffix *-ṇya* is applied and the vowel is increased (*vṛddhi*).
369. The vowel *a* is elided, and there is also the elision of *ye*.
The vowel *avaṇṇa* undergoes elision when followed by the *taddhita* suffix *ya*. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that the vowel *ivaṇṇa* also [undergoes elision];

thus, there is the elision of the letter *i*. According to the rule, “In the case of the consonants *ta*, *la*, *na*, *da*, and *ka*, as well as *la*, *ña*, and *ja*, they become *ca*,” the *ca* replaces the conjunct *tya*.
By the rule, “In place of two following [consonants], there is doubling,” there is doubling (*dvitta*). Thus: *ādicco*. Likewise, the son of *Diti* is *decco*.
When the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of "the son of Kuṇḍanī," the rule "kvacādimajjhuttare" (at times, [substitution occurs] in the beginning, middle, or end) applies.
370. Among those [cases], there are [instances of] vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*), elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification (*vikāra*), and reverse substitution (*viparitādēsa*).

Among those [words] whose characteristics are not prescribed for the beginning, middle, or end, there occur—in accordance with the word of the Victor (*jinavacana*)—in certain instances, vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), elision (*lopa*), augment (*āgama*), modification (*vikāra*), reversal (*viparīta*), and substitution (*ādesa*).
Thus, even when ending in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoganta*), there is strengthening of the initial vowel (*ādivuddhi*); with the elision of the letter *i*, there is the substitution of *nya*:
*koṇḍañño*. *Kuruno putto* becomes *korabyo*; here too, by that same rule, there is the substitution of *ava* for the letter *u*. *Bhātuno putto* becomes *bhātabyo*.
In the analysis [of the compound] *upagussāpacca* (“the descendant of Upagu”), [rule] 371 applies: *Ṇavopagvādīhi*.
After the groups of names beginning with *upagu*, which end in *u* and denote lineages (*gotta*), the suffix *Ṇava* optionally occurs in the sense of “his descendant” (*tassāpacco*).

[Regarding] *atthe*: because the word *ādi* here expresses "a type" (*pakāra*), this [suffix] occurs only after a stem ending in *-u*. Examples include: *opagavo*, *opagavī*, *opagavaṃ* (from *upagava*);
*mānavo* (the descendant of *manu*)—this form arises when the suffix *ṇa* is applied and the augment *s* is added, resulting in *mānuso*;
*bhaggavo* (the descendant of *bhaggu*); *paṇḍavo* (the descendant of *paṇḍu*); *opavindavo* (the descendant of *upavindu*), and so forth.
Regarding the meaning "offspring of a widow":
372. *Ṇa* after *vidhavā*, etc.
The suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs after *vidhavā* and others in the sense of offspring (*apacca*). She whose husband (*dhava*)—that is, her lord (*pati*)—has departed is a *vidhavā*.
Vedhavera, bandhukera— the son of a female messenger (abhisāriṇī) by a kinsman (bandhu)— and sāmaṇera, meaning "a novice who is like a son" because he is the son of a monk’s preceptor (upajjhāya),
as well as nāḷikera, and so forth. These are examples of words not formed with secondary suffixes (apaccataddhita).

Regarding the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffixes with multiple meanings, such as *saṃsaṭṭha*: in the analysis of the compound "mixed with sesame" (*tilena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ*), [the rule states]: 373.
The suffix *ṇika* is applied after a word with which one is mixed, or by means of which one crosses, moves, or carries.

The suffix *ṇika* optionally occurs after a word ending in the third case (*tatiyanta*)—whether that word denotes with whom one is associated (*saṃsaṭṭha*), by means of what one crosses (*tarati*), by means of what one moves (*carati*), or by means of what one is carried (*vahati*)—to express those meanings of being associated and so forth. *Telikaṃ bhojanaṃ*: food prepared with sesame oil;
the meaning is "prepared with sesame oil. *Telikī yāgu*: rice gruel [prepared with sesame oil]. *Egāḷikaṃ*: a mixture associated with sugar. Likewise: *ghātikaṃ*, *dādhikaṃ*, *māricikaṃ*, *loṇikaṃ*.
One who crosses by means of a boat is a *nāvika*; one who crosses by means of a raft is an *oḷumpika*. In the alternative where there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), it is *uḷumpika*.
Likewise for *kullika* and *gopucchika*. One who travels by means of a cart is a *sākaṭika*. Likewise for *pādika* and *daṇḍika*.
One who acts or proceeds according to the Dhamma is *dhammika*. One who carries on the head is *sīsika*; by the inclusion of the suffix *-ika*, there is the strengthening (*vuddhi*) of the vowel *ī*.
There is no [suffix]. Likewise with *aṃsika*, *khandhika*, *hatthika*, and *aṅgulika*.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of the word "again" (*puna*), the suffix *ṇika* occurs even in other senses: from *paradāraṃ gacchati* comes *pāradāriko*; from *pathaṃ gacchati* comes *pathiko*.
Or, in the analysis of the compounds *vinayam adhīte* and *aveccādhīte*—
“Ṇika” is understood [as the governing suffix].

374. [The suffix Ṇika is applied] after the word “tam” (that) in the sense of “one who studies that,” and after the words “tena kata” (made by him), etc., in the senses of proximity, appointment, craft, merchandise, and livelihood. This [sutta] consists of four words.
In the sense of “one who studies that” (*tam adhīte*), and in the senses of “made by him” (*tena kato*) and so forth, there is the application of that [suffix] in the sense of proximity; therein—

The suffix *ṇika* optionally occurs after nominal stems ending in the second case (*accusative*) and subsequent cases when expressing these meanings: "appointed to," "his craft," "his merchandise," or "his livelihood.
Examples: *venayiko* (one appointed to the discipline), likewise *suttantiko* (one appointed to the discourses) and *ābhidhammiko* (one appointed to the Abhidhamma).
When the sense is "he studies grammar" (*byākaraṇam adhīte*), and the suffix *ṇika* and others have been applied—

While the rule “*vuddhādisarassa vā saṃyogantassa saṇe cā*” (there is optionally *vuddhi* for a vowel beginning with *vuddhi*, etc., when followed by *saṇ*; and also for a conjunct-final [vowel] before *saṇ*) is in force:
375. *Māyūnamāgamo ṭhāne*:

For *mā*, *u*, *ī*, *ca*, *e*, *bhe*, and *saṃ*—when they do not end in a conjunct consonant—there is no *vuddhi* before *saṇ*. Instead, there is an augment (*āgama*) of *vuddhi* in that very place; thus, there is the augment of the *vuddhi* vowel *ē*.
And here, because of the word "in its place" (*ṭhāne*), since [the substitute] has become a replacement for the *yū* vowels,
the *vṛddhi* substitutions *e* and *o* occur as augmentations even before the *yava*s.
There is a doubling of the letter *y*.

One who explains is a *veyyākaraṇika*; one who has studied the Nyāya is a *neyyāyika*. Likewise, there are the *takki* (reasoner), the *vedika* (one who knows the Vedas), and the *nemittika* (one who knows omens).
That which is performed by the body is *kāyika*; action performed by the body is *kāyika*, and action performed by speech is *vācasika*.

Likewise, there is the *mānasika* (mental). And here, according to the rule "there is the augment *s-* before *sa-ṛ-ṣa-ṣa-sa-ha-va-y-ā-v-ā-m-ya-va-ra-la-na-ṅa-na-ma-na-ja-ña-bha-ga-gha-ḍha-dha-ja-cha-śa-kha-pha-tha-ta-tha-ca-ṭa-ṭa-pa" (*sasare vāgamo*), the augment *s-* occurs even when followed by an affix, due to the word *vavatthita* (restricted) [in the rule].

The *therikā* (recitation by the elders) was performed by those [elders]. Thus, in the cases of the *pañcasatikā* (five-hundredth) and *sattasatikā* (seven-hundredth), the suffix *-ī* does not occur here because the word "vāk" (speech) is understood from the rule beginning with "*ṇavaṇikā*" and so on. In the sense of proximity:
pain (*vedanā*) residing in the body (*sarīre sannidhānā*) is *sārīrikā*; bodily suffering is *sārīrikaṃ*. Likewise, mental is *mānasikā*; mental [suffering] is *mānasikaṃ*.

One appointed at the door of a specific meaning is a *dovārika* (doorkeeper); here, by the rule “there is the augment *o* before the letter *v* in the place [of the suffix] *ya*,” there is the augment *o* preceding the letter *v*.

In the same way: *bhaṇḍāgārika* (treasurer), *nāgarika* (citizen), *navakammika* (workman), *vanakammika* (forester), *ādikammika* (beginner), *odarika* (gluttonous), *rathika* (charioteer), *pathika* (traveler).
One appointed in a means (*upāya*) is *opāyika*; those appointed in the mind (*cetasi*) are *cetasika*.

In the sense of a craft (*sippa*): *vīṇāvādanaṃ vīṇā*; "the lute is his craft" is a lute-player (*veṇiko*). Likewise: a drummer (*pāṇaviko*), a player of the *modiṅga* drum (*modiṅgiko*), a flute-player (*vaṃsiko*).

In the sense of merchandise (*bhaṇḍa*): "merchandise is his" is a merchant (*gandhiko*). Likewise: an oil-seller (*teliko*), a seller of balls (*goḷiko*), a baker (*pūviko*), a seller of leaves (*paṇṇiko*), a betel-seller (*tambūliko*), a salt-seller (*loṇiko*).

In the sense of a livelihood (*jīvikā*): he lives by killing a ram; "a ram is his livelihood" is a butcher (*orabbhiko*). Likewise: a hunter of deer (*māgaviko*)—here there is the insertion of the letter *v*. A pig-killer (*sūkariko*), a fowler (*sākuṇiko*), a fisherman (*macchiko*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by him made, etc.," here the inclusion of "etc. refers to:

by him killed, by him bound, by him bought, he plays with it, it is his weapon, it is his affliction, devoted to that, belonging to him, its measure, a heap of it, it is worthy of it, his habit, born there, dwelling there, known therein.
The suffix *ṇika* occurs in such senses as: "it conduces to that," "come from that," "arisen from that," or "that is its purpose.
For example: one struck by a net (*jāla*), or one who strikes with it, is called a *jālika*.
Likewise, a fisherman (*bāḷisika*), a fowler (*vākarika*), one bound by thread is a *suttika*, and an elephant bound by a leather thong is a *vārattika*.

Goods purchased with cloth are "cloth-dealers. Likewise, there are those who deal in pots (*kumbhika*), those who deal in ploughshares (*phālika*), those who deal in gold (*sovaṇṇika*), and those who deal in swords (*sātika*).

One who plays with dice is a "dice-player" (*akkhika*); likewise, there are those who play with sticks (*sālākika*), those who play with *tinduka* nuts (*tindukika*), and those who play with mango fruits (*ambaphalika*). One whose weapon is a bow is a "bowman" (*cāpika*);
likewise, there are those who carry a lance (*tomarika*), those who carry a club (*muggarika*), and those who carry a pestle (*mosalika*).
One for whom wind is a disease is "windy" (*vātiko*). Likewise, one who has phlegm is "phlegmatic" (*semhiko*), and one who has bile is "bilious" (*pittiko*).

One who has faith in the Buddha is "devoted to the Buddha" (*buddhiko*); likewise, one devoted to the Dhamma is "Dhamma-devoted" (*dhammiko*), and one devoted to the Saṅgha is "Saṅgha-devoted" (*saṅghiko*). A dwelling belonging to the Buddha is "Buddha-owned" (*buddhiko*); likewise, a dwelling belonging to the Dhamma is "Dhamma-owned" (*dhammiko*), a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha is "Saṅgha-owned" (*saṅghiko*), land belonging to the Saṅgha is "Saṅgha-owned" (*saṅghikā bhūmi*), and a robe belonging to the Saṅgha is "Saṅgha-owned" (*saṅghikaṃ cīvaraṃ*).

That which belongs to an individual is "personal" (*puggalikaṃ*). That whose measure is a jar is "measured by a jar" (*kumbhikaṃ*); likewise, that measured by a *khāri* is "khārika," and that measured by a *doṇa* is "doṇika. A heap of jars is "a jar-heap" (*kumbhiko*).

One who is worthy of a *kumbha* is a *kumbhika*. Likewise, there are those worthy of a *doṇa*, a *aṭṭhamāsa*, a *kahāpaṇa*, the eighty-verse [text], the ninety-verse, the hundred-verse, and the thousand-verse.
One who is worthy of being seen face-to-face is *sandivṭṭhika*; one who is worthy of the procedure "Come, see for yourself" is *ehipassika*.

In the sense of virtue (*sīla*): wearing rags from a dust heap is *paṃsukūla*; one who has that as his virtue is a *paṃsukūlika*. Likewise, one who has the virtue of [wearing] only three robes is a *tecīvarika*; one whose habit is eating at a single sitting is an *ekāsanika*; one whose habit is dwelling at the foot of a tree is a *rukkhamūlika*;

similarly, an *āraññika*, a *sosānika*. In the sense of birth (*jāta*): one born in a state of misery is an *āpāyika*. Likewise, one bound for hell is a *nerayika*; a fish born in the sea is a *sāmuddika*; one born in the rains is a *vassika*, such as a *vassika* flower;
likewise, a *sāradika*, a *hemantika*, a *vāsantika*, or a *cātuddasika* [flower]. [One born] in Rājagaha...
A person born in Rājagaha and living there is called a *rājagahika*; one born in Magadha and living there is a *māgadhika* (male), *māgadhikā* (female), or *māgadhikaṃ* (neuter).
One born in Sāvatthī and living there is a *sāvatthika*; likewise, one from Kapilavatthu is a *kāpilavatthika*, and one from Vesālī is a *vesālika*.

Known in the world, it is *lokika*; or, that which leads to the world, it is also *lokika*. Similarly, a name derived from the mother is *mātika*, and that derived from the father is called *pettika*.

In the sense of being produced (*sambhūtatthe*), that which is produced from a mother is "maternal" (*mātika*); likewise for "paternal" (*pettika*). That which has a purpose related to acquisitions (*upadhi*) is "pertaining to acquisitions" (*opadhika*).

Even when used in its own sense (*sakatthe*), that which is without volitional effort is "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*); likewise for "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*). That which is a name itself is "nominal" (*nāmika*);
likewise for "verbal" (*ākhyātika*), "prepositional" (*opasaggika*), and "derivative" (*nepātika*). Those who have devotion (*bhatti*) toward the Four Great Kings are "Cātumahārājikas."
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.
Regarding the analysis of the compound *kasāvena rattaṃ*: 376. The suffix *ṇa* [is added] after *rāga*;
that by which something is colored is called *tena-rattaṃ*, and this suffix is also used in other senses.

The suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs after a word denoting color (*rāga*) in the sense of "dyed by that" (*tena rattaṃ*), following a word ending in the sixth case (*tasse*), and in the sense of "this" (*idaṃ*) or other meanings.

For example: *kāsāvaṃ vatthaṃ* (a yellow robe). Likewise, *kāsāyaṃ*. Dyed with safflower: *kosumbhaṃ*; dyed with turmeric: *hāliddaṃ*; *pattaṅgaṃ*, *mañjiṭṭhaṃ*, *kuṅkumaṃ*; dyed with indigo: *nīlaṃ*. Likewise, *pītaṃ* (yellow).

In the sense of "this belongs to a buffalo," *māhiṃsaṃ* means the meat of a buffalo, or curd, ghee, hide, and so forth; in the sense of "this belongs to a pig," *sūkaraṃ*; and in the sense of "this belongs to Kaccāyana," *kaccāyanaṃ* refers to the grammar. Likewise for the teaching of the Sugata (*sogataṃ sāsanaṃ*).

When the suffix *-ṇa* is applied in the sense of "this belongs to a seer" (*isissa idan*), and the vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) has been effected, the rule "in place of *saṇ*, there is the augment *yūna*" continues to apply.
377. *Āttañ-ca*.

In these [rules], when the suffix *saṇa* follows, the vowel *i* becomes *ā* for these vowels beginning with *i*; by the word "and" (*ca*), there is also the insertion of the vowel *ri*, and the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *i*.
Because of the governing context of "substitution" (*ṭhāna*), this applies to [vowels] such as those following *is*, *us*, *sabha*, and *auja*.
But for *issā*, the suffix *-ika* occurs when there is no interval [between the base and the suffix]. *Ārisyaṃ*:
this is the state of a bull (*usabha*), hence it is the "bull-like state" (*āsabhaṃ*); or it is the speech of a bull (*āsabhī vācā*).
By the inclusion of the word "elsewhere," however, there are the following meanings: being near, existing therein, born therein, or come from that; such is its [meaning].

The suffix *ṇa* is applied in such senses as: "dwelling," "its lord," "the month associated with Kattika and so forth," "its deity," "he studies that [text]," "the region which is its domain," "it exists in that region," "produced from that," "it deserves that," "a modification thereof," and "that is its measure.
For example: *vediso*, meaning "situated not far from the intermediate direction (*vidisā*)."
A village; a celestial mansion belonging to Udumbara, situated not far from Udumbara, is *odumbara*.
That which exists in the mind (*manas*) is mental happiness (*mānasa*); this includes the suffix *-a*. That which exists in water (*saras*) is a *sārasa* bird;

a *sārasī* is a female *sārasa* bird; a *sārasa* is a flower. That which exists in the breast (*uras*) is a breast-born son (*orasa*), because he was reared in the breast; those who exist among friends (*mitra*)...
*Mettā* or *mettī* means friendly; *purā* means ancient or polite speech. Regarding [words derived from] seasons and so forth:
born in the rainy season (*pāvusa*) is a "rainy-season friend" (*pāvuso*), such as a cloud; the rainy-season night; the rainy-season sky.

Likewise, born in autumn (*sārada*) is the month of autumn, the autumn night, or an autumn flower. Similarly for the cool season (*sisira*), winter (*hemanta*), spring (*vasanta*), and summer (*gimha*). In Mathurā...
A person born in Mathurā, a courtesan of Mathurā, cloth from Mathurā. One who has come from Mathurā is "Māthura"; one for whom Mathurā is his residence is "Māthura";

a king who is the lord of Mathurā is "Māthura. In the expression "sabbatoko," by the repetition of the word *sabba*, there is sometimes the addition of the suffix *-ka* even after a taddhita derivative;
thus, "māthurako" means born in Rājagaha or come from Rājagaha.
It is called *rājagaha* because it is his residence, or because he is the lord of Rājagaha; thus one is a *rājagahaka*.
Likewise, *sāgala* or *sāgalaka*, *pāṭaliputta* or *pāṭaliputtaka*, or *vesāla* or *vesālaka* in the sense of "born in Vesālī," and so forth;
likewise, *kosināra* or *kosināraka* in the sense of "born in Kusinārā"; and similarly, *sāketa* or *sāketaka*, *kosamba*, and so on.
Whether one is from Kosambī, or Indapatta, or Indapattaka; from Kapila, or Kapillaka;
or from Bhārukaccha, or Bhārukacchaka—one who is born in a city, has come from a city, or dwells in a city is called a *nāgara* or a *nāgaraka*. Thus it is with respect to a province (*janapada*).
However, in all cases regarding names of provinces, only the plural form is used. For example: "born in Aṅga," or "from Aṅga."
He has come from Aṅga—whether he be a native of Aṅga, a lord of Aṅga, or an inhabitant of Aṅga—or from Magadha, whether he be a native of Magadha or an inhabitant of Magadha;

or from Kosala, whether he be a native of Kosala or an inhabitant of Kosala; or from Vedeha, whether he be a native of Vedeha or an inhabitant of Vedeha; or from Kamboja, whether he be a native of Kamboja or an inhabitant of Kamboja; or from Gandhāra, whether he be a native of Gandhāra or an inhabitant of Gandhāra;

or from Sovīra, whether he be a native of Sovīra or an inhabitant of Sovīra; or from Sindhava, whether he be a native of Sindhava or an inhabitant of Sindhava; or from Assaka, Kaliṅga, Pañcāla, or Sakka.
Likewise, one born in Suratta, or the lord of Suratta, is a *soraṭṭha* or a *soraṭṭhaka*. Similarly, [one from] Mahāraṭṭha or a *mahāraṭṭhaka*, and so forth.
Regarding the conjunction of constellations (*nakkhattayoga*), the month joined with the full moon of Kattikā is *Kattika*; [the month] joined with the moon of Magasira...
The month joined with the constellation Maghā is Māgasira; likewise, the month joined with Phussa is Phussa,
the month joined with Maghā is Māgha, the month joined with Phagguṇī is Phagguṇa, the month joined with Cittā is Citta, the month joined with Visākhā is Vesākha,
the month joined with Jeṭṭhā is Jeṭṭha, and the month joined with Uttarāsāḷhā is Āsāḷha, [and also] Āsāḷhī.

Or, a month joined with the month of Śrāvaṇa is *sāvaṇo*, [and its full moon day] is *sāvaṇī*. A month joined with the month of Bhadra is *bhaddo*; a month joined with the month of Āśvayuja is *assayujo*.
One whose deity is Buddha is *buddho*. Likewise: *sogato*, *māhindo*, *yāmo*, *somo*.

One who has studied grammar after having mastered it is *veyyākaraṇo*. Likewise: *mohutto*, *nemitto*, *aṅgavijjo*, *vatthuvijjo*. A region that is the domain of the Vasātīs is *vāsāto*; a region where there are *udumbara* trees in that place is *odumbaro*.

A moat produced by a thousand [units] is *sāhassī*; rice-milk produced by [the same] is *pāyāsa*; that which deserves a thousand is *sāhassī*, as in a verse; iron is a transformation (*vikāra*) of non-iron (*ayasa*). Likewise for "golden" (*sovaṇṇa*). That water has a man as its measure is *porisaṃ* water.
By the inclusion of the particle "ca," the suffix *ṇeya* is applied in such cases as "born there," "dwells there," "beneficial for him," or "deserves that.
One who is born in or dwells in Benares is *bārāṇaseyyaka*; the letter *k* is inserted here as it was in the case of *pura*. Likewise, one from Campā is *campseyyaka*.
A person from Sāgala is a *sāgaleyyaka*; the people of Mithilā are *mithileyyaka*; a fish born in the Ganges is *gaṅgeyya*; what is produced from a stone is *seleyyaka*;
a dog born in a noble family is *koleyyaka*; a flower grown in the forest is *vāneyya*. Likewise, a human being from the mountains is *pabbateyya*;
a river from the mountains is *pabbateyyā*; a medicinal herb from the mountains is *pabbateyya*; what is beneficial for a journey is *pātheyya*; and wealth beneficial for a master is *sāpateyya*.
"Oil for lighting a lamp; filial devotion toward one's mother; likewise, filial devotion toward one's father. "Worthy of offerings" means *dakkhiṇeyyo*, and so forth. 378.
*Imi* and *iya* are also [suffixes] after words such as *jāta*. The suffixes *imi* and *iya* optionally occur in the sense of words such as *jāta* (born), etc.

*Pacchā-jāto*, *pacchimo*, *pacchimā janatā*, *pacchimaṃ cittaṃ*; *ante jāto*, *antimo*, *antimā*, *antimaṃ*. Likewise, *majjhimo*, *purimo*, *uparimo*, *heṭṭhimo*, *paccantimo*, *gopphimo*, *ganthimo*.
