Similarly, with the suffix *-iya*: born of the human species (*manussajātiyā*), *manussajātiyo*, *manussajātiyā*, *manussajātiyaṃ*. Likewise, *assajātiyo*, *hatthijātiyo*, *bodhisattajātiyo*, *dabbajātiyo*, *samānajātiyo*, *lokiyo*, and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), this suffix *iya* occurs not only in the sense of "connected with that," "that belongs to him," or "existing in that," but also in other such cases;
furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *ika* is also included. For example: *antima*, *antiya*, and *antika* mean "situated at the end";
*puttimo*, *puttiyo*, and *vuttiko* mean "one who has a son" or "one in whom a son exists"; and *kappiyo* means "one who has a ritual period (*kappa*)".

One who has matted hair (*jaṭā*) is a *jaṭī*; one who possesses the portion of decline (*hānabhāga*) is a *hānabhāgiya*. Likewise, one who possesses the portion of stability (*ṭhitibhāga*) is a *ṭhitibhāgiya*.
Those belonging to the side of awakening (*bodhi*) are the *bodhipakkhiyā*; those belonging to the group of five are the *pañcavaggiyā*. Likewise, the *chabbaggiyā* (the group of six).
*Udariya* means "belonging to the belly. *Attaniya* means "one's own" (*attano idaṃ*); here, the letter *na* is inserted [as a euphonic augment].

By the inclusion of *ca* (and), the suffixes *iya* and *yaṇ* are also [included]. That which is connected with birth (*jāti*) is *jātikiya*. Likewise, *andhakiya*; that which is connected with those born blind (*jaccandha*) is *jaccandhakiya*. That which belongs to him (*sassa ayan*) is *sakiya*. Likewise, *parakiya*.
The suffix *ya* occurs in the senses of "good for," "beneficial to," "originating from," "born from," and so on. For example: good for work is *kammañña*;

good for an assembly (*sabhā*) is *sabbha*, with the vowel *u* etc., according to the rule beginning with "the elision of *ta*" (*yavataṃ talanā*). Likewise, beneficial to the intellect (*medhā*) is *mejja* (clarified butter). Of the feet...
*Hitaṃ pajaṃ telaṃ*: beneficial for offspring; *hitā racchā*: a road suitable for a chariot; *gamme bhavo gammo*: born in a village; *gave bhavaṃ gabyaṃ*: produced from a cow.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the sutta "osare ca," the substitution of *ava* occurs even when the suffix *ya* follows. *Kavimhi bhavaṃ kabyaṃ*: produced in poetry; *divi bhavā dibyā*:
existing in heaven; *thanato jātaṃ thaññaṃ*: born from the breast; *dhanāya saṃvattatīti dhaññaṃ*: it leads to wealth, thus it is "grain" (*dhañña*).

The suffix *Ṇya* [is applied] as follows: one who is good in an assembly is *pārisajja*; there is the insertion of the letter *da*. That which is beneficial for recluses (*samaṇa*) is *sāmañña*, and that which is beneficial for brahmins is *brāhmañña*. Those existing in the formless realm are *āruppa*, and so forth.
In the analysis (*viggahe*) "a collection of princes" (*rājaputtānaṃ samūho*), [the suffix] *kaṇaṇa* is applied in the sense of a collection (Pāṇini 4.2.37).
After the sixth [suffix] *-i*, the suffixes *kaṇ* and *aṇ* occur in the sense of "a collection of those.
Thus: *rājaputtako*, *rājaputtakaṃ*, or *rājaputto*. Likewise: *mānussako*, *mānusso*; *māthurako*, *māthuro*; *porisako*, *poriso*.
A collection of elders (*vuddhānaṃ*) is *vuddhako* or *vuddho*. Likewise: *māyūrako*, *māyūro*; *kāpoto*, *kokilo*; *māhiṃsako*, *māhiṃso*.
*Oṭṭhaka*, *orabbhaka*; a group of eight is *aṭṭhaka*; a group of kings is *rājaka*; a group of alms-foods is *bhikkha*; a group of trainings is *sikkha*;
a group of two is *dvayaṃ*, where the substitution of *ay* for the vowel *i* occurs according to the rule beginning with "in those cases, there is *vuddhi*" (*tesu vuddhi*).
Likewise, a group of three is *tayaṃ*, and so forth.
The term “in the sense of a collection” (samūhatthe) recurs. 380.
From words such as *gāma*, *jana*, *bandhu*, and *sahāya*, the suffix *tā* occurs in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). For example: the collection of villages is *gāmatā*.
In this way, there is the state of being a person (*janatā*), a kinsman (*bandhutā*), a companion (*sahāyatā*), or a citizen (*nāgaratā*).
Regarding the word "tā," through the analysis of its grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*), it refers to the deity itself as "devatā"; the suffix *-tā* is always feminine in gender. 381.
And that is his place (*ṭhāna*) and object (*iya*).
In the sense of "that would be the place for it," the suffix *iya* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case. For example:
the place for intoxication (*madana*) is *madaniya*, *madaniyā*, or *madaniyaṃ*; the place for binding (*bandhana*) is *bandhaniyaṃ*. Likewise, *mucchaniyaṃ*.
Also, *rajanīyaṃ*, *gamanīyaṃ*, *dassanīyaṃ*, *upādāniyaṃ*, and *pasādaniyaṃ*. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the suffix *iya*] also occurs in the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*) and so forth.
"Beneficial to the clingings" means "clinging-inducing," and so forth.
382. *Āyitatta* (the state of appearing like).

When the sense of "appearing like" [is intended], the suffix *-āyitatta* occurs by virtue of the gender of the word expressing the comparison. That which is seen as if it were smoke is *dhūmāyitatta*. Likewise, *timirāyitatta* (the state of appearing like darkness/glaucoma).
The phrase “*tadassa ṭhānan*” (that is its basis) continues [from the previous rule]. 383.

Regarding the sense of being dependent on that (*tannissita*): the suffix *la* occurs in the sense of “dependent on that” (*tannissita*) and in the sense of “that is its basis” (*tadassa ṭhāna*). In the case of *duṭṭhulla*—meaning either “badly dependent” (*duṭṭhu nissita*) or “a bad basis” (*duṭṭhu ṭhāna*)—or “vulgar speech” (*duṭṭhullā vācā*), there is a doubling of the *la* suffix. Thus, [the formation of] *vedalla*.
In the analysis of the phrase “covetousness is his nature, covetousness is his abundance”:
384. *Ālu* is used when there is an abundance of that. The suffix *ālup* occurs after a word ending in the first case (nominative) in the sense of “that is abundant for him. Example: *abhijjhālu*.
*abhijjhālū*, *abhijjhālavo*. Likewise, *sītālu*, *dhajālu*, *dayālu*.
In the case of *sabbato ko*, by the repetition of the word *sabba*, there is the insertion of the letter *k*: *abhijjhāluko*, *abhijjhālukā*, *abhijjhālukaṃ*.
Likewise, *sītāluko*, *dayāluko*; similarly, *hīno* becomes *hīnako*. Likewise, *potako*, *kumārako*, *māṇavako*, *muduko*, *ujuko*, *appamattakaṃ*.
“Oramattakaṃ, sīlamattakaṃ,” and so forth.
By the rule “yadanupapannā nipātanā sijjhanti,” the suffix *ka* is applied in the senses of resemblance (*paṭibhāga*), contempt (*kucchita*), compassion (*anukampā*), and so on.
In the sense of resemblance: *hatthino iva hatthikā* (like an elephant, a little elephant); likewise, *assakā*. In the sense of contempt: *kucchito* (contemptible).

A *samaṇa* is a *samaṇaka*; likewise, a *brāhmaṇaka*, a *muṇḍaka*, a *paṇḍitaka*, and a *veyyākaraṇaka*. In the sense of being made by perception (*saññā*), there are the suffixes *-kata* and *-ka*, as in *bhaṭaka*.
In the sense of compassion, there is *puttaka*.
Similarly, the suffixes *-kiṃyat*, *-ita*, *-tata*, *-parimāṇa*, *-tta*, and *-ka* occur in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*). For example: "What is its measure? means *kittakaṃ*.
In this way: *yattakaṃ*, *tattakaṃ*, *ettakaṃ*. Regarding *yāvā*: because it has a measure (*parimāṇa*) that can be vomited out (*vatumhi āttañca*), it is *yāvā*;
*yāvanto* is equal to those possessing qualities (*guṇavantu-sama*). Likewise: *tāvā*, *tāvanto*; *etāvā*, *etāvanto*, and so forth.
In the analysis (*viggahe*) of the compound "made with gold" (*suvaṇṇena pakataṃ*):
385. *Tappakativacane mayo*.

The suffix *maya* occurs in the sense of expressing the material cause (*tappakativacana*). That which is made is the "cause" (*pakati*); thus, that which is its cause is the "material cause" (*tappakati*).
The expression or statement regarding that material cause is "tappakativacana. For example: *suvaṇṇamayo ratho* (a chariot made of gold) or *sovaṇṇamayo* (made of gold).

A variety of vessels made of gold is a "golden vessel. Likewise, there are those made of silver (rūpiya), those made of tin (rajata), those made of lac (jata), those made of wood (dāru), those made of clay (mattikā), and those produced by supernormal power (iddhi) are "supernormally produced" (iddhimaya).

Those produced from the mind are "mind-made" (manomaya); that which is fashioned from iron is "iron-made" (ayomaya). And here, while the phrase "of the group beginning with the mind" (manogaṇādīnaṃ) is being applied—
386. *Etesaṃ lope*:
When there is elision of these [suffixes] belonging to the *manogaṇa* and other groups, the letter *o* is substituted for the final vowel when a case ending (*vibhatti*) is elided. For example:

*gavena pakataṃ karīsaṃ*, or "produced from a cow" (*goto nibbattaṃ*), is *gomayaṃ*. By means of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the word *maya* can also express the same meaning as the base itself; thus, giving itself is "consisting of giving" (*dānamayaṃ*), virtue itself is "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamayaṃ*), and so forth.
The taddhita suffixes *saṃsaṭṭha* and so forth have multiple meanings. Regarding the taddhita suffix *bhāva*,
in the analysis (*viggaha*) of "the state of being lazy" (*alasassa bhāvo*):
387. *Ṇya*, *tta*, and *ta* [are used] in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*).

After a word ending in the sixth case, these suffixes—*ṇya*, *tta*, and *ta*—occur in the sense of "the state of that" (*tassa bhāvo*), and by the inclusion of the particle *tu*, the suffixes *ttana*, *ṇeya*, and so forth are also included.
That from which cognition arises is called "state" (*bhāva*); it is the cause for the occurrence of a word.

It is said, and it has been stated: "When a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, there is the application of the suffixes *ṇya*, *tta*, *na*, and so forth, for the purpose of denoting that [quality].
The suffixes *ṇya*, *tta*, and *na* are always neuter; the suffix *tāpa* is always feminine by its very nature.

This suffix *ṇya* occurs after words such as *brāhmaṇa* when expressing a quality. In that case, by the rule "the vowel *a* is elided and *ye* is dropped," there is the elision of the vowel *a*, followed by the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening.

Laziness (*ālasya*). Likewise: the state of being healthy is health (*ārogya*); the state of being elated is elation (*audagrya*); the state of being a friend is friendship (*sakhya*); the state of being debt-free is freedom from debt (*āṇaṇya*); the state of being a widow is widowhood (*vaidhavya*); the state of being weak is weakness (*durbalya*); the state of being fickle is fickleness (*cāpalya*).

The state of being clever is cleverness (*vaiyattiya*); the state of being stingy is stinginess (*mātsarya*). Similarly: lordship (*aiśvarya*), laziness (*ālasya*), shaven-headedness (*muṇḍiya*), and delusion (*mūḷhiya*). Here, in words such as *vaiyattiya*, the augment *i* is inserted by the rule beginning with "In those [cases], there is an increase" (*tesu vuddhi*).

In such cases as “the state of a wise man is wisdom (*paṇḍitya*)”, the substitution of *ca*, *laṃ*, *ja*, and *ka* for the conjuncts beginning with *tya*—namely, *calañaja-kāratta*—and the doubling of the consonant [occur].

Wisdom is *paṇḍiccaṃ*; the state of one who is well-versed is erudition (*bāhussaccaṃ*), where the vowel *u* becomes *a* according to the rule “among those, it is a vowel increase (*vuddhi*)”, and so too with *porohiccaṃ*. The state of a lord is sovereignty (*ādhipaccaṃ*).
The state of one with muddled mindfulness is *muṭṭhassaccaṃ*; here, the vowel *i* is elided. The state of one who is skillful is *kosallaṃ*. Likewise, *vepullaṃ*.

The state of those who are similar is *sāmaññaṃ*. The state of one who is ill is *gelaññaṃ*; according to the rule beginning with "kvacādimajjhuttarā," there is shortening of the vowel before a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).

The state of one who is well-disposed (*suhada*) is *sohajja*. Likewise, the state of one who is confident is *vesārajja*; the state of one who is indolent is *kosajja*, where the vowel *ī* becomes *a* according to the rule beginning with "in those [cases], there is growth" (*tesu vuḍḍhi*).

Similarly, in examples such as "the state of a man is *porisa*," the rule regarding the suffix *-ya* (contained in the sutta "the substitution of *ya* for *ta*") prescribes that for the letters *sa*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and the labials (*pa-vagga*), there are substitutions by *sa*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and the labials respectively. The state of one who is well-minded (*sumana*) is *somanassa*.
In the same way, *domanassa*, *sovacassa*, and *dovacassa*—here there is the addition of the letter *sakāra*.

Likewise, the state of being *nipaka* is *nepakka*; there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*). Similarly, *ādhikka*; the state of being unfortunate is *dobhagga*; the state of being a merchant is *vāṇijja*;
the state of being a king is *rajja*, with shortening of the vowel by the rule "kvacā" and so forth. The state of being well-proportioned is *sāruppa*. In the same way, *opamma* and *sokhumma*.

The state of being *tatha* is *taccha*; the state of being dull-witted (*dummedha*) is *dummejjha*; the state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*) is *sāmañña*. Likewise, the state of being a brahmin is *brāhmañña*;

the state of being subtle (*nipuṇa*) is *nepuñña*. In the case of *taccha* and the others as well, by the inclusion of the causal suffix (*kāra*), there is the substitution of the letters *cha*, *jha*, and *ña* for the letters *tha*, *dha*, and *ṇa* respectively.

Regarding the *taddhita* suffixes: the state of being a refuse-rag wearer (*paṃsukūlika*) is "refuse-rag wearerness" (*paṃsukūlikattaṃ*), or "refuse-rag wearerness" (*paṃsukūlikatā*). Likewise: the state of being one who owns only three robes is "three-robe-ness" (*tecīvarikattaṃ*), or "three-robe-ness" (*tecīvarikatā*);

the state of being gluttonous is "gluttony" (*odarikattaṃ*), or "gluttony" (*odarikatā*); the state of being human is "humanity" (*manussattaṃ*), or "humanity" (*manussatā*); birth; the state of being blue is "blueness" (*nīlattaṃ*), or "blueness" (*nīlatā*); a quality; the state of being a beggar is "beggarhood" (*yācakattaṃ*), or "beggarhood" (*yācakatā*); an action;

the state of being a staff-bearer is "staff-bearing" (*daṇḍittaṃ*), or "staff-bearing" (*daṇḍitā*); a substance; truthfulness is "truth-speaking-ness" (*saccavāditā*); and perfection is "parami-ness" (*pāramitā*).
In the sense of gratitude (*kataññutā*), omniscience (*sabbaññutā*), the shortening of the vowel occurs before the suffix *tāp* in words such as “kvacā”;
in the sense of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), non-association (*asaṃsaggatā*), delight in talk (*bhassārāmatā*), delight in sleep (*niddārāmatā*), lightness (*lahutā*), and so forth.
In the sense of the suffix *ttana*: the state of an ordinary person is *puthujjanattanā*, the state of feeling is *vedanattanā*, and the state of being born is *jāyattanā*.

*Ṇeyya*: *Sucissa bhāvo* (the state of one who is pure) is *soceyyaṃ*. Thus, by way of division according to the suffixes: *kavissa bhāvo* (the state of a poet) is *kāveyyaṃ*; *thenassa bhāvo* (the state of a thief) is *theyyaṃ*, with the elision of the letter *n* according to the rule for great declension (*mahāvutti*).

Regarding the phrase “*Ṇyattatā*”: through the analysis of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*), the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* apply in the sense of the object (*kamma*) and in their own inherent meaning (*sakattha*).

Thus, *vīrānaṃ bhāvo* (the state of heroes) or their action is *vīriyaṃ*; the action of a servant (*paribhaṭa*) is *pāribhaṭyaṃ*; the state of being a servant is *pāribhaṭyatā*. In this same manner...

*So-vacassatā* (tractability) is the state or the action of one who is easy to speak with. *Bhesajja* (medicine) is the action of a physician. *Veyyāvacca* (service) is the action of one who is occupied.
*Sāṭheyya* is either the state of a rogue or the action of a rogue.

However, when used in its own sense (*sakatthe*), it is as follows: *yathābhūtaṃ* (as it really is) is the same as *yathābhuccaṃ*; *karuṇā* (compassion) is the same as *kāruññaṃ*; *pattakālaṃ* (opportune time) is the same as *pattakallaṃ*; *ākāsānantaṃ* (infinite space) is the same as *ākāsānañcaṃ*; and *kāyapāguññaṃ* (bodily proficiency) is the same as *kāyapāguññatā*, and so forth.
In the analysis [of the compound] as “the state of being uneven” (*visamassa bhāvo*),
the rule “*tattā*, in the sense of state (*bhāve*)" applies;
and [the suffix] *ṇa* is added after words such as *visama*.
The suffix *ṇap* occurs after words such as *visama* ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhivanta*), in the sense of "the state of that" (*tassa bhāvo*).
This is an *ākati-gaṇa* (an open class). Thus: *vesamaṃ*, *visamattaṃ*, *visamatā*. The state of being pure is *socaṃ*, *sucittaṃ*, *sucatā*;
the state of being venerable is *gāravo*, with an initial vowel increase (*ādivuddhi*). By the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *o sare ca*, the letter *u* [is replaced by *ā*].
And there is the substitution of *av*. The state of being clever (*paṭu*) is *pāṭavaṃ*, *paṭuttaṃ*, or *paṭutā*.

The state of being straight (*uju*) is *ajjavaṃ*; the state of being soft (*mudu*) is *maddavaṃ*. In these cases, by the rule "āttañca," when the suffix *ṇa* is applied, the vowels *i* and *u* become *āt* (long *ā*), there is doubling of the consonant, and the first letter of the conjunct becomes nasalized (*assatta*).
Thus: *ujutā*, *mudutā*. In the same way, the state of being a seer (*isi*) is *ārisyaṃ*.

The state of a bull (*āsabha*), the state of a youth (*kumāra*) which is *bhāvokomāra*, the state of a young man (*yuvā*) which is *yobbana*—the letter *na* is added by the rule for great usage (*mahāvutti*)—the state or action of those who are supreme (*paramānaṃ*) is the perfection (*pāramī*), namely the act of giving and so forth;
the suffix *ī* is applied by the rule beginning with “*ṇavaṇikā*,” and the state of those who are harmonious (*samaggānaṃ*) is harmony (*sāmaggī*).
389. From *ramaṇīya* and others, the suffix *kaṇa* [is applied].
In this way, from the word *rāmaṇīya*, there arises the suffix *-ka* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).
Thus: the state of being beautiful is *rāmaṇīyakaṃ*, *ramaṇīyattaṃ*, or *ramaṇīyatā*. Likewise: *mānuññakaṃ*, *manuññattaṃ*, *manuññatā*;
*piyarūpakaṃ*, *piyarūpattaṃ*, *piyarūpatā*; *kalyāṇakaṃ*, *kalyāṇattaṃ*, *kalyāṇatā*; and *corakaṃ* or *corikā*, *corattaṃ*, *coratā*.
*Addhakaṃ*, *addhattaṃ*, *addhatā*, and so forth. These are derivative suffixes (*taddhita*) expressing abstract state (*bhāva*).
They are specific derivative suffixes (*visesa-taddhita*).
In the case of a comparative judgment such as, “All these are evil;

this one among them is especially evil,” the following suffixes are added in the sense of comparison (*visesa*): *tara*, *tama*, *isika*, *iya*, and *iṭṭha*. Thus: *pāpataro*, *pāpatarā*, *pāpataraṃ*.
Even more than that: *pāpatamo*, *pāpatamā*, *pāpatamaṃ*; *pāpisiko*, *pāpisikā*, *pāpisikaṃ*; *pāpiyo*, *pāpiyā*, *pāpiyaṃ*;
*pāpiṭṭho*, *pāpiṭṭhā*, *pāpiṭṭhaṃ*. To an even greater degree: *pāpiṭṭhatara*. Likewise:
*paṭutaro*, *paṭutamo*, *paṭisiko*, *paṭiyo*, *paṭiṭṭho*. Of all [these], to the highest degree: *varataro*.
*Varatama*, *varisika*, *variya*, *variṭṭha*. Likewise, *paṇītara* and *paṇītatama*.
When the sense is "all these are superior" (*vuḍḍha*) and "this one among them is superior by distinction," the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* occur. 391.
For the word *vuḍḍha*, the substitute *ja* occurs before the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha*.
In all instances of the word *vuḍḍha* (grown/elder), when followed by the suffixes *iya* or *iṭṭha*, [the following forms arise]: *jeyya* and *jeṭṭha*.
Herein, in the rule "saralopādi," instead of applying elision (*lopa*) by the inclusion of the letter *t*, the preceding vowel is dropped according to the rule "sarā sare lopa.
Then, by the rule "kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte," the letter *e* is substituted.
“*Iyiṭṭhesu*” (in the case of desired forms) is the governing rule, and “*jo*” (the suffix *ja*) is also understood from the preceding context. 392. Regarding the word *pasattha* (praised):

for the entire word *pasattha*, there is a substitution of *sā* (the suffix *sa*), and [the suffix] *ja* occurs when it is among those that are desired (*iyiṭṭhesu*). Thus: “This one is praised, this one is praised; all these are praised”; “this one is especially praised”—[from which arise] *seyyo*, *seṭṭho*, *jeyyo*, *jeṭṭho*.
393. *Antika* becomes *nedi*.
The substitution of *nedi* occurs for the word *antika* in its entirety when followed by suffixes beginning with *i* or *ī*. Specifically, *antika* becomes *nediya* and *nediṭṭha*.
394. *Bāḷha* becomes *sādu*.
In the case of the word *bāḷha*, there is a substitution of *sādhi* for the whole word when followed by suffixes beginning with *i* or *ī*. Specifically, *bāḷha* becomes *sādhiya* and *sādhiṭṭha*.
395. For the word *appa*, there is *kaṇa*.
For the whole word *appa*, there is a substitution of *kaṇa* when followed by suffixes beginning with *i* or *ī*. Specifically, *appa* becomes *kaṇiya* and *kaṇiṭṭha*.
Regarding the phrase “especially for *yuvan*,” the term *kaṇa* is supplied.
396. *Yuvānañca*:

For the entire word *yuvan*, *kaṇa* is substituted when suffixes beginning with *i* or *iṭ* follow. By the rule “*tesu vuddhī*” and so forth, the letter *ṇ* is replaced by *n*. Thus: *kaniyo*, *kaniṭṭho*.
397. *Vantu*, *mantu*, and *vīna*: elision.

There is elision of the suffixes *vantu*, *mantu*, and *vī* when followed by suffixes beginning with *i*. For example: "All these are virtuous" (*guṇavanto*) and "this one among them is especially virtuous" (*visesena guṇavā*) result in *guṇiyo* and *guṇiṭṭho*.
"Especially mindful" (*visesena satimā*) results in *satiyo* and *satiṭṭho*. Especially... [and so on].
"Medhāvī" [is derived from] "medhiya," "medhiṭṭha," and so forth.
This is a specific secondary derivative (visesataddhita). It is a secondary derivative based on existence (assatthitaddhita).
Regarding the analysis (*viggaha*): “He who has wisdom (*medhā*), in him it exists.
[The rule states: 398. *Tadassatthīti vī ca*.
After a word ending in the first case, the suffix *vī* occurs in the sense of “that belongs to him” (*tadassa atthi*) or “it exists in him” (*tasmiṃ vijjati*).
And by means of the words *medhā* and *māyā*: [the masculine forms are] *medhāvī*, *medhāvino*.

In the feminine, because it ends in the vowel *ī*, the suffix *inī* is applied according to the rule “after *pati*, *bhikkhu*, and words ending in *r* or *ī*, [the suffix] *inī* [is added]”; thus: *medhāvinī*, *medhāviniyo*. In the neuter: *medhāvi kulaṃ*. Likewise: *māyāvī*, *māyāvinī*, *māyāvi cittaṃ*.
By the inclusion of the particle *ca* (and), there are also the suffixes *so*, *i*, *lava*, *ālādi*, and so forth; for example: one in whom *sumedhā* exists, or in whom it is found...
*Sumedhaso*: [the suffix] *rassattaṃ*. Likewise, *lomaso*. That which has *picchaṃ* (feathers/down), or that in which it exists, is *picchilo*.
Likewise, *phenilo*, *tuṇḍilo*, *jaṭilo*. That which has *kesā* (hair) is *kesavo*; likewise, *vācālo*, and so forth. In the analysis:
“That which has *tapo* (asceticism), or that in which it exists.”
“*Tadassatthī*” (it has that as its purpose) is the governing rule.
399. *Sī* follows *tapa*, etc.

The suffix *sī* occurs after *tapa* and so forth in the sense of “*tadassatthī*. There is doubling of the *s*. [Examples: *tapassī*, *tapassino*, *tapassinī*, *tapassi*. Likewise: *tejassī*, *yasassī*, *manassī*, *payassī*.
In the analysis [of the compound] "daṇḍo assa atthi, tasmiṃ vā vijjati" (the staff exists for him, or it is found in him):

400. From *daṇḍa* and so forth, the suffixes *ika*, *ī*, and *a* are added. This word *ādi* (and so forth) has the sense of "manner"; thus, from *daṇḍa* and other such words ending in *avaṇṇa*, the suffixes *ika*, *ī*, and *a* occur in the sense of "that belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*).
In this sense [the suffix -in is applied]: *daṇḍiko*, *daṇḍī*, *daṇḍino*, *daṇḍinī*. Likewise: *māliko*, *mālī*, *mālinī*;
*chattiko*, *chattī*; *rūpiko*, *rūpī*; *kesiko*, *kesī*; *saṅghī*, *ñāṇī*, *hatthī*, and so forth. 401.
After *madhu* and others, *-ra* [is added].

The suffix *rappa* occurs after [stems ending in] *madhu*, etc., in the sense of "having that as its purpose" (*tadassatthī*). Because it has honey (*madhu*) for its purpose, or because it exists therein, it is *madhuro* (sweet) sugar;
*madhurā* (sweet) candied sugar; *madhuraṃ* (sweet) milk. Because he has temples (*kuñja*)—that is, jaws—[he is] *kuñjaro* (an elephant).

In every instance where something ought to be said, because he has a mouth (*mukha*), he is *mukharo* (loquacious); because he has a cavity (*susi*), he is *susiro* (hollow). Likewise, *ruciro* (beautiful); *nagaro* (a city).
In the analysis [of the compound] “guṇo assa atthi, tasmiṃ vā vijjati” (there is a quality in it, or it exists in that), [the rule applies]:
402. *Guṇāditovantu*.
The suffix *-vantu* occurs after words such as *guṇa* and others in the sense of “that which has this. When the case ending is elided, it receives the designation of a noun (*nāma*).
And when *kate* occurs, there is the arising of *y*. Regarding *guṇavant*, having taken [the rule] “*savibhattissa, ntussā*,” it is stated “*ā simhī*”;
thus, *guṇavā puriso*. The rest is to be understood. Similarly, *gaṇavā*, *kulavā*, and so forth.

In the feminine, by the rule “*ṇava ṇika ṇeyyaṇantūhī*,” the suffix *ī* is applied; while the word “*vā*” is still in force, by the rule “*ntussa tamīkāre*,” the letter *t* is replaced; thus, *guṇavatī*.
“Guṇavantī,” and so forth. In the neuter, by the rule “*aṃ napuṃsake*,” there is the substitution of *am* for the stem ending in *-nt-* along with its case-suffix;
thus, “guṇavaṃ,” and so forth. In the analysis “*sati assa atthi, tasmiṃ vā vijjatī*” (it exists in him, or it is found in that), the phrase “*tadassatthī*” is supplied as a governing rule.

493. The suffix *mantu* is applied after words such as *sati*, provided they are devoid of other suffixes (*avaṇṇantara*) and end in the nominative case, in the sense of "one who possesses that" (*tadassatthī*).
The remainder is the same as for the suffix *guṇavantu*. [Examples: *satimā*, *satimatī*, *satimantī*, *satimaṃ*.
Likewise, [there are examples] such as *dhitimā* (possessing fortitude) and *gatimā* (possessing movement).
Similarly, in the case of the expression *“āyu assa atthīti āyumanto”* (he has life, thus he is "possessing life"), [the rule applies]:
404. *Āyussa-kārā-samantumi*. (The suffix *mantu* is added after *āyu*, *sukha*, and *asama*.)

In the word *āyu*, the vowel *u* becomes *a* according to the rule "in a mantra," resulting in the substitution of *as*. Thus, *āyasmā*; the remainder is the same [as previously explained]. [Gomā: Because he has cows (*gāvaḥ*), he is *gomā*, *gomanto*, *gomatī*, *gomantī*, or "the family possessing cows" (*gomam kulam*), and so forth.
In the analytical statement (*viggahe*) "faith exists in him": 405.
After *saddhā* and other such words, the suffix *ṇa* [is applied].

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after words such as *saddhā* and *paññā* in the sense of "that which possesses this" (*tadassatthi*). Thus: *saddho puriso* (a faithful man), *saddhā kaññā* (a faithful girl), *saddhaṃ kulaṃ* (a faithful family).
Likewise: *pañño*, *amaccharo*; similarly, *buddhaṃ* [is explained as] one who has awakening (*buddhi*) is a *buddho*, and so forth.
This is a *taddhita* derivative in the sense of possession.
Regarding the *saṅkhyātaddhita* [derivative]:

in the analysis of the phrase “the filler of five” (*pañcannaṃ pūraṇo*), [the rule] states: 406. *mo* is substituted for the word-final [element] when expressing the completion of a number (*saṅkhyāpūraṇe*).
That by which one completes a number is a "completer" (*pūraṇa*); a completer of a number is a "number-completer" (*saṅkhyāpūraṇa*).
In the sense of being a number-completer, the suffix *ma* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case. Thus, *pañcamo* (the fifth). A female completer of five is *pañcamī*;

the suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule "optionally *ī* after words beginning with *nada*," and the suffix *ā* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ā* occurs for the feminine after a word ending in *a*. Thus, *pañcamā* is the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramī*), and *pañcamaṃ* is the fifth jhāna.
Thus: *sattamo*, *sattamī*, *sattamā*, *sattamaṃ*; *aṭṭhamo*, *aṭṭhamī*, *aṭṭhamā*, *aṭṭhamaṃ*; *navamo*, *navamī*, *navamā*, *navamaṃ*;
*dasamo*, *dasamī*, *dasamā*, *dasamaṃ*, and so forth. The governing rule is:
"In the sense of completing a number."
407. *Catucchehi thaṭhā*.

From *catu* and *cha*, the suffixes *tha* and *ṭha* occur in the sense of completing a number. That which completes four is *catuttha* (fourth); [with the suffix *ī*] *catutthī*, [with the suffix *ā*] *catutthā*;
[with the suffix *a*] *catutthaṃ*. That which completes six is *chaṭṭha* (sixth); [with the suffix *ī*] *chaṭṭhī*, [with the suffix *ā*] *chaṭṭhā*.
*Chaṭṭhaṃ*: "Sixth"; *chaṭṭhamaṃ* is simply "sixth.
In such cases as *chāhaṃ* and *chaḷāyatanaṃ*, there is optionally the substitution of *sa* for *cha*.

In enumeration, the substitution of *cha* for *sa* occurs optionally. Examples include: *chāham assa jīvitaṃ sāhaṃ* (six days of his life were mine), *chāhaṃ vā*, and *saḷāyatanaṃ* (the six sense bases).
In the analysis of the compound *dvinnaṃ pūraṇo* ("the completer of two"), [the following applies]: 409. From *dvi* and *ti*, [the suffix] *iya* is added.
The suffix *tiya* occurs after the words *dvi* and *tī* in the sense of completing a number. When the forms *dvi* and *tīṇṇaṃ* are present—according to rule 410:
*Tiye dutāpi ca*—the substitutes *duta* and *api* respectively take the place of *dvi* and *tī* when the suffix *tiya* follows. Thus: *dutiyo puriso*, *dutiyā*, *dutiyaṃ*.

Thus, for the three [words], *pūraṇa* is the third [form]: *tatiyo*, *tatiyā*, *tatiyaṃ*. By the inclusion of the particle *api*, the substitution of *du-* for the word *dvi-* occurs in other instances as well;

and by the particle *ca*, the form *di-* also occurs. Examples: two nights = *durattaṃ*; of two kinds = *duvidhaṃ*; two limbs = *duvaṅgaṃ*; two nights = *dirattaṃ*; twofold = *diguṇaṃ*; a pair = *digu*. 411.
When combined with the prefix *aḍḍha-*, they become: *aḍḍhuḍḍha-*, *divaḍḍha-*, *diyaḍḍha-*, *aḍḍhatiya-*.
For those [words]—the fourth, second, and third—with the prefix *aḍḍha*, there are the substitutions *aḍḍhuḍḍha*, *diyaḍḍha*, and *aḍḍhatiya* when combined with the prefix *aḍḍha*.
And here: "Those preceded by *aḍḍha* have the power to denote a quarter (*pāda*) as a secondary element."

By the word *tesam* (of them), the fourth, second, and other case endings are understood. When the sense is "half and four" (*aḍḍhañca catutthañca*), it is the compound *aḍḍhuḍḍha*; when the sense is "half and two," it is *divaḍḍha* or *diyaḍḍha*; and when the sense is "half and three," it is *aḍḍhatiya*.

In the sense of "one and ten," when a *dvanda* compound is formed, or in the sense of "ten plus one," when a *tappurisa* compound is made, while the rule "in the context of numerals" (*saṅkhyāne*) is in force, the substitution of *ā* for the place of "two" and "one" is prescribed by the rule "the vowel *ā* optionally replaces the place of two and one" (*dvekaṭṭhānamākāro vā*). This word *vā* (or) has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*).
And herein, by this [method], he illuminates the number of bases: Two places always have ten; Of the two, ninety-eight have nine;
And for the others, there are none; Thus he demonstrates the count of bases.
“In the counting from one to ten”: this refers to *rattaṃ*.

The substitution of *ra-* occurs because it is merely a phoneme (*vaṇṇamattattā*); and even though there is the possibility that it is merely a phoneme, it may [be understood as such] because of its proximity to the cause (*nimitta*), namely the word *dasa* itself.

Then, regarding the plural form: the *akāra* of "five" (*pañca*) and so forth is the substitution for the final portion including the case-ending. *Ekārasa* and *ekādasa* are the same across all three genders. The particle *vā* (or) is understood [from the previous rule].
412. After *eka* and so forth, the suffix *dasī* [is applied].
The suffix *īp* optionally occurs after the first of a series ending in ten (*dasa*) in the sense of completion.
Because the suffix cannot be attached to "ten," the meaning is "having obtained the end";
thus, by its very nature, it arises only in the feminine gender.
The eleventh, which completes eleven, is *ekādasī*; elsewhere it is *ekādasamo* or *ekādasamaṃ*. As for *dvādasa*:
two and ten, or ten with two added—thus in the expression "dvi dasa," the word "vā" (or) is understood from the previous rule.

By the substitution rule "bā replaces dvi before viṃśati and dasa," *dvi* becomes *bā*, and *da* becomes *rā*. Thus, *bārasa*; elsewhere it is *āttaṃ* (with long ā), i.e., *dvādasa*. That which completes twelve is *bārasamo*, *dvādasamo*, or *dvādasī*.
Three and ten, or ten plus three, is thirteen (*terasa*). By the rule “*tesu vuddhi lopā*,” etc., *tissa* becomes *teā* before *daso*, as in *ānavuti*;
thus we have *terasamo* (the thirteenth) and *terasī* (the thirteenth day). Four and ten, or ten plus four, is fourteen (*cuddasa*).
Here, while the rule “*gaṇane dasassā*” is in force, by the rule “*catūpapadassa lopo tuttarapadādi cassa cucopi navā*,” there is elision of *tu*, and *cu* is substituted for *ca*.
*Ca*: *Cuddasa*, *coddasa*, *catuddasa*. *Cuddasamo*, *catuddasamo*, *cakuddasī*, or *cātuddasī*.

Five and ten, or ten with five added, is fifteen (*pañcadasa*). In this context, by the rule "In place of the word *pañca*, when followed by *dasa* or a particular number, there is substitution of *panna*, *paṇṇa*, or *ā*," the word *pañca* is replaced;
furthermore, by the rule "And after *aṭṭha*, etc.," the vowel is lengthened. Thus: *pannarasa*, *pañcadasa*. *Pannarasamo*.
*Pañcadasamo*, *pannarasī*, *pañcadasī*.

When the compound is formed as “six and ten” (*cha ca dasa ca*) or “ten with six added” (*chahi vā adhikā dasā*), while the term *chassā* is being applied, the rule *dase so niccañcā* applies the substitution *so*;
furthermore, the term *saṅkhyānaṃ, vā* is also in force. The letter *l* is substituted by the rule *la darānaṃ*. This word *vā* has the sense of a restrictive option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*).
The letter *ḷ* always occurs as *soḷasa*, *terasa*, and *cattālīsa*;
it does not occur otherwise, according to the established rule of optional usage (*vibhāsā*).
In some instances there is no distinction between *la* and *ḷ*: *soḷasa*, *teḷasa*, *cattālīsaṃ*, *cattārīsaṃ*, *soḷasamo*, and *soḷasī*.
Regarding the statement, “*vā*, *dasara*, *saṅkhyāne*,” the suffix *-ra* is added after the word *aṭṭha* and others. Thus: *aṭṭhārasa* (eighteen), *aṭṭhādasa* (eighteen); [the form] *āttaṃ*.
That which completes eighteen is the eighteenth (*aṭṭhārasamo*), or the eighteenth (*aṭṭhādasamo*). Likewise: *sattarasa* (seventeen), *sattadasa* (seventeen);
the seventeenth (*sattarasamo*), the seventeenth (*sattadasamo*).
"Starting from eight": for what purpose? [To indicate] fourteen.

"Twenty less one" is a *tappurisa* compound; thus, "nineteen. Numbers beginning with nineteen up to ninety should be understood as having the singular number (*ekavacananta*) and being feminine in gender (*itthiliṅga*).
These function both as numerals (*saṅkhyāna*) and as the things numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*); when they refer to the numeral itself...

When [the number] is occurring, it is as follows: *bhikkhūnam ekūnavīsati tiṭṭhati*, *bho bhikkhūnam ekūnavīsati tiṭṭhatu*, *bhikkhūnam ekūnavīsatiṃ passa*, *bhikkhūnam ekūnavīsatiyā kataṃ*, and so forth.
But when it is the object of counting (*saṅkhyeyya*), it is: *ekūnavīsati bhikkhavo tiṭṭhanti*, *bho ekūnavīsati bhikkhavo tiṭṭhatha*.

"Behold nineteen bhikkhus; [an act] performed by nineteen bhikkhus," and so forth. In this way, it should also be applied to twenty and so on. That which completes nineteen is the "nineteenth" (*ekūnavīsatimo*). Regarding the expression "ten and ten":

having formed a *dvanda* compound for the sense of "ten and ten," and when one should have said "dasadasā," the single-remainder (*ekasesa*) rule "of similar forms, the single remainder is used" is applied, whereby the nominative plural ending is added to the word "ten. Thus, in the phrase "Dasa yo": [The commentary continues: Here, in the case of "Dasa yo"— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here. The following is a continuation of the grammatical explanation based on the context of Pali grammatical treatises. ...the word "ten" (*dasa*) is repeated to indicate the number twenty. By the rule of single-remainder (*ekasesa*), only one instance of the word remains, and the plural marker is attached to that single remaining form to denote the group. This is how the formation of such ordinal numbers and collective expressions is explained.

413. In enumeration, for the words related to "ten" (*dasa*)—namely *dvika*, *tika*, *catukka*, *pañcaka*, *chakka*, *sattaka*, *aṭṭhaka*, and *navaka*—when they are used as the remainder of a compound, there are respectively the substitutions *vīti*, *cattāro*, *paññā*, *cha*, *satta*, *asa*, and *nava* in the masculine (*yosu*).

[The rule] stands thus: *tīti*. In enumeration, for the words related to "ten"—namely *dvika*, *tika*, *catukka*, *pañcaka*, *chakka*, *sattaka*, *aṭṭhaka*, and *navaka*—when they are used as the remainder of a compound, there are respectively the substitutions *vīti*, *cattāro*, *paññā*, *cha*, *satta*, *asa*, and *nava* in the masculine (*yosu*).
[The rule] stands thus: *tīti*. (This means that these substitutions apply when the words are used in the masculine dual.)

In the place of *dasa* (ten), which expresses the number twelve, the substitute *vīsa* occurs; for the word ending in *yu*, there is the substitute *īsa*, with the elision of the preceding vowel (*saralopa*), etc.
The phrase "or at the end of numerals" also continues [to apply].
At the end of those [numerals] ending in *ti*, there is optionally the addition of the letter *ti*. This word "optionally" (*vā*) has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*).
Optionally, the addition of *ti* occurs at the end of twenty (*vīsa*) and thirty (*tiṃsa*).
It does not exist elsewhere, because it is restricted by its specific definition (*vavatthita-vibhāsato*).

In the phrase "and in the consonant" (*byañjane ca*), there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra); then, because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it receives the designation of a noun (*nāma*) and the case endings (*syādi*) arise.
Examples include: *bhikkhūnaṃ vīsati*, *vīsaṃ*, *vīsati bhikkhū*, or *vīsaṃ*. [The ordinal is] *vīsatimo*. Likewise, there are twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses (*kusalacitta*).
Or twenty-one. The twenty-first. Twenty-two, or twenty-two. The twenty-second.
Twenty-three, or twenty-three. The twenty-third. Twenty-four, or twenty-four. The twenty-fourth.
Twenty-five, or twenty-five. The twenty-fifth. Twenty-five, or twenty-five. The twenty-fifth.
*Chabbīsati*, or *chabbīsaṃ*. The twenty-sixth (*chabbīsatimo*). *Sattavīsati*, or *sattavīsaṃ*. The twenty-seventh (*sattavīsatimo*).
*Aṭṭhavīsati*, or *aṭṭhavīsaṃ*. The twenty-eighth (*aṭṭhavīsatimo*). *Ekūnatiṃsati*, or *ekūnatiṃsaṃ*. The twenty-ninth (*ekūnatiṃsatimo*).

Regarding "ten and ten and ten," where one should have said "ten, ten, tens" (*dasa dasa dasā*), by applying the rule of single-remainder (*ekasesa*) according to the formula "in counting, of ten," etc., [the form *dasā* is established].
There are thirty forms: by the rule "kvacā" and others, there is shortening and the insertion of *niggahīta*;
the remainder is the same as for twenty. Examples include *tiṃsati*, *tiṃsaṃ*, *tiṃsa* (thirty years), with the elision of *niggahīta*;
*tiṃsaṃ*, *tiṃsāya*, and so forth. Also *ekatiṃsati* or *ekatiṃsaṃ*, *bāttiṃsaṃ*, *dvattiṃsaṃ*, *tettiṃsaṃ*, and so on.
In the case of *das* (ten) when its final syllable is elided (*katékasesa*) after the word *catuddasa* (fourteen), the form is *cattāro*; in the case of the word *yava*, it is *īsā*.

[Thus we have] *cattālīsaṃ* (“forty”), where the short *l* replaces the long *l* according to the rule “*la darānan*” (Pāṇini 8.2.35), or alternatively *tālīsaṃ*. [The ordinal number is] *cattālīsatimo* (the fortieth).
[Cardinal numbers include] *ekacattālīsaṃ* (forty-one), *dvācattālīsaṃ* (forty-two), *dvicattālīsaṃ* (forty-two), *tecattālīsaṃ* (forty-three), *ticattālīsaṃ* (forty-three), and so forth.

In *pañcadasa* (fifteen), the word expressing the number ten (*dasa*) becomes *paññā*, and the word expressing the unit (*yova*) becomes *āsa*. Thus, it is *paññāsaṃ*; or, by the rule “*tesu vuddhi lopā*,” etc., there is the substitution of *paṇṇā*, making it *paṇṇāsaṃ*. [Examples: *ekapaññāsaṃ*, *dvepaññāsaṃ*, *dvipaññāsaṃ*.

In *chadasa* (sixty), the word expressing the number ten (*dasa*) becomes *cha*, and the word expressing the unit (*yova*) becomes *ṭhi*. By the rule “*sa chassa vā*,” there is the substitution of *sa* for the *s*. Thus, it is *saṭṭhi*. [Examples: *dvāsaṭṭhi*, *dvesaṭṭhi*, *dvisaṭṭhi*, *tesaṭṭhi*, *tisaṭṭhi*.

For the word *das* expressing the number seventeen, *satta* is substituted, and for the word *yava*, *ri* and *ti* are substituted. Thus: *sattari*, *sattati*, *dvāsattari*, *dvāsattati*, *dvisattari*, *disattati*, *tesattati*, *tisattati*, and so forth.

For the word *das* expressing the number eighteen, *asa* is substituted, and for the word *yava*, the substitution *īti* occurs. Thus: *asīti*, *ekāsīti*, *dveasīti*, *teasīti*, *caturāsīti*; [the lengthening of the vowel] occurs by the rule "kvacā" and so on.

For the word *dasa* (ten) following *nava* (nine), there is *nava*; for the word *yava* (up to), there are *uti*: *navuti*, *dvānavuti*, *dvenavuti*, *dvinavuti*, *tenavuti*, *tinavuti*, *catunavuti*, *channavutiyā*, and *channavutīnaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ*.
The phrase “in counting, after *dasa*” also recurs.
415. Ten times ten is a hundred; a hundred times ten is a thousand, when the suffix *yo* is present.

In the context of calculation, for the word *dasa* (ten), which expresses the meaning of a "decad" (*dasaka*), there is a hundred (*sataṃ*); for the word *dasa*, which expresses the meaning of a "hundred decad" (*satadasaka*), there is a thousand (*sahassaṃ*).

By this grammatical rule (*nipātanena*), the suffix *yo* is elided. Because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it again receives the designation of a noun (*nāmabyapadesa*), resulting in the application of the case endings beginning with *si*.
There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (the nasal *m*), and by the rule "si," there is the substitution of *am*. Thus, there is a hundred or a thousand of *yojanas*. *Sataṃ*.
It is neuter and takes the singular number; likewise for *sahassa*. However, when there is a division into groups (*vagga*), the plural is used in all cases.
For example: "two twenties. Similarly for thirties and so on. Also: "two hundreds," "many hundreds," "two thousands," "many thousands.

When forming a genitive tappurisa compound in the sense of "a pair of a hundred" (*satassa dvikaṃ*), although one should say "a pair of a hundred" (*sataṃ dvikaṃ*), [in the case of] "dvika" and so forth...

And because of the statement in the Vutti, “the words ending in *tad* are also treated as indeclinables (*nipacca*”), by this rule of formation (*nipātana*), there is the prior placement of the final member and the elision of the letter *k*. Thus, two hundred (*dvisataṃ*).

In this way, three hundred is a triple-hundred (*tisataṃ*), and likewise four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, nine hundred, and ten hundred becomes a thousand (*sahassaṃ*).
Alternatively, *dvesatāni* is a *digusamāsa* compound meaning "two hundreds. Likewise for *tisataṃ*, *catusatam*, and so forth.
416. *Yāva taduttari dasaguṇitañ ca*:
up to the point where those numbers increase further, they must be multiplied by ten; here, the letter *da-* is a euphonic (*sandhi*) insertion.
For example—ten times ten is a hundred; ten times a hundred is a thousand;
ten times a thousand is ten thousand, which is also called a *nahuta*; ten times ten thousand is a hundred thousand, which is also called a *lakhā*;
ten times a hundred thousand is one million (*dasasatasahassa*).
“The statement ‘those formations which are unestablished succeed’ continues [to apply]. 417.
By their own names: those forms belonging to numbers whose names have not been specifically mentioned are declined by their own respective names.”
A hundred of one hundred thousand is a *koṭi*; the feminine gender is used and it takes the singular number, though in the division of groups, the plural may also occur.
A hundred of one hundred thousand *koṭis* is a *pakoṭi*; a hundred of one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is a *koṭippakoṭi*.
Likewise, there are a *nahuta*, a *ninnahuta*, an *akkhobhinī*, a *bindu*, an *abbuda*, a *nirabbuda*, an *ahaha*, and an *ababa*.
Aṭaṭa, Sogandhika, Uppala, Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, Paduma, Kathāna, Mahākathāna, and Asaṅkhyeya.
Thus, from one station to the next, it is considered to be multiplied by a hundred thousand;
for the numbers beginning with ten million (koṭi), the sequence follows the same order.
In the analysis [of the compound] “there are two measures for this,” [the rule applies]: 418. *Dvāditō konekatthe ca*.

From *dvi* and so forth, when used in the sense of enumeration and in various meanings (*anekattha*), the suffix *ka* occurs. Thus, *dviko rāsi* (a group of two) becomes *dvikaṃ*; likewise, *tikaṃ* (a group of three).
A group of four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, and so forth. These are derivative taddhita formations from numerals (saṅkhyātaddhita).
Derivative taddhita formations from indeclinables (abyayataddhita).
Regarding the dispute: "He eats once," or "He eats twice"—419. From *eka*, *dvi*, etc., the suffix *kkhattum* is applied in the sense of "time" (*vāra*) for one's own [number].
After words such as *eka*, *dvi*, and *ti*, the suffix *kkhattum* occurs in place of the numeral in the sense of "time. For example: *ekakkhattum*.
He eats twice; [in this case] there is elision of the *si* suffix by the rule beginning with “*sabbāsam āvuso*.
Likewise: three times, four times, five times, six times, seven times, eight times, nine times, ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, many times, how many times.
In the analysis (viggaha) of the phrase “by one division” (ekena vibhāgena), the application of the term *saṅkhya* (number) from the rule for frog-leaping (*maṇḍūkagati*) is carried over. 420.
[The suffix] *dha* occurs after the word *vibhāga*.

The suffix *dhā* occurs after the numerals one (*eka*), etc., when the sense is division. By the word "and" (*ca*), [it is understood that] *jjha* follows *eka* and *dvi*, and *so* follows *sutta*, etc.
*Ekadhā*. From two divisions: *dvidhā*, or *dudhā*, or *dvedhā*. From three divisions: *tidhā*, or *tedhā*;
here, by the rule “*tesu vuddhī*,” etc., the vowel *i* becomes *e*. Likewise: *catudhā*, *pañcadhā*, *chadhā*, *sattadhā*.
Eightfold, ninefold, tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, manifold, manyfold.
With the suffix *jjha*, from "he makes into one" comes *ekajjhaṃ*. Likewise, *dvejjhaṃ*.

With the suffix *so*, there is "by way of the Sutta through division" as *suttaso*. Likewise, *byañjanaso* (by way of syllables), *padaso* (by way of phrases), *atthaso* (by way of meaning), *bahuso* (many times), *sabbākārena sabbaso* (in every way entirely), *upāyaso* (by way of means), *hetuso* (by way of cause), *ṭhānaso* (by way of occasion), and *yoniso* (properly).
421. Regarding the suffix *tha* after all nouns in the sense of manner (*pakāra*).
After all nouns, the suffix *tha* occurs in the sense of manner; by the word *tu*, the suffix *tā* also occurs.
A particularity (*visesa*) that differentiates a general category (*sāmañña*) is "manner" (*pakāra*); the meaning is "in the expression of that. That manner is *tathā*; that manner is *taṃ tathā*.
In that manner is *tathā*; in whatever manner is *yathā*. Likewise, there are the suffixes for state (*tattāpaccaya*):

*sabbathā*, *aññathā*, *itarathā*, *ubhayathā*, and *tathattā* in the sense of "in that manner"; likewise, *yathattā* and *aññathattā*. What is the meaning of "manner" (*pakāra*)? It refers to the sense of a way or mode.
422. *Kimimehi thaṃ*.

The suffix *thaṃ* occurs after *kiṃ* and *ima* in the sense of expressing a manner (*pakāra*). In the phrase *“kissa ka ve ca”* (from *kiṃ*, *ka* is substituted, and *ca*), the word *ca* indicates that *kiṃ* undergoes the substitution of *kā*.
How so? In what manner is “how”? By what manner is “how”? This manner is “thus” (*itthaṃ*).

*Imaṃ pakāraṃ itthaṃ*: in this manner, thus. By this manner, thus; [the form] *itthaṃ* is derived from the word *ima*, where the vowel *i* replaces *ma* and doubling occurs according to the rule *“imasmiṃ thaṃ dāniha to dhesu ca”*.

For here, since words ending in suffixes such as *kkhattuṃ*, *ādi*, *thaṃ*, and *pariyosāna* are indeclinable (*avyaya*) and possess the designation of a noun (*nāma*) due to being taddhita derivatives, when a case-ending is applied, the elision of the case-suffix occurs according to the rule *“sabbāsamāvuso”* etc. [And] “in some cases... (*kvaci*).
Because it is stated [in the grammatical rules] as "to the sense of the fifth case," etc., the suffixes beginning with *ādi* are included here within the category of indeclinable taddhita suffixes.
423. Regarding those that are established by conventional usage (*nipātana*):

those words which are not established by grammatical rule—that is, whose formation is not indicated by a formal rule—whether they originate from a root (*akkhara*), or from a noun (*nāma*), a prefix (*upasagga*), or a particle (*nipāta*), or from a compound (*samāsa*) or a taddhita derivative, are established by conventional usage (*nipātana*).
First, regarding secondary derivatives (*taddhita*):
from the word *ima*, the suffix *jja* occurs in the sense of time; furthermore, after the words *samāna* and *apara*, the suffix *ju* occurs.
Moreover, the vowel *a* of the word *ima* and the vowel *o* of the word *samāna* may be substituted [with the respective vowels of the suffixes].

In the sense of "at this time," "on this day," or "today" (*ajja*), the suffix *tan* is applied to the word *bhava*. In the sense of "at the same time," it is *sajju*; in the sense of "on another day," it is *aparajju*.
The suffix *tan* occurs after the word *bhava* when used with particles (*nipāta*). For example: *Ajja bhavaṃ* becomes *ajjatanaṃ* (today); *ajja bhavā* becomes *ajjatanī* (today [feminine]);

*sve bhavaṃ* becomes *svātanaṃ* (tomorrow). Similarly, *purātanaṃ* (ancient); *hiyyo bhavaṃ* becomes *hiyyattanaṃ* (yesterday); *hiyyo bhavā* becomes *hiyyattanī* (yesterday [feminine]), and so forth.
The Indeclinable Derivative (abyayataddhita).
The derivative suffix (taddhita) arising from an indeclinable (abyaya) that expresses a general state or condition is threefold;
therein, the first type is fourfold, consisting of secondary suffixes (paccaya) with various meanings, as well as those denoting possession and number.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Section on Taddhita Derivatives, within the *Padarūpasiddhi*. 6.
The Section on Verbs (*Ākhyātakaṇḍa*).
The Rules for Case Endings in the Bhūvādi Group:
Now, the verbal case endings (ākhyāta-vibhattiyo) are stated as occurring after roots that express action.

In this context, that which "explains action" (ācikkhati) is called *ākhyāta*, the verb. For it has been said: "The characteristic of a verb (*ākhyātika*) is that which indicates time, the agent, and the person, and possesses the characteristic of action.
Here, "time" refers to the past and so forth; "agent" refers to the object, the doer, and the state [of being]; "person" refers to the first, middle, and last [persons];
and "action" refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), such as going, cooking, and so on. This is the characteristic of action.
That which has this as its sign is a *kriyālakkhaṇa* (action-characteristic) and it is also a gender-indicator (*liṅga*).
And this has been said:
“That which [expresses] the three times, the three persons, expresses action, and [denotes] the three factors of action;”
"The dual number is *atiliṅga*; that is called *ākhyāta*.

They are called *vibhattis* (inflections) because they divide the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) according to time and other factors; they are the forms beginning with *ti*. These, moreover, are eightfold: the present, the fifth (imperative), the seventh (optative), the *parokkhā*, the *ahiyattanī*, the *ajjatanī*, the future, and the conditional (*kālātipatti*).

They are called *dhātus* (verbal roots) because they bear the action; they are those beginning with *bhū* and so forth, as well as the verbal roots ending in suffixes such as *khādi*. These, furthermore, by way of their meaning...
They are of two kinds: transitive and intransitive. Among these, those that express an action requiring an object are transitive, such as:
"he makes a mat," "he goes to the village," and "he cooks rice";
whereas those that express an action independent of an object are intransitive, such as: "he sits," "he lies down," and "he stands."
Furthermore, these [roots] are sevenfold according to the distinction of their suffixes (*vikaraṇa-paccaya*); how so? Those without a suffix are the *bhū-vādi* group;
those with a nasalized prefix as their suffix are the *rudh-ādi* group; those with *y* as their suffix are the *div-ādi* group; those with *ṇu*, *ṇā*, or *uṇā* as their suffix are the *sv-ādi* group;

those with *nāp* or *ṇhā* as their suffix are the *ky-ādi* group; those with *oyir* as their suffix are the *tan-ādi* group; and those ending in *ṇ* in the sense of self-agency (*sakatthe*) are the *cur-ādi* group.

Therein, among the non-causative roots beginning with *bhū*, the first root, which is intransitive, is taken; from this root *bhū*, suffixes such as *tya* and others are applied. Regarding the statement "the root *bhū* is in the sense of existence":
the meaning is that this root *bhū* functions in the sense of existence (*sattā*), that is, it functions in the state of being (*bhavana*) which constitutes the generality of action.
When the form "*bhū*" stands [as the base]—
424. *Bhūvādayo dhātavo*.

Those groups of words (*saddagaṇa*) denoting action, such as *bhū* and others, receive the designation *dhātu*. Those for which *bhū* is the first are *bhūvādayo*; alternatively, those for which *bhūva-ādi* (the letter *v*) is the initial [marker] are *bhūvādayo*.
Among the *bhūvādayo*, this letter *v* should be known as arising from an augment (*āgama*) and euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
Or, roots (dhātu) are of two kinds: those with objects (sakamma) and those without objects (akamma), according to their meaning.
From the beginning [of the rule], "kvaci" (in some cases) is supplied from the phrase "kvaci dhātū" (in some cases, roots).
425. In the case of a root, there is elision (lopa) of a vowel consisting of more than one syllable.
In the case of a verbal root (dhātu) consisting of more than one syllable, there is sometimes elision [of the final vowel].

The inclusion of the word "sometimes" (kvaci) is for the purpose of excluding cases such as *mahīyati* and *samatho*; thus, because these lack the quality of having more than one syllable (*anekassaratta*), there is no elision of the final syllable of the root here.

Consequently, when there is the possibility of various suffixes (*paccaya*) prescribed under the heading of roots, one should follow the principle that "the realization of words proceeds according to the speaker’s desire"; therefore, when there is a desire to express the present tense—
426. *Vattamānā* (the present tense) consists of: *anti*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *nte*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, *mhe*.

The twelve beginning with *ti* are designated as "present" (*vattamāna*). Because they have the meaning of the present as their domain, those beginning with *ti* are designated as "present. 427. [This applies] to time.
This is the governing heading (adhikāra).
From here onwards, it applies everywhere in the formulation of the case endings beginning with *tya*. 428.
The present tense (*vattamānā*) is used for the present time (*paccuppanna*).

In the present time, when an action is being performed (*gamyamāna*), the present tense suffix (*vattamāna-vibhatti*) occurs. Here, "time" (*kāla*) refers to the action (*kriyā*); "kāra" means the instrument (*karaṇa*). By changing the letter *r* to *l*, it becomes "kāla.
Therefore:
Because the suffixes are prescribed when an action is being performed, [the present tense applies].
“Dhātūheva bhavanti” (the roots themselves become [the forms])—thus the case endings beginning with *ti* are established.
Here, however, because time is divided sixfold according to the distinctions of past, future, present, indefinite, hypothetical, and attained time, one specifies it as “in the present.
That which has arisen in dependence upon various causes is the present; its own-nature (*sabhāva*) has been acquired.
The meaning is "not yet past.
Even in proximity to the present, [the term] may be applied to the past through the figurative usage of that designation, according to the speaker's intention regarding that time.

Having applied the present tense suffix (*vattamānavibhatti*) to that [root], and having applied the present suffix after the verbal root (dhātu) according to the rule "suffixes follow the roots and genders" (*dhātuliṅgehi parā paccayā*) within the determination of its positions,
when there arises the contingency of non-restriction among them, then— according to the principle "the application of words follows the sequence of desire"—
in the case of the desire for the third-person form (*parassapada*):
429. Now, the six preceding *parassapada* verbal endings.

Now, among all the eightfold verbal endings—beginning with the present (*vattamāna*) and so forth—which are stated immediately after the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), whichever six preceding endings there may be, they are by meaning designated as *parassapada*, numbering exactly forty-eight.

In the passage beginning with *honti*, there is the designation *parassapada* (third person) for the six [terminations]. Words whose referents are others are *parassapadāni*; they are designated as such because of the predominance of that [usage].
While the rule “*ṇe* and *ṇaya* after verbal roots” (*dhātūhi*) and so forth is in force, [it is stated: 430.
The *parassapada* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).

When the agent (*kattarikāraka*) is to be expressed, the *parassapada* (active voice) endings occur after all verbal roots; thus, having applied the *parassapada*, and because there was the possibility of its application being unrestricted, by the will of the author—through a change of form—the terms "of the *parassapada*" and "of the *attanopada*" (middle voice) are carried forward. 431.
There are two each for the first, middle, and highest persons.

Of those case endings, both the *parassapada* (active) and *attanopada* (middle) have two forms each, which are designated respectively as first person (*paṭhamapurisa*), middle person (*majjhimapurisa*), and third person (*uttamapurisa*).
For example: *ti*, *anti* are first persons; *si*, *tha* are middle persons; *mi*, *ma* are third persons.
In the *attanopada* as well, *te*, *ante* are first persons; *se*, *vhe* are middle persons; *e*, *mhe* are third persons.
In this same way, it should be applied to the remaining seven case-endings as well.

Thus, within the ninety-six types of verbal forms according to the eight cases, there are thirty-two first, middle, and last persons for each; therefore, in the present tense parassapada and other forms, the designation "first person" applies to two [forms] each.
432. Even when a noun (*nāma*) is employed that has the same grammatical core (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), the first person [suffix] is used.

When a noun expressing an agent (*sādhaka*) that possesses the same grammatical core as [the verb] is employed—whether it is actually expressed or not—except for the words *tumha* and *amha*, the first person is applied after verbal roots;
thus, having established the first person, even when there is the contingency of non-restriction regarding that [first person], [the rule applies] to the agent of the action.

When the singularity of the agent (*kattṛ*) is intended to be expressed, the singular number (*ekavacana*) applies according to the rule: "In the singular [number] when one [is to be expressed]. This refers to the first person singular of the *parassapada* (active voice) in the present tense.

Furthermore, the governing context (*adhikāra*) consists of the terms "the other" (*paro*), "suffix" (*paccaya*), and "root" (*dhātu*). From this point, the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kattari*)—which was introduced in the rule for prescribing suffixes (*vikaraṇa-paccaya*) by the phrase "as in the case of the agent" (*yathā kattari ca*)—governs all subsequent instances. 433. After roots beginning with *bhū*, etc., [the suffix] *a* [is applied].
After the group of roots beginning with *bhū*, the suffix *ap* occurs when case-suffixes prescribed for the agent follow. This [suffix] is mixed only within the domain of all roots (*sabbadhātuka*).
The rule “there is *vṛddhi* for that which does not end in a consonant cluster” also continues to apply. 434.
And in other cases as well.

By virtue of their function, there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) for those verbal roots ending in consonants when combined with other suffixes. By the inclusion of the particle *ca* ("and"), strengthening also occurs for the suffix *ṇu*.
Here, the word "or" (*vā*) from the phrase "or of *ghaṭa*, etc. should be understood as recurring; furthermore, it has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*).
By this [rule], [strengthening applies] to roots ending in *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels, and to roots whose penultimate letter is light (*lahu*).
Vṛddhi occurs for the subsequent [vowel] only when the preceding sounds are *i* or *u*;
it does not occur for *y* or *v* before suffixes such as *ya*, *ṇu*, *ṇa*, *nā*, or *aniṭṭha*.
Furthermore, it does not occur in the case of the *vikaraṇa* of roots beginning with *tud*, nor in cases such as *chettvā*.

In the case of this [substitution] as well, where there is the possibility of non-restriction, the vowel *o* is the *vṛddhi* substitute for the vowel *ū*, according to the metarule (*paribhāsa*): "The *vṛddhi* substitute occurs for *a* and *u* vowels.
By way of transference (*vipariṇāma*), the term "of roots" (*dhātūnam*) is understood to carry over.
435. *O* becomes *ava* before a vowel.

When a vowel follows the final element of the *okāra* (the letter *o*), it is replaced by *ava*. Once the elision of the vowel (*saralopa*) and other such changes have been made according to the rule "elision of the vowel, substitution of *m*, etc.," the subsequent application of the rule must be carried out according to the principle: "that which is further [applied] is joined.
Thus: *so puriso sādhu bhavati*, *sā kaññā sādhu bhavati*, *taṃ cittaṃ sādhu bhavati*.
For in this case—
Because the agent has already been expressed by the noun (kattunobhihitattā), it is not expressed by the verb (ākhyātena);
thus, disregarding the gender-meaning, the third person becomes the first person.

Even though there is unity of action, because there is plurality of agents, the plural form of the first person in the *parassapada* (active voice)—which occurs when the plural must be expressed—is used.

The suffixes *anti*, etc., are like the augment *vuddhi* and the substitute *avādesa*, as well as the elision of *sara* (vowels), and so forth. Those persons become [the endings]; even when not employed, it becomes [the form] *bhavati*; when employed, it becomes *bhavanti*.
The phrase “when the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same” also continues [to apply].
436. *Tumhe* is the middle [person].
Even when the word *tumha* is used as having a common grammatical base (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), or even when it is not used, the middle person (*majjhimapurisa*) occurs after verbal roots.
Thus, in the present tense, third-person singular form, [the suffix] is applied; the rest is the same as before. [Examples:
*tvaṃ bhavasi*, *tumhe bhavatha*; even when [the word *tumha*] is not used: *bhavasi*, *bhavatha*.
What is the purpose of [the term] "having the same substratum" (tulyādhikaraṇa)? [Example: *Tayā paccate odano* ("Rice is cooked by her").
Within that very same context: 437.
*Amhe uttamo* ("I am the best among us").

Even when the word *amhas* is employed or not employed as having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), the first person is used after verbal roots. Thus, for the present tense third-person singular ending *mi*, there is the suffix *app*, the vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and the substitution of *ava*.
438. The letter *a* becomes long before *him* and *ima*.
The letter *a* undergoes lengthening before these case-endings: *him* and *ima*. [Examples: *ahaṃ bhavāmi* (I am), *mayaṃ bhavāma* (we are); *bhavāmi*, *bhavāma*.
“Of the case-endings, six,” this [phrase] continues.
439. The subsequent six words for the middle voice (attanopada).
Of all the eight kinds of case-endings that occur, whichever are the subsequent six words, they receive the designation *attanopada*; thus, *te* and so forth receive the designation *attanopada*.
The phrase "from verbal roots, the ātmanepada endings" continues [from the previous rule]. 440.
And when the agent is expressed.

When the agent (*kattar*) is the factor to be expressed, the ātmanepada endings occur after verbal roots. The inclusion of the word *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of excluding [the application of these endings] in certain instances.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated for the third person. [The forms are: *bhavate*, *bhavante*, *bhavase*, *bhavavhe*, *bhave*, *bhavāmhe*.

In the root *pac* (to cook), there is the elision of the final vowel of the root due to its designation as a verbal root (*dhātu*). The derivation of the suffixes beginning with *ti* occurs according to the same method stated above; however, the specific distinction here is the absence of the *vṛddhi* strengthening because of the absence of the vowels *i* and *u*.
[Examples: *so devadatto odanaṃ pacati* (that Devadatta cooks rice), *pacanti* (they cook), *pacasi* (you cook), *pacatha* (you [plural] cook).

I cook, we cook; he cooks that rice, they cook; you cook, you (plural) cook; I cook, we cook. Regarding the possibility of the first person and the others occurring in a single sentence, he states the following paribhāsa: 441.
When all [persons] are expressed by a single word, the subsequent person [prevails].
When it is necessary to express three persons—the first, middle, and last; or the first and last;
or the middle and last—of all [categories], the third person (*para*) should be joined. This [rule] applies only when they are expressed as being at the same time.
Thus, in the context of a synonymic construction such as "He cooks and you cook," the form becomes "You two cook" (*tumhe pacatha*). Likewise, "He cooks and I [cook]"...
"I cook" means "we cook"; likewise, "you cook" and "I cook" mean "we cook," as do "he cooks," "you cook," and "I cook.
Thus it should be applied in all cases. For what purpose is the term "single expression" (*ekābhidhāna*) used?
In the phrase "He cooks, you will cook, and I cooked," because the times [of the actions] are different, the form "we have cooked" (*pacimhā*) does not occur.
In the case of *gamu* in the sense of "going," as before, there is the elision of the final phoneme of the root when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*dhātu-anta-lopa*).
The suffixes *tya* and so forth arise in the active voice (*kattari*). 442. Before all [suffixes], *ccha* optionally replaces the root-final in the future tense (*gamissanto*).

In all case endings, the *m* of the word *gamuiccetassa* optionally becomes *cch*. By the inclusion of the term "all," this applies to words ending in *-māna* and to *kārita* suffixes as well. This word *vā* (or) has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*). Therefore, this [rule] is explained as follows:
The word *vā* indicates that the rule is compulsory in the case of the agent (*kattar*) for those ending in *-māna*, but it is non-compulsory elsewhere;
however, in the *parokkhā* tense, it is compulsory for those not ending in *-māna*.

Regarding the substitution of the second person (*appaccaya*): when the verb *gacchati* (he goes) becomes *gacchanti* (they go), the letter *re* optionally replaces the third-person plural ending according to the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātu" (in some cases, after a root), provided that the preceding syllable is heavy (*garu*). Thus, *gacchare*. You go (*tvaṃ gacchasi*), you all go (*tumhe gacchatha*).
I go (*ahaṃ gacchāmi*), we all go (*mayaṃ gacchāma*).

In the absence of a suffix, by the rule “*lopañcettamakāro*,” the letter *e* replaces the zero-suffix (*appaccaya*). Thus: *gameti*, *gamenti* (with the elision of the *r* vowel). *Gamesi*, *gametha*. *Gamemi*, *gamema*. In the middle voice (*attanopada*) as well:
*so gāmaṃ gacchate*, *gacchante*, *gacchare*. *Gacchase*, *gacchavhe*. *Gacche*, *gacchāmhe*.

However, in expressions such as “*kuto nu tvaṃ āgacchasi, rājagahato āgacchāmī*” (“From where do you come? I am coming from Rājagaha”), the verb form expresses the present tense in its proximity to the current moment.
The word “vā” (or) is understood [from the previous rule]. 443. *Gamissa ghammaṃ*:
for this root *gamu*, there is optionally the substitution of *ghamma* for the whole [root]. Thus: *ghammati*, *ghammanti*, and so forth.
Regarding the *attanopada* endings in the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*): 444.

In both the sense of becoming and the object, when the agent (*kāraka*) is to be expressed, the *attanopada* endings are used; by the word "and" (*ca*), they are also used when the agent is the object (*kammakattṛ*).

*Bhāvanam* means the state of becoming (*bhāva*). This is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), such as *bhava* (to become) or *lava* (to cut), existing in its entirety and uncombined with any other agent.
That which is performed is called an object (*kamma*). Even roots that are intransitive (*akammaka*) become transitive (*sakammaka*) when accompanied by prefixes (*upasagga*).
Therefore, in the sense of the object, from the root *bhū*, the form *te* is derived as the present tense, active voice, first person singular.

From the rule beginning with “*Dhātūhi ṇe ṇaya*,” while the term “*dhātūhi*” (from roots) is still in force: 445. *Bhāvakammesu yo*: The suffix *ya* comes after all verbal roots (*dhātu*) when expressing the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the passive/objective (*kamma*).

This [suffix] will be treated as having the scope of the *attanopada* endings; however, because the word “*aññesu ca*” (and in others) is carried over from the previous sutta, there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) in the *ya* suffix. Example: *anubhūyate sukhaṃ devadattena* (pleasure is experienced by Devadatta).
Because it is not expressed by the verb, the third case (instrumental) occurs for the agent;
because the object is already expressed, the second (accusative) and first (nominative) cases do not occur.
Prosperities are experienced by you. You are being experienced by Devadatta. You all are being experienced. I am being experienced by you. We are being experienced.
When the word "kvaci" (sometimes) is present from the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātu," [the following applies]:
446. The *attanopada* endings take the place of the *parassapada* endings.
Sometimes the *attanopada* endings undergo the substitution of *parassapada* endings; this occurs only when there is no agent (*akattari*). There is doubling of the letter *ya*.
"I experience pleasure," "it is experienced," or "they are experienced. "You experience," "you [plural] experience.
"I experience," "we experience. In the absence of the dual—*anubhūyati*, *anubhūyanti*.
Why say "sometimes"? (As in: *anubhūyate*.

In the sense of a state (*bhāve*), because the state is a single entity for one whose conduct is not material, there is only the singular number, and that belongs only to the first person: *bhūyate devadattena*, meaning "Devadatta is being [in a state] right now.

When the suffix *ya* is applied after the root *pac* in the passive sense (*kammani*) with the *attanopada* endings, and while the word "of which" (*yassa*) is being stated through euphonic change (*vipariṇāmena*).

447. The substitution of a palatal (*ca-vagga*), *ya*, or *va* occurs for that suffix *ya* when it has the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva*) or an object (*kamma*), together with the final letter of the verbal root (*dhātu-anta*), as far as possible.
And here, the word "optionally" (*vā*) should be carried over by "lion's gait" (*sīhagati*) from the rule "the augment *ivaṇṇa* optionally" (*ivaṇṇāgamo vā*).
And that has the meaning of a fixed analysis. By means of it:
"The *ca*-group is the limit of the *ta*-groups [consonants] ending in a root-vowel (*dhātu*);
and for the *ra*-vowels, there is the sequence of *sa*, *ya*, *pa*, *ca*, and *yā* respectively."

When the *cavagga* (the *c*-group) at the end of the verbal root is changed to *ca*, the doubling of the *ca* occurs according to the rule: “There is doubling of a following consonant in its place. Thus:

*paccate odano devadattena* (“Rice is being cooked by Devadatta”). According to the rule beginning with “In some cases, for roots,” etc., the third-person plural ending (*aṃ*) is sometimes replaced by *re* after a heavy initial syllable.
Thus: *paccare*, *paccante*. [The second-person forms are: *paccase*, *paccavhe*. [The first-person forms are: *pacce*, *paccāmhe*.

In the case of the substitution of the *parassapada* endings: *paccati*, *paccanti*; *paccasi*, *paccatha*; *paccāmi*, *paccāma*. Likewise, when the agent is also the object (*kammakattari*), as in "the rice cooks by itself": *paccate odano sayameva*, *paccante*; or *paccati*, *paccanti*, and so forth.
When the suffix *-ita* is applied to the object (*kammani*) and the *attanopada* endings and the *ya*-suffix are added—[the following rule applies]:
"From roots, in that [context], those [suffixes]... (this phrase continues the governing context).
448. *Ivaṇṇāgamo vā*.

When any verbal root (*dhātu*) is followed by the suffix *ya* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the passive (*kamma*), the vowel *i* (the *ivaṇṇa*) may optionally be inserted—that is, the vowel *ī* may be inserted.
This word *vā* has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*). [The *cha* substitute occurs: *gacchīyate gāmo devadattena*, *gacchīyante*.
*gacchīyase*, *gacchīyavhe*; *gacchīye*, *gacchīyāmhe*.
In the absence of the substitution of *ccha*—the rule "from verbal roots, *ya* or *vā*" also continues to apply.
449. *Pubbarūpaṃ* (Original Form).

This [rule] applies only to subsequent roots from those mentioned below; that is, after roots ending in the consonants *ka*, *pa*, *ya*, *ga*, *ra*, *sa*, and *ha*, the suffix *ya* undergoes the original form (*pubbarūpa*).
Thus, the *m* of the subsequent [root] becomes *m* for the *y*. Examples: *gammate*, *gamīyate*, *gammante*.
*Gamyante*. *Gammase*, *gamīyase*, *gammavhe*, *gamīyavhe*. *Gamme*, *gamīye*, *gammāmhe*, *gamīyāmhe*. In the passive voice (*parassapada*):
*gacchīyyati*, *gacchīyyanti*; or *gacchīyati*, *gacchīyanti*; *gammati*, *gammanti*; *gamīyati*, *gamīyanti*.
With the insertion of the vowel *i*: *gamiyyati*, *gamiyyanti*. Likewise, *ghammīyati*, *ghammīyanti*, and so forth.
Present Tense Endings. 450.
The fifth [case] consists of *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *ssu*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*.
These twelve, beginning with *tu*, are designated as the fifth (the imperative endings).
451. The fifth case ending occurs in the sense of command (*āṇatti*) and in the sense of benediction (*āsīsa*), provided it is not a time [already governed by another rule].

Even though the category of time (*kāla*) was already under discussion, the mention of "time" again [here] serves to include cases such as injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantana*), entreaty (*ajjhesanā*), consent (*anumati*), aspiration (*patthana*), attainment (*patta*), and so forth.
And the fifth [case ending]. *Āṇāpana* is the act of commanding; *āsīsanā* is the state of being commanded. That is the aspiration for a desired object not yet attained;
it occurs in that state of being commanded and directed. *Anutta-kāla* means the time of what has not been uttered, that is, the present time;
or, *anutta-kāla* means the time when it has not been uttered. The meaning is that it occurs without referring to a specific time.

In that context, for the purpose of expressing a wish (*āsīsana*), from the root *bhū* (to be), there is the fifth case, the third person singular ending *-tu*, with the suffix *appaccaya*, the vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and the substitution of *ava*. Thus: *so sukhī bhavatu* (may he be happy); *te sukhitā bhavantu* (may they be happy).
By way of reversal, the term "from the letter *a*" (*akārato*) is understood to carry over. 452. Or, there is the elision of the suffix *hi*.

After the letter *a*, the following case endings (*vibhatti*) optionally undergo elision (*lopa*). In the active voice (*parassapada*): *Tvaṃ sukhī bhava*, or *bhavāhi*; [the vowel] becomes long before *him*. *Tumhe sukhitā bhavatha*. *Ahaṃ sukhī bhavāmi*, *mayaṃ sukhino bhavāma*.
In the middle voice (*attanopada*): *So sukhī bhavataṃ*, *te sukhitā bhavantaṃ*. *Tvaṃ sukhī bhavassu*, *tumhe sukhitā bhavavho*. *Ahaṃ sukhī bhave*, *mayaṃ sukhitā bhavāmase*.
In the passive voice (*kammani*): *Anubhūyataṃ tayā*, *anubhūyantaṃ*. *Anubhūyassu*, *anubhūyavho*. *Anubhūye*, *anubhūyāmase*.
In the passive voice (parassapada): *anubhūyyatu*, *anubhūyyantu*; or *anubhūyatu*, *anubhūyantu*; and *anubhūyāhi*, etc. In the impersonal sense (*bhāve*): *bhūyatam*.

In the injunctive mood (*āṇatti*) with the agent (*kattari*): "Now let Devadatta cook the rice"—*pacatu*, *pacantu*; *paca*, *pacāhi*, *pacatha*; *pacāmi*, *pacāma*; *pacatam*, *pacantam*; *pacassu*, *pacavho*; *pace*, *pacāmase*.

In the *kammani* (passive/objective) voice, the *ya*-suffix and the *cavagga* (the *c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*, *ñ*) groups are used: *paccati odano devadattena* (rice is being cooked by Devadatta), *paccantaṃ*.

[Imperative: *paccassu*, *paccavho*. [Optative: *pacce*, *paccāmase*. In the *parassapada* (active/subjective) endings: *paccatu*, *paccantu*. [Imperative: *pacca*, *paccāhi*, *paccatha*. [Optative: *paccāmi*, *paccāma*. Likewise:
*so gāmaṃ gacchatu, gacchantu*. [Imperative: *gaccha*, *gacchāhi*, *gacchatha*. [Optative: *gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*.
Let he go: *gametu*, *gamentu*. Let them go: *gamāhi*, *gametha*. Let me go: *gamemi*, *gamema*. Let them go: *gacchataṃ*, *gacchantu*. Go thou: *gacchassu*, *gacchavho*.
