He causes a man to cook rice; they cause [him] to cook. He causes [it] to be cooked; they cause [it] to be cooked. As for the object:
that rice is caused to be cooked by him—it is being cooked, it is being caused to be cooked, it is being caused to be caused to be cooked.

Likewise: let him cook, let him cause to cook, let him cause to be cooked, let him cause to be caused to be cooked. Let it be cooked, let it be caused to be cooked, let it be caused to be caused to be cooked, let it be caused to be caused to be cooked.
*pācāpiyataṃ*, *pācāpiyatu*, *pācāpayīyataṃ*, *pācāpayīyatu*. *Pāceyya*, *pācayeyya*, *pācāpeyya*, *pācāpayeyya*.
*Pācīyeyya*, *pācīyeyyuṃ*. *Apācesi*, *apācayi*, *apācāpesi*, *apācāpayi*.
*Pācessati*, *pācayissati*, *pācāpessati*, *pācāpayissati*. *Apācissa*, *apācayissa*, *apācāpissa*, *apācāpayissa*—and so forth.
In the sense of "he causes one who is going, or who is about to go," the suffix *ṇe* is applied; thus [we have] *nayādayo*.
When the vowel-vṛddhi has been achieved, the rule "vṛddhi occurs for a word ending in a non-conjunct consonant when a causative suffix (*kārita*) follows" applies.
Or, as in the case of *ghaṭādayo*.

Regarding the statement, "There is either growth (*vuddhi*) or causal activity (*kārita*) for roots such as *ghaṭ* which end in a non-conjunct consonant," here, by the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), there is no growth; this particle *vā* has the sense of a fixed alternative (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*).

He causes that man to go to the village: *gameti*, *gamayati*, *gacchāpeti*, *gacchāpayati*. He is caused to go to the village by him: *gamīyati*, *gamayīyati*, *gacchāpīyati*, *gacchāpayīyati*, and so forth. This should be applied in all cases. The same applies to what follows.

The root *ghaṭ* [means] "to strive"; it causes one who is striving to apply himself, thus *ghaṭeti*. There is no vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*) in *ghaṭādīnaṃ*. [In the causative: *ghaṭayati*, *ghaṭāpeti*, *ghaṭāpayati*. The term "in the causative" (*kārite*) is understood [from the previous rule].
543. In *guha* and *dusa*, there is lengthening of the vowel.
In these roots *guha* and *dusa*, the vowel becomes long when followed by a causative suffix (*kārita*);

this is an exception to the general rule of *vuddhi*. *Guha* (to conceal): one causes another to conceal is *gūhayati*, *gūhayanti*. *Dusa* (displeasure): one causes another to be displeased is *dūsayati*, *dūsayanti*, and so forth.

Likewise, one causes another who desires to desire is *icchāpeti*, *icchāpayati*, or *eseti*, *esayati*. One causes another who is determining to determine... [niyacchantaṃ payojayati]... [is expressed as *niyāmeti*, etc.]
He causes one who is restraining to restrain: *niyāmeti*, *niyāmayati*. He causes one who is sitting to sit:
*āseti*, *āsayati*, *acchāpeti*, *acchāpayati*. He causes one who is obtaining to obtain: *lābheti*, *lābhayati*. He causes one who is speaking to speak:
*vāceti*, *vācayati*, *vācāpeti*, *vācāpayati*. Likewise: *vāseti*, *vāsayati*, *vāsāpeti*, *vāsāpayati*. *Vāheti*, *vāhayati*, *vāhāpeti*...
He causes to carry (*vāhāpayati*). He causes to age: *jīreti*, *jīrayati*, *jīrāpeti*, *jīrāpayati*. He causes to kill: *māreti*, *mārayati*, *mārāpeti*, *mārāpayati*.
He causes to show: *dasseti*, *dassayati*, and so forth.
Likewise, he causes one who is piercing to act: *todeti*, *todayati*, *todāpeti*, *todāpayati*. He causes one who is entering to act...
He causes one to enter, or he enters himself; he causes to enter, or causes to be caused to enter. He employs one who is reciting:
he causes to recite, or causes to be caused to recite. He employs one who is able: he causes to flow forth, or causes to be caused to flow forth. He employs one who is lying down:

he causes to lie down, causes to be caused to lie down, causes to be caused to lie down by another, or causes to be caused to be caused to lie down by another. Here, there is the substitution of *āy* for the vowel *e*: *sayāpeti*, *sayāpayati*.
By the rule beginning with “kvaci dhātu,” there is shortening of the vowel *ā* in the forms *ṇāpeti* and *ṇāpayati*.
He causes one who is leading to lead: *nayāpeti*, *nayāpayati*. He causes one who is establishing to establish: *paṭṭhāpeti*, *paṭṭhāpayati*, or *paṭṭhapeti*.
In the sense of "he causes one who is killing to kill," the suffixes *ṇe*, *ṇaya*, and so forth are applied.
The word “Ṇamhi” is understood [from the previous rule]. 544. *Hana* becomes *ghāta*.

For this root *hana*, the substitution *ghāta* occurs when followed by a causative suffix (*kāritappaccaya*) containing the letter *ṇ*. Thus: *ghāteti*, *ghātayati*, *ghātāpeti*, *ghātāpayati*. Alternatively, according to the rule “*vadhā vā sabbattha*” (or *vadha* everywhere), with the substitution of *vadha*, there are: *vadheti*, *vadhāpeti*.
He instigates one who is sacrificing: *juhāveti*, *juhāvayati*. He instigates one who is abandoning:
*jahāpeti*, *jahāpayati*, *hāpeti*, *hāpayati*. He instigates one who is giving: *dāpeti*, *dāpayati*. He instigates one who is closing:
*pidhāpeti*, *pidhāpayati*, *pidahāpeti*, *pidahāpayati*.
He causes one who is obstructing to obstruct: he obstructs, he causes to obstruct, he causes to be obstructed, he causes to be caused to obstruct.

He causes one who is cutting to cut: he cuts, he causes to cut, he causes to be cut, he causes to be caused to cut. He causes one who is yoking to yoke: he yokes, he causes to yoke, he causes to be yoked, he causes to be caused to yoke.
He causes one who is eating to eat: he feeds, he causes to feed, he causes to be fed, he causes to be caused to feed.
One causes that which is being released to release: *moceti*, *mocayati*, *mocāpeti*, *mocāpayati*.
One causes that which is playing to play: *deveti*, *devayati*. One causes that which is arising to arise: *uppādeti*, *uppādayati*.
One causes that which is awakening to awaken: *bodheti*, *bodhayati*. By the rule “*dādhāntato yo kvaci*,” there is the augment *y*; thus: *bujjhāpeti*.
He causes [someone] to awaken: *bujjhāpayati*. He instigates one who is pleased; he pleases, he causes to please, he causes to be pleased, he causes to be made pleased:

*toseti*, *tosayati*, *tosāpeti*, *tosāpayati*. He instigates one who is calming oneself; he calms, he causes to calm: *sameti*, *samayati* (there is no increase because it begins with *gha*). He instigates one who is becoming angry; he makes angry, he causes to become angry:
*kopeti*, *kopayati*. He instigates one who is being born; he gives birth, he causes to be born: *janeti*, *janayati* (there is no increase because it begins with *gha*).

He causes one who is hearing to engage [in hearing], he causes to announce, he causes to proclaim. He causes one who is reaching to engage [in reaching], he causes to cause to reach, he causes to cause to reach.

He causes one who is selling to engage [in selling], he causes to cause to sell, he causes to cause to sell. He causes one who is winning to engage [in winning], he causes to cause to win, he causes to cause to win.

He causes one who is knowing to engage [in knowing], he causes to cause to know, he causes to cause to know. He causes one who is grasping to engage [in grasping], he causes to cause to grasp, he causes to cause to grasp.
*gāhāpeti*, *gāhāpayati*, *gaṇhāpeti*, *gaṇhāpayati*.

One causes one who is spreading [a canopy] to act: *vitāneti*, *vitānayati*. Whoever does something, another says to him, "Do it! Do it!", thus causing the one doing it to act; or one causes someone to do what was to be done: *kāreti*, *kārayati*, *kārāpeti*, *kārāpayati*, and so forth. One causes one who is stealing to act: *corāpeti*, *corāpayati*.
One causes one who is thinking to act: *cintāpeti*, *cintāpayati*. One causes one who is worshipping to act: *pūjāpeti*, *pūjāpayati*, and so forth. In all cases, it is easily understood.
Furthermore, there may be [forms] based on the *dhātu* suffix and the *kārita* suffix;
for instance, from roots ending in *yu* and *nu*, such as *titikkhati* and *tikicchati*.

Here, the observation of forms with the *kārita* suffix serves as an indicator. Thus, one causes someone who is enduring to endure: *titikkheti*; one causes someone to cause another to endure: *titikkhāpeti*. One causes someone who is healing to heal: *tikiccheti*.

He treats medically (*tikicchati*), he causes to treat medically (*tikicchāpeti*), he causes to cause to treat medically (*tikicchāpayati*). Likewise, *bubhukkheti*, *bubhukkhayati*, *bubhukkhāpeti*, *bubhukkhāpayati*;

*pabbatāyantam payojayati* results in *pabbatāyayati*. *Puttīyayati* and so forth are also established in this way. This is the method [concerning] verbal roots, suffixes, and word endings (*dhātuppaccayantaniyo*).
This which has been pointed out for the sake of the Dispensation and explained through my own intelligence—
let the discerning contemplate this by the power of their own extensive learning.
[The suffixes] *bhavati*, *tiṭṭhati*, *seti*, *ahosi*, and so forth;
They should be understood as "intransitive" by one who knows the characteristics of objects (kamma).
Even those that are intransitive become transitive when suffixed by verbal endings expressing a cause;
for example: "The bhikkhu develops the path which destroys lust and the other defilements."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Verbs, within the *Padarūpasiddhi*. 7.
The Chapter on Primary Derivatives (*Kibbidhānakaṇḍa*).

The Method of the Temporal Relation of Functions: Now, the formation of verbal derivatives (*kibbidhāna*) is commenced by means of verbal roots themselves, together with the grammatical factors (*sādhana*) such as the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In this context, conditions (*paccaya*) are twofold, according to whether they are by way of function (*kicca*) or by way of having been performed (*kata*). Among these, because they are mentioned first under the designation "function" and because functions are few in number, the functional conditions (*kiccappaccaya*) are stated first.

The root *bhū* is used in the sense of existence (*sattā*). In the analysis (*viggha*)—"*bhūyate*, *abhavittha*, or *bhavissate* by Devadatta"—the term "*dhātuyā*" from the rule "*Dhātuyā kammādimhi ṇo*" applies here;
it recurs in all subsequent rules for the application of suffixes and so forth. Furthermore, the governing terms "*parā*" and "*paccayā*" remain in force.
545. *tabba* and *anīya* after the sense of the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*).

After these meanings of the passive and the object, the suffixes *tabba* and *anīya* follow all verbal roots (*dhātu*). By means of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), they also occur in other senses.
Therein—
Those [suffixes] that are intransitive (akammaka) form abstract nouns (bhāva);
those that are transitive (sakammaka) denote the object (kamma), illustrating the meanings of "worthy" (araha) and "honored" (sakkata), and so forth.
And they—
546. *Ṇādayo tekālikā*.

Those belonging to the three times (*tekālika*) are those connected with the three times. Since the suffixes beginning with *ṇ* that are prescribed here in this third section on verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*) have their time not specifically indicated, by virtue of this maxim (*paribhāsa*), they belong to all three times.
The phrase "in some cases" (*kvaci*) from the rule on the lion’s gait (*sīhagati*) continues [to apply].
547. *Yathāgamamikāro*:

According to the tradition and according to usage, in accordance with the word of the Jina (*jinavacana*), there is sometimes the addition of the letter *i* after a root (*dhātu*) when followed by certain suffixes (*kicca*, *kit*, *ka*) beginning with a consonant.

By the rule "vṛddhi for other vowels," there is the substitution of *vṛddhi*; by the rule "o becomes ava before a vowel" (*o ava sare*), there is the substitution of *ava*; and by the rule "after *na*, [the following vowel is] long" (*naye paraṃ*).
"Yutte": that which is to be led by another [should be supplied]. 548.
Those [suffixes]—namely the *tabba*, *anīya*, *ṇya*, *teyya*, and *rica* suffixes—which are stated here, should be understood as having the designation "kicca" (obligatory).

Then, because of the statement "so that others may [know]," since the *kicca* suffixes do not possess the quality of being a *kita*, and before the designation of a noun (*nāmabyapadesa*) has been reached, the designation of a noun occurs here by the inclusion of the particle "ca" in the rule "Taddhita-samāsa-kita-ka nāmaṃ vā tavetunādīsu ca.
From that, the case endings beginning with *si* arise. Since there is oneness of the state (*bhāva*), there is only the singular number;
thus, by the substitution rule for *am*, "si" becomes "am. It is to be become by you who are wise; it is to be become.

Here, because there is no suffix beginning with a consonant (*byañjana*), there is no addition of the vowel *i* due to the inclusion of the term "following a vowel" (*anuvattita-kavagga*). When [the suffix] exists, those ending in kṛtya-suffixes are neuter;

when [the suffix] denotes the object (*karman*), they have three genders. With respect to the object, preceded by *abhi-*: *abhibhūyate*, *abhibhūyittha*, *abhibhūyissati*—anger is to be overcome (*abhibhavitabbo*) by the wise;
craving is to be overcome; suffering is to be overcome. Thus, it is to be overcome (*abhibhavanīyo*), they are to be overcome (*abhibhavanīyā*).
"O man, it is to be overcome,"—this should be understood according to the method of the "mind-sound" (cittasaddanaya); thus it is in all cases.
For here, because the action is stated by those very words beginning with "tabbā" (to be done), there is no repetition.
Because there is no [form] to be stated, the second [suffix] does not occur after the first. Regarding the root *ās* (to sit):

*āsīyittha*, *āsīyate*, *āsīyissati*—thus, "you must sit" (*āsitabbaṃ*) or "that which is to be sat upon" (*āsanīyaṃ*). Regarding the object (*kamma*): one who is to be served is "venerable" (*upāsitabbo*, *upāsanīyo*).

Regarding the root *sī* (to lie down): *asīyittha*, *sīyate*, *sīyissati*—thus, "you must lie down" (*sayitabbaṃ*) or "that which is to be lied upon" (*sayanīyaṃ*); here, by the rule "e ayā," the substitution of *ay* occurs. One who is to be surpassed is "surpassable" (*atisayitabbo*, *atisayanīyo*).
Regarding the sense of "going" (*gati*), that which is to arise—as in "it has arisen," "it arises," or "it will arise"—is called *uppajjitabba*. It is also called *uppajjanīya*.

Here, the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule "after roots beginning with *div*, [the suffix] *ya*" even without an explicit governing heading; then, by the rule "for that, the group of *ca*-consonants and the letter *y* [are substituted]," the *ca*-group is substituted;
and by the rule "doubling occurs in place of the following consonant," there is doubling. Thus, it is to be understood as *paṭipajjitabba*.

*Magga* means that which is to be traversed. *Budha* means to awaken; because one has awakened, is awakening, or will awaken, it is the *dhamma* that is to be awakened to (*bujjhitabba*), that which is to be understood.

*Su* means to hear; because one has heard, is hearing, or will hear, it is the *dhamma* that is to be heard (*sotabba*). Here, by taking the form according to the traditional grammatical source (*yathāgama*), there is an absence of the augment *i*. [Thus] it is *suṇitabba*. By the rule "after *svādita*, the suffixes *ṇu*, *ṇā*, and *uṇā* [are applied]," even without the application of the governing rule (*vinādhikāra*), the suffix *ṇā* is added, resulting in *savaṇīya*. It is that which is to be heard.
The suffixes *tabba* and *anīya* occur in the sense of "to be done" (*karaṇe*), "was done" (*karīyittha*), "is being done" (*karīyati*), and "will be done" (*karīyissati*).
The phrases "of *anta*, of *kara*, and of *tatta*" are also understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
549. The suffixes *tuṃ* and *tu* optionally occur in place of *tabba*.
The letter *ra* within the verbal root *kara*, when followed by the suffixes *tuṃ*, *tu*, or *tabba*, optionally becomes *ta*. Thus:
*kattabbo bhavatā dhammo* (the Dhamma is to be done by you), *kattabbā pūjā* (worship is to be performed), *kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ* (wholesome action is to be done).

In the absence of the suffix *ta*, when the present form *karoti* is used, the substitution of *ka* for *kara* occurs before the suffixes *tava*, *etu*, and so forth; here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the suffix *tabba* is also included, as in *kātabbaṃ hitaṃ* (benefit is to be accomplished).
550. *Rahādito ṇa*.

After verbal roots beginning with the letter *ra* or *ha*, the following letter *na*—such as that found in *anāniya* and so forth—is changed to *ṇa*. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), it is also understood to apply after [roots] such as *ramu* and *apaññāta*.
Here, because a letter *na* cannot follow immediately after [roots] beginning with *ra* or *ha*, [the rule applies to those cases where such a change is possible].
The presence of the letter *ṇ* here is for the sake of the suffix *anīya* and others.
"Dhamma that ought to be done" (*karaṇīyo dhammo*) means it is fit to be performed; [the forms] are *karaṇīyā* (feminine) and *karaṇīyaṃ* (neuter).
From the root *bhṛ* in the sense of supporting: it is to be supported (*bharitabbo*), thus "that which ought to be supported" (*bharaṇīyo*).
*Gaha* (seizing) is derived from *upādāna* (clinging). It is to be grasped (*gahetabbo*) because it has been seized (*agayhittha*), is being seized (*gayhati*), or will be seized (*gayhissati*).

By the rule "the vowel *i* [becomes] *e*" in the phrase "there is growth in those," the vowel *i* becomes *e*. It is to be included (*saṅgaṇhitabbo*). By the rule "from *gaha*, etc., the suffix *ppaṇhā*," the suffix *ṇhā* is applied without the need for a governing rule or a division of connection; following the elision of the final consonant (*halopa*) and the elision of the preceding vowel (*asaralopa*), it becomes *saṅgaṇhaṇīyo* and *gahaṇīyo*.

By the inclusion of "ādi" (and so forth), from the root *ram* in the sense of sporting: *ramīyittha*, *ramīyati*, *ramīyissati*—thus it is "to be enjoyed" (*ramitabba*), and "delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) is a dwelling place.

From the root *ap* in the sense of reaching, with the suffix *-uṇā*: *pāpīyati*—thus it is "to be reached" (*pāpuṇitabba*). By the rule "of *gup* and others," there is elision of the final part of the root, and doubling [of the initial consonant]; thus: *pattabba*, *patteyya*, *pāpuṇaṇīya*, *pāpaṇīya*.
The phrase "of the internal [consonant], optionally" also continues to apply.

551. In the case of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, and *han*, the final *n* is optionally retained before suffixes beginning with *t*, such as *tuṃ*, *tabba*, *tave*, *tuna*, *tvā*, *ānatvā*, and so forth. For instance: *agacchīyittha*, *gacchīyati*.
*gacchīyissati* means "it will be gone to"; thus it is *gantabbo* (to be gone), *gamitabbaṃ* (to be gone), or *gamanīyaṃ* (to be gone).

Regarding the root *khanu* in the sense of digging: from *akhaññittha*, *khaññati*, and *khaññissati*, there is *khantabbaṃ* (to be dug), *khanitabbaṃ* (to be dug), and—by the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātū"—there is also the suffix *-ṇa-* for one who digs, resulting in *khaṇitabbaṃ*, *khaṇaṇīyaṃ*, or *khananīyaṃ* (all meaning "to be dug," referring to a pit).

Regarding the root *hana* in the senses of harming and going: from *ahaññittha*, *haññate*, and *haññissati*, there is *hantabbaṃ*, *hanitabbaṃ*, or *hananīyaṃ* (meaning "to be killed" or "to be harmed").

Regarding *mana* (to think): it was thought (*amaññittha*), it is thought (*maññate*), and it will be thought (*maññissati*). It is to be thought (*mantabbo*), it is to be thought (*manitabbo*), and in the sense of the *yapaccaya*, there is the substitution of the *cavagga* sounds, etc., resulting in *maññitabbaṃ* and *maññanīyaṃ*.

Regarding *pūja* (to worship): in the sense of "it was worshipped" (*apūjīyittha*), "it is worshipped" (*pūjīyati*), and "it will be worshipped" (*pūjīyissati*), the suffixes *-tabba* and *-anīya* are used. According to the rule "from *curādi* [roots], *ṇe* and *ṇaya*," the suffix *ṇe* is applied even when there is no agent;
and among those suffixes ending in *i* that undergo the *anīya* replacement, by the rule "elision of *sa-ra*" and so forth, there is the elision of the *kārita-sa* (the causative *sa*).
The Blessed One is to be honored, to be worshipped, to be revered.

In the case of the suffix *-anīya*, through the analysis of grammatical relations (*yogavibhāga*), it is used for both the agent and the instrument; thus, that which leads to attainment is the "leading" (*niyyānīka*) path. That which they go by are "to-be-gone-to" (*gamanīya*) enjoyments. That by which one bathes is "for bathing" (*nahānīya*) powder. The governing rule here is:
"in the sense of the state of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*)."

552. And *ṇya*. The suffix *ṇya* occurs after all verbal roots in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*); by the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *teyya* also occurs in cases such as *ñāteyya*. 553.
A suffix with an indicatory letter *ṇ* is treated like a causative (*kārita*).

The suffix *an* is without functional application (*appayogī*); however, a suffix with the letter *ṇ* as its adjunct should be regarded as having a functional application (*kārita*), and thus receives the designation "functional.

According to the rule "the *ṇ* is elided after functional suffixes" (*kāritānaṃ ṇo lopa*), the *ṇ* is elided; according to the rule "vṛddhi occurs before a functional suffix after a word ending in a non-conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogantassa vuddhi kārite*), vṛddhi occurs, followed by the augment *ik*.

That which is to be done is called "functional" (*kāriya*). From the root *hṛ* (in the sense of "taking away"), we have *aharīyittha*, *harīyati*, or *harīyissati*; thus, that which is to be taken away is "to-be-taken-away" (*hāriya*).
*Bhara* means supporting; that which is to be supported is *bhāriya*.

*Labha* means obtaining; that which is to be obtained is *labbha*. In the sutta beginning with "yavataṃ talana," by the inclusion of the suffix *-ka*, the letter *bha* becomes *bha* after the letter *ta*; this is a doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*). *Sāsa* means instruction;
one who is to be instructed is a *sisso* (disciple). By the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātū," the vowel *ā* becomes *i*.
In the word *vaca*, when the suffix *ṇya* and others are applied, the rule "of final vowels, when followed by a suffix with *ṇ* as an anubandha" continues to apply.
554. *Kagā cajānaṃ*:

For the final consonants *ca* and *ja* of verbal roots, the substitutes *ka* and *ga* respectively occur when a suffix with *ṇ* as an anubandha follows; thus, there is the substitution of *kā* for *ca*. [The derivative is] *vacanīyaṃ*, meaning "speech."
"Bhaja" means "for service. "Bhajanīyaṃ" means "fortune worthy of being honored," of which this is the root.

"Ci" means "to accumulate": *acīyittha*, *cīyati*, *cīyissati*—thus it is that which is to be accumulated (*cetabbaṃ*), called *ceyyaṃ*. [In the formation of *viniccheyyaṃ*: there is the vowel increment (*vuddhi*) of *i* to *e*; the doubling of the letter *y*;
and by the rule "vinipubbo ‘do dhassa cā’" (with the inclusion of the letter *ca* in the sutta), the letter *c* becomes *ch*. Thus: *viniccheyyaṃ*.

*Vinicchitabbaṃ*, *vinicchanīyaṃ*. Regarding the question "From what root [is this derived]?", by means of the suffixes *tabba*, *anīya*, *tuṃ*, *tuna*, and so forth—apart from the application of the *vinā* prefix and the *adhikāra* (governing rule)—the suffix *na* is applied: *vinicchinitabbaṃ*, *vinicchinanīyaṃ*.
From the root *nī* (to lead/attain): *anīyittha*, *nīyati*, *nīyissati*—thus it is *neyyo*, *neyyā*, *neyyaṃ*. Also: *netabbaṃ*.

The mention of *ṇya* follows by way of the genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*), and the mention of the suffix *anta* follows by way of the instrumental case (*tatiyā*) through the "frog-leap" method (*maṇḍūkagati*). 555. *Bhūto vva*.
After the root *bhū*, the suffix *ṇya* undergoes the substitution *abb* together with the end of the verbal root. Thus: *bhavitabbo*, *bhabbo*, *bhabbā*, *bhabbaṃ*.
“After [a root] ending in a vowel,” this also continues to apply.

556. After the roots *vada*, *mada*, *gamu*, *yuja*, and those beginning with *garaha*, or after a root ending in long *ā* that is eligible for the suffix *ya*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied to the following [root].
Thus, after roots such as *vada*, *mada*, *gamu*, *yuja*, *garaha*, and so forth, and after those ending in long *ā*, the suffix *ṇya* is added to the subsequent [root].
Together with the final vowel of the base, these substitutions—*jja*, *mma*, *gga*, *yyha*, *e*, and *yya*—occur respectively, or alternatively, the substitution of *gāra* for *gara*.
This *gāra* is the same as *gāra* derived from *garaha*. The word *vā* here has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthita-vibhāsa*). [The root] *vad* means "to speak clearly.
That which has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken is called *vajja*; it is that which is to be spoken. It becomes short (by rule). *Vajja* means fault (*dosa*).

That by which one becomes intoxicated (*mada*), has been intoxicated, is intoxicated, or will be intoxicated, is *majja*, meaning intoxicating. The suffix *-nya* is applied even when expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) through the inclusion of the root *mad*.
From *gamu* in the sense of going: that which is to be gone to is *gamma*. From *yuja* in the sense of joining:

that which has been joined, is joined, or will be joined is *yogga* or *niyojja*. From *garaha* in the sense of censuring: that which has been censured, is censured, or will be censured—this being the meaning—the suffix *-nya* is applied. In this case, there is a substitution of *yh* for the end of the root, and a substitution of *gār* for *gara*. Thus: *gārayha*, *gārayhā*, *gārayhaṃ*, or *garahaṇīyaṃ*.

By the word *ādi* (and so forth), other taming-controllers (*damajahantā*) are also included. From the root *gada*, meaning "articulate speech," one speaks (*gajjate*); thus, that which is to be spoken is *gajja*.

From the root *pada*, meaning "to go," that which is to be traversed is *pajja*; [here] it refers to a verse (*gāthā*). From the root *khāda*, meaning "to eat," that which is eaten is *khajja*, i.e., food to be chewed (*khādanīya*).

From the root *damu*, meaning "to tame," that which was tamed (*adammittha*), is being tamed (*dammate*), or will be tamed (*damīyissati*) is *damma*, i.e., that which is to be tamed (*damanīya*). From the root *bhuja*...

That which is protected and maintained—having been enjoyed, being enjoyed, or will be enjoyed—is called *bhogga* or *bhojja*. By the inclusion of the term "kāra," that in which the letter *j* occurs [is included].
That which is to be taken is *gayha*, and so forth.

Furthermore, from a root ending in long *ā*, such as *dā* in the sense of giving (*dāne*), in the meanings of "was given," "is given," or "will be given," there is the suffix *ṇya*; by means of this [suffix], [the form *deyya* is derived].
With the final vowel of the root *dhā*, there is the substitution of *eyya*; thus, *deyyaṃ* (to be given) and *dātabbaṃ* (should be given).

Regarding the suffix *-anīya*, when the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*) would otherwise apply according to the rule "saralopo," etc., that is prohibited by the inclusion of *tu* in that very rule; then, by the rule "sarā sare lopa," the vowel *ā* is elided, and the long vowel of the following vowel occurs, resulting in *dānīyaṃ*.

The root *pā* means "to drink": *apīyittha* (was drunk), *pīyati* (is drunk), *pīyissati* (will be drunk); thus, *peyyaṃ* (drinkable), *pātabbaṃ* (should be drunk), and *pānīyaṃ* (beverage). The root *hā* means "to abandon": *ahīyittha* (was abandoned).

*Hīyati* (is abandoned), *hīyissati* (will be abandoned) = *heyyaṃ*, that which is to be abandoned, that which is subject to abandonment (*hānīyaṃ*). *Mā* (to measure): *amīyittha*, *mīyati*, *mīyissati* = *meyyaṃ*, that which is to be measured, that which is to be measured out (*mātabbaṃ*), or that which is to be meted out (*metabbaṃ*).

*Ñā* (in the sense of understanding): *aññāyittha*, *ñāyati*, *ñāyissati* = *ñeyyaṃ*, that which is to be known, that which is to be understood (*ñātabbaṃ*), or that which is to be cognized (*ñāteyyaṃ*).

Regarding the substitution of *j* for *ñā* according to the rule *“ñāssa jā jaṃ nā”* (for *ñā*, there is *ja* and *jaṃ* as substitutes), and by the separation of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *“kiyādito nā”* (the suffix *na* follows roots beginning with *kiya*), [the form *ñeyyaṃ* is established].

*Nāpaccaya* (the suffix *na*) and the augment *ikāra* are to be understood; [the forms] *vijānitabbaṃ* and *vijānanīyaṃ* [are derived thus]. In the sense of "making known," [the forms] *saṅkhyātabbaṃ* and *saṅkhyeyyaṃ* occur, and so forth.
557. After the root *kara*, the suffix *ricca* occurs in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).
558. *Ramhi ranto rādi no*.
When a suffix beginning with the letter *r* follows, every final *r* of a verbal root (dhātu) becomes *no*; the meaning is that it undergoes elision (*lopa*).

In the word *rantō*, the letter *r* is a euphonic junction (*sandhija*), and the function to be performed is [the application of this rule]. By means of the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) of the term *riccā*, [the rule applies] even from roots beginning with *bh*.

The *ricca* suffix: for example, from *bharati*, *bhacca* (to be carried), with the elision of *ra*. From the root *i* in the sense of "going," *pati* + *etabba* = *paṭicco* (one who must be approached). 559.

The *kicca* suffixes occur in the senses of sending (*pesa*), excellence (*atisagga*), and the time for what ought to be done (*pattakāla*). The *kicca* suffixes occur in these senses: sending (*pesa*), excellence (*atisagga*), and the time for what ought to be done (*pattakāla*). Sending (*pesana*) means "this is to be done."

[This refers to] commanding and entreating [someone], saying, "Do this by you. Excessive generosity (*atisagga*) means granting permission for what ought to be done—either when one is asked, "What should be done by me?
or by way of demonstrating the proper course of conduct, such as "Living beings must not be killed," and so forth.
The "proper time" (*pattakāla*) means the opportune moment; it is for one who does not act without first examining the time for performing their own duty.

There is no formal request (*ajjhesanā*) in that case; rather, because it is stated that [the suffixes] *tabba*, *anīya*, and *attha* occur in the sense of the passive and the gerundive (*bhāvakamma*), they occur only in the passive and gerundive senses.

First, regarding the sense of commissioning (*pesana*): in the sense of "let the work be done by you," there are the suffixes *tabba*, *anīya*, and *attha*; the rest is exactly as previously explained. [Examples: *kattabbaṃ kammaṃ bhavatā* (the work is to be done by you), *karaṇīyaṃ kiccaṃ bhavatā* (the duty is to be performed by you).

In the sense of "let him eat more," the suffixes *tabba* and so forth are applied; by the rule "and in other cases," there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). The word "tassa" (of it) is understood [from the previous rule].
560. For roots beginning with *bhuj*, the suffix *na* is added at the end, and the final consonant is not doubled.

For roots such as *bhuja* ending in *j*, there is no substitution of *n* for the final letter; rather, there is doubling of the *t* of the suffixes *kicca*, *kita*, and *kappa*. Thus: *bhottabbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā* (food to be eaten by you), *bhojanīyaṃ bhojjaṃ bhavatā* (food fit to be eaten by you).

However, regarding the *t* joined with the augment *i*, the prohibition against the elision of the root-final and so forth occurs through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the phrase "of those ending in *n* or *m*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *n*" (*namakarānamantānaṃ niyuttatamhī*), specifically by the portion "when followed by a suffix beginning with *n*" (*antānaṃ niyuttatamhī*).

Furthermore, the form "preceded by a nasal" (*niggahītapubba*) in the rule "from *rudh* etc., preceded by a nasal" (*rudhādito niggahītapubbaṃ*) occurs without the governing heading (*adhikāra*) or the division of the rule.

Or, in the case of the expression "niggahītañca," there is the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). [Examples are: *bhuñjitabbaṃ tayā* (it must be eaten by you) and *yuñjitabbaṃ* (it must be joined).

However, in the announcement of the occasion (*samayārocane*)—in the sense that "you are studying" (*adhīyatam bhavata*)—there is the prefix *adhi-* before the root *i-*. The suffixes *-tabba*, *-anīya*, and so forth, apply;

there is the insertion of the vowel *i*, the vowel increase (*vuddhi*), the substitution of *ā* for *e*, and the substitution of *ajjha* for *adhi*. But when the suffix *ṇya* is applied, there is vowel increase and the doubling of the letter *y*; thus, it becomes *ajjhayitabbaṃ*.

In the sentences "it must be studied by you," "it is to be studied by you," or "it is necessarily to be done," the suffix *tabba* and others are applied after the word *kicca* (to be done) according to the rule "after words meaning 'necessary' or 'debt,' the suffix *ṇī* or *cā* [is added]," as in *avassakādhamiṇesu ṇī cā*. Thus:
"my house must be built by you" (*me bhavatā gehaṃ kattabbaṃ*), *karaṇīyaṃ*, *kāriyaṃ*. Likewise: "one hundred must be given by you to me" (*me bhavatā sataṃ dātabbaṃ*), *dānīyaṃ*, *deyyaṃ*.

The root *dhṛ* (to hold) takes the suffix *ṇic* because it belongs to the *cur-ādi* group; there is vocalization (*vṛddhi*) and the insertion of the vowel *i*, resulting in forms such as *dhāretabbaṃ* (should be held) and *dhārayitabbaṃ* (should be caused to be held).

Regarding the rule "After roots beginning with *nud*, the suffixes *yu*, *ṇvu*, *man*, *ana*, *nā*, *kāna*, and *na* are added when there is a causative (*sakārita*)," one should understand that by the very prescription of the substitutes *yu*, *ṇvu*, etc., the functional suffixes (*kicca*), participial suffixes (*kita*), and potential suffixes (*kappa*) also arise from both verbal roots and suffixes.
Therefore, [the form] *titikkhāpīyati* (is endured) [is derived accordingly].
It should be made to endure; thus, it is "to be treated" (*tikicchāpetabbo*) or "one who is to be treated" (*tikicchāpanīyo*).
Because it was cultivated, is being cultivated, or will be cultivated, the path is "to be cultivated" (*bhāvetabbo*).

Because it was done, is being done, or will be done, it is established as "to be done" (*kāretabbaṃ*), "to be caused to be done" (*kārayitabbaṃ*), "to be caused to be performed" (*kārāpetabbaṃ*), "to be caused to be performed" (*kārāpayitabbaṃ*), "to be caused to be performed" (*kārāpanīyaṃ*), and so forth.
*Kattabba*, *karaṇīya*, *kāriya*, *kicca*,
as well as *kāretabba* and *kārāpetabba*, are included among the *kicca* suffixes.
This is the method for the *kicca*-suffixes.
The Method for the Condition of Nutriment at One Time:
Now the conditions of nutriment are being stated.
*Kara* is used in the sense of making (*karane*); it is like *dhātu-saññādi* [in the previous example].
*Kumbha* is the secondary word (*upapada*); therefore, the second case ending is applied.
In the analysis (*viggaha*): "He makes a jar," "he made," or "he will make."
The terms “after” (parā) and “conditioned by” (paccayā) are understood [to carry over].

561. After a verbal root (dhātu), when there is an object (kamma) or one of the other [grammatical relations] at the beginning, the suffix *ṇa* occurs. When an object or another such relation stands at the beginning, the suffix *ṇa* follows the verbal root.
And so—562.
*Aññe kita* (Others are *kita*).

In the third section on bases (*dhātu*), it is stated that those suffixes (*paccaya*) prescribed for functions other than *kicca* receive the designation *kita*; thus, the designation *kita* is applied.
563. *Kattari kita*.

The suffix *kita* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*); this is established by rule as being in the agentive case. Furthermore, because it is stated that "the suffixes beginning with *ṇa* pertain to all three times," it also occurs in all three tenses.
As before, there are the designations of causative, passive, elision, and vowel strengthening; and because the suffix is devoid of gender, [it is applied accordingly].

If the suffix *kitaka* had not been reached [by the rule], then because of the rule “*taddhita-samāsa-kitakā nāmaṃ vā ta-vetunādīsu ca*” (Taddhita suffixes, compounds, and *kitaka* are optionally called nouns when followed by *ta*, *vetuna*, etc.), the noun-form would have arisen upon its formation.

Consequently, in the sense of “he makes a jar,” the second case ending would have occurred according to the rule “*am-ādayo parapadehi*” (the endings *am* and so on [are elided] before subsequent words), resulting in a *tappurisa* compound.

Then, by the rule “*nāmānan*” and so forth, it would have received the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saññā*), and by the rule “*tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca*” (the case-endings of these are elided), the case-ending would have been dropped, leaving the base form (*pakati*).
In the case of *cassa sarantassā* (“of him who remembers”), there is the state of being a base form (*pakatibhāvo*);

then, because it has been made as if it were a noun due to its inclusion in a compound, the case endings (*syādyuppatti*) arise. Thus: *so kumbhakāro* (“that potter”), *te kumbhakārā* (“those potters”), and so forth. In the feminine: *kumbhakārī*, *kumbhakāriyo*, and so forth.
Likewise, one who performs work is a *kammakāro*. Similarly: *mālākāro* (garland-maker), *kaṭṭhakāro* (wood-worker), *rathakāro* (chariot-maker), *suvaṇṇakāro* (goldsmith), *suttakāro* (weaver).

The author of the *Vutti*, the author of the *Ṭīkā*. [In the sense of] grasping (*gaha*) or taking hold (*upādāna*): one who has taken a bowl, takes it, or will take it is called a "bowl-grasper" (*pattaggāha*).

Likewise, a "rope-grasper" (*rasmiggāha*), a "cord-grasper" (*rajjuggāha*). [In the sense of] weaving (*ve*), which means the continuous extension of thread: one who has woven, weaves, or will weave thread is a "weaver" (*tantavāya*). Here, the substitution of *ā* occurs according to the rule “*te āvāyā kārite*” (Pāṇini 3.1.146). However, in this specific context, the substitution of *ā* occurs through a division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) as in “*te āvāyā*”. Likewise, a "tailor" (*tunnavāya*).

When the sense of "measuring" (*parimāṇa*) is intended—such as in the words *dhaññaṃ amini*, *mināti*, or *minissati*—and the suffix *ṇa* has been added, the phrase "after [a root] ending in *ṇ*" (*ṇamhī*) is understood to carry over.
564. For roots ending in long *ā*, the suffix *āya* is applied.

For verbal roots ending in the vowel *ā*, the substitution of *āy* occurs for the final *ā* when a suffix with the marker *ṇ* follows, after which the *a* and following letters are elided, and so forth. For example: *dhaññamāyo*. Similarly, one who gives a gift is called *dānadāyo*. The root *kamu* means "to desire.

One who has desired, desires, or will desire the Dhamma is a person who "desires the Dhamma" (*dhammakāmo*); a maiden who desires the Dhamma is *dhammakāmā*; a mind that desires the Dhamma is *dhammakāmaṃ*. Likewise:

one who desires welfare (*atthakāmo*), one who desires benefit (*hitakāmo*), one who desires happiness (*sukhakāmo*); and one who protects the Dhamma is a "guardian of the Dhamma" (*dhammapālo*), and so on.

In *damu damane*, regarding the analysis (*viggaha*) as "I have subdued the enemy," "he subdues," or "he will subdue," the governing rule is "after a verbal root" (*dhātuyā*); furthermore, the phrase "at the beginning [of an object, etc. (*kammādimhi*) is understood to carry over.
565. *Saññāyamanu*.

When an object (*kamma*) is present at the beginning as an accompanying word (*upapada*), provided that a name (*saññā*) is implied, the suffix *a* (*appaccaya*) occurs after the verbal root, [the accompanying word] being placed at the end.

And there is the augment *nu*. Furthermore, in this context, because of the statement "the nasal *niggahīta* [is inserted] at the end of a word" (*nu niggahītaṃ padante*) in the sutta, it should be understood that the augment *nu* occurs only when [the word] ends in a word-base (*upapada*).
By the rule beginning with "among those, [there is] vowel-lengthening" (*tesu vuddhi*), there is the elision of the letter *u*.
However, it should be known that this augment *nu* occurs only after the compound has been formed and the case-ending of the subordinate word (*upapada-vibhatti*) has been elided.
566. Now, regarding the *niggahīta* at the end of a word:

the augment *nu*-kāra occurring at the end of a noun that functions as an upapada undergoes the state of *niggahīta*; for *niggahīta*, the rule of being the final letter of its respective class (*vagga*) applies. The rest is the same; the only distinction is the absence of vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), as in *arindamo rājā*.

Likewise, from the root *tara* (to cross), one who crosses over the world of commoners (*vessa*) is *Vessantara*. The Blessed One is *Taṇhaṅkaro* because he effects the destruction of craving (*taṇhaṃ karoti hiṃsati*). Similarly: *Medhaṅkaro*, *Saraṇaṅkaro*, *Dīpaṅkaro*.
The [term] "ādimhi, a" also recurs [from the previous rule]. 567. Regarding *pura* and *dadā*:
when the word *pura* occurs at the beginning, the suffix *a* is applied to the root *dad* (in the sense of "giving"), and the vowel *a* of the word *pura* [is elided].

And here it is so. Furthermore, in this context, according to the grammatical rule (*paribhāsa*), it should be understood that the substitution *iṃ* occurs only for the final syllable of the word *pura* in the expression "without obstructing that" (*tadanuparodhena*).

Although the suffixes beginning with *ṇ* (such as *ṇvu*) pertain to all three times, it should be understood that this primary suffix (*appaccaya*) occurs only in the past tense due to the specific meaning of the accompanying word (*upapada*). For example:
"He gave a gift formerly" (*pure dānam adadī*) is *purindada*, [an epithet of] Sakka. Here too, the substitution *iṃ* occurs only after the case ending has been elided.
The phrase “after *kamma* and so forth, *a*” is understood [from the previous rule]. 568.

After every [verbal] root (*dhātu*), when there is an object (*sakamma*) or no object (*akamma*), the four suffixes *ṇvu*, *tu*, *āvi*, and *vā* optionally occur. The inclusion of the word “optionally” (*vā*) is for the purpose of providing an alternative, namely that it may also occur when there is no object.
First, regarding the secondary suffix (*appaccaya*): *dhara* means "to hold. One who has held the Dhamma, holds it, or will hold it is a *dhammadhara*.
Likewise, one who has held the Vinaya is a *vinayadhara*. Similarly, one who does that [action] is a *takkara*; there is a doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*). Thus:
*hitakara*, *divasakara*, *dinakara*, *divākara*, *nisākara*. One who takes a bow is a *dhanuggaha*. Likewise: *kaṭaggaha*, *sabbakāma*.
“He gives” means he is a giver of all desires, a giver of everything.
Furthermore, from the root *ā*: “he gave food, he gives, he will give” is *annada* (giver of food). Likewise, *dhanada* (giver of wealth). From *sandahati* (“he connects”):

*saccasandha* (one who is true to his word). From *pā* (“to drink”): “he drinks liquor” is *majjapa* (drinker of liquor). From *tā* (“to protect”): “he protects the sound of cows” is *gotta* (clan). Thus [the suffixes] are used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).

Furthermore, regarding *akammādi* (non-objective, etc.): because of the inclusion of the word "fear" (*bhaya*) in the Sutta rule "because it causes one to obtain," the suffix *ap* is applied even to other instruments.
*Nī* in the sense of "reaching," preceded by *vi-*: from *vinesī*, *vineti*, and *vinessati*; [the term] *vinaya* means "by this" or "in this.

By the rule "and in others," there is vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*) and the substitution of *ay*. *Naya* means "leading. *Si* in the sense of "service," preceded by *ni-*: from *nissīyittha*, *nissīyati*.
Or, "it will lean out" (nissīyissati) is *nissaya*. Or, "it lies down" (*si*), "it has lain down" (*anusayi*), "it lies down" (*anuseti*), or "it will lie down" (*anusessati*) is *anusaya*.

The root *i* in the sense of "going," preceded by *paṭi*, [means] that which attains its fruit depending on one [thing]; thus it is *paccaya* (condition). It is *samudaya* (origin). The root *ci* in the sense of "accumulation":
that by which something is determined, or the act of determining, is *vinicchaya*; the act of heaping up is *uccaya*, as is *sañcaya*. One who discerns the Dhamma is [a *viniścāyaka*].

*Dhammavicaya*: *dhamma-vicaya*. *Khī* means destruction (*khaye*); the act of destroying is *khayo*. *Ji* means to conquer (*jaye*); the act of conquering is *vijayo*, or simply *jayo*. *Kī* means bartering goods (*dabbavinimaye*);

the act of selling is *vikkayo*, or *kayo*. *Lī* means clinging (*silesane*); that to which one clings is *ālayo*, or *layo*. Thus [the forms] ending in the vowel *i*. They obey (*āsuṇanti*), thus they are *assavā*; there is a substitution of *ava* for *su*.
The act of listening back is *paṭissavo*. *Su* means to go (*gatimhi*); they flow up to the peak of existence (*ābhavaggā*), thus [they are *savā*].
*Āsavā*. *Ru* means sound; it resounds, thus it is *ravo* (noise). It comes into being, thus it is *bhavo* (existence). It originates from this, thus it is *pabhavo* (source).
*Lū* means cutting; the act of cutting is *lavo*. Thus [the suffix] *-ava* is added.
*Niggaṇhāti*, or the act of restraining, is *niggaho* (restraint); *paggaho* (exertion); by means of it one gathers together, or the act of gathering is *saṅgaho* (inclusion).
*Vara* means choosing; *saṃvaraṇaṃ* (restraining) is *saṃvaro* (restraint). *Dara* means respect; *ādaraṇaṃ* (honoring) is *ādaro* (respect).
It comes, or it is coming, thus it is *āgamo*; or, they come here by means of this, or the meaning is obtained through this, thus *āgamo* is the *pariyatti* (the sacred scriptures).
It hisses, thus it is *sappo* (a snake). He shines, thus he is *devo* (a god). *Kamu* means to step; stepping forth is *pakkamanaṃ*, or he steps forth, thus it is *pakkamo*. Likewise with *vikkamo*.

One who moves in the forest (*vana*) is a forest-dweller (*vanacara*). That world where desire (*kāma*) moves about is the sense-sphere world (*kāmāvacara-loka*); likewise, there is sense-sphere perception (*kāmāvacara-saññā*) and sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*). That wherein cattle move is a pasture (*gocara*); this is a genitive *tappurisa* compound.
That which drinks with its foot is a tree (*pādapa*). Similarly, "tortoise" (*kacchapa*) is a third-case *tappurisa* compound.
From the root *ruha* (to grow), that which grows on the head is hair (*siroruha*); that which lies in a cave is a mind dwelling in a cave (*guhāsaya*). Thus.

The winds dwell in the belly (*kucchisaya*). The word *aṭṭha* [is used] in the sense of "stopping from motion" (*gatinivatti*): a man who stands on a mountain is called "one standing on a mountain" (*pabbataṭṭha*), as are "a river standing on a mountain" (*pabbataṭṭhā nadī*) and "a medicinal herb standing on a mountain" (*pabbataṭṭhaṃ osadhaṃ*).
Likewise, there are "land-dwellers" (*thalaṭṭhaṃ*) and "water-dwellers" (*jalaṭṭhaṃ*); these are seventh-case tappurisa compounds. 569.
[The suffix -ka is added] optionally after the word *gaha* when it follows [another word].

Regarding this element *gaha*, there is the form *upadha*. The term *upadha* is a designation for the vowel preceding the final consonant. That which is grasped (*gahati*) is a *geha* or *gaha*. With the suffix *ṇvu*:

in the sense of "one who makes a chariot" (*rathaṃ karoti*), the suffix *ṇvu* is applied; and because it is designated as *kita* by the rule "others are *kita*," it occurs in the sense of the agent according to the rule "the *kita* [suffixes] denote the agent. Thereafter, the causative designation, the elision of *ṇ*, and the vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) occur.
570. After vowels, [the suffixes] *yu*, *ṇu*, and *ūna* [are applied].

Since these suffixes (*paccaya*) are added after the [root] *yuṇ*, these substitutions (*ādesa*) occur; thus, there is the substitution of the letter *a*. The remainder is the same as in the word *kumbhakāra*:
*rathakāraka* (a chariot-maker). Likewise, one who gives food is *annadāyaka*; here, by the rule "for those ending in long *ā*, the suffix *āya*," there is the substitution of *āya*.

Then, by the rule "in the feminine, the suffix *ā* follows [the stem] ending in *a*," the suffix *ā* is added. By the rule beginning with "among those, the vowel is increased," the letter *a* becomes *i*, resulting in *annadāyikā* (a girl who gives food), and *annadāyakaṃ* (that which gives food).

A family (*kula*). One who leads the world is a "Leader of the World" (*lokanāyaka*); one who disciplines beings is a "Guide" (*vināyaka*), with the substitution of *ā* for *e* according to the rule "those [stems] ending in *ā* are used.

One who performs an action when there is no accompanying object is an "agent" (*kāraka*), "female agent" (*kārikā*), or "instrumental agent" (*kārakaṃ*). One who gives is a "giver" (*dāyaka*), "female giver" (*dāyikā*), or "instrumental giver" (*dāyakaṃ*).
One who leads is a "leader" (*nāyaka*), "female leader" (*nāyikā*), or "instrumental leader" (*nāyakaṃ*). He has heard, hears, or will hear the instruction and admonition of the Blessed One.

Or [the forms] *sāvako* (disciple), *sāvikā* (female disciple) are examples of the suffix *-aka*. One who cuts is a *lāvako*. The root *pu* means to purify; one who purifies is a *pāvako*; one who exists is a *bhāvako*;
one who worships is an *upāsako*, [and] *upāsikā*. One who takes is a *gāhako*. One who cooks is a *pācako*.
One who has sacrificed, sacrifices, or will sacrifice is a *yājako*. For here, by the rule "for *ca* and *ja*, *ka* and *ga*," since *ca* and *ja* have attained the state of *ka* and *ga*—
571. *Na kagattaṃ cajā ṇvumhi*.

When the suffix *ṇvu* follows, the letters *ca* and *ja*, when they constitute the final element of a verbal root (*dhātu*), do not undergo the change to *ka* and *ga*. This does not occur because it is prohibited by the rule [stating that] *ṇvu* is added.

From the root *jana* (to be born), *janetīti janako* (he causes to be born, thus "progenitor"), and *janikā*. By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule "or for *ghaṭa* etc.," there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*).
It does not exist. One who digs is a *khanaka*; one who brings together is a *samaka*;

one who goes is a *gamaka*; one who tames is a *damaka*. One who has killed, kills, or will kill is a *vadhaka*; in the sense of "killing everywhere," there is a substitution of *vadha* for *hana*. One who strikes is a *yātaka*;
in the sense of "the killing of *hana*," there is a substitution of *ghāta* when the suffix *ṇvu* is present. One who kills cows is a *goghātaka*. One who obstructs is a *rundhaka*.

There is the insertion of *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and because it ends in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). Thus: one who eats is a *bhuñjaka*; one who buys is a *kāyaka*;

one who protects is a *pālaka*; one who worships is a *pūjaka*. 572. From the roots *nud* and others, the suffixes *yu*, *ṇvu*, *mana*, *ana*, *na*, *ka*, *ana*, and *ka* are added, as well as those with the sense of causing action (*sakārita*).

After roots beginning with *nud* and after roots that take the *sakārita* (causative) suffix, the affixes *yu* and *vuṇ* undergo, respectively, the following substitutions: *ana*, *āna*, *ana*, *ānana*, and *akanaka*.
For here, because the grammatical operation is prescribed for the *yu* and *vuṇ* affixes after those [roots] that take the *sakārita* suffix—
The state of being a "doer" (kattṛ) is also to be understood through verbal roots (dhātu) and suffixes (paccaya).

In the sense of "to push away," "to expel," with the prefix *pa-*—as in *panudi*, *panudati*, or *panudissati*—there is the suffix *ṇvu*. By this [suffix], there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel [of the root]; by the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātū," there is lengthening of the vowel in *nud*, resulting in *panūdaka*.

*Sūd* in the sense of "to flow"—as in *sūdati*—results in *sūdaka*. *Ñā* in the sense of "to understand"—as in *aññāsi*, *jānāti*, or *jānissati*—takes the suffix *ṇvu*. By this [suffix], there is the substitution of *āna* for the vowel; by the rule "ñāssa jā jaṃ nā," there is the substitution of *jā*; and following the elision of *sa-ra*, etc., it becomes *jānanaka*.

Furthermore, regarding the causative (*sakārita*) forms used in the sense of commanding or sending forth—such as *āṇāpesi*, *āṇāpeti*, or *āṇāpessati*—the suffix *ṇvu* is applied by the rule “*sabbato ṇvutvāvī vā*”.

In this case, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the suffix-initial *n*, there is elision of the preceding vowel (*saralopa*), and so on, resulting in *āṇāpaka*. Similarly, from *saññāpeti* comes *saññāpaka*, meaning "one who causes to perceive" or "one who makes known";
here, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the suffix-initial *n*, and the causative suffix is dropped according to the rule “*kvaci dhātū*” and so forth. Likewise, from *dāpeti* comes *dāpaka*.

In the word *anaka*, there is the substitution of *a* for *yu*. One who establishes is an *patiṭṭhāpaka*; one who causes [others] to reach Nibbāna is a *nibbānasampāpaka*; one who causes to do is a *kārāpaka*;
likewise, a female agent is a *kārāpikā*, and so forth. Regarding the suffix *tu*:

in the sense of "he did," "he does," or "he will do," the suffix *tu* is applied by the rule "after all [roots], *ṇvu* or *tu*. Because it is designated as *kita*, this *tu* suffix functions in all instances as the agentive (*kattari*) suffix, just like the suffix *ṇvu*.
“*Anta*” is understood [from the previous rule]. 573.
*Kara* also becomes *tatta* before the suffix *tu*.
The letter *r* at the end of this root *kara* becomes the letter *t* when the suffix *tu* follows. By the word *ca* (also),...

And in the case of *bharādi* (the roots beginning with *bhṛ*), from that [root] there is the arising of the *syādi* suffixes as if it were a noun (*nāma*). According to the rule, “In the case of *satthu*, *pitā*, etc., there is elision (*silopa*) of the *ā* in the locative (*āsismiṃ*),” there is elision of the *ā*.
[Thus: *tassa kattā* = *takattā*; this is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). Likewise, he supports (*bharati*) is *bhattā*.

From the root *hṛ* in the sense of taking away (*haraṇe*), he takes away (*harati*) is *hattā*. He breaks (*bhindati*) is *bhettā*, or *bheditā*. He cuts (*chindati*) is *chettā*. He gives (*dadāti*) is...
A giver (*dātā*); one who has the nature of giving food is a "giver of food" (*bhojanadātā*); one who joins together (*sandahati*) is a "connector" (*sandhātā*);

one who has spoken, speaks, or will speak is a "speaker" (*vattā*), with the elision of the final root-vowel and the doubling of the consonant according to the rule: "for *bhuj* and others, the final [consonant] is not doubled. One who eats is an "eater" (*bhottā*).

One who has awakened, awakens, or will awaken is an "awakened one" (*bujjhitā*), with the addition of the vowels *ya* and *i*. One who knows is a "knower" (*ñātā*). One who conquers is... [a conqueror] (*jinātīti*).
One who conquers is a *jetā*; one who hears is a *sotā*; one who grasps is a *gahetā*; one who becomes is a *bhavitā*; one who remembers is a *saritā*; one who goes is a *gantā*.

According to the rule, “In the case of the suffixes *tuṃ*, *tabba*, and so forth, there is no substitution of *n* for the final letter of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, and *han*,” the final letter of the root undergoes this change.
Thus: one who digs is a *khantā*; one who kills is a *hantā*; one who thinks is a *mantā*; one who protects is a *pāletā* or *pālayitā*.

One who causes [something] to be made and develops it is a *bhāvetā*, that is, a developer (*bhāvayitā*). Likewise: one who causes to remember is a *sāretā*, a causer to remember (*sārayitā*); one who causes to give is a *dāpetā*, a causer to give (*dāpayitā*); one who causes to abandon is a *hāpetā*, a causer to abandon (*hāpayitā*);

one who causes cessation is a *nirodhetā*, a causer of cessation (*nirodhayitā*); one who causes awakening is a *bodhetā*, a causer of awakening (*bodhayitā*); one who causes to know is a *ñāpetā*, a causer to know (*ñāpayitā*); one who causes to hear is a *sāvetā*, a causer to hear (*sāvayitā*);

one who causes to enter is a *gāhetā*, a causer to enter (*gāhayitā*); one who causes to make is a *kāretā*, a causer to make (*kārayitā*); one who causes to have made is a *kārāpetā*, a causer to have made (*kārāpayitā*)—and so forth.

The suffix *āvī* occurs in the sense of "seeing fear" (*bhayaṃ apassi*, *passati*, or *passissati*). According to the rule "in some cases, [the root] *dis* [is replaced]," the root *dis* is replaced by *dass*.
Thus, one forms *bhayadassāvī* (one who sees fear) and *bhayadassāvino* (those who see fear), which should be understood in the same way as *daṇḍī* (a staff-bearer).
In the feminine, it is *bhayadassāvinī*; in the neuter, *bhayadassāvi cittaṃ* (a mind that sees fear).
Regarding the meaning "he instructs the world together with its devas by way of matters pertaining to the present life and so forth" in the word *sāsati*:
574. *Sāsādīhi ratthu*.
The suffix *ratthu* occurs after verbal roots such as *sāsa* and others.

In the phrase “*ramhi ranto rādi no*,” there is the elision of *rādi*, followed by the elision of the vowel (*saralopādi*), the designation as a noun (*nāmabyapadeso*), the arising of the case endings beginning with *-si* (*syādyuppatti*), the substitution of *ā* (*āttaṃ*), and the elision of the suffix (*silopo*). Thus: *satthā*, *satthāro*.
In the sense of "protecting" (*pā rakkhaṇe*), in the meaning "he protects his son" (*puttaṃ pātīti*), [the rule] 575 applies: *pādito ritu*.

From the group of roots beginning with *pā*, the suffix *ritu* occurs; there is elision of the initial *r*, as well as the elision of vowels (*saralopa*), and so forth. *Pitā*. From the root *dhṛ* (in the sense of "bearing"), [the word] *dhītā* ("daughter") is derived, meaning "she who is borne by the mother and father"; the long vowel for the letter *i* is applied according to the rule "sometimes from roots" (*kvaci dhātū*), etc.
From the root *mān* (in the sense of "honoring"), in the sense of "he honors his son according to the Dhamma"—576.
The suffix *rātu* is added after *mān* and others.

The suffix *rā* occurs after verbal roots such as *mā* and *bhās*; there is elision of the *r*, resulting in *mātā*. The root *bhās* is used in the sense of distinct speech; one who spoke before is called *bhātā*, and so forth.
With the prefix *pa-* added to *vis* in the sense of "entering"—as in *pāvisi*, *pavisati*, or *pavisissati*—[the following rule applies]:
577. After the roots *vis* and *ruj*, and others, the suffix *ṇa* is applied.

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after verbal roots such as *visa*, *ruja*, and others; thus it is called the *ṇa*-suffix. Because it is designated as *kit*, it applies to the agent (*kattari*). [In this case, there is] the designation of the causative (*kārita*), the elision of the suffix *ana*, and the *vṛddhi* strengthening.

[Thus we have] *paveso*. Likewise, from the root *ruja* in the sense of "afflicting," we have *aruji*, *rujati*, or *rujissati*—meaning "disease. By the rule "the substitution of *ga* for *ja* after *ka* and *ga*," the letter *ja* becomes *ga*. From the root *uppajj* in the sense of "arising," we have *uppādo*.
From the root *phusa* in the sense of "touching," we have *aphusi*, *phusati*, *phusissati*, or *phusanti* by means of that [suffix].

“Associated” (*sampayutta*) refers to contact (*phassa*); by the rule beginning with “in some cases *dhātu*,” the *u* of *phusa* becomes *o*, and because it is a terminal *saṃyoga*, there is no lengthening (*vuddhi*).

It exists, thus it is “being” (*bhāva*). The root *uc* means to assemble; that which assembles is a “dwelling” (*oka*), where the letter *c* becomes *k*. The root *aya* means to go: from *ayi*, *ayati*, *ayissati*, or *ayati vā iti*, it is “coming” (*āya*).
The root *budh* means to understand; one who perfectly awakens is “perfect awakening” (*sambodha*). That which brings forth is... [the text continues].
*Āhāra*; it destroys, thus it is *upaghāta*. In the case of *hana*, there is the substitution of *ghāta* according to the rule "of *hana*, *ghāta*.
*Ranja* means "in passion"; the suffix *ṇa* is applied in the sense of "one who colors" (*ranjati*).
578. A nasal (*niggahīta*) [is dropped] when it is the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).

In a conjunct, the letter *n* becomes *niggahīta* (the nasal stop). The *niggahīta* becomes the final consonant of its respective class (*vagganta*); for the letter *j*, it becomes *g*. 579. When the suffix *ṇa* follows the root *ranj* in the senses of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), the *j* at the end of this root is replaced by *j*.
That is, when the suffix *ṇa* is prescribed after the root *ranj* in the meanings of the abstract noun or the instrument, the *j* at the end of that root undergoes substitution with *j*.
For here: because the substitution of *ja* for the root *rañj* is prescribed after the suffix *ṇam*,
it should be understood that the suffix *ṇa* can occur even when there is no agent (*akartari*), since its possibility exists within the category of grammatical factors (*kārake*).
*Rāga* is so called because one is colored by it (*rañjati anena*), or because one is colored by means of it (*rañjīyati anena*), or because it itself colors (*sayaṃ rañjati*).

The letter *ja* [in place of *na*] occurs through the rule of grammatical division (*yogavibhāga*) stating: "In the suffix *ṇam*, there is *ja* for *ranj*. *Pāda* is so called because one goes by means of it (*pajjati anena*); *patoda* because one drives with it (*patujjati anena*); *jāra* because one ages by means of it (*jarīyati anena*).
Likewise is *dāra*. Similarly, in the case of *kamma* and so forth: *bhoga* because one enjoys it (*bhujjati*). Thus also is *bhāga*.

It is a burden (*bhāra*); it is obtained, thus it is gain (*lābha*); it is expressed in common usage, thus it is usage (*vohāra*); it is given, thus it is a gift (*dāya*); one is afflicted by this, thus it is affliction (*vighāta*);

they dwell in this, thus it is a dwelling (*vihāra*); they delight in this, thus it is a pleasure grove (*ārāma*). In this way, [the suffixes apply] after *papāta*, etc. The term "Ṇa" is understood [as a governing rule].

580. *Bhāve ca*. The suffix *ṇa* occurs after verbal roots when the sense is that of an abstract state (*bhāva*), that is, when an abstract state is to be expressed. For example: from *bhū*, "to be," we have *bhūyate* (it is being) or *bhavanaṃ* (the act of being), which is *bhāva*; from *pac*, "to cook," we have *paccate* (it is cooked) or *pacanaṃ* (the act of cooking), which is *pāka*.

[In this last case,] by the rule "for *ca* and *ja*, there is *ka*," there is the substitution of *ka* for *ja*. From *sic*, "to pour," we have *secanam* (the act of pouring), which is *seka*. From *suc*, "to grieve," we have *socanam* (the act of grieving), which is *soka*. From *caj*, "to abandon," [we have] *acajjittha* (he abandoned).

*Ca* means to abandon; [the forms] *cajjate*, *cajjissate*, or the act of abandoning (*cajana*) is relinquishment (*cāga*). *Yaja* is used in the senses of worshiping deities, forming associations, and giving;
[the forms] *ijjittha*, *ijjate*, *ijjissate*, or the act of sacrificing (*yajana*) is sacrifice (*yāga*). *Yuñjana* is application (*yoga*). *Bhaja* means to serve;

[the forms] *abhajjittha*, *bhajjate*, *bhajjissate*, or the act of serving (*bhajana*) is a portion (*bhāga*). *Arajjittha*, *rajjate*, *rajjissate*, or the act of coloring (*rajana*) is passion (*rāga*); in this case, the letter *g* is replaced by *j*.
In the sense of "furthermore," "having been burnt," "was burnt," "is being burnt," "will be burnt," or "the act of burning," the suffix *ṇa* is applied.
The phrase "and [the rule] 'before *ṇa*, optionally'" also continues to apply.
581. For the root *dah*, *da* becomes *la*.

Furthermore, the letter *da* of this root *daha* becomes *la* when followed by the suffix *ṇa*. Thus: *pariḷāho*, *paridāho*. From the root *bhanja* in the sense of crushing: *bhañjanaṃ*, *bhaṅgo*. From the root *sanja* in the sense of clinging: *sañjanaṃ*, *saṅgo*; here the nasal (*n*) is elided.

In the sense of "that which is produced by coming together with conditions" or "that by which one is conditioned," the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "after *visaruj*, *pada*, etc. or by the rule "also in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*)," resulting in *saṅkhāraṇaṃ*.
The phrase "when *ṇa* follows" is understood to carry over.
582. *Pura*, *saṃ*, *upa*, and *pari*: these [prefixes] optionally become the substitutes *kha* and *khara* for the root *karoti* when followed by a *tappaccaya* or a *ṇappaccaya*.
By the use of the plural form in the phrase "in *tappaccayas*," it is indicated that this also applies to suffixes such as *tuṃ* and *tvā*.

Because even a substitute for a root (dhātu-ādesa) is designated as a "root" through metaphorical application to its original place, there is a *vuddhi* [vowel strengthening] according to the rule “*asaṃyogantassa vuddhi kārite*” [“there is *vuddhi* for a non-conjunct final before a *kārita* suffix”];
thus, *saṅkhāra*. Likewise, *parikkhāra* and *purekkhāra*. Why [is it] said “or” (*vā*)?
[To exclude: *upakāra*.
*Lobha* (greed): it is greed because one is greedy for gain, or because one is greedy by means of it, or because one is oneself greedy, or because it is merely the state of being greedy;

thus it is greed. *Dosa* (hatred): it is hatred because one hates through lack of affection, or because one hates by means of it, or because one is oneself hateful, or because it is merely the state of being hateful;

thus it is hatred. *Moha* (delusion): it is delusion because one is deluded by way of mental confusion, or because one is deluded by means of it, or because one is oneself deluded, or because it is merely the state of being deluded; and so forth.
This should be applied appropriately to the states of the agent and the instrument.
[In the word *gaha*: the root *gah* means "to be grasped"; by the rule beginning with *visarujapadādi*, the suffix *ṇa* is added in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
583. For *gaha*, there is the substitution of *ghara* or the suffix *ṇe*.

The substitution of *ghara* for the root *gah* optionally occurs before the suffix *ṇa*, with the elision of the vowel *a* and so forth; thus, *gharaṃ* (a house) and *gharāni* (houses). Why "optionally"?
[Because otherwise it would be] *gaṇhāti* (he takes), *gahaṇaṃ* (taking), or *gāho* (grasping).
In the sense of "it arises": [the following applies].
584. *Kvi ca*.
The suffix *kvip* occurs after all verbal roots (*dhātu*); and because it is designated as *kit*, it functions in the sense of the agent (*kattṛ*). 585.
*Kvilopa ca*. And there is the elision (*lopa*) of *kvip*.

There is the elision of the final syllable of *kvip*. Having treated it as a noun because it ends in *kit*, the case endings (*syādi*) arise; then there is the elision of the suffix (*silopa*), resulting in *sambhū*. Likewise, from *vibhavati* comes *vibhū*; from *abhibhavati*, *abhibhū*; and from *sayambhavati*, *sayambhū*.

Similarly, from *dhū* in the sense of "shaking," *sandhunāti* becomes *sandhū*. From *bhā* in the sense of "splendor": *vibhāti* becomes *vibhā*; *pabhāti* becomes *pabhā*. Regarding *sabhā*: [it is derived from] *saṅgamma* (coming together) or *bhanti* (they shine) or *bhāsanti* (they speak) *ettha* (here); thus *sabhā*. There is the substitution of *sa* for *saha*, and the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
In the sense of "going by means of the arms" (*bhujena gacchati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied.
586. Elision of the final of a verbal root before *kvip*.
When the suffix *kvip* follows, there is elision of the consonant at the end of a verbal root. [Examples of] the elision of *kvip*: *bhujaga* (a snake).
Likewise, "that which moves on its breast" is *uraga*; "that which moves swiftly and rapidly" is *turaga*; "that which moves in the sky" is *khaga*.
It goes through the sky (*vihāyas*), thus it is a *vihaga* (bird); there is a substitution of *vi* for *vihā*. It does not go, thus it is *ago*;

[with the prefix *na-*] it is *nago* (a mountain). The root *khanu* means "to determine" when preceded by the prefix *sam-*: it is a *saṅkhani*, or it is called a *saṅkha* because it scratches (*saṅkhanati*) or it will scratch (*saṅkhanissati*).

The root *ramu* means "in play": it delights in a thicket (*kuñja*), thus it is a *kuñjara* (elephant). The root *jana* means "birth": in the sense of "born from an action," the suffix *kvip* is applied; [there is] the end of the verbal root...

The elision (*lopādi*) and so forth are the same as in the previous [compound]; the distinction is that it is a *pañcamī-tappurisa* (genitive determinative compound). "Born of karma" (*kammaja*), "rebirth-linking born of karma" (*kammajā paṭisandhi*), "matter born of karma" (*kammajaṃ rūpaṃ*).
Likewise: "mind-born" (*cittaja*), "element-born" (*utuja*), "nutriment-born" (*āhāraja*), "self-born son" (*attajo putto*). "Born in water" (*vārimhi jāto vārijo*). Likewise:

"land-born" (*thalajo*), "mud-born" (*paṅkajaṃ*), "water-born" (*jalajaṃ*), "egg-born" (*aṇḍajaṃ*), "head-born" (*sirajaṃ*). These are locative compounds (*sattamī-samāsa*). "Born twice" (*dvikkhattuṃ jāto*).
“Dvijo,” “pacchājāto,” “anujo,” and so forth.
The root *vid* means “to know”; in the sense of “he knew the world” (*lokaṃ avedī*), there is the *kvip* suffix.
The word “in *kvip*” (*kvimhi*) is supplied [from the previous rule].
587. *Vidante ū*.
The vowel *ū* is added as an augment (*āgama*) after the root *vid*, when the suffix *kvip* follows; there is elision of *kvip*. [Thus: *lokavidū* (knower of the world).
[The root] *dis* means "to see. In the sense of "he saw him as this," "he sees him," "he will see him," or "he is seen like this," the suffix *kvip* is applied.

When the elision of the final vowel of the verbal root (dhātu) is reached by the rule “*Dhātvantassa lopo kvimhī*” [the final vowel of the root is dropped before the suffix *kvim*], [the following applies]:

**588.** For the pronouns *ima*, *ya*, *ta*, *amha*, *kiṃ*, and *eta*, when they function as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or a subordinate term (*upapada*), the final vowel of the word *disa* [“direction”] becomes long in some instances;

furthermore, the substitution of *guṇa* for *disa* occurs, and *raṃ* is substituted for *sakkhi*. [Thus, from the words *ima*, *ya*, *ta*, *amha*, *kiṃ*, and *eta*—all being pronouns (*sabbanāma*)—acting as a standard of comparison or a subordinate term, the word *disa* undergoes these changes.]
In the case of the word *dhātu*, the vowel at the end becomes long; furthermore, for the final syllable of this word *dhātu*, the substitutions *sa*, *kha*, and *ī* occur.

Regarding the rule "the letter *da* of the word *disa* becomes *ra*," having applied the substitution of *sasadda* for the end of the verbal root (*dhātu*) when the suffix *kvim* follows, and having performed the elision of *kvim* and so forth, by means of the grammatical injunction (*nipātana*), the letter *i* of the word *ima* is replaced by *ī*; and by the rule *tassiminā*...
And when the vowel *i* is lengthened, there is the arising of the suffix *yya*:

"such a man," "such a girl," or "such [a thing]," "such a mind. Likewise, "as one sees him" or "as he is seen" is *yādiso*, *yādisā*, *yādisī*, *yādisaṃ*. "As one sees him" or "as he is seen" is likewise [expressed by these forms].
*Vā tādiso*, *tādisā*, *tādisī*, *tādisaṃ*. Or, "he sees him as like me" or "he is seen as like me," thus *mādiso*, *mādisā*, *mādisī*, *mādisaṃ*;
here, by means of the grammatical rule of substitution (*nipātana*), the word *amha* is replaced by *ma*.
Or, "how does he see him? or "how is he seen?"—thus *kīdiso*, *kīdisā*, *kīdisī*, *kīdisaṃ*. Or, "he sees him as like this"—thus *etamiva naṃ passati*.

*Ediso* or *etādiso* means "it is seen as such" (*eso viya dissati*). In the forms *edisā*, *edisī*, and *edisaṃ*, the vowel *e* replaces the word *eta* by means of a grammatical substitution (*nipātana*).
*Sādiso* means "he sees it as equal" (*samānaṃ katvā naṃ passati*) or "it is seen as equal" (*samāno viya dissati*).

In the forms *sādisā*, *sādisī*, *sadisā*, *sadisī*, *sādisaṃ*, and *sadisaṃ*, the substitute *sā-* replaces *samāna* by means of a grammatical substitution (*nipātana*), or there is a lengthening of the final vowel of that which ends in *-ta*. Thus we have *sādisā*, *sādisī*, *sadisā*, *sadisī*, *sādisaṃ*, and *sadisaṃ*.
When there is the substitution of *ra* for *da*, [the forms are]: *īriso*, *yāriso*, *tāriso*, *māriso*, *kīriso*, *eriso*, *sāriso*, *sariso*.
When there is the substitution of *kkha*, [the forms are]: *īdikkho*, *yādikkho*, *tādikkho*, *mādikkho*, *kīdikkho*, *edikkho*, *sādikkho*, *sadikkho*.
When there is the substitution of *ra*, [the forms are]: *sārikkho*, *sarikkho*. When there is the substitution of *ī*, [the forms are]: *īdī*, *yādī*, *tādī*, *mādī*, *kīdī*, *edī*, *sādī*.

By means of the suffix *sad*, even when there is an upapada such as *tumha* (you), it is seen as *tumhe* (you); thus, one who is like you is *tumhādiso* or *tumhādisī*. Because the aggregates (*khandhā*) are seen as if they were [like] you, they are called *khandhādisā*, and so forth.

In the sense of "to hold" (*dhara dhāraṇe*): it holds beings who have not fallen into the states of misery (*apāya*), such as those who have attained the Path; or, by which [beings] are held; or, it holds its own characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*); or, it is held by conditions—in these senses, from the root *dhara* etc., the word *ramma* [is derived]. 589. From *dhara* etc., *ramma*.
The suffix *ramma* occurs after verbal roots such as *dhāra* and others. And that [suffix]—
it should be understood here— that it is used in the sense of the agent (*kattar*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the state (*bhāva*), and the object (*kamma*).
"Akattaripi hoti" means that the suffix -amman occurs after a verb root (*kāra*).
There is the elision of the *r* and so forth, resulting in *dhamma*. That which is thus performed is "action" (*kamma*).

From the root *vara* in the sense of warding off, we have *vamma*. The root *saṃsa* in the sense of praising is preceded by *pa*; with *piya* as the subordinate term (*upapada*), it means "one whose nature is to praise what is dear," or "one whose nature is to praise the dear," or "one who is skillful in praising the dear"—such are the meanings.
590. *Tassīlādīsu ṇī tvā vī ca*. "Sīla" means natural disposition (*pakati*).

When the senses of "having that as one's disposition," "having that as one's nature," or "practicing that well" are implied, the suffixes *ṇī*, *tu*, and *āvī* occur after all verbal roots. Thus, the suffix *ṇī* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). Because it ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoganta*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening.

The rest is to be understood accordingly. [Example: *piyapasaṃsī rājā* (the king who praises what is dear). Alternatively, one who by way of disposition (*sīlena*) or by way of nature (*dhammena*) has praised, praises, or will praise what is dear.
Or: one who praises what is dear is a *piyapasaṃsī*, a *piyapasaṃsinī*, or a *piyapasaṃsi* family. Or:
one whose conduct (*sīla*) is the holy life (*brahma*) is a *brahmacārī*, a *brahmacārinī*, or a *brahmacāri*; that is, one who lives the holy life through virtue and through the Dhamma. Likewise:
a speaker of truth (*saccavādī*), a speaker of Dhamma (*dhammavādī*), one who goes quickly (*sīghayāyī*), an evildoer (*pāpakārī*), a garland-maker (*mālākārī*), and so forth.
By means of the suffix *adda*, there is also the form *mānī*. One who considers himself wise is "wise-conceited" (*paṇḍitamānī*); likewise, "learned-conceited" (*bāhusstutamānī*), and so forth.
The root *vat* (to speak) is preceded by *pa*; in the sense of "one whose nature it is to proceed by force," the suffix *tu* is applied by this rule, resulting in *pasayhapavattā*.

Alternatively, from the root *vac* (to speak articulately), in the sense of "one whose nature it is to proceed by force," the suffix *tu* is applied, resulting in *pasayhapavattā* (singular) or *pasayhapavattāro* (plural).
The suffixes -ita, -anta, -lopa, and -dvitta [are applied] after the root *bhuj*; the remainder is the same as for the agent (*kattu*).

Alternatively, one whose nature (*sīla*) it is to see fear is "one who sees fear" (*bhayadassana-sīla*); or one whose characteristic (*dhamma*) is to see fear; or one who is skilled (*sādhukārī*) in seeing fear—thus one is "one who sees fear" (*bhayadassāvī*), feminine *bhayadassāvinī*, and neuter *bhayadassāvi cittaṃ*. Likewise for "one who sees danger" (*ādīnavadassāvī*). The governing rule is:
"In the sense of 'having that as one's nature' (*tassīlādīsu*)."

591. *Yu* [is the suffix] after verbal roots meaning sound (*sadda*), calling (*kūta*), shaking (*dhuta*), moving (*cala*), ornamenting (*maṇḍa*), and after those beginning with *ruca* (to shine), in the sense of habit (*tassīla*) and so forth.

After verbal roots having the meanings of sound, calling, shaking, moving, and ornamenting, as well as those beginning with *ruca*, the suffix *yu* occurs in the senses of habit and so on. From the root *ghusa* (in the sense of sounding):
one whose nature it is to sound, or one who has the habit of sounding, is called *aghosayi*, *ghosayati*, or *ghosayissati*.

In the sense of "good by virtue of morality (sīla) and by virtue of the Dhamma," the suffix *yu* is applied; for that [suffix], there is the substitution of *an* according to the rule "for *ana*, *yu* and *ūna*";
then, by the rule "and in other cases," there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening, resulting in *ghosana*. Regarding *bhāsana*: it means distinct speech (*viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ*);
or, one whose nature is to speak is "one who speaks" (*bhāsanasīlo*) or "one whose nature is speaking" (*bhāsanadhammo*); or, one who acts skillfully in speaking is "one who speaks" (*bhāsano*).
*Kudha* means anger. One who has the habit of being angry, or whose nature is to be angry, is *kodhana*;
[the forms] *kodhanā*, *kodhanaṃ* follow. *Rusa* means resentment; one who has the habit of resenting, or whose nature is to resent, is *rosana*.
*Cala* means shaking; one whose nature is to shake, or who shakes by nature, is *calana*. *Kapi* means shaking; [one who has the habit of] shaking...
