Alternatively, *akampano* means "one whose virtue is unshakable," or "one who shakes, will shake, or has shaken by means of virtue.

Regarding the suffix *-ano*, the nasal (*niggahīta*) is inserted according to the rules beginning with "in some cases, after a root vowel" (*kvaci dhātū*) and "and the nasal" (*niggahītañca*). *Phandano*: from the root *phadi* meaning slight movement;
it is "one whose nature is to quiver," or "one who quivers by means of virtue."

*Maḍana*: that which has the nature (*sīla*) of adorning (*maṇḍayituṃ*) one’s own ground (*bhūsāyaṃ*), or that which adorns by its nature; thus it is *maḍana*. [The root] *bhūs* is used in the sense of ornamenting (*alaṅkāre*). That which has the nature of ornamenting is *bhūsana*; or, that which has adorned (*abhūsayi*), adorns (*bhūsayati*), or will adorn (*bhūyayissati*) by its nature is *bhūsana*, *bhūsanā*, or *bhūsanaṃ*.

*Ruc* is used in the sense of shining (*dittimhi*). That which has the nature of shining—whether it has shone (*arucci*), shines (*ruccati*), or will shine (*ruccissati)—is *rocana*. *Jut* is used in the sense of shining. That which has the nature of shining—whether it has shone (*ajoti*), shines (*jotati*), or will shine (*jotissati)—is *jotana*. *Vaḍḍh* is used in the sense of increasing (*vaḍḍhane*). That which has the nature of increasing is *vaḍḍhana*, and so forth. 592. From the root *gam* preceded by *pārā-* (etc.), the suffix *rū* is applied.

When *pāra* and other words are used as prefixes (*upapada*), the suffix *rūpa* follows the root *gami*, but only when the agent (*kattā*) is intended in the senses of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
Those whose beginning is *pāra* are "those starting with *pāra*" (*pārādayo*); from these, [the suffix follows] after *gami*, hence *pārādigami*. There is elision of the *r*-group (*rādilopa*).

Thus, one whose nature is to go to the further shore of existence (*bhava-pāra*) is "one whose habit is to go to the further shore of existence" (*bhava-pāra-gamana-sīlo*), or "one whose dharma is to go to the further shore of existence" (*bhava-pāra-gamana-dhammo*), or "one who goes to the further shore of existence" (*bhava-pāra-gāmī*).
One who acts well in going is called *bhavapāragū* or *bhavapāraguṇo*. One whose nature is to go to the end is *antagū*. Likewise for *vedagū* and *addhagū*.
The term "ru" is understood [to apply here]. 593. And [the suffix -u applies] after *bhikkhu* and so forth.
The suffix -aka arises after verbal roots such as *bhikkha* and others in the senses of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
The root *bhikkha* means "to beg. One who has the habit of begging is a *bhikkhu*; or, one who begs, will beg, or is characterized by begging is a *bhikkhu*;

or, one whose nature is to beg, or one who is skillful in begging, is a *bhikkhu*. The shortening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule beginning with "in some cases, of roots" (*kvaci dhātū*). The root *ikkha* means "seeing" or "marking."
One who sees fear in *saṃsāra* is a *bhikkhu*; one whose nature is to discern (*vijānituṃ*) is a *viññū*, or one whose nature is discernment;
one who knows all is *sabbaññū*. In this same way, there are terms such as *mattaññū*, *dhammaññū*, *atthaññū*, *kālaññū*, and *kataññū*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.138) The suffix *ṇuka* is applied after roots such as *han* and others.

The suffix *ṇuka* occurs after roots such as *hana* and others in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth, when denoting the agent; the genitive case is used here in reference to the root ending.
The letter *ṇ* serves to indicate vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). One whose habit is to strike is *āghātuka*; here, *ghāta* is the substitute, with the elision of the vowel *a* and so forth.

One whose habit is to act is *kāruka*, a craftsman. The root *bhī* means fear; one whose habit is to fear is *bhīruka*, with the addition of the letter *r*. The root *ava* means protection; one who protects is *āvuka*, a father.
595. *Saṃhanaññāya vā ro gho*:

After the root *hana* preceded by the prefix *sam*, and after any other root, the suffix *ra* occurs, and for *hana*, there is the substitution *gho*. The inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of conjunction or for the purpose of providing an alternative; by this, *saṅghāta* is also established.
This substitution *gho* applies only to *hana*, according to the specific designation.
And because it is not combined (*asaṃpuṇṇā*) with that *ro*, the form *paṭigho* is also established.

The root *hana* is used in the senses of "harming" and "going. With the prefix *saṃ*, it means: "it brings together" (*saṃhanati*), that is, it approaches a unified action; or, "it destroys the distress of the defilements in a proper way" (*sammadeva kilesadarathe hanati*)—thus it is called *saṅgho*.
There is the elision of the *r*-sound (from *saṃ*). It is called a *parikhā* because it is dug (*khaññati*) all around the exterior of the city; [this occurs] in the feminine gender.
The suffix *āpa* [is applied]; "one who makes an end" (*antaṃ karoti*) is thus *antaka*, meaning death (*maccu*).
The phrase "in the sense of the agent and the object" (*bhāvakammesu*) is understood [from the previous rule]. 596. The suffix *yu* is added after *nanda* and others.

After roots such as *nand*, the suffix *yu* occurs in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*). According to the rule “*anakā yuṇvūna*,” there is the substitution of *an* for the suffix *yu*.
Thus: *nanda* in the sense of prosperity (*samiddhi*), or *nandana* (the act of gladdening). In the sense of the abstract state: that which is gladdened is *nandana*. In the sense of the object:
that which was gladdened, is being gladdened, will be gladdened, or that which ought to be gladdened, is the forest called *nandana*; it is grasped.

That which is to be grasped is *gahaṇīyaṃ*, or *gahaṇaṃ*, or *gaṇhanaṃ*; that which is to be practiced is *caritabbaṃ*, or *caraṇaṃ*; that which is being is *bhūyate*, or *bhavanaṃ*; that which is offered is *hūyate*, or *havanaṃ*.
That which is to be obstructed is *rundhitabbaṃ*, or *rundhanaṃ*, or *rodhanaṃ*; that which is to be eaten is *bhuñjitabbaṃ*, or *bhuñjanaṃ*, or *bhojanaṃ*.

That which is to be awakened is *bujjhitabbaṃ*, or *bujjhanaṃ*, or *bodhanaṃ*. It is heard (*sūyati*), or the hearing (*suti*) is *savaṇaṃ*; it reaches (*pāpīyati*), thus it is reaching (*pāpuṇanaṃ*), or causing to reach (*pāpanaṃ*).
It protects, thus it is *pālanaṃ*, and so forth. The term “*yū*” recurs.
597. And [it applies] in the case of words expressing the agent (*kattṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The suffix *yu* occurs after all verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the sense of "the agent" (*kattā*), "the instrument" (*karaṇa*), and "the location" (*padesa*).

Here, "location" (*padesa*) refers to the grammatical factor of the locus (*adhikaraṇakāraka*). First, regarding the agent (*kattā*): That which carries away dust is "dust-cleansing water" (*rajoharaṇaṃ toyaṃ*).

That which cognizes the object is "consciousness" (*viññāṇaṃ*); or it is "cognizing" (*vijānanaṃ*), with the substitution of *ā* for *ana*. The root *ghā* means "to take up odor"; that which smells is "the nose" (*ghānaṃ*).
*Jhāna*: from the root *jhā*, meaning "to meditate"; thus it is *jhāna*. The vowel *ā* is substituted according to the rule beginning with "in some cases, [the vowel] *ā*.

*Karaṇa*: from the root *kṛ*, meaning "to do" (*kara karaṇe*). It is *karaṇa* because one acts by means of it (*karoti tena*). *Byākaraṇa*: words are analyzed (*byākarīyanti*) according to their respective forms (*yathāsārūpaṃ*) by means of this;

thus it is *byākaraṇa*. *Pūraṇa*: from the root *pṛ*, meaning "to fill" (*pūra pūraṇe*). It is *pūraṇa* because one fills by means of it (*pūrayati tena*). *Dāna*: it is given (*dīyati*) by means of this; thus it is *dāna*. *Pamāṇa*: it is measured (*pamīyati*)...
*Anena* means "by this," hence it is called *pamāṇa*. That by which one speaks is *vacana*; or, that by which one drives away (*panudati*) or is driven away (*panujjate*) is *panūdano*.
*Sūda* means to flow; that which flows (*sūdati*) or is purified (*sujjate*) by it is *sūdano*; or, that by which one hears (*suṇāti*) or is heard (*sūyati*) is *savaṇaṃ*. *Lū* means to cut;
that which cuts (*lunāti*) or is cut (*lūyati*) by it is *lavanaṃ*, *lavaṇaṃ*, or *loṇaṃ*. *Nayati* means to lead; that which is led (*nīyati*) [is *neyya*].

"By this" is the leading (*nayana*). "Pavana" means purification (*pū*); it purifies (*punāti*), or that by which one is purified (*pūyate*) is *pavana*. "Samaṇa": it pacifies (*sameti*) or is approached (*samīyati*) by evil;
thus it is *samaṇa*, or one who is *samaṇa*. Likewise, "bhāvanā": it develops (*bhāveti*), is developed (*bhāvīyati*), or is brought to singleness (*ekāya*);
thus it is *bhāvanā*. In the same way, there are *pācana* (cooking), *pācāpana* (causing to cook), and so forth.

Regarding *adhikaraṇe*: the root *ṭhā* means "cessation of motion"; that wherein one stands is a *ṭhāna* (locus). Similarly, it is a *sayana* (bed), *sena* (army), or *āsana* (seat); it is called *adhikaraṇa* because it is that wherein something is placed (*adhikarīyati*).

By the word *ca* ("and"), [the suffix] is also applied in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*): that from which one gives correctly is the recipient (*sampadāna*); that depending upon which one takes [something] is the point of departure (*apādāna*). 598.
The suffix *i* is added after the roots *dā* and *dhā* when forming a technical name (*saññā*).

When the verbal root *saññā* (cognition) is to be understood, the suffix *i* is applied after the roots *dā* and *dhā*; this occurs within the governing context of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*kamma*), and involves the elision of the vowel *a*, among other changes.

The root *dā* means "to give" and is preceded by the prefix *ā*. That which is taken is called *ādi* (beginning). Similarly, there is *upādi*. The root *dhā* means "to hold. That which holds water is *udadhi* (the ocean);

in this case, through the elision of the vowel *a* and other changes, the word *udaka* (water) undergoes the substitution of *udā* within the technical term (*saññā*). That in which water is held is *jaladhi* (the ocean).
It holds hairs (*vālāni*) in it, thus it is a *vāladhi*; it is joined (*sandhīyati*), or it joins (*sandadhāti*), thus it is a *sandhi*; it is deposited (*nidhīyati*), thus it is a *nidhi*.

Likewise, it is performed (*vidhīyati*), it performs (*vidadhāti*), or it is an arrangement (*vidhāna*), thus it is a *vidhi*; it properly (*sammā*) or evenly (*samaṃ*) places the mind (*cittaṃ*), thus it is *samādhi*.
[The suffix] *-mat* or *-ya* is used here.

When a feminine referent is intended, the suffixes *aka*, *ara*, and *ti* are optionally applied after all verbal roots in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*kamma*), and so forth.

First, regarding the absence of a suffix (*appaccaya*): *jara* [denotes] the decline of age; it is called *jarā* because "one ages" (*jīrati*) or "the act of aging" (*jīraṇa*). According to the rule "in the feminine, the suffix *āp* follows from this," the suffix *āp* is added, resulting in *jarā*.
That which is analyzed (*paṭisambhijjati*) is *paṭisambhidā*. That by means of which one proceeds (*paṭipajjati*) is *paṭipadā*. In the same way, *sampadā*.

It is a calamity (*āpadā*). It is grasped (*upādīyati*), thus it is grasping (*upādā*). One perceives (*sañjānāti*), thus it is perception (*saññā*); one understands (*pajānāti*), thus it is wisdom (*paññā*). One looks on with equanimity (*upekkhati*), thus it is equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Thinking is thought (*cintā*). A foundation is a footing (*patiṭṭhā*). Training in the acquisition of knowledge is training;

it is training because of the act of training, or that which is trained in, thus it is training (*sikkhā*). Likewise for alms-food (*bhikkhā*). In the sense of thinking, "one meditates intensely upon the excellence of another," thus it is covetousness (*abhijjhā*).
One who meditates after having established what is beneficial is an *upajjhā*; [with the suffix -aya] it becomes *upajjhāyo*. That wherein one meditates rightly is *sajjhā*.

In the root *isu*, meaning "to desire," the suffix *-ana* is applied to form the sense of "seeking" (*esanā*); by the rule "in *isu*, *yamūna*, and *manta*, there is the substitution of *ccha*," the letter *ccha* replaces [the final], resulting in *icchā* (desire).
In the root *puccha*, meaning "to ask," the act of asking is *pucchā*; curing is *tikicchā*; the desire to eat is *jighacchā*.

*Titikkhā* (endurance), *bubhukkhā* (hunger), *pipāsā* (thirst) [from the desire to drink]. Due to the governing rule (*vādhikāra*), there is an absence of the augment *v*. *Vicchā* (the desire to pervade), and so forth. With the suffix *ti*, from *sambhū* comes *sambhūti* (origination).

Due to the governing rule, there is no *vṛddhi* in the suffix *ti*: from *śru* comes *sutī* (hearing); from *nī* comes *nītī* (leading, or that by which one is led). From *man* (in the sense of knowing), *maññati* (he conceives/thinks), thus *mati* (thought). The terms *te*, *no*, and *timhī* also recur [as governing rules].

600. The final consonant of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, *han*, *ram*, and so forth, ending in *m* or *n*, is not [retained] before a suffix beginning with *t*; and because of the rule "and before *ti*," there is elision of the final phoneme of the root.
Thus: *gamanam* (the act of going), or *gantabbā* (to be gone); likewise, *upahananam* (the act of striking) becomes *upahatī*.
They delight by means of it, or delighting is *rati*. *Tan* means extension; extending is *tati*. *Yam* means to cease; restraining is *niyati*.
However, in cases such as *ramato* and *ramatī*, there is no elision of the final consonant of the root because it is separated by the vowel *a*. Eating is *bhutti*; yoking is *yutti*.

Here, there is elision of the final consonant of the root and doubling [of the remaining consonant] according to the rule: "In the case of *bhuj* and others, the final [consonant] becomes *n*, and there is no doubling. Entering into [meditative attainment] is *samāpajjanaṃ*.
*Samāpatti* (attainment) is derived from *samāpajjati* (to enter); it is a formation where the final vowel of the root is elided and doubled according to the rule "gupādīnañca.
By the rule "kvaci dhātū," etc., the suffix *ni* is substituted for *ha* and so on; thus we have *hāni* (loss), *jāni* (destruction), and so forth. Regarding the suffix *yu*:

in the sense of "consciousness" (*cita*) or "to perceive" (*sañcetane*), the suffix *yu* is applied to the root *cetayati* (to perceive); there is substitution of *a* for the root vowel, vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and the addition of the suffix *ā*.

*Cetanā*. [The root] *vid* means "to experience"; that which experiences is *vedanā*. [The root] *dis* means "to express"; that which is expressed is *desanā*; that which is cultivated is *bhāvanā*, and so forth.
The phrase "in the feminine" (*itthiyaṃ*) or "optionally" (*vā*) also continues [from the previous rule].
601. The suffix *-riya* is added after the verb *kar*.

The suffix *riya* occurs after the verbal root *kṛ* when a feminine or non-feminine referent is to be expressed; the letter *r* is elided. [The word] *karaṇīya* means "action to be performed" (*kiriyā*).
The term "agent" (*kattar*) is understood [to carry over]. 602.
The suffix *ina* is applied everywhere after the root *ji*.

When the suffix *ina* follows a verbal root ending in *i*, it forms a word for the agent (*kattar*) at all times. From the root *ji* (to conquer): he has conquered, he conquers, or he will conquer evil, unwholesome states; thus, he is a *jina*.
The term *ina* is understood [from the previous rule]. 603. And after a word ending in *su*.
The suffix *in* occurs after a verbal root ending in a vowel (*sup*) when followed by the word *para*. From the root *sup* (to lie down): *supine*, *supinaṃ* (a dream).
From the root *sī* (to lie down), with *īsaṃ* as an accompanying word (*upapada*), in the sense of "he lies down slightly": 604. *Īsaṃ-dus-ūhi kha*.
(The suffix *kha* occurs after roots ending in *īsaṃ*, *du*, or *u*).
The suffix *kha* occurs after verbal roots when followed by these particles: *īsaṃ*, *du*, and *su*.
And that [suffix]—605—is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*), with the meanings of *kicca*, *akta*, and *khattha*.
Regarding these meanings of *bhāva* (state/abstract action) and *kamma* (object), since the suffixes *kicca*, *ktā*, and *kkhatta* occur [by rule], they necessarily apply only to *bhāva* and *kamma*.

In the phrase “in some cases, from a root,” there is the elision of the suffix *kkha*, vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), the substitution of *ay* by virtue of the *dvitta* rule, and the elision of the long *ī*. Thus:
*bhavatā* (by being); that which is endured with difficulty is *dussaya*; that which is endured with ease is *sussaya*.
Kamma: it is done with effort, thus kamma is "effortful" (*īsakkara*). Likewise, that which is done with difficulty is "difficult to do" (*dukkara*) for one who seeks welfare;
evil is "easy to do" (*sukara*) for a fool. That which is maintained with difficulty is "difficult to maintain" (*dubbhara*), such as one of great desire.

That which is maintained with ease is "easy to maintain" (*subhara*), such as one of few desires. That which must be guarded with difficulty is a "difficult-to-guard" (*durakkha*) mind. With difficulty...
"It should be seen" means the Dhamma is difficult to see. "It should be seen with ease" means the faults of others are easy to see.
"It should be awakened to with difficulty" means the Dhamma is hard to awaken to. "It should be awakened to with ease" means it is easy to awaken to, and so forth.
Regarding the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding": it refers to one who has awakened, is awakening, or will awaken to all phenomena—whether conditioned, unconditioned, or conventional.
The term "ta" is understood [to recur]. 606. *Budhagamāditthe kattari*:
When the sense of those roots beginning with *budha* and *gama* is to be understood, the suffix *ta* occurs in all tenses when the agent (*kattar*) is expressed.
“Of that” (tassā) is understood [from the previous rule]. 607. *Dhaḍhabhahehi dha ḍhā ca*:
After verbal roots ending in *dha*, *ḍha*, *bha*, or *ha*, the letter *ta* of a subsequent suffix is respectively replaced by *dha* and *ḍha*.

*Honti* means that the letter *ta* becomes *dha* by virtue of the rule for *dha*. Because the letter *ha* is included in the phrase "the fourth [consonant] after *ha*," there is also the substitution of *dha* in some instances even from the letter *ha*, provided there is no intervening element.
Therefore, in cases such as *rundhati*, *ārādhito*, *vaḍḍhito*, *labhitvā*, and *gahito*, this does not occur because they are separated by suffixes or augments.
608. *Hacatutthānamantānaṃ do dhe*:
For the fourth letters of the *ha*-group (*ha*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*) occurring at the end of a verbal root, there is a substitution of *da* when followed by *dha*. *Buddho bhagavā*.

One who has gone for refuge—whether he has gone, is going, or will go—is called a lay follower (*upāsaka*), according to the rule: "The final [consonants] of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, *han*, and *ram* [are dropped]."
There is elision of the final element of the verbal root (*dhātvantalopa*). Thus, from *jñā* (to know), one who knows is *ñāta*. From *i* (in the sense of going), one who approaches is *upeta*.
From *cit* (in the sense of thinking), one who thinks is *citta*; here, by the rule “and for *gup* and others,” there is elision of the final element of the root and doubling of the consonant.

From *sañj* (in the sense of clinging), one who has clung, clings, or will cling to forms and so forth is *satta*; here, by the rule “for *bhuj* and others, the final [consonant] becomes *n*, and there is doubling,” there is elision of the final element of the root and doubling.
The term "of a noun" (saññāya) is understood [to carry over]. 609. *Tikicca-āsiṭṭhe*:

When a benediction (*āsiṭṭha*) is implied with respect to a noun as the object denoted, the suffix *ti* and the suffix *ita* occur after verbal roots. For example: *jinabuddhi*, meaning "may he awaken this [person] as a Conqueror" (with the substitution of *dha* for *da*); and *dhanabhūti*, meaning "may wealth be his."

“May he exist through the support of books” means *bhūto*; “may the Dhamma give him [support]” means *dhammadinno*, where the suffix *inna* (or *anna*, *īṇā*) is substituted for the primary suffix *ta* according to the rule “*bhidādito inna anna īṇā vā*”.
“May he increase” means *vaḍḍhamāno*, where the suffix *māna* takes the *appa*-suffix according to the rule “*bhūvādito a*” among those ending in *māna*.
“May he rejoice” means *nandako*; “may he live” means *jīvako*, and so forth.
610. *Āgamā tuko*.

After the root *gam* preceded by *ā*, the suffix *tuka* occurs; because it denotes the agent (*kattā*), it is used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). That which comes is an *āgantuko*. The word "from a village" (*gamā*) is understood [as the governing term].
611. *Bhabbe ika*. The suffix *ika* occurs in the sense of capability (*bhabba*). A monk who is capable of going is a "goer" (*gamiko*).
This is the method for suffixes ending in *te-kālika*.
The Method of the Past Condition (Atītappaccayantana): 612. *Atīte ta tavantu tāvī*.

In the past tense, the suffixes *ta*, *tavantu*, and *tāvī* occur after all verbal roots (*dhātu*). These very same [suffixes] are also used according to the common convention (*parasamaññā*) for other tenses.
Those ending in *niṭṭha* also become agent nouns (*kattari*) because they possess the sense of the past participle (*kitasaññattā*). *Bhabhī* means "one who has been" (*bhūto*), *bhūtā*, *bhūtaṃ*.

By the inclusion of the word "and others" (*aññesu ca*) which recurs from that rule, there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) in the suffixes *-ta*, *-tavant*, and *-tu*. The root *hu* is used in the senses of giving, eating, sacrificing, and bestowing.

*Ahavī* means "the fire that has been sacrificed into" (*huto aggiṃ*). With the suffix *-tavant*: by the rule "ā simhī," the vowel *ā* is substituted; thus *aggiṃ hutavā*, *hutavanto*, etc., are identical in form to those ending in the suffix *-vant* (denoting possession of qualities).
*Tāvīmhi*—in the sense of "one who has offered oblations," as in *aggiṃ hutāvī*, *aggiṃ hutāvino*, and so forth, it is similar to *daṇḍī*. In the feminine, the suffix *-inī* is applied:
*hutāvinī*. In the neuter, there is shortening: *hutāvi*.

From the root *vasa* (to dwell), in the sense of "he dwelt" (*vassaṃ avasī*), the suffix *-ta* is applied; because it ends in *s*, the substitution of *ṭha* occurs according to the rule beginning with "for *sa* and *dīrgha," etc.
“Of that” (*tassā*) is the governing reference, as is “with *sā*.
613. *Vasato uttha*:

After the verbal root *vas*, the substitution of *uttha* occurs for the following letter *t*, provided it is preceded by a consonant such as *s*; there is also the elision of the vowel *a*, and so forth.

Having completed the rains retreat (*vassa*), that [retreat] is completed. According to the rule beginning with “*saralopo*” (the elision of *sa* and *ra*), because of the inclusion of *tu*, there is no elision of the preceding vowel;
thus, in cases such as “*adhivatthā devatā*” (deities dwelling therein) and “*vatthabban*” (to be dwelt), there is elision of the subsequent vowel.
The form “*vasassā*” occurs through a grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*).

614. *Vassa vū*. When the letter *va* of this phoneme (*dhātu*) is followed by the letter *ta*, it becomes *u*, and there is optionally an insertion of the letter *va* therein. This [rule] applies only when the *ta* is a final consonant (*niṭṭha*).
Alternatively, in the word *vū*, the letter *va* is a euphonic junction (*sandhi-ja*); according to the method of the treatise (*tantra-naya*), the second [letter] here is [the result].
The inclusion of the term *vāk* (speech) is intended; by that, the substitution of *u* for *a* is also established, as in *usito brahmacariyaṃ*, *vusito*, and likewise *vusitavā*, *vusitāvī*.
Due to the intervention caused by the addition of the vowel *i*, the substitution of *u* does not occur [in cases like *vusitavān*].

The root *bhuja* is used in the senses of protecting and consuming; in the sense of "he consumed rice," there are the forms *tatavant* and *tātāvī*. [In the rule] "for *bhuja* and others, the final [consonant]... [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a portion of a grammatical commentary on Pāli morphology, specifically concerning vowel substitutions (*ādesa*) and suffix formations.]
In *no dvi ca*, there is elision of the final vowel of the root and doubling of the letter *t*: *bhutto*, *bhuttavā*, *bhuttāvī*. Likewise, from *rañja* (to color/passion):
*arañji* means colored, *ratto*, *rattā*, *rattaṃ*. From *yuja* (to join/yoke): *ayuñji* means joined, *yutto*, *yuttā*, *yuttaṃ*.
From *vica* (to separate), preceded by *vi-* (*vivicati*): *vivicci* means secluded, *vivitto*, *vivittā*, *vivittaṃ*. From *muca* (to release): *amuñci*...
"Released from bondage. Likewise, in the case of the *t*-suffix: by this [rule], there is the elision of the final vowel of the root and the doubling of the consonant.
*Āsajjanaṃ* (assaulting) is *āsatti*; *vimuccanaṃ* (releasing) or "that by which one is released" (*vimuccati etāya*) is *vimutti*.

In the root *kudha*, meaning "anger," the suffix *ta* is applied in the sense of "one who does not get angry"; for that [suffix], there is the substitution of *dha* according to the rule: "In place of *dha*, *ḍha*, *bha*, and *ha*, there are *ḍha*, *ḍha*, and *ba* respectively. Thus, it becomes *kodha*.
By the rule “*hacatutthānam antānaṃ do dhe*,” the letter *dh* becomes *d*: *kuddho*. From the root *yudh* (in the sense of combat), *ayujjhīti yuddho*, [and thus] *yuddhaṃ*.
From the root *sidh* (in the sense of accomplishment), *asijjhīti siddho*. With the prefix *ā-*, from the root *rabh* (in the sense of rashness/undertaking), *ārabhīti āraddho gantuṃ*.
With the prefix *sam-*, from the root *nah* (in the sense of binding), *sannayhīti sannaddho*. [The rule continues: “*dhaḍhabhahehi dhaḍhā*...”
And in the word *cā*, the letter *ta* is changed to *dha*.

In the root *vaḍḍha* (meaning "to increase"), the suffix *tappaccaya* is applied in the sense of "having increased"; its *ḍha* becomes *tta*, the vowel *ā* of the root is elided according to the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātū," and the *ḍa* is also elided.
The phrase "of the fourth letters following *ha*" is understood to carry over.
615. Regarding the letter *ḍha*:

for the fourth letters of the *ha*-group at the end of verbal roots (*dhātu*), there is the substitution of the letter *ḍa* when followed by the letter *ḍha*. [Examples: *vuḍḍho*, *vuḍḍhā*; according to the rule "bo vassā," *buḍḍho* [is formed].
In the case of the suffix *tippaccaya*: *bujjhanaṃ* (the act of awakening), or that by which one awakens is *buddhi*. Likewise, *siddhi* and *vaḍḍhi*.
In that context: "it is to be understood," and so forth.
And the governing rule is "internal, not [external].
616. After *tara* and the others, the suffix *iṇ* is applied.
By means of the roots beginning with *tara*, there is the substitution of *iṇ* for the suffix *ta*, and the final vowel of the root does not remain;

this includes the elision of the vowel *a* and so forth. From the root *tara* (to cross): one who has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra is "crossed" (*tiṇṇo*); [the optative] "may he cause to cross" (*tāreyyaṃ*). Likewise, *uttiṇṇo* or *tiṇṇaṃ*. From the root *pūra* (to fill):

one who has filled completely is "full" (*saṃpuṇṇo*). According to the rule beginning with "elision of the vowel *a*" (*saralopo*), because of the inclusion of the letter *t* [in the rule], there is no elision of the preceding [nasal].
Due to the elision of the following vowel according to the rule "or another [vowel] of a different form," there is shortening in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).

From the root *tura* (in the sense of speed), *aturī* becomes *tuṇṇaṃ* or *turitaṃ*. From *jara* (in the sense of loss of age), *parijīrī* becomes *parijiṇṇo*. From *kira* (in the sense of scattering), *ākirī* becomes *ākiṇṇo*, and so forth.
617. After *su*, *pa*, *ca*, and *ka*, [the suffixes] *to*, *kkha*, and *kkā* [are applied].

The letters *k*, *kh*, and *kha* are substituted for the suffix *ta* after the roots *su*, *pac*, and *sak*. Furthermore, the final consonant [of these roots] is not elided. By the word "and" (*ca*), the substitution of *kk* occurs after *muc* and others.
*Sus* means drying; since it has dried (*asuṣi*), it is a dry (*sukka*) tree. *Apac* means to ripen; that which has ripened (*apacci*) is a ripe fruit.
*Sak* means capability; since he was capable (*asakkhi*), he is Sakka. *Omuñc* means to release; that which has been released (*omucci*) is a removed (*omukkā*) sandal. "To cook" (*pacitum*).
However, in cases such as *pacitabba*, [the suffix] does not occur because it is separated by the vowel *i*. Thus, in all instances, it does not occur when there is an intervention.
The mention of the word *tī* (three) follows the rule for the lion’s gait (*sīhagati*). 618. [The suffix] *nto* occurs after *pakkam* and so forth.
With roots ending in the letter *m*, such as *pakkama* and others, there is a substitution of *nt* for the following *tappaccaya* suffix, and the final vowel of the root is elided.
By the word *ca* (and), there is also the substitution of *nti* for the *tippaccaya* suffix. In the case of *kamu* (to step), as in *pakkamīti pakkanto* ("having stepped forth, he has stepped").
Likewise, *saṅkanto*, *nikkhanto*. According to the rule *do dhassa cā*, by the inclusion of *ca* in that sutta, there is the substitution of *kha* for *ka*. *Bhamu*...
In *anavaṭṭhāne*, "vibbhamīti" means one who has strayed (*vibbhanto*), i.e., one who is wavering. In *khamu* (to endure), "akkhamīti" means patient (*khanto*).
In *samu* (to be calmed), "asamīti" means peaceful (*santo*). In *damu* (to tame), "adamīti" means tamed (*danto*).
Regarding the suffix *-ti*: "saṅkamanaṃ" becomes "saṅkanti. Thus, there are forms such as *okkanti*, *vibbhanti*, *khanti*, *santi*, *danti*, and so forth.

619. And in the case of *jana* and so forth, [the vowel becomes long]. In the case of roots such as *jana* and the like, the final consonant is replaced by its corresponding long vowel (*āttam*) when the suffix *ta* follows, and also when *ti* follows. By means of a division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), this also applies in other instances.

In the root *jana* (to be born): *ajanīti jāto* (he was born); *vijāyīti puttaṃ vijātā* (she gave birth, having brought forth a son); *jananaṃ jāti* (the act of being born is "birth"). [This occurs] when the suffix *ta* follows.

Even though the letter *ta* exists [in the rule], the repetition of the word *ti* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *ā* when another condition (*paccayantara*) ending in *ta* is present, as in *jantu*.
However, in cases such as *janitvā* and *janituṃ*, it does not occur because [the *ta*] is separated by the letter *i*.
Furthermore, the phrase “*ā*, and before *tim*” continues to apply.
620. *Ṭhāpānam i ī ca*.
For the vowels *ā* and *āi* within these roots, the substitutions *i* and *ī* respectively occur before the suffix *ta*, as well as before *ti*.
By the word "and" (*ca*), this also occurs in some instances elsewhere. *Ṭhā* means "ceasing of motion"; thus, *aṭṭhāsi* means "he stood," and *upaṭṭhito* means "established."

*Garuṃ*, *ṭhitavā*, *adhiṭṭhitvā*, *ṭhānaṃ*, *ṭhiti*. *Pā* means "to drink"; *apāyi* means "drank," *yāguṃ pītavā* means "having drunk rice-gruel," *pānaṃ pīti* means "drinking a beverage," and *pītvā* means "having drunk. 621. *Hantehi ho hassa lo vā adahanahānaṃ*: After verbal roots ending in *h*, the substitute *ho* occurs for the following suffix *tappaccaya*, and there is optionally the substitution of *l* for the final *h* of the root.

(The *ho* is the substitute for *t*. *Garum*: from the root *gṛ* ("to take"), with the suffix *tumun*. *Ṭhitavā*: from the root *sthā* ("to stand"), with the suffix *tavantu*. *Adhiṭṭhitvā*: from the root *sthā* with prefix *adhi*, with the suffix *tvā*. *Ṭhānaṃ*: from the root *sthā*, with the suffix *anaṇ*. *Ṭhiti*: from the root *sthā*, with the suffix *ktin*. *Apāyi*: from the root *pā* ("to drink"), with the suffix *a*. *Yāguṃ pītavā*: from the root *pā*, with the suffix *tavantu*. *Pānaṃ pīti*: from the root *pā*, with the suffix *ktin*. *Pītvā*: from the root *pā*, with the suffix *tvā*. Regarding the rule: after roots ending in *h*, the suffix *tappaccaya* becomes *ho*, and the final *h* of the root is optionally replaced by *l*. For example, from the root *dah* ("to burn"), one forms *daho* ("burning"). From the root *han* ("to kill"), one forms *hano* ("killing"). The *ho* is the substitute for the suffix *t*.

The letter *l* occurs optionally in place of *d*, excluding the root *dah* (to burn); this is an exception to the rule for *ḍh*. The root *ruh* means "to grow"; *aruhī* means "ascended" (as in *aruḷho rukkhanti*). There is no distinction between *l* and *ḷ*;
thus, *ārulho* is equivalent to *āruḷho*. The root *ruh* also means "to grow"; *ruhanam* is "growth," and *ruḷhī* is "conventional usage. The root *gāh* means "to stir";

*agāhī* becomes *gāḷho*, as in *ajjhogāḷho mahannavam* ("plunged deep into the great ocean"). The root *bah* means "to increase"; *abahī* becomes *bāḷho*, with the vowel lengthened by the rule beginning with "in some cases, the root [vowel]. The root *muh* means "confusion of mind."

*Amuyhīti* means "he is deluded" (*mūḷho*). *Guha* is in the sense of concealing; *aguhīti* means "concealed" (*gūḷhaṃ*). *Vaha* is in the sense of reaching; *upavahīti* means "carried near" (*upavuḷho*). This is stated in the grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) as:
"In the case of *vaca*, *vasa*, *vaha*, and others, the letter *u* [is substituted] for the vowel *a*.

For what purpose is the prohibition against burning (*adahanahāna*) stated? [To prevent it from applying to: *daḍḍho* ("burnt") and *sannaddho* ("armed"). Why is *vā* mentioned? [To exclude: *duddho* ("milked") and *siniddho* ("smooth"). However, in cases such as *gahitaṃ* ("taken") and *mahitaṃ* ("honored"), the substitution does not occur because the [original vowel] is separated by the augment *i*.

Also from the perspective of the *dhātu* and *paccaya*: in the phrase “*atīte ta tavantutāvī*,” there is the *tappaccaya*; for example, *abubhukkhī* becomes *bubhukkhito*. Likewise, *jighacchito*, *pipāsito*, and so forth.
Thus ends the method of derivation (*niṭṭhanaya*) regarding the agent (*kattar*).
The term “in the past” (*atīte*) continues to apply.

622. *Bhāvakammesu ta*: When the past tense (*atīte kāle*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ta* occurs after all verbal roots (*sabbadhātūhi*) in the senses of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the passive (*kamma*). First, regarding the abstract action (*bhāve*):
[examples follow].
In the sense of "singing," "singing," or "has sung," there is the *tappaccaya* suffix. 623.
In all instances, *ge* becomes *gī*.

For this root *ge*, the substitution *gī* occurs in all cases, specifically when the *tappaccaya* or *tipaccaya* suffixes follow. From that [root], there is *gītaṃ*, *gāyanaṃ*, or *gāyitabbaṃ*; thus, it is called *gīti*.
In the sense of state (*bhāve*), words ending in that suffix are neuter; in the sense of object (*kammani*), they are of three genders.
In the sense of "bending of a limb" (*nata-gatta-vināme*) or "dancing" (*naccanaṃ*) or "having danced" (*anaccittha*), the suffix *tappaccaya* occurs.
624. The suffixes beginning with *da* are established through grammatical convention (*nipātanā*).
Those words here that have suffixes (*sappaccaya*) and have not reached their final form through those suffixes are established by means of *nipātana* (irregular substitution).
Thus, with the end of the verbal root, there is the substitution of *cca* for the suffix *ta*. Examples: *naccaṃ*, *naṭṭaṃ*. In the case of the root *hasa* (to laugh), *hasanaṃ* becomes *hasitaṃ*;

there is the insertion of the vowel *i*. *Gamanaṃ* becomes *gataṃ*. Likewise, *ṭhitaṃ* and *sayitaṃ*. Because the section on *vā* (optionality) is a rule of restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). [The same applies to] *ruda*.
In *assu-vimocane* (the shedding of tears): *aruñjhittha* means wept, or *ruṇṇaṃ*, etc. In the sense of an object (*kammani*):
*abhibhūyittha* means anger was overcome by you; [forms] *abhibhūtā*, *abhibhūtaṃ*. In *bhāsabyattiyaṃ* (clarity of speech), it refers to speech.

It was spoken by him, thus it is the "spoken Dhamma" (*bhāsito dhammo*); the verses were spoken (*bhāsitā gāthā*); the discourse was spoken (*bhāsitaṃ suttaṃ*). The root *dis* means "to utter"; because it belongs to the *curādigaṇa*, the suffix *-ṇe* is applied.

It was pointed out by the Blessed One, thus it is the "pointed-out Dhamma" (*desito dhammo*); with the addition of the vowel *i*, there is the elision of the causative suffix and the following consonant.

The root *ji* means "to conquer"; he was not conquered, thus Māra was "conquered" (*jito*). The root *nī* means "to reach"; they were led to the village, thus the goats were "led" (*nītā*). The Dhamma was heard by you, thus it is "known" (*ñāto*).
In the meanings "he instructs" (*anusāsati*) and "he was instructed" (*anusāsīyati*), the suffix *tappaccaya* occurs.
625. *Sāsadisato tassa riṭṭho ca*:

after the verbal roots *sās-* and those similar to it, the substitution of *riṭṭha* for the following suffix *tappaccaya* takes place; by the word *ca*, [the substitution of] *riṭṭhi* for *ti* also occurs.
And from the root *dis* (to see), the forms *raṭṭha*, *raṭṭhuṃ*, and *raṭṭhā* arise due to the suffixes *-tu*, *-tuṃ*, and *-tva*, etc., with the elision of the initial *r*.

It was instructed by me (*anusiṭṭho so*), she was instructed (*anusiṭṭhā sā*), it was instructed (*anusiṭṭhaṃ*). From the root *dis* in the sense of seeing: "it was seen" (*adissittha*) thus becomes *diṭṭhaṃ*—I saw the form.
In the feminine suffix *-ti*: instruction is *anusāsanaṃ* or *anusiṭṭhi*; seeing is *dassanaṃ* or *diṭṭhi*.
Regarding the functions (*kicca*) and so forth: *dassanīyaṃ* means "to be seen"; *daṭṭhabbaṃ*, *daṭṭheyyaṃ*, and *passituṃ* mean "in order to see," as in "he goes to see";

*passitvā* means "having seen," as in "having seen renunciation. Due to the insertion of the vowel *i*, the nasalization (*na-bhava*) does not occur for the internal [consonant], as in *anusāsitaṃ*, *anusāsitabbaṃ*, *anusāsituṃ*, *anusāsitvā*, *dassitaṃ*, and so forth.
In the phrase *tussa pītimhi*, *atussī* means "he rejoiced"; here the suffix *ta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).
The term "*tassa*" is the governing heading (*adhikāra*).
626. The suffix *ṭṭha* is applied after [roots ending in] *sādi*, *santa*, *puccha*, *bhañja*, *hansa*, and so forth.

“Sādi” means that which occurs together with *sa* and so forth. When a *ta* following roots ending in *s*, such as *pucch*, *bhanj*, *haṃsa*, and others, is immediately preceded by a consonant from the group beginning with *sa*, it undergoes substitution by *ṭṭh*.

Although *haṃsa* is already included [in the list], its separate mention is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution by *ṭṭh* is not invariably obligatory in certain instances; hence [the form] “viddhasto.”
In such cases as "utrasto" (frightened), there is no [suffix]. "Tuṭṭho" means satisfied; it is derived from the root *tuṣ*. "Bhasa" means speaking;
"abhassī" becomes "bhaṭṭho" or "bhassito. "Nasa" means disappearance; "nassī" becomes "naṭṭho. "Daṃsa" means biting; "adaṃsīyittha" becomes "daṭṭho" by a snake, or "ḍaṃsito";
here, by the rule "kvaci dhātū," etc., the substitution of *ḍa* for *da* occurs. "Phusa" means touching; "aphusīyittha" becomes "phuṭṭho" by a disease.

*Phussita*: or touched. *Isu* means desire; that which was desired (*esīyittha*) is *iṭṭha*, *icchita*, or *esito*. *Masu* means to touch; that which was touched (*āmasīyittha*) is *āmaṭṭha*. *Vasu* means to sprinkle;

that which has been sprinkled (*avassī*) is *vuṭṭha* (as in "the rain fell"), that which has entered (*pavisīyittha*) is *paviṭṭha*, and that which has been pointed out (*uddisīyittha*) is *uddiṭṭha*.
*Puccha* means to ask; that which was asked (*apucchīyittha*) is *puṭṭha* (a question) or *pucchita*. *Bhanja* means to crush.
*Abhañjiyittha* means "it was broken," thus *bhaṭṭhaṃ* (broken) and *dhaññaṃ* (grain). The root *haṃs* is used in the sense of joy; from *ahaṃsi*, we have *haṭṭho*, *pahaṭṭho*, and *pahaṃsito*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [roots such as] *yaja* in the senses of worshipping deities, joining together, and giving are included; from *ijjittha*, the suffix *tappaccaya* occurs, and for that, there is a substitution of *ṭṭha*. 627.
In the case of the root *yaj*, when followed by a vowel and the suffix *ṭṭha*, [the *j* is replaced].

In the place of the vowel *i* of this root *yaj*, there is the substitution of the vowel *i* when followed by the suffix *ṭṭha*. Thus: *yiṭṭho mayā jino* ("the Conqueror was sacrificed to by me"). *Saj* is used in the sense of emission; preceded by *sam*, it becomes *saṃsaṭṭho* (mixed) from *saṃsajjittha* ("he mixed with that"), and *vissaṭṭho* (emitted).

*Maj* is used in the sense of cleansing; *amañjī* becomes *maṭṭho* ("polished"), and so forth. Regarding the gerundives (*kicca*) such as those ending in *ta*: *tussitabbaṃ* becomes *toṭṭhabbaṃ*; *phusitabbaṃ* becomes *phoṭṭhabbaṃ*; *pucchituṃ* becomes *puṭṭhuṃ*; *yajituṃ* becomes *yiṭṭhuṃ*;
*abhiharituṃ* becomes *abhihaṭṭhuṃ*. The noun forms are: *tosanaṃ* becomes *tuṭṭhi*; *esanaṃ* becomes *eṭṭhi*; *vassanaṃ*... [and so on].
*Vuṭṭhi*, *vissajjanaṃ*, *vissaṭṭhi*, and so forth.
The phrase “of that, [the suffix] sādi” also continues [from the previous rule].
628. For the root *bhañj*, there is also *gga*.
When the root *bhañj* (to break) is used, the letter *g* is substituted for the suffix *tappaccaya* along with its initial consonant (*sa*). Thus: *bhaggo rāgo anena* (“passion was broken by this”).

In the sense of dwelling (*vasanivāse*), from the verb *parivasati*, we have *parivuṭṭho* (one who has completed his stay) and *parivāso* (probation). [From *vas* in the sense of having lived: *vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ* (“the holy life has been lived”). Here, *u* is the substitute for *ṭṭha*.

In the sense of covering (*vasa acchādane*), from *nivasati*, we have *nivatthaṃ vatthaṃ* (“clothed in a garment”). By the rule beginning with “*kvaci dhātū*,” the conjunct consonant *st* [is changed].
*tthattaṃ*, thus it should be worn. *Saṃsa* means to praise; that which has been praised is "praised" (*pasattha*) or "extolled" (*pasaṃsita*), and the act of praising is "praise" (*pasatthi*).
*Badha* means to bind; that which has been bound is "bound by the king" (*baddho raññā*), and that which has been obtained is "wealth obtained by me" (*alabhīyittha*);
[examples of] *dhatta* and *datta*. *Rabha* means impetuosity; that which has been undertaken is "vigor begun" (*ārabbha* / *āraddhaṃ vīriyaṃ*). *Daha* means to reduce to ashes.
*Adayhitta* means "a forest that was burnt"; *abhujjittha* means "rice that was eaten. In *bhujāditā*, there is elision of the end of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and doubling of the consonant.
*Caja* is used in the sense of "loss"; *pariccajīyittha* means "wealth that was relinquished," i.e., *pariccatta*.
*Amuccittha* means "an arrow that was released. *Vaca* is used for distinct speech; *avacīyittha* is used in the sense of [the object], with the suffix *ta* applied.
“*Anto*, *no*, *dvi*, and *cā*” is the governing rule (*adhikāra*). 629.
*Vaca vā vu*. This consists of four words.
For the consonant *v* of the verbal root *vaca*, there is optionally a substitution of *u*; and [the same applies to] the end of the root.

The letter *c* does not occur [in place of *v*], and there is a doubling of the suffix *tappaccaya*. The inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of restriction; it means that the augment *va* occurs at the beginning of the root.
This was spoken by the Blessed One, or it was uttered (*uttaṃ*). 630.
And [the augment occurs] after *gup* and the others.
In the case of roots such as *gup*, etc., there is neither a final vowel nor a consonant; furthermore, the following letter *t* becomes doubled. The root *gup* means "to protect.
In the form *sugutto* (well-protected), it is derived from *sugopīyittha* (was well-protected). Because the vowel *i* intervenes, there is no elision of the final part of the root.

According to the rule "and in other cases," because the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of that sutta is subject to a fixed option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), there is sometimes a vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) even when the suffix *niṭṭha-ta* follows. Protection (*gopana*) is *gutti*.

*Lipa* means to smear; that which has been smeared (*alimpīyittha*) is "smeared" (*litto*) with fragrance. *Tapa* means to heat; that which has been heated (*santapīyittha*) is "heated" (*santatto*) by fire.

*Dīpa* means splendor; that which has been ignited (*ādīpīyittha*) is "blazing" (*āditto*) with fire. The shortening of the vowel occurs because "splendor" (*dīpana*) is the same as "splendor" (*ditti*). *Apa* means to reach;

that which has been reached (*pāpīyittha*) is "attained" (*patto*) as in "the village is reached," or "he attains" (*pāpuṇīti*) as in "he attains happiness. "Reaching" (*pāpuṇana*) is "attainment" (*patti*), that which is to be attained (*pattabba*).
