"You ought to be; you are worthy to speak. It is possible to conquer by means of wealth; it is possible to obtain; he will be able to do.
He is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness; he is incapable of doing. You are worthy to receive this gift.
This is fitting to do. It is appropriate to give the gift; one may both give and speak; thus it is proper to say."
“It is not allowable to cut,” and so forth. Likewise: “it is the right time to eat,” “it is the proper occasion to eat,” “it is the hour to eat.
The word “tu” (but/however) is understood [from the previous rule]. 639. [The suffix -tva] occurs after words expressing a vessel and after words having the sense of “sufficient.”
When there is the expression "attained" (*patto*) regarding the meanings of *alaṃ*, the suffix *tuṃ* occurs after all verbal roots. The meanings of the word *alaṃ* are the meanings of *alamattha*:
adornment, mastery, and prohibition; [the suffix occurs] in those meanings of *alaṃ*. The term *pattavacanaṃ* is the statement of what has been attained (*patto*).
The meaning is: "it is sufficient indeed to give gifts," "it is sufficient indeed to perform meritorious deeds," or "mastery has indeed been attained."
In the sense of "having done the work, he went," "he goes," or "he will go":
640. *Tuna*, *tvāna*, or *tvā* [are used] for roots having a single agent in the prior time.

"Prior time" means the prior action; "having a single agent" means those whose agent is one. For those roots having a single agent—that is, having the same agent—these suffixes *tuna*, *tvāna*, and *tvā* optionally occur after a root expressing the prior time.
Because the particle *vāsa* has a fixed optionality (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), the suffix *tuṇ* occurs only in certain instances.

And because those [suffixes] have the technical designation *kita*, and because it is stated that they apply "to those having a single agent," they occur only in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). In the case of *tuṇ*, there is the substitution of *kā* according to the rule "in *tava*, *tuṇ*, etc., *kā* [is substituted]," and due to its being a particle (*nipāta*), there is elision of the *s*.
That [agent] goes to the object (*kamma*) by means of *kātuṇ*: "Sentient beings will suffer for merit not done."

In *tvānatvāsu*, by the rule "and the letter *r*," there is elision of the final of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Having performed a good deed—that is, having performed meritorious acts such as giving—one goes to heaven;
[this means] having conditioned [the action], having done it. Likewise: having sewn, having been born, having caused to be born, having heard the Dhamma.
"Having heard the Dhamma, one rejoices"; [this means] having listened, having reached, having attained. Having bought, having conquered.
*Jinitvā*, *jitvā*; *coretvā*, *corayitvā*; *pūjetvā*, *pūjayitvā*. Likewise: *mettaṃ bhāvetvā*, *bhāvayitvā*;
*vihāraṃ kāretvā*, *kārayitvā*, *kārāpetvā*, *kārāpayitvā*—they will go to heaven, and so forth. For what purpose [is the rule] regarding the "past time" (*pubbakāle*)?
[Examples: *paṭhati*, *pacati*. Why [specify] "having a single agent" (*ekakattukānaṃ*)? [Example: *Bhutte devadatte yaññadatto vajati* (When Devadatta has eaten, Yajñadatta goes).

In such instances as “Having reached the river, the mountain [remains],” and “Having crossed the mountain, the river [flows],” the sense of a single agent and a prior temporal sequence is understood through the connection with the verb “it exists” (*bhavati*).
The particle “or” (*vā*) continues to apply.
641. After all [roots], the suffixes beginning with *tu* [occur].
The substitution of *ya* for the suffix *tun* and others that follow all verbal roots (*dhātu*), whether preceded by prefixes (*upasagga*) or not, is optional.

In the case of *vanda* (to worship), preceded by *abhi*: - For the suffix *tvā*, there is the substitution of *ya* and the augment *i*; thus: *abhivandiya bhāsissaṃ* (I shall speak after having worshipped).

- Alternatively: *abhivanditvā*. - Or: *vandiya*, *vanditvā*. Likewise: - *abhibhuyya* (having overcome); due to the doubling of the consonant and the shortening of the vowel: *abhibhavitvā*, *abhibhotvā*.

In the sense of service (*sevā*), [the form] *nissāya* is derived from the root *ni*, where the vowel *i* becomes *ā* according to the rule beginning with "in some cases, of the roots" (*kvaci dhātū*); [thus: having relied upon, having depended.

In the sense of service (*sevā*), [the form] *bhajja* is derived from the root *bhaj*, where the prior form (*pubbarūpa*) is applied according to the rule "likewise in the agent" (*tathā kattari ca*); [thus: having divided, having distributed, having analyzed.

In the sense of assigning (*atisajjana*), [the forms] *uddissa*, *uddisiya*, and *uddisitvā* [are derived from the root *dis*]. [The forms] *pavissa*, *pavisiya*, and *pavisitvā* [are derived from the root *vis*].
*Nī*: having reached, having brought near, having led. *Atiseyya*: having surpassed. *Ohāya*, *ohitvā*, *jahitvā*, *hitvā*: having abandoned, having left behind. *Ādāya*, *ādiyitvā*: having taken;
[here] the suffix *-ya* occurs by the rule "after roots beginning with *diva*, *-ya*," and the final vowel of the root is elided by the rule "in some cases, the roots...
etc. *Datvā*, *datvāna*: having given. *Pidhāya*, *pidahitvā*: having covered. *Bhuñjiya*, *bhuñjitvā*, *bhotvā*: having eaten. *Viceyya*, *vicinitvā*: having discriminated, having investigated.
*Viññāya*, *vijānitvā*, and *ñatvā* [mean] having understood, having discerned, and having known.
The phrase “according to the source, in cases such as *tuna* and so forth” also applies.
642. The suffix *-dadhanta-* occurs in some instances.
The augment *y* is inserted according to the tradition after roots ending in *d* or *dh*, in certain cases such as before suffixes beginning with *tu*.
From *yava*, the *d* becomes *j*: having entered into, having arisen, having broken, having been cut off, it has gone.

In the root *budh* (to understand), by the rule “*tathā kattari ca*,” the *y* at the end of the *sakhi*-group undergoes the change to the *ca*-group (*cavagga*): *bujjhiya*, *bujjhitvā*. *Virajjhiya*.
Having become detached (*virajjhitvā*). Having obstructed (*rundhiya*, *rundhitvā*).
The governing rule is "of *tu*-beginning [roots]," and there is also the option (*vā*).
643. After roots ending in *-can*, the suffix *-ra* is added.

After verbal roots ending in the letters *c* or *n*, there is optionally the substitution of *racca* for the suffixes beginning with *tu*; by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "racca," this substitution occurs after other [roots] as well.
The word "optionally" (*vā*) here has the sense of a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*). There is the elision of the letter *r*. The root *vic* preceded by *vi* means "separation";
thus we have *vivicca* and *viviccitvā*. By the division of the rule stating "the augment *ya* occurs wherever [possible]," the augment *ya* is inserted.
In the case of *paca* (to cook): *pāke*, *pacca*, *pacciya*, *paccitvā*. In the case of *vimuca* (to release): *vimucca*, *vimuccitvā*.
In the case of *hana* (in the senses of killing and going): *āhacca*, *upahacca*, *āhantvā*, *upahantvā*.
Why [is it] *vāti*? [As in: *avamañña*, *avamaññitvā*, *mantvā*; [and] the letter *ñ* in *nyassa*.

In *gatimhi*, there is the substitution of *racca* by way of *yogavibhāga*; [the forms are] *paṭicca*, *avecca*, *upecca*, and *upetvā*. In *kara* [meaning] instrument (*karaṇe*), [the forms are] *sakkacca*, *adhikicca*, and *kariya*, where there is the addition of the vowel *i*.
In *disa* [meaning] seeing (*pekkhaṇe*)—644. In *disā*, there is the elision of *svāna* and *svānta*.

In place of the suffix *disa*, there is optionally the substitution of *svā* for the following conditions such as *tunā* and so forth, or else there is elision of the final vowel of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Examples: *disvānassa etadahosi* (this occurred to him after seeing), *cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā* (having seen a form with the eye). Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? [To show that it does not apply here:
*nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhuṃ* (to see renunciation), *daṭṭhā* (having seen). [Other forms include] *passiya*, *passituna*, *passitvā*.
The mention of "end" (*anta*) and the mention of "elision of the end" (*antalopa*) continue to apply [in subsequent rules].

645. *Ma-ha-da-bhehi mma yha jja bba ddhā ca.* After verbal roots ending in *m*, *h*, *d*, *b*, *bh*, and *c*, the suffixes beginning with *tu* undergo, respectively, the substitutions *mma*, *yha*, *jja*, *bbha*, *ddhā*, optionally;
furthermore, there is elision of the final letter of the root. First, after roots ending in *m*: *āgamma*, *āgantvā*.
With *k*-ending [gerunds]: *padavikkhepe*, having stepped; *okkamma*, having descended; *okkamitvā*, having descended;

*nikkhamma*, having gone out; *nikkhamitvā*, having gone out; *abhiramma*, having delighted. With *hakāra*-endings: *paggayha*, having taken up; *paggaṇhitvā*, having taken up; *paggahetvā*, having taken up. With *muhā*-endings: *sammuyha*, having become confused; *sammuyhitvā*, having become confused. With the addition of *y*: *āruyha*, having ascended; *āruhitvā*, having ascended; *ogayha*, having plunged; *ogahetvā*, having plunged. With *dakāra*-endings: *uppajja*, having arisen;

*uppajjitvā*, having arisen; *pamajja*, having neglected; *pamajjitvā*, having neglected; *upasampajja*, having attained; *upasampajjitvā*, having attained. With *chid* in the sense of cutting into two: *acchijja*, having cut; *chijja*, having cut; *chijjitvā*, having cut; *chindiya*, having cut; *chinditvā*, having cut; *chetvā*, having cut.

With roots ending in *bhakāra*: *rabha* (to begin) and *rābhasse* (rashness); *ārabbha* (having begun), *kathesi* (he spoke), *āraddhā* (undertaken), *ārabhitvā* (having begun). *Labha* (to obtain) and *lābhe* (in obtaining); *upalabbha* (having obtained), *upaladdhā* (obtained), as in "having acquired faith, they perform meritorious deeds," and so forth.
This is the method for suffixes ending in *tavetunādi*.
Now, the method for suffixes ending in *mānantapaccaya*, which expresses the present tense.
646. *Vattamāne mānantā*.

When the sense (*attha*) is commenced but not yet completed, it is "present" (*vattamāna*). While that present time is being understood, these suffixes ending in *māna* and *anta* occur after all verbal roots (*dhātu*). Because they are designated as *kita*, they apply to the agent (*kattari*) according to the rule “*kittā kitā*.

Furthermore, because the suffixes *anta* and *māna* are subject to the designation of *parassapada* and *attanopada* by virtue of the rule “*parasamaññāpayoge*,” just as in the case of *ty-ādi* suffixes, the *vikaraṇa* suffixes also occur before these *anta* and *māna* suffixes.

By that very same *māna* suffix, it occurs also in the sense of the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*), as in the rule: “*attanopadāni bhāve ca kammani*. Furthermore, for that [suffix], there is sometimes a replacement of the *anta* suffix by the form *parassapadatta*, as in:

“*attanopadāni parassapadattaṃ*. In the case of *gamu* and *sappa* in the sense of “going” (*gatimhi*): 1. Regarding the meaning “he goes” (*gacchatīti*), the *anta* suffix is applied. 2. By the rule “*bhūvādito a*,” the *a* suffix is added. 3.

By the rule “*gamissanto ccho vā sabbāsū*,” the final part of the root (*dhātvanta*) is replaced by *ccha*. 4. Following the elision of vowels (*saralopa*), etc., the designation of a noun (*nāmabyapadesa*) occurs, and the case endings beginning with *si* (*syādi*) arise.

In the case of *gacchanto si*, when the particle *vā* is applied here, the rule *“siṃhi gacchantādīnaṃ ntasaddo aṃ”* prescribes the substitution of *am* for the suffix *nt*. Because the particle *vā* functions as a delimiter (*vavatthi*), a restriction (*bhava*), or an alternative (*vibhāsa*), this substitution does not occur when the suffix follows a single vowel *o* or *ā*;

thus, there is the elision of the vowel and so forth: *so puriso gacchaṃ*, *gacchanto gaṇhāti*. The remainder is the same as in the masculine form ending in *-vantu*. In the feminine, by the rule *“nadādito vā ī”*, the suffix *ī* is added.

Then, by the rule *“sesesu ntuvā”* which prescribes the designation *ntu*, and depending on the particle *vā*, the rule *“ntussa tamīkāre”* applies the substitution of *ta*. Following the elision of the vowel and the elision of the final syllable (*silopa*), we have: *sā kaññā gacchatī*, *gacchantī*, and so forth; this is the same as the feminine form.

In the neuter gender, as in the case of *puri*, there is the substitution of *am* for the ending; thus, *taṃ cittaṃ gacchaṃ*, *gacchantaṃ*, *gacchantāni*, and so forth, are identical to the masculine gender.
Likewise, in the sense of "going," the suffix *māna* is applied, with the substitution of *cch* and so on;

thus, *so gacchamāno gaṇhāti*, *te gacchamānā*, and so forth, are identical to the word *purisa* (man). *Sā gacchamānā*, *tā gacchamānāyo*, and so forth, are identical to the word *kaññā* (woman). *Taṃ*...
“Gacchamānaṃ,” “tāni gacchamānāni,” and so forth, are identical in form to the word *citta*.

In the sense of “it is being gone by,” the suffix *māna* is applied in the passive (*kammani*) according to the rule “*attanopadāni bhāve ca kammanī*”; the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or passive (*kamma*) according to the rule “*bhāvakammesu yo*”;
the vowel *i* is inserted according to the rule “*ivaṇṇāgamo vā*”; and there is the substitution of *ccha*. Thus, it is being gone by that; she...
*Gacchiyamānā*, *taṃ gacchiyamānaṃ*.

In the absence of a suffix (*cchādesābhāve*), by the rule “the preceding form also” (*pubbarūpañca*), the letter *y* becomes *m*: *dhammo adhigammamāno hitāya bhavati*, *adhigammamānā*, *adhigammamānaṃ*.
Likewise, from the root *maha* in the sense of worship (*pūjāyaṃ*): *mahatīti mahaṃ*, *mahanto*, *mahatī*, *mahantī*, *mahaṃ*, *mahantaṃ*, *mahaṃmāno*.
*Mahamānā*, *mahamānaṃ*. Regarding the grammatical function (*kamma*): by the rule “*yamhi dādhāmāṭhāhāpā maha mathādīnamī*,” the vowel *a* at the end of the verbal root is replaced by *ī*;
thus: *mahīyamāno*, *mahīyamānā*, *mahīyamānaṃ*. Likewise: that which moves is *caraṃ*, *caratī*, *carantī*, *carantaṃ*, *caramāno*, *cariyamāno*. That which cooks is *pacaṃ*.
*Pacatī*, *pacantī*, *pacantaṃ*, *pacamāno*, *paccamāno*: by the rule beginning with “*tassa cavagga*,” there is substitution of the *ca*-group (*cavagga*), as well as doubling (*dvitta*).

*Bhū* in the sense of existence (*sattāyaṃ*): in the sense of “he exists” (*bhavatīti*), the suffix *ant* is applied; there is the elision of the suffix (*appaccaya*), the *vṛddhi* vowel substitution, and the replacement of *bha* for *bhava*.
Thus: *so bhavaṃ*, *bhavanto*. In the feminine, the suffix *ī* is applied. By the rule “*bhavato bhoto*,” there is the replacement of *bhavaṃ* with *bhoto*. Thus: *bhotī*, *bhotī*, *bhotiyo*.

In the neuter: *bhavaṃ*, *bhavantaṃ*, *bhavantāni*, *abhibhavamāno*. In the sense of becoming (*bhāve*): *bhūyamānaṃ*. In the sense of an object (*kammani*): *abhibhūyamāno*. Regarding *jara* (decay) in the sense of the loss of youth:

by the rule "in *jara* and *marana*, etc.," there is the substitution of *jīra* for *jīrya*. Thus: *jīratīti jīraṃ*; *jīrantī*, *jīrantaṃ*, *jīramāno*, *jīrīyamāno*, *jīyaṃ*, *jīyantī*, *jīyantaṃ*, *jīyamāno*, *jīyyamāno*.
Regarding *mara* (death) in the sense of the relinquishing of life: by the rule "sometimes in roots, etc.," there is the elision of one *y*-sound. Thus: *maratīti mīyaṃ*; *mīyantī*.
*Mīyantaṃ*, *mīyamāno*, *mīyyamāno*, *maraṃ*, *marantī*, *marantaṃ*, *maramāno*, *marīyamāno*. *Labhaṃ*, *labhantī*, *labhantaṃ*, *labhamāno*, *labbhamāno*.
*Vahaṃ*, *vahantī*, *vahantaṃ*, *vahamāno*, *vuyhamāno*. By the rule “*Isuyamūnamanto ccho vā*,” there is the substitution of *ccha*;
thus, one who desires is *icchaṃ*, *icchantaṃ*, *icchamāno*, *icchamānā*, *icchamānaṃ*. *Icchantī*, *icchantaṃ*, *icchamāno*.
“Icchīyamāno” means desiring. Regarding “disassa, passadissadakkhā vā”:
*passa*, *dissa*, and *dakkhā* are substitutes; one who sees is *passaṃ*, *passantī*, *passantaṃ*, *passamāno*, *vipassīyamāno*, *dissamāno*, *dissanto*;
[in the case of] *māna*, there is the substitution of the final syllable, as in *disaṃ*.
*dissantī*, *dissantaṃ*, *dakkhaṃ*, *dakkhantī*, *dakkhantaṃ*, *dakkhamāno*, *dakkhiyamāno*, and so forth.

*Tuda* in the sense of "to strike" or "to afflict": *tudatīti tudaṃ*, *tudantī*, *tudantaṃ*, *tudamāno*, *tujjamāno*. *Pavisatīti pavisaṃ*, *pavisantī*, *pavisantaṃ*, *pavisamāno*, *pavisīyamāno*, and so forth.
*Hū* and *bhū* in the sense of "existence": with the elision of the suffix (*appaccayalopa*), *pahotīti pahonto*, *pahontī*, *pahontaṃ*, *pahūyamānaṃ*.

By that [root]. *Seti* means lying down; [the forms are] *sentī*, *sentaṃ*, *semāno*, *sayaṃ*, *sayantī*, *sayantaṃ*, *sayamāno*, or *sayāno*—wherein there is the substitution of *ā* for *māna*—and *atisīyamāno*.

From the root *asa* in the sense of existence: according to the rule “*sabbatthāsassādilopo ca*,” there is the elision of the vowel *a*; thus [the forms are] *atthīti saṃ*, *santo*, *satī*, *santī*, *santaṃ*, *samāno*, *samānā*, *samānaṃ*.
In the sense of cessation of motion (*gatini-vatti*), when the particle *vā* is understood, there is the substitution of *ṭhā* for *tiṭṭha*: *tiṭṭhaṃ*, *tiṭṭhantī*, *tiṭṭhantaṃ*, *tiṭṭhamāno*.
In the sense of non-motion (*ṭhābhāve*), by the rule beginning with "in some cases, [the augment is added] to roots" (*kvaci dhātū*), the letter *h* is inserted after *ṭhā* and it is shortened:
*upaṭṭhahaṃ*, *upaṭṭhahantī*, *upaṭṭhahantaṃ*, *upaṭṭhahamāno*. Also: *ṭhīyamānaṃ* (by him), *upaṭṭhīyamāno*, *upaṭṭhahīyamāno*.
*Pā* in the sense of drinking: *pā* becomes *piba* by the rule "pā piba" [when followed by certain suffixes]; thus, *pibatīti pibaṃ*, *pibantī*, *pibantaṃ*, *pibamāno*.
By the rule beginning with "kvaci dhātū," the letter *b* undergoes *vattā*-substitution; thus, *pivaṃ*, *pivantī*, *pivantaṃ*, *pivamāno*, *pīyamāno*, *pīyamānā*, *pīyamānaṃ*, and so forth.
*Hu* in the sense of giving, eating, sacrificing, and bestowing: when the zero-suffix (*appaccaya*) follows, there is reduplication as before; thus, *juhotīti juhaṃ*, *juhantī*.
*Juhantaṃ*, *juhamāno*, *hūyamāno*. Likewise: *jahaṃ*, *jahantī*, *jahantaṃ*, *jahamāno*, *jahīyamāno*.
"He gives" (*dadāti*) thus: *dadaṃ*, *dadantī*, *dadantaṃ*, *dadamāno*; in the absence of reduplication (*dvitta*), [it is] *dānaṃ*, *dento*, *dentī*, *dentaṃ*, *dīyamāno*.

*Rudh* in the sense of obstructing: by the rule "after *rudh* etc., there is the augment *niggahīta* before the suffix," there is the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) before the suffix; thus: *rundhati*.
*rundhaṃ*, *rundhantī*, *rundhantaṃ*, *rundhamāno*, *rujjhamāno*. Regarding *bhuñjatīti*: *bhuñjaṃ*, *bhuñjantī*, *bhuñjantaṃ*, *bhuñjamāno*, *bhujjamāno*, and so forth.
In the root *divu* in the sense of playing, the suffix *ya* is applied by the rule "after *div* and others, *ya*";
then, by the rule "likewise for the agent," there is the substitution of the prior form (*pubbarūpattaṃ*) and the change to *vattaṃ*.
It shines, thus it is *dibbaṃ*; [the forms] *dibbanti*, *dibbantaṃ*, and *dibbamāno*. Likewise, it awakens, thus it is *bujjhaṃ*, *bujjhanto*, and *bujjhamāno*;

here there is the substitution of the *ca*-group (*cavaggādeso*). The root *jan* is used in the sense of manifestation; by the rule "of *jan* and so forth, *ā*" through the division of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāgena*), the vowel *ā* is substituted:
it is born, thus *jāyaṃ*, *jāyamāno*, and *jaññamāno*.

In the case of *su-*, by the rule "after *su*, [the suffixes] *ṇu*, *ṇā*, and *uṇā*," we have *suṇaṃ*, *suṇanto*, *suṇamāno*, *sūyamāno*, and *suyyamāno* (he hears). From *pāpuṇāti* (he reaches), we have *pāpuṇaṃ*, *pāpuṇamāno*, and *pāpīyamāno*.
By the rule "after *kiyādi*, [the suffix] *nā*," there is *nā*; with the shortening of the vowel, from *kiṇāti* (he buys), we have *kiṇaṃ*, *kīṇamāno*, and *kīyamāno*.
From *vinicchināti* (he decides), we have *vinicchinaṃ*, *vinicchinamāno*, and *vinicchīyamāno*; likewise, *cinaṃ* and *cīyamāno*. From *jānāti* (he knows), we have *jānaṃ* and *jānamāno*.
*Jādeso*: when it is understood as *ñā*. *Gaṇhāti* means "he takes"; thus, *gaṇhaṃ*, *gaṇhamāno*, and *gayhamāno*.

In the sense of "doing" (*kara*), in the meaning of "he does," the suffix *-anta* is applied by the rule "in the present tense, the suffix *-anta* [is added] after a root ending in *-m*. Then, by the rule "after *tan* and so on, *o* replaces *i*," the *i* becomes *o*.

Then, having applied the rule "optionally for that," the *utta* (the augment *u*) is inserted before the final syllable. Finally, by the rule "and *u* replaces the *a* of *kara*," the *a* is replaced by *u*. Thus, *kurumāno* is formed.
In the phrase “yavakārā ca,” there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel, the doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*), and by the rule “bo vassā,” the doubling of the letter *b*.
Then, by the rule “kvaci dhātū” and others, there is the elision of *r*. Thus: *kubbaṃ*, *kubbanto*, *kubbatī*, *kubbantī*, *kubbantaṃ*. In the absence of the augment *utt*:
*kammaṃ karonto*, *karontī*, *karontaṃ*. In the honorific (*māna*): the two forms of *utt*, *kurumāno*, *kurumānā*, *kurumānaṃ*.
*kubbāno* (doing). *Kammani kayiramāno*, *karīyamāno* (being done), and so forth.
Regarding *cura* (to steal): by the rule "from *cura* etc. (*curādito*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied;
thus, from *coreti*, we have *corento*, *corentī*, *corentaṃ*, *corayaṃ*, *corayati*, *corayantaṃ*, *corayamāno*, *corīyamāno*. From *pāleti* (to protect), we have *pālento*, *pālentī*, *pālentaṃ*.
*pālayaṃ*, *pālayantī*, *pālayantaṃ*, *pālayamāno*, *pālīyamāno*, and so forth. In the causative (*kārita*), [from the root *bhū*]:
*bhāveti* means "he causes to be," thus *bhāvento*, *bhāventī*, *bhāvantaṃ*, *bhāvayaṃ*, *bhāvayantī*, *bhāvayantaṃ*, *bhāvayamāno*, *bhāvīyamāno*.
From *kāreti* ("he causes to do"): *kāronto*, *kārentī*, *kārentaṃ*, *kārayaṃ*, *kārayantī*.
*kārayantaṃ*, *kārayamāno*, *kārīyamāno*, *kārāpento*, *kārāpentī*, *kārāpentaṃ*, *kārāpayaṃ*,
*kārāpayantī*, *kārāpayantaṃ*, *kārāpayamāno*, *kārāpīyamāno*, and so forth.
This is the method for present-tense forms ending in the suffix *-māna*.
The method for suffixes whose time-reference is the future (*anāgatakālika*) begins with the heading "In time" (*kāle*). 647.
After [roots] such as *gam*, there are the suffixes *ṇī*, *ghi*, and *ṇa* when referring to the future.

When the sense of "future time" (*bhavissati-kāla*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *ṇī*, *ghi*, and *ṇa* are added to verbal roots such as *gam* and others. The letter *ṇ* serves to indicate vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*).

In the sense of "one whose nature is to go in the future," the suffix *ṇī* is applied; [here] there is strengthening and the elision of the suffix marker *ṇ*. Thus: *gāmī*, *gāmino*, *āgāmī kālo* ("a future time"). With the suffix *ghi*:
by the rule "in some cases the root [is modified]" (*kvaci dhātu*), etc., there is the elision of the *gha* suffix marker. Thus: *gāmaṃ gāmi*, *gāmī*, *gāmayo*.

*Bhājī*: one whose nature is to associate (*bhajati*) or serve (*sevāyaṃ*) in the future (*āyati*). *Bhāji* is formed by the rule of separation (*yogavibhāgena*) "there is no substitution of *ka* for *ga*," whereby the suffix *gattaṃ* does not occur according to the rule "for *ja* and *na*, *ka* and *ga* do not follow when *ṇa* is attached.

*Passāvī*: from the root *su* (in the sense of going), with the causative suffix (*kārite*), the vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*) and the substitution of *āva*. One whose nature is to urinate (*passavituṃ*) in the future is a *passāvī*; *passāvi*. *Paṭṭhāyī*: one whose nature is to stand firm (*paṭṭhānaṃ*) in the future. *Paṭṭhāyi* is formed by the substitution of *āya* according to the rule "for those ending in long *ā*, there is *āya*.
The governing heading is "it will be" (*bhavissati*).

648. The suffixes *ṇvu* and *tu* are used for the sense of action (*kiriyā*). When the sense of action is understood from the verbal roots, these suffixes, namely *ṇvu* and *tu*, occur in the future tense. In the case of *ṇvu*: there is elision of *ṇ*, vowel-lengthening (*vuddhi*), and the substitution of *a*. "He goes to do" (*karissaṃ vajati*) is thus *kārako vajati*. In the case of *tu*:

by the rule "the letter *t* replaces the final *ra* of *kara* before the suffix *tu*," the letter *t* is substituted; the remainder is the same as for the agent (*kattusama*). Thus: *kattā vajati*, *kattuṃ*.
The meaning is "he goes. Thus, *pācako vajati* ("the cooker goes") means "he goes thinking, 'I shall cook,'" and *pacitā vajati* ("the cooker goes").
*Bhuñjako vajati* ("the eater goes") means "he goes thinking, 'I shall eat,'" and *bhottā vajati* ("the eater goes"), and so forth. 649.
The suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
When *kamma* is the subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇa* is added to verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the sense of the future tense;
there is elision of *ṇa* and vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). One who will build a city is called a *nagarakāra*. From the root *lū* (to cut), one who will reap rice is called a *sālilāva*.
From *vapa* (to sow), one who will sow grain is called a *dhaññavāpa*. One who will give wealth is called a *bhogadāya*. [One who will cross] the Sindhu...
"He will drink" (*pivissati*) is used in such expressions as "he goes to the river-drinker" (*sindhupāyo vajati*). The term "after a verbal root" (*kammani*) continues [from the previous rule]. 650.
After the remaining [roots], the suffixes *ssaṃ*, *ntu*, *māna*, and *āna* [are applied].

When *kamma* is the subordinate term (*upapada*) and a sense of incompleteness (*aparisamatta*) is intended, the suffixes *-ssam*, *-tu*, *-māna*, and *-āna* occur after verbal roots when a future time (*bhavissati-kāla*) is understood;

these suffixes function in the active voice (*kattari*) because they denote the agent (*kitakattā*). In the sense of "he will do the work" (*kammaṃ karissati*), the suffix *-ssam* occurs, there is the augment *i* (*ikārāgama*), and the elision of the final vowel (*silopa*).
Thus, "I shall go to do the work" (*kammaṃ karissaṃ vajati*) is formed. Because it is dependent (*sāpekkhattā*), no compound (*samāsa*) is formed. [In the case of] the suffix *-ntu*:

In the phrase “*tanādito oyirā*,” *o* [is the suffix]; in “*simhi vā*,” the final *nt* of *ntu* becomes *atta*; and in “*kammaṃ karissatīti kammaṃ karonto vajati*,” etc., it is the same as when there is a person possessing a quality (*guṇavantu*).
Alternatively, regarding the rule “*bhavissati gamādīhi ṇī ghiṇa*,” because of the word “*bhavissati*” here, [the suffix] is *ssantu*.
Only one condition is to be observed: from that, [the form] *simhi* or *vā* [is derived];

by the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the word *am* is *a*," there is the substitution of *am*; [then] the elision of *s*. [The forms are: *karissāmi*, *karissāmo*; *karissasi*, *karissatha*; *karissati*, *karissanti*;
*karissantaṃ*, *karissante*; *karissantā*, *karissantena*, *karissantehi*; *karissato*, *karissantassa*, *karissataṃ*, *karissantānaṃ*; *karissatā*, *karissantehi*.
*karissato*, *karissantassa*, *karissataṃ*, *karissantānaṃ*, *karissati*, *karissante*, *karissantesu*, and so forth, should be understood as being similar to those ending in the suffix *-vant*.
Regarding the honorific (*māna*):

there is the substitution of *utta* for the vowels *o* and *ā*. Thus, one who will do work is expressed as *kammaṃ karissanto*, *kammaṃ karāno*, or *vajati*. Likewise, one who will eat food is expressed as *bhojanaṃ bhuñjissanto*, *bhuñjanto*, *bhuñjamāno*, or *bhuñjāno*, and so forth.
In all instances involving the agent (*kattar*), the respective verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa-paccaya*) must be applied to nouns ending in *ntu* or *māna*.
For example: "He goes to eat" (*khādanaṃ khādissati*) is expressed as *khādanaṃ khādissaṃ vajati*; likewise, *khādanaṃ khādanto*, *khādanaṃ khādamāno*, and *khādanaṃ khādāno vajati*.
Similarly, "he goes to walk on the path" (*maggaṃ carissati*) is expressed as *maggaṃ carissaṃ*, *maggaṃ caranto*, *maggaṃ*...
"Caraṃ" means "going," as in "he goes while walking on the path. Regarding the term *bhikkha* (alms): "He goes for alms" (*bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissati*) means "I shall go for alms";

thus one goes for alms (*bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissaṃ carati*), or "going for alms" (*bhikkhaṃ bhikkhanto*), "while going for alms" (*bhikkhaṃ bhikkhamāno*), or "having gone for alms" (*bhikkhaṃ bhikkhāno carati*), and so forth.
This is the method [of application] for suffixes whose time-reference is future (*anāgatakālika*).
The Method of the *uṇādi* Suffixes.
Now the *uṇādi* suffixes are being stated.
“From a verbal root (*dhātu*)” is the governing rule (*adhikāra*).
651. *Ṇvu* and other suffixes occur when the past or the present time is indicated.
When the past time or the present time is understood, the suffix *ṇu* is added to verbal roots. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), *yu*, *kta*, *mi*, and so forth are also included.

In the sense of "to do" (*kara*) or "having done" (*akāsi*) and "he does" (*karoti*), the suffix *ṇu* is applied; there is elision of *ṇu*, and the vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*. Thus: *kāru* (an artisan), *kārū* (a craftsman).
*Kāru*: from *kṛ*, "to do. *Vāyu*: from *vā*, "to go" or "to blow"; it is called *vāyu* because it has blown (*avāyi*) or it blows (*vāyati*), with the substitution of *ā* for *o*.

*Sādu*: from *sad*, "to taste"; it is called *sādu* because it is tasted (*assādīyati*). *Sādhu*: from *rādha* or *sādha*, "to accomplish"; it is called *sādhu* because welfare is accomplished by means of it (*anena*). *Bandhu*: from *bandha*, "to bind";

it is called *bandhu* because it binds another to itself (*attani paraṃ bandhati*). *Cakkhu*: from *cakṣ*, "to speak clearly"; it is called *cakkhu* because it sees (*cakkhati*). *I*: from *i*, "to go."
*Āyu*: beings go, proceed, or move by means of this; thus it is *āyu*. *Daru*: from the root *dar*, meaning "to split";

that which is split is *dāru*, wood. *Sanu*: from the root *san*, meaning "to give. That which gives is *sānu*, a certain part of a mountain. *Janu*: from the root *jan*, meaning "to be born"; that which is born is *jānu*, the knee joint. *Cāru*: from the root *car*, meaning "to move";

that which moves is *cāru*, beautiful or lovely to behold. *Rahu*: from the root *rah*, meaning "to abandon"; that which abandons is *rāhu*, the lord of the asuras. *Tālu*: from the root *tar*, meaning "to cross"; [the form] *tālu* [is derived here], with the *l* becoming short.

In this context, however, there is no vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*) for *maru* and so forth, due to the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule "of *ghaṭa* and so forth. Thus: *maru*, *taru*, *tanu*, *dhanu*, *hanu*, *manu*, *asu*, *vasu*, *vaṭu*, *garu*, and so on. From the root *cad* in the sense of "rubbing" (*hilādane*), with the suffix *yu*:

by the rule "after *nud* and so forth, there is the substitution of *an*, *ān*, *anak*, *anakā*, and *sakā* [for the suffix] when followed by a causative," there is the substitution of *an* and the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*).

Thus: *candanaṃ*. That in which something exists is *bhuvanaṃ*; here, by the rule "for *jhal* sounds, there is optionally the substitution of *u* or *ū* before a consonant," there is the substitution of *ū*.
*Kira* means scattering; *kiraṇo*. *Vicakkhaṇo*. It causes trembling (*kampanaṃ karoti*), thus it is *karuṇā*; here the letter *a* is elided. In the *ktap* suffix: *kalopo*, *abhavi*;

or, that which becomes (*bhavati*) is *bhūtaṃ*, such as a *yakkha* and so forth; [plural] *bhūtāni*. That which blows is *vāto*; that which protects is *tāto*. In the suffix *min*: that wherein things exist is *bhūmi*; that which leads is *nemi*, and so forth. 652.
After roots beginning with *khī*, *mana* is added, and *ca* and *ta* are optionally substituted.
The suffix *man* occurs after verbal roots such as *khī*, *bhī*, *su*, *ru*, *hu*, *vā*, *dhū*, *hilū*, *pī*, *ad*, *icc*, and so forth; and the *m* of this suffix optionally becomes *t*.
This change of *m* to *t* occurs only when the root does not end in *d*;
it does not occur after any other [root], due to the fixed optionality of the rule.

In the sense that "calamities, obstacles, and the like perish (*khīyanti*) here," the suffix *man* is applied; by the rule "in some cases [there is] elision of *na* from the root" (*kvaci dhātū*), there is elision of *na*, and by the rule "and in other cases," there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), resulting in *khemo*.
Likewise, from *bhī* in the sense of fear (*bhaye*), it is "that from which they fear" (*bhāyanti etasmā*), thus *bhīmo*;

because of the governing rule [of the preceding section], there is no *vṛddhi*. From *su* in the sense of flowing (*abhisave*), it is "it flows" (*savati*), thus *somo*. From *ru* in the sense of motion (*gatimhi*), *romo*. From *hu* in the senses of giving, eating, and bestowing (*dānādanahabyappadānesu*), [it is *homa*].
It is called *homa* because it is offered (*hūyati*). From the root *vā*, meaning "to go" or "to smell," comes *vāma*. From *dhū*, meaning "to shake," comes *dhūma* because it shakes (*dhunāti*).

From *hi*, meaning "to go," comes *hema* because it causes one to go (*hinoti*). From *lū*, meaning "to cut," comes *loma* because it is cut (*lūyati*). From *pī*, meaning "to satisfy," comes *pema* as the act of satisfying (*pīṇanaṃ*).

From *ada*, meaning "to eat," comes *atta* in the sense that it eats (*adati*); the *m* becomes *t*, and the *t* is substituted for *d* according to the rule "for *da*, there is *ta*. Thus: *attā*, *ātumā*; [also] "in some cases..."
By [the rule] beginning with "dhātū," there is lengthening of the vowel *a* and the insertion of the letter *u*. In the sense of "going" (*yā*), it becomes *yāma*.
While the particle "or" (*vā*) is being carried over—[rule] 653: "After *samā*, [the suffix] *thamā* [is added]."

The suffixes *tha* and *ma* optionally occur after roots such as *sama*, *dama*, *dara*, *raha*, *lapa*, *vasa*, *yu*, *du*, *hi*, *si*, *dā*, *sā*, *ṭhā*, *bhasa*, and *bahau*. *Sama* means "to pacify. Because of the governing rule regarding the inclusion of certain letters (*kvaciggahaṇādhikārā*), there is no elision of the final vowel of the root.
Thus, that which pacifies the defilements (*kilese*) is *samatha*, which is *samādhi* (concentration).

Similarly, *damana* is *damatho* (taming). *Dara* means "to burn"; the act of burning is *daratho*, which is feverish distress (*paridāho*). *Raha* means "to take up" (*upādāne*); that which is taken up is *rahīyati*.
In *ratha*, there is the elision of the consonant (*halopa*) according to the rule beginning with “*kvaci dhātū*. In *akkosa* (abuse), *sap* [is the root]; the state of swearing is *sapatha*.
In *vasa* (to dwell), *āvasatho* means that which they dwell in. In *yu* (to mix), *yūtho*; [here] the vowel is long. In *du* (in the sense of movement and growth), *dumō* means that which grows;
thus it is a tree (*duma*). In *hinoti* (he impels), *himō* means dew. In *si* (binding), *sīmā* means that which is bound; [here] the vowel is long. In *dā* (cutting), *dāmo* (a tether).

The root *sām* means "to be capable"; [from it comes] *sāma*. The root *ṭhā* means "cessation of motion"; [from it comes] *ṭhāma*, where the state of being stationary (*thattaṃ*) is derived from *ṭha*.

The root *bhas* means "to reduce to ashes"; [from it comes] *bhasmā*, with the vowel lengthening (*āttaṃ*) by the rule "after *brahma*, etc., *syā*. The root *bah* means "increase"; [from it comes] *brahmā*, where *ba* becomes *bro* by way of irregular derivation (*nipātanato*).
The root *usu* means "to burn"; [from it comes] *usmā*, and so forth.
654. *Masussa sussa ccharaccherā*.

For the root *masu*, when followed by the suffix *su*, the substitutes *cchara* and *cchera* occur. [In the sense of] *masu* = *macchera*, with the suffix *kvip*, and the substitutions *cchara* and *cchera*, we have *maccharo* and *macchero*.
The phrase “*cchara ccherā*” continues [to apply].
655. *Āpubbacarassa ca*:
For the root *cara* preceded by *ā*, the substitutes *cchara* and *cchari* occur; by the word *ca* (and), the substitute *cchariya* also occurs.
In the sense of "wandering intensely," there is the suffix *kvip*, the substitution of *cchariya* and so forth, and shortening of the vowel. Thus: *acchariyaṃ* (marvelous) and *accharaṃ* (a clap).
*Accheraṃ*. It is called *acchariyaṃ* because it is worthy of clapping one's hands (*accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti*).

656. From the roots *ala*, *kala*, and *sala*, the suffixes *la* and *ya* occur. *Ala* in the sense of completion: *allaṃ*, *alyaṃ*. *Kala* in the sense of counting: *kallaṃ*, *kalyaṃ*. *Sala* and *hula* in the sense of going (*pada-gatimhi*): *sallaṃ*, *salyaṃ*.
The rule “kala salehi” applies.
657. *Yāṇa* and *lāṇā*:
after those roots beginning with *kala* and *sala*, the suffixes *yāṇa* and *lāṇa* occur. Examples: *kalyāṇaṃ*, *paṭisalyāṇaṃ*, *kallāṇo*.
Regarding *paṭisallāṇo*: when the verbal root is *silesana*, then [the form] *paṭisallayanaṃ* or *paṭisallāṇaṃ* is established by means of the suffix *-ya*.
Therein, the nasal (*niggahīta*) of the prefix is replaced by *l*; the *n* is replaced by *ṇ* because it is followed by *ra* and so forth;
and the vowel *e* is replaced by *a* by the rule beginning with "In some cases, [the suffix] *at* [is added] to roots."
658. *Mathissa tha-lassa lō*. For the letter *tha* of this root *math*, there is the substitution of *la*;
by the word *ca* (and), the suffix *la* is also included. The root *math* means "to stir" (*viloḷane*). Thus, *mallō*; and that very thing is *mallakō*, just as *hīnakō* [is derived from *hīna*].
The term "kicca" (grammatical operation) is understood to carry over.
659. The suffix *ṇī* occurs after the words *avassaka*, *adhammiṇa*, and *icca*.

Regarding these meanings, the suffix *ṇī* is applied; because it is a *kicca*-suffix, the *ṇī*-suffix [is used]. [In this case,] there is elision of *ṇ*, vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and elision of the feminine suffix (*silopa*).

"You are fit to perform my work necessarily" means: "my work is necessarily to be done by you" (*me kammaṃ avassaṃ kātuṃ yutto si*); "my work is necessarily to be done by the doer" (*kārino me kammaṃ avassaṃ*).
"You will certainly bear my burden"—this is the sense of *dhārī asi*.

"You are capable of paying me a hundred [coins] of debt"—thus, "you are a payer (*dāyī*) of a hundred-debt to me," or "you are a bearer (*dhārī*) of a thousand-debt to me," and so forth. However, the suffixes for the verbal action (*kicca-paccaya*) have already been shown above.
660. From *vajja* and other roots, words such as *pabbajjā* are derived as primary nouns (*nipacca*).

This is the section on *ākati* (irregular) groups. Words such as *pabbajjā* and others are derived through the application of suffixes, substitutions, elisions, augmentations, prohibitions, and rules for gender and so forth, according to their respective definitions, from verbal roots such as *vaja*.

The root *vaja* in the sense of "going" is preceded by the prefix *pa-*. In the sense of "that which must first be gone to," with reference to the rule "for the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule "*ṇyocā*.
Following the elision of *ṇ* and other operations, when the form *pavvajjā* is reached, this [rule] effects the substitution of *jjā* for *jjha*, and [the doubling] of the two *v* sounds.
The two forms *baka*, the prohibition of *vuddhi* (vowel strengthening), and the feminine gender are applied in the following derivations: *pabbajjā*.

Likewise, from the root *iñj* in the sense of shaking, *iñjana* becomes *ijjā*; from *yaja* in the sense of worshipping a deity, *yajana* becomes *ijjā*, with the substitution of *it* for the suffix according to the rule “*yajassādissī*”;

from *añj* in the senses of excellence and motion, preceded by the prefix *sam-*, *samañjana* becomes *samajjā*, with the substitution of *jj* for *ñjh*. From *sad* in the senses of departing, going, and ending—

*Nisīdana* means sitting. *Vid* means knowledge; thus, the act of knowing (*vijānana*) or that which knows (*vidati*) is *vijjā*. *Saja* means to release; thus, the act of releasing (*vissajjana*) is *vissajjā*.
*Pada* means to go; thus, the act of lying down (*nipajjana*) is *nipajjā*. *Hana* is used in the senses of harming and going;

when the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of "that which is to be killed," the substitution of *vadha* for *hana* occurs according to the rule: "Or *vadha* [is substituted] for *hana* in all cases."
By the rule *jhassiminā*, there is the substitution of *jjh*; thus, he is one to be slain (*vajjha*), she is one to be slain (*vajjhā*).
From the root *sī* (to lie down), there is the word *seyyā*—meaning "lying down" or "that wherein they lie"—with the suffix *ya* and the doubling of the letter *y*.

From the root *dhā* (to hold) with the prefix *sam-*, meaning "by which one properly directs the mind," or "one has faith oneself," the suffix *atiyava* is applied in the feminine according to the rule *“itthiyamatiyavo vā”* when the form *sandhā* is reached.

By this [rule], *n* becomes *d*: *saddhā*. In the root *cara* (to walk), when the sense is "walking" (*caraṇa*), after applying the suffix *ṇya* and the augment *i*, by this [rule] the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is applied: *cariyā*.

In the root *ruj* (to afflict), when the sense is "afflicting" (*rujana*), after applying the suffix *cha*, [the rule] "and for that which ends in a consonant, *c* is substituted before the suffixes beginning with *cha*" applies.
The letter *c* at the end of the verbal root is established by the suffixes *ucchā*, *rujā*, and *a*. Likewise, from *kuc* (contraction), with the suffix *cha*, *kocanaṃ* becomes *kucchā*.
From *labh* (to obtain), with the suffix *cha*, there is the substitution of *c*, resulting in *lacchā*. From *rad* (scratching), *racchā*.
From *muh* (bewilderment), *muyhanaṃ* becomes *mucchā*, or alternatively, *mucchanam* becomes *mucchā*. From *vas* (dwelling), *vacchā*. From *kac* (splendor), [with the suffix *cha*, *kacchā*].
*Kacchā*: The root *katha* means "to speak. With the prefix *sam-*, in the sense of "speaking together," the suffix *ṇya* is applied;
by this [rule], there is the substitution of *cch* for *thya*, and the substitution of *s* for the word *sam*; thus, *sākacchā*. *Tuda* means "to afflict. *Tucchā*. *Pada* means "to go.

In the sense of "afflicting" (*byāpajjana*), when the suffix *ṇya* is applied, the form *byāpādyā* is reached; by this rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the substitution of *jj* for *dya* and shortening of the vowel; thus, *byāpajjā*.
From the root *mṛ* (to die), by means of this [suffix] *tya*, with the elision of the final consonant of the verbal root (*dhātu*), and then by the rule “*yavata*” etc., the letter *c* is added:
thus *macca* (mortal) and *maccu* (death). From *sat* (to exist) and *sāt* (to endure), by means of this [suffix] *ya*, the *t* becomes *c*:

thus *sacca* (truth). Likewise, from *nat* (to bend the limbs), *nacca* (dance). From *nit* (to go out), *nicca* (constant). From *mā* (to measure/pride), *māyā* (illusion/deceit). From *jan* (to be born),...
In the case of *jāyā*, *kana* is substituted for the [final] vowels (*ditti-kantīsu*), and *ñatta* and *dvitta* are replaced by *kaññā*. In the case of *dhana* and *dhañña*, it is *dhañña*.
That which purifies is *puñña*; there is the addition of the letter *n*, and so forth.
661. When preceded by *ve*, *pu*, *sī*, *da*, *va*, *mu*, *ku*, *dā*, *bhū*, *hva*, etc., the suffix *ṇi* is produced after the root vowel (*thutti*).

From roots such as *vep* (to tremble), *sīd* (to sink), and *muc* (to release), and from *ku*, *dā*, *bhū*, and so forth, as well as from *hvā* and others, the suffixes *thu* and *maṇi* respectively occur in the sense of "produced from" (*nibbatta*).
In the case of *vep* (trembling), the suffix *thu* is added; by the rule "in some cases [there is] an augment of *a* to the root," there is the insertion of the vowel *a*.
Alternatively, it should be understood that although one ought to say *athū*, the form *thū* is stated after eliding the initial vowel. Thus, [it means] "produced by trembling."
*Vepathu*: trembling. From *sī*, meaning "to lie down"; produced by lying down is *sayathu*. From *dav*, meaning "to play"; produced by playing is *davathu*.
From *vam*, meaning "to vomit"; produced by vomiting is *vamathu*.
*Kutti* means "making"; produced by that is *kuttimaṃ*. Due to the grammatical substitution (*nipātana*) of *karassa* (of making) as *kuttaṃ*, [it becomes *kuttimaṃ*]. From *dā*, meaning "to give."
*Dāti* means giving; that which is produced by that is *dattima*, with the shortening of the vowel. *Bhūti* means existence; that which is produced by that is *bhottima*.

*Avahuti* means carrying away; that which is produced by that is *ohāvima*, [formed] by the elision of the suffix *-ṇa*, the lengthening of the vowel, and the substitution of *ā* for *o*. 662. In the sense of abuse, the suffixes *-namha* and *-ani* are applied.
When the words *akkose* (in abuse) and *gammamāne* (being reviled) are present as co-occurring terms (*upapada*), the suffix *āni* arises after a verbal root.

In the sense of "O wretch, that place is not to be gone to," the suffix *āni* is applied; because it is treated like a noun due to its *kit*-character, when the feminine suffix *si* is added, there is a *kammadhāraya* compound in the sense of "one who does not go" (*na gamānī*).
The *na* takes the form of the stem (*atta*), and again, because it is a compound, it is treated like a noun, resulting in the addition of case endings (*syādi*).
"Your birthplace has come to you; no deed should be done by you, my child—thus, my child, do not perform such a deed.
Why "namhi"? As in: "Failure has come to you. Why "akkose"? As in:
"A bad path has come to you. 663. *Sunassa-suno-ṇava-anu-vā-anu-nuna-khuṇā-nā.*

For the word *sunetta*, which is related to *pāṭipadika* (the first day of the lunar fortnight), the substitutes *oṇa*, *vāna*, *uvāna*, *una*, *unakha*, *uṇa*, *ā*, and *āna* occur [in place of the final syllable].

When the substitutes beginning with *oṇa* have been applied to *sunassa* and the subsequent case-ending (*paranayana*) has been effected, the formation of the case-endings (*syādyuppatti*) results in:
*soṇo*, *soṇā*; *svāno*, *svānā*; *suvāno*, *suvānā*; *suno*, *sunā*; *sunakho*, *sunakhā*; *suṇo*, *suṇā*.
*sā sāno*, *sānā*, and so forth.
664. *Taruṇassa susu ca*:
for the word *taruṇa*, the substitute *susu* occurs. The particle *ca* has the sense of non-restriction; thus, it may be either *susu* or *taruṇa*.
665. *Yuva*, *suvassu*, *vassu*, *vānu*, *nūna*.

For the word *yuvan* occurring at the beginning of a compound, the substitutes *uva*, *uva*, *ānu*, *āna*, *ūna*, and *ūna* are applied. Thus: *yuvā tiṭṭhati*, *yuvāno tiṭṭhati*, *yuno tiṭṭhati*, *yūno tiṭṭhati*.
666. From *chada* and others, the suffix *tatraṇa*.
The suffixes *tatraṇa* and others occur after verbal roots such as *chad* and so forth. The root *chad* means "to cover" (*apavāraṇe*).
By the rule "sometimes [the suffix] after a root," etc., the letter *t* is substituted for the final letter of the root. That which covers the sun is *chattaṃ* (an umbrella); it is also *chatraṃ*.

In the three consonants, there is the elision of one of those that are identical in form. The root *cint* means "thinking. That which thinks is *cittaṃ* (mind). Because the letter *n* is followed by a conjunct consonant, it becomes a nasal stop (*niggahīta*). Its elision occurs by the rule "also before a consonant. [From the same root: *citram* (variegated), where there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) because of the rule "optionally for *ghaṭa* and others."

In the case of *su* in the sense of "pressing," its doubling occurs by the rule "doubling [occurs] in the sense of place" (*paradvebhāvo ṭhāne*), resulting in *sutta*, which means "that which presses out meaning.

In *sūda* in the sense of "flowing," it means "it flows out meaning," hence *sutta*; here there is shortening, elision of the suffix *dal* due to its being listed among the *bhujādi* group, and doubling. In *su* in the sense of "hearing," it means "he hears," hence *sota* (ear) or *sotra*;

here there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). In *ni* in the sense of "leading," it means "it leads," hence *netta* or *netra*. In *vida* in the sense of "auspiciousness," the suffix *ta* replaces *da*, resulting in *pavitta* or *pavitra*. In *pū* in the sense of "purifying," it means "it purifies," hence *pavitta* or *pavitra*; here there is the insertion of the letter *i*, vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and the substitution of *ava* for the root vowel.
*Pat* in the sense of going: it goes, thus *patta*, *patra*; it protects one who goes, thus *patto*, *patro*.
*Tan* in the sense of spreading: it spreads, thus *tanta*, *tantra*. *Yat* in the sense of effort: *yatta*, *yatra*. *Yā* in the sense of wandering:
wandering, thus *yāpanā*, *yatrā*. *Yam* in the sense of ceasing: *yanta*, *yantra*. *Ad* in the sense of eating: it eats, thus *atta*, *atra*. *Yuj* in the sense of joining: it joins, thus...
*yottaṃ* (cord), *yotraṃ* (cord); due to the suffixes *bhujādi* and the doubling of the final radical (*dvittā*).
*Vatu* in the sense of turning: *vattaṃ* (turn), *vattraṃ* (turn). *Mida* in the sense of moistening: that which is moistened is *mittaṃ* (friend), *mitraṃ* (friend).

*Mā* in the sense of measuring: *mattā* is measurement; [the forms] *dvitta*, *rassatta*, and *ni*. Likewise, he purifies (*punāti*) thus: *putto*, *putro* (son). *Kala* in the sense of counting: *kalattaṃ* (wife).
*Kalatra* means wife (*bhariyā*). *Vara* is in the sense of restraining; hence *varatta*, *varatra*, meaning a leather thong. *Vepu* is in the sense of trembling;
that which trembles is *vetta*, *vetra*.
*Gupa* is in the sense of concealing; hence *gotta*, *gotra*. By the rule "and for *gup* etc.," there is elision of the final radical and doubling of the consonant, resulting in *gatta*.
Or, by the rule beginning with “kvaci dhātū,” the letter *u* becomes *a*. From the root *dā* (to cut), we have *dāttaṃ* and *dātraṃ* (sickle).
From *hu* (to sacrifice), *aggihuttaṃ* (fire-sacrifice). From *vaha* (to carry), *vahittaṃ* and *vahitraṃ* (boat).
From *cara* (to move), *carittaṃ* and *caritraṃ* (conduct). From *muc* (to release), *muttaṃ* (urine/excrement). From *bhāsa* (to shine), *bhastrā* (bellows), and so forth.

667. The suffix *ṇit* occurs after roots such as *vada*, *cara*, *vara*, and so forth, when the sense of a "group" (*gaṇa*) is implied. *Vada* means "distinct speech": the group of those who speak is *vāditta*. *Cara* means "wandering":
the group of those who wander is *cāritta*. *Vara* means "choosing": [the group of those who choose is *varitta*].

*Vārittaṃ* is the state of having avoided (*varitānaṃ*) [unwholesome conduct]. Alternatively, it is *cārittaṃ* because those who fulfill [the training] practice (*caranti*) therein. It is *vārittaṃ* because they protect themselves (*tāyanti*) from what has been prohibited (*vāritaṃ*) by means of this [training], or in this [training].
[The suffix] *-tta* occurs after roots such as *mid*.

The suffixes *mi*, *tti*, and *ti* occur according to their respective designations after verbal roots such as *mida*, *pada*, *ranja*, *tanu*, *dhā*, and so forth. *Metti*: it is called *metti* because one is moistened (*mijjati*) or cleansed (*siniyhati*);

there is elision of the final part of the root. *Patti*: it is called *patti* because one reaches (*pajjati*). *Ratti*: from the root *ranja* in the sense of coloring (*rāge*); it is called *ratti* because one is colored therein (*ranjati ettha*).

*Tanti*: it is called *tanti* because it is expanded (*vitthārīyati*). *Dhāti*: it is called *dhāti* because she supports (*dhāreti*). *Pāti*: from the root *pā* in the sense of protecting (*rakkhaṇe*), it is *pāti*. *Vasati*: from the root *vasa* in the sense of dwelling (*nivāse*), it is *vasati*.
669. *Usuranjadaṃsānaṃ daṃsassa daḍḍho ḍha ṭhā ca.* After the roots *usu*, *ranja*, and *daṃsa*, the substitution *daḍḍha* occurs for *daṃsa*;
after the remaining roots, the suffixes *ḍha* and *ṭha* occur. [The roots are] *usu* (to burn), *ranja* (to color/attach);
with the suffixes *ḍha* and *ṭha*, [the form is derived] by [the rule] "In some cases, [the root undergoes change]... and so forth.

There is elision of the final vowel of the base, doubling of the consonant, and the substitution of *uḍḍha* for *raṭṭha*. From the root *daṃsa* in the sense of biting, with the suffix *kvip*, there is elision of *kvip* and the substitution of *daḍḍha* for *daṃsa*;
thus, *daḍḍhaṃ*. 670. After *sū*, *usāna*, *mū*, and *usāna*, *tha* is substituted for *a*.
When *sū*, *vu*, and *asa*—these roots—end in *ū*, *u*, or *as*, there is a substitution of *ataicc* (the suffix *icca* with the replacement of *a*), and the suffix *tha* is added at the end.
*Sū* in the sense of harming: *satthaṃ* (weapon). *Vu* in the sense of covering: *vatthaṃ* (garment). *Asa* in the sense of existence: *attho* (meaning/purpose).

However, when the roots *sa* in the sense of harming, *vas* in the sense of covering, and *ara* in the sense of going are used, then by the rule “*samādīhi tha mā*,” the suffix *tha* is applied; [and] “*kvaci*”...

By the rule beginning with "dhātu," there is the elision of the final vowel of the root; by the rule beginning with "vagge ghosā," there is doubling of the consonant. That which cuts is "satthaṃ" (weapon);
that which is worn is "vatthaṃ" (garment);
that which is sought after is "attho" (meaning/object). 671. After roots such as *ranj*, the suffixes *dha*, *di*, *da*, and *ki* are applied, and in some cases, the letters *ja* and *da* are elided.

From verbal roots such as *rañj*, *ud*, and others, the suffixes *dha*, *da*, *idda*, *ka*, and *ira* occur in certain instances; furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letters *ja* and *da* at the end of the verbal roots.

In the sense of "coloring" (*rāge*), from the root *rañj*, with the suffix *dha* and the elision of *ja*, we have *randhaṃ*. In the senses of "exuding" and "moistening" (*pasavanakledanesu*), from the root *ud* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *da*, we have *samuddo*;

[without the prefix] *uddo*. In the sense of "hunger" (*pipāsāyaṃ*), from the root *khud*, we have *khuddo*. In the sense of "cutting into two" (*dvidhākaraṇe*), from the root *chid*, we have *chiddo*. In the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyaṃ*), from the root *rud*...

*Ruddha* means cruel; *luddha*, *lo* (the short form). *Bhadi* means auspicious; *bhadda*. *Nidi* means contempt; *niddā* (sleep). *Muda* means laughter; *muddā* (a seal). *Dala* means in a miserable state;
with the suffix *-idda*, it becomes *dalidda* (poor). *Susa* means drying up, or *suca* means sorrow;

with the suffix *-ka*, the final consonant of the root becomes *k*, thus *sukkaṃ* (white/dried). *Vaca* means distinct speech; or *vaka* means taking; thus *vakkaṃ* (kidney). *Saka* means power; *sakka* (Śakra/Indra). *Usu* means burning; *ukkā* (a torch).
In the root *vaja* (to go), with the suffix *-ira*, it becomes *vajira*, meaning "that which moves unimpeded. In the root *mada* (intoxication), it becomes *madirā*.
Likewise: *mandira*, *rudhira*, *ruhira*, *rucira*. In the root *badha* (binding), it becomes *badhira*, *badhirā*, *badhiraṃ*;
*timira*, *timiraṃ*, *siro*. In the root *sara* (injury), it becomes *sarira*. In words such as *kalila* and *salila*, there is the substitution of *la* for *ra*.
*Kuṭila*, *kokila*, and so forth. 672.
*Paṭita* [is derived] from *hiraṇa* and *hīraṇa*.
For the root *hi* meaning "to go," preceded by *paṭi*, the substitutes *hiraṇa* and *hīraṇa* occur. *Hi* [is used] in the sense of going, preceded by *paṭi*.

In the sense of "going after having crushed the adversary," the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvicā"; there is the elision of *kvip*, and by this [rule], the substitution of *heraṇa* for *hīraṇa* occurs;
then the elision of *ṇa*, and by the rule "vṛddhi in those [cases]," there is the *vṛddhi* of the first vowel of the prefix *paṭi*, resulting in *pāṭiheraṃ* or *pāṭihīraṃ*.
However, when the root is *hara* in the sense of "carrying away," then it is established as *pāṭihāriyaṃ* by means of the suffix *ṇya*, in the sense of "one who carries away the adversary."
673. *Kaḍyādīhi ko*:
The suffix *ka* occurs after verbal roots such as *kaḍi* and others.

After the root *kaḍi* (in the sense of cutting), when the suffix *ka* is applied, [the vowel *i* is elided] by the rule "In some cases, of a root," etc., or by the rule "And a nasalized consonant (*niggahīta*)," since it has the letter *i* as its marker.

There is the insertion of a *niggahīta* (anusvāra) after the root-vowel, and the addition of the suffix *-ka*. The *niggahīta* becomes the final letter of its respective class (*vaga*). Thus: from *kaṇḍ* with the sense of "arrow," we have *kaṇḍo*; and with the sense of "measure," *kaṇḍo*.

Likewise, from *ghaṭ* in the sense of "striking," we have *ghaṭṭo*, or *ghaṇṭo* and *ghaṇṭā*. From *vaṭ* in the sense of "turning," or from *vaṭ* in the senses of "supporting," "binding," or "joining," we have *vaṇṭo*.
From *karaḍ* in the sense of "receptacle," we have *karaṇḍo*. From *maḍ* in the sense of "adornment," we have *maṇḍo*. From *saḍ* in the sense of "cluster," [we have *saṇḍo*].
*Saṇḍo*: [from] *saṇḍi*, in the sense of being broken; *saṇḍa*. *Bhaḍi* is in the sense of a commodity; *bhaṇḍa*. *Paḍi* is in the sense of deficiency of gender;

*paṇḍo*, which is the same as *paṇḍaka* (a eunuch). *Daḍi* is in the sense of command; *daṇḍo* (a staff). *Raḍi* is in the sense of harming; *raṇḍo* (a widower). *Taḍi* is in the sense of movement; *vitaṇḍo* (sophistry). *Caḍi* is in the sense of ferocity; *caṇḍo* (fierce).

*Gaḍi* is in the sense of accumulation; *gaṇḍo* (a boil). *Aḍi* is in the sense of an egg; *aṇḍo* (an egg). *Laḍi* is in the sense of disgust; *laṇḍaṃ* (excrement). *Meḍi* is in the sense of crookedness.
*Meṇḍa*, *meṇḍaka*. From the root *eraḍi* in the sense of harming: *eraṇḍa*. From *khaḍi* in the sense of cutting: *khaṇḍa*. From *madi* in the sense of laughing: *manda*.
From *idi* in the sense of supreme sovereignty: *inda*. From *cadi* in the sense of desire and longing: *canda*. From *khura* in the sense of cutting: *khura*, and so forth.
The word "ko" (who) is understood to carry over.
674. Regarding *khanda*, *andha*, and *gandha*:
for the roots *khād* (to eat), *am* (to go), and *gam* (to go), these substitutes—*khanda*, *andha*, and *gandha*—are applied, and the suffix *kappa* is also added.
*Khād* means "eating"; it is called a *khandha* (aggregate) because it is devoured by the sufferings of saṃsāra, such as birth, aging, and death.

*Āma* means disease; *andha* means blind. *Gama* means a snake; *gandha* means odor. By the inclusion of the suffix *-ka*, there are the forms *khandhaka*, *andhaka*, and *gandhaka* when the collective sense (*kalāpa*) is absent.

Alternatively, *khandha* is used in the sense of a heap (*rāsa*). *Gandha* means to indicate (*sūcana*); it is called *gandha* because it indicates or points out its own support. 675. It is sufficient [to explain] with the examples beginning with cloth (*paṭa*).
The suffix *ala* occurs after roots such as *paṭa* and others, as well as after primary nouns (*pāṭipadika*). In the sense of "going" (*gati*), there is the root *aṭa*;
in the sense of "sufficient" (*alaṃ*) or "capable" (*samattha*), the suffix *ala* is applied by this rule. With the insertion of *si*, there is the substitution of *am*. Thus: *paṭalaṃ*, *paṭalāni*.
Likewise, from *kala* in the sense of "mud" (*kalala*), we have *kalalaṃ*. From *kusa* in the senses of "cutting," "giving," and "accumulating," we have *kusalaṃ*. But when [the root] *sala* is...

The root *lā* means "to move. Thus, it is derived as *kusala* either through the sense of moving (*salana*) in a base way, or through the sense of cutting (*lavana*) weeds (*kusa*), or through the sense of being cut like a weed, or because it is to be obtained by means of a weed (*kusa*).
The formation of the word should be understood through the suffixes *appa* or *kappa*.
*Kada* means "intoxication" (*made*); hence *kadalaṃ*. *Bhagaṇda* means "to sprinkle" (*secane*); hence *bhagandalaṃ*. *Mekha* means "a variegated waistband"; hence *mekhalaṃ*, *mekhalā*.
Or: from the root *vakk* (to bark), *vakkalaṃ* (bark); from *takka* (tree-resin), *takkalaṃ* (resin); from *palla* (low-lying place), *pallalaṃ* (marsh);
from *sadda* (greenery), *saddalaṃ* (grass)—here there is elision of the final vowel (*paralopa*). From *mūla* (foundation), *mulālaṃ* (root)—here there is shortening of the vowel.
From *bila* (support), *bilālaṃ* (cat). From *vida* (existence), *vidālaṃ* (cat). From *caḍi* (fierceness), *caṇḍālo* (outcaste)—here there is lengthening of the vowel.
The root *vā* is used in the senses of going and smelling; thus, *vālaṃ*. The root *vasa* means to cover; thus, *vasala*. The root *paci* means extension;
thus, *pacalo*, *pañcālo*—the latter being derived as "the territory (*ala*) of five kings (*pañca-rājūnaṃ*).

The root *maca* means to steal; thus, *macalo*. The root *musa* means theft; thus, *musalo*. The root *gotthu* means lineage; thus, *gotthulo*. The root *puthu* means extension; thus, *puthulo*. The root *bahu* means enumeration; thus, *bahulaṃ*, with the elision of the final vowel (*paralopa*). However, when the root is *lā* in the sense of taking, then *gotthuṃ lāti* (he takes the lineage) becomes *gotthulo*. Likewise for *puthulo* and *bahulaṃ*.
From the root *maṅg* in the sense of "auspiciousness," *maṅgalaṃ*. From *baha* in the sense of "increase," *bahalaṃ*. From *kamb* in the sense of "movement," *kambalaṃ*.
From *sab* in the sense of "a circle," *sambalaṃ*; there is the addition of the *niggahīta*, or it is *sabalaṃ*. From *agg* in the sense of "going" or "crookedness," *aggalaṃ*.
From *maḍi* in the sense of "adornment," *maṇḍalaṃ*. From *kuḍi* in the sense of "burning," *kuṇḍalaṃ*, and so forth.
676. *Puthassa puthu-pathā vā*.
For this root *putha*, the substitutes *puthu* and *patha* occur, and the suffix *am* optionally follows; in some instances, this word "optionally" (*vā*) has that specific meaning.
The root *putha* means "to spread"; in the sense of "spread out," the suffix *kvip* is applied. By this [rule], the substitutes *puthu* and *patha* are substituted for *putha*.

There is elision of *kv*. When forming the feminine, the suffix *ī* is added; by the rule *“o sare ca”* (and before a vowel), the word *ca* indicates the substitution of *ava* for *o*, resulting in *puthavī*, *pathavī*, or *padhavī*.
The substitution of *tha* for *th* occurs [by another rule]; when the suffix *ama* is added, there is the substitution of *pa* for *tha*, resulting in *pathama*.
677. From *sasva* and so forth, the suffix *tu* is added.
The suffixes *du* and *iccete* arise after verbal roots such as *sasū*. In the sense of "harming" (*hiṃsā*) and "going" (*gati*), from the root *sas*, the suffix *tu* is applied;

by the rule "in some cases [the final letter of] a root," etc., the final *t* of the root is changed to *k*, resulting in *sattu*. From *jana* in the sense of "producing" (*janana*), *jattu*. From *dada* in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), *daddu* (a specific type of leprosy).
From *ada* in the sense of "eating" (*bhakkhaṇa*), *addu*. From *mada* in the sense of "intoxication" (*ummāda*), *maddu*, and so forth.

678. The suffix *īvara* occurs after roots such as *ci*, *pā*, and *dhā*. From *ci* (to accumulate): that which is accumulated is *cīvara* (a robe). From *pā* (to drink): one who drinks is *pīvara* (fat). From *dhā* (to hold): a holder [of nets] is *dhīvara* (a fisherman). 679.
The suffix *ci* occurs after *muna* and other roots.

The suffix *ippaccaya* occurs after the verbal roots *muna*, etc., and by the word "and" (*ca*), it also occurs after the *pāṭipadika* (base) words. *Muna* means "knowledge"; one who knows (*munāti*) is a *muni*. Due to the governing rule [of the preceding section], there is no *vuddhi* (vowel strengthening).
*Yata* means "exertion"; one who exerts himself (*yatatīti*) is a *yati*. *Agga* means "going" and "crookedness"; hence *aggi*. *Pata* means "going"; hence *pati*.
*Suca* means "the act of grieving"; hence *suci*. *Ruca* means "splendor"; hence *ruci*. *Isa* means "seeking"; one who seeks virtues such as moral conduct (*sīla*) is a *isi*.
*isi*: in the sense of sound (*sadda*), there is the substitution of *kavi*, *vuddhi*, and *ava*. *ru*: in the sense of sound (*sadda*), *ravi*, *dadhi*, *kuṭi*.
*asu*: in the sense of throwing (*khepana*), *asi*. *rāja*: in the sense of shining (*ditti*), *rāji*. *gapu*: in the sense of going (*gati*), *sappa*; *sappi*. *acca*:

in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), *acci*. *juta*: in the sense of shining (*ditti*), *joti*; *nandi*, *dīpi*, *kimi*—there is the change of *a* to *i*. *tamu*: in the sense of doubt (*kaṅkhā*), *timi*. *budha*: in the sense of awakening (*bodhana*); "one who awakens" (*bujjhati*)—thus [it is formed].
*Bodhi*. From the root *vilikh* (to scratch), *kasi*; from *kap* (to move), *kapi*, *kali*, *bali*, *masi*, *dhani*, *hari*, *ari*, *giri*, and so forth.
Furthermore, from the first vowel (*pāṭipadika*), there are *mahāli*, *bhaddāli*, *maṇi*, *araṇi*, *taraṇi*, *dharaṇi*, *saraṇi*, *dhamaṇi*, *avani*, *asani*, *vasani*, and so on. 680.
After *vid* and others, the suffix *ūra* [is applied].

The suffix *ūr* occurs after verbal roots such as *vid*, etc. After the root *vid* (in the sense of "obtaining"), the suffix *ūr* is applied in the sense of "sufficient for the purpose of worshipping because it is not near," resulting in *vidūra*.

Alternatively, from *vijjūro*, [we have] *vedūra*, a gem produced in a distant place (*vidūre*). After the roots *vala* and *valla* (in the senses of "common" and "binding"), [we have] *vallūra*. After the root *masa* (in the sense of "touching"), [we have] *masūra*.
After the root *sida* (in the sense of "ornamentation"), [we have] *sindūra*, with the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta*. After the root *du* (in the sense of "going"),...
*dūra-*; *ku-* in the sense of sound, *kūra-*; *kap-* in the senses of harming, cutting, and fragrance, *kappūra-*, a pair [of forms];
*may-* in the sense of going, *mayūra-*, or alternatively, *mayūra-* because it cries on the earth (*mahiyam*).
“The addition of a phoneme and the substitution of a phoneme...”
"And two others: change of phoneme and elision;
the application of a root with a fourth [consonant] as a suffix—this is called the fivefold etymology."

The derivation of forms should be understood according to the characteristics of the stated grammatical rules, such as "among those, *vuddhi* [vowel strengthening]" and so forth, and "in some cases, roots" and so forth. From the root *udi* in the sense of "flowing" and "moistening":

one who is capable (*alam*) of flowing is an *undūra* (mole). From the root *khajja* in the sense of "eating": that which is capable of being eaten is a *khajjūra* (date palm). From the root *kura* in the sense of "reviling": that which is capable of reviling is a *kurūra* (a type of grain). From the root *su* in the sense of "injuring": a *sūra* (hero). 681. By means of the suffixes *ṇu*, *nu*, and *tu* following roots such as *han* and others: [the forms are derived].

From the verbal roots beginning with *hana*, these suffixes—*ṇu*, *nu*, and *tu*—are applied. In the case of the suffix *ṇu*: from *hana* (in the senses of harming and going), *hanati* (he strikes) becomes *haṇu*.

From *jana* (in the sense of being born), *jāyati* (he is born) becomes *jāṇu*; here there is elision of the final vowel of the root and lengthening of the vowel. From *bhā* (in the sense of shining), *bhāti* (it shines) becomes *bhāṇu*.

From *ri* (in the sense of continuity), *rayati* (it flows/extends) becomes *reṇu*, meaning dust. From *khanu* (in the sense of digging or splitting), *khanti* (it digs) or *khaññati* (it is dug) becomes *khāṇu*.
In the sense of going and so forth, it does not go (*amatīti*), thus it is *aṇu*;

there is elision of the final consonant of the root. With the suffix *nup*: *ve* means the continuous weaving of threads; it weaves (*vāyatīti*), thus it is *venu* or *veṇu*. *Dhe* means to drink; it suckles (*dhāyati*) the calf, thus it is *dhenu*.

It shines (*bhātīti*), thus it is *bhānu*. With the suffix *tu*: *dhā* means to hold; it holds an action or a characteristic (*lakkhaṇaṃ*), thus it is *dhātu*. *Si* means to bind; it is bound (*sīyati*).
It is called *setu* because it binds (*bandhati*). It is called *ketu* because it goes upward (*uddham gacchati*) in the sense of departing (*ki*) from wealth or in the sense of rising (*unnatimhi*).

It is called *hetu* because it impels (*hinoti*) in the sense of going (*hi*). It is called *jantu* because it is born (*jāyati*) in the sense of being produced (*jana*). It is called *tantu* because it extends (*tanoti*) in the sense of spreading (*tanu*).

It is called *vatthu* because the fruit dwells (*vasati*) therein due to its dependence on that [basis], in the sense of abiding (*vasa nivāse*). By the rule beginning with "in some cases, of roots" (*kvaci dhātū*), there is the substitution of *tth* for the cluster of *s-t*.

682. *Kuṭādīhi ṭha*. The suffix *ṭha* occurs after verbal roots such as *kuṭa* and others. From *kuṭa* (in the sense of cutting): *kuṭati* (he cuts) thus *kuṭṭho* (a disease). From *kusa* (in the senses of cutting, filling, and fragrance):
*kusati* thus *koṭṭho* (the belly); here there is elision of the final root-consonant and doubling of the preceding vowel. From *kaṭa* (in the sense of crushing): [kaṭṭho].
It is called *kaṭṭha* because it cuts (*kaṭati*) or crushes (*maddati*). *Kaṇṭha* is derived from the root *kaṇ*, meaning "to close.
683. The suffixes *-ussa*, *-anu*, *-su*, and *-na* follow roots such as *manu*, *pūra*, *suṇa*, and others.
These suffixes, namely *-ussa*, *-anu*, *-su*, and *-sa*, occur after verbal roots such as *manu*, *pūra*, *suṇa*, and so forth, as well as after primary nouns (*pāṭipadika*).

*Manu* means to awaken; according to the *Ussanāsutta*, one who thinks or knows is a *manusso* (human), or *mānuso*; the final vowel of the root is changed to *ā*. *Pūra* means to give or to fill; one who fills is a *puriso* (man);

there is shortening [of the vowel], and in *poso*, there is the elision of the letters *r* and *o*, as well as the vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). One who dwells in a high place (*pura*) is a *puriso*. *Suṇa* means to harm, to be afflicted, or to connect;
one who connects with the family is a *suṇisā* (daughter-in-law). *Ku* means contemptible; one who acts wickedly is a *kavī*.
*Karīsa* means dung; *kussa* means yellowish-brown; and *dīgho* means long. The root *su* is used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*);

because he destroys the fear of beings by dispelling darkness, he is called *sūriyo* (the sun), with the addition of the letter *r* and the change of *s* to *y*. The root *maha* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*); "he is great" thus he is *mahiso* (a buffalo), or alternatively, *mahiso* is so called because he lies upon the earth (*mahiyam*).
The root *si* is used in the sense of binding (*bandhana*); it is called *sīsaṃ* (the head) because it is bound (*sīyati*) or fastened. And so forth.
684. *Akkharehi kāra*.
The suffix *kāra* occurs after syllables—that is, after phonemes (*vaṇṇa*) that denote syllables.

By the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*ca*) in the rule on taddhita suffixes and so forth, the designation "noun" (*nāma*) applies, and the case endings beginning with *si* arise: *akāro*, *akkāraṃ*, *akārena*, and so on; likewise *ākāro*, *okāro*, *kakāro*.
The letter *ya*, the letter *ha*, and the letter *ḷ*. Furthermore, in words such as *evakāra*, the term *kāra* means "that which is made" or "pronounced," thus it is a sound (*sadda*).
Since it is both *eva* and *kāra*, it is called *evakāra*. In the same way, there are *dhikāra*, *huṃkāra*, and *sādhukāra*.
The letter *i* occurs in the *Dhātuniddesa* [in the rule] *vikaraṇandhito*.
"Bhavanta," "gamissa," and "hanatya" are the indicators here.
This is the method for suffixes ending in *uṇ* and so forth.
Those beginning with *tabba* and ending with *ṇa* are the terminations (*niṭṭhā*); likewise, those beginning with *tave* and *tuṇ*.
*Mānantādi* and *uṇādī*: thus is the sixfold compendium of *kitaka*.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the derivation of *kibbidhāna*, in the *Padarūpasiddhi*.
The conclusion (nigamana), sandhi, nouns (nāman), the agent (kāraka), compound (samāsa), secondary derivative (taddhita),
verb (ākhyāta), primary derivative (kitaka), and noun stem (kaṇḍā)— these seven [topics] constitute the *Rūpasiddhi*.
The *sandhi* is threefold, the *pada* fourfold, and the nominal (*nāmika*) fivefold;
the analysis of suffixes (*byāsa*) is sixfold, as are the *kārakas*, the *samāsa*, and the *taddhita*;
the verb (*ākhyāta*) is eightfold, the *kitaka* is sixfold, and there are various divisions of suffixes (*paccaya*).
May he, illuminating the perfection of form, long bring about the increase of the wisdom of the people here.
He is the disciple of the eminent preceptors known as the renowned Ānanda Thera, who bear the banner of Tambapaṇṇi;
he is the one called Dīpaṅkara, whose fame was attained on the land of the Damilas.
He who, dwelling for two years at Bālādicca and other locations, illuminated the Dispensation—
this very ascetic named Buddhappiya composed this straightforward *Rūpasiddhi*.
Thus ends the treatise on the derivation of word-forms (*Padarūpasiddhi*).
